#3455. If You Loved 'Cupertino,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Cupertino is one of those TV shows that arrived just when we all needed it. In this economy, a story about two lawyers who get shafted by the “move fast and break things” culture of Silicon Valley and decide to use their legal chops to fight back was almost destined to be a hit, and the great performances by Mike Colter and Rachel Keller sealed the deal. If you love the sharp legal wrangling and tech-focused storylines and want a movie that perfectly complements the show, it’s time to watch (or re-watch) Aaron Sorkin and David Fincher’s 2010 masterpiece, The Social Network.

Just like Cupertino, The Social Network arrived at precisely the right moment in history—just when everyone was beginning to wonder if the social media revolution kicked off by Facebook and Mark Zuckerberg was actually a good idea or not. While it might seem hard to imagine, there was a time when Facebook was the social media platform—everyone was on it, and it dominated the conversation like nothing else. And the outsized wealth and influence Zuckerberg accrued as a result were just starting to make people a little uneasy.

At its core, The Social Network is a legal drama—the framing narrative involves dual lawsuits brought against Zuckerberg and the depositions he is giving, which prompt flashbacks to the formation and success of Facebook in the early 2000s. Like Cupertino, the story is soaked in the “apologize later” culture of tech startups, and traces the ruthlessness and cold genius of Zuckerberg as he cements his control over the platform, ices out former partners, and generally behaves like a sociopathic genius (Jesse Eisenberg’s performance as Zuckerberg is coldly compelling).

The film doesn’t have any kind of clear-cut ending where the good guys win, but there’s a certain satisfaction in the way Sorkin’s script and Eisenberg’s performance strip away the glamour of Zuckerberg’s money and success, reducing him in many ways to an aggrieved loner who translated his rage into a brilliant idea, and then has to isolate himself from everyone in order to maintain his control over it. The Zuckerberg depicted in the film is a lonely, bitter dude, and it’s as much of a happy ending as you’ll get. It’s a fascinating story of legal maneuvering and bickering lawyers against a backdrop of one of the foundational social media moments that shaped modern culture, and fans of the show will dig it. Stream The Social Network on Pluto or rent it on Prime Video.

Still craving legal drama, tech-sector skulduggery, or more David-versus-Goliath courtroom fireworks? Here are a few more movies that fans of Cupertino will love.

It’s set nowhere near Silicon Valley, but Michael Clayton is a real barn-burner of a paranoid legal thriller. George Clooney plays the title role, a “fixer” for a big-money law firm. When his mentor and friend, Arthur Edens (Tom Wilkinson), suffers a mental breakdown while working on a case involving a toxic weedkiller produced by one of the firm’s clients and becomes a security threat, he’s assassinated, and Clayton is forced to reckon with his role in the world and how much injustice he’s willing to tolerate in exchange for money. It’s tense, smart, and has a wonderfully satisfying conclusion that fans of legal dramas where the good guys are willing to sacrifice (and win) will cheer. Rent Michael Clayton on Prime Video.

Based on real events, Dark Waters will appeal to anyone who likes to see smart lawyers take on enormous corporations in a search for the truth. A successful corporate lawyer, Robert Bilott (Mark Ruffalo), looks into a series of bizarre cattle deaths in rural West Virginia and stumbles onto evidence that the DuPont corporation has been dumping illegal, unregulated chemicals into the groundwater. Bilott’s years-long effort to hold DuPont responsible for the health impact on the community nearly costs him everything, but his determination to make the system work is ultimately the kind of inspiring legal story fans of Cupertino will appreciate. Rent Dark Waters on Prime Video.

If you just want the simple pleasures of a thrilling legal procedural, you can’t do much better than A Civil Action. John Travolta (at the height of his comeback) plays attorney Jan Schlichtmann, who takes on a class action lawsuit against two huge corporations because he thinks the case will be lucrative and relatively straightforward. As the case saps his resources and brings his firm to the brink of collapse, however, Schlichtmann slowly realizes that he’s fighting for more than just a big payday. Fair warning: This isn’t a feel-good movie in many ways, but it definitely brings those David-versus-Goliath vibes that Cupertino trades in. Rent A Civil Action on Prime Video.

The true story behind the effort to license the video game Tetris from the Soviet-era Russian government doesn’t have the same stakes as many of the stories in Cupertino, and it’s certainly no longer timely. But the globe-trotting legal maze that Henk Rogers (Taron Egerton) must navigate to secure the rights, which seem to keep twisting and slipping from his grasp as various political and corporate interests weigh in, is just as fun and fascinating as the legal battles on the show. Tetris may no longer be a novel sensation in the gaming world, but it’s fascinating to see how something so baked into modern pop culture achieved that status. Stream Tetris on Apple TV or rent it on Prime Video.

If your favorite part of Cupertino is its exploration of the way tech companies impact our lives, and the way decisions made in obscure corporate offices can have enormous consequences, BlackBerry will be a favorite. Based on true events, it tells the story of how Research in Motion (RIM) created what was, for a time, the most dominant phone in the world—and how the company lost everything when its leaders took their eye off the ball and let personal obsessions and grudges impede their work. With a cast that includes Jay Baruchel and Glenn Howerton, this story of Silicon Valley hubris is right on target for Cupertino fans. Stream Blackberry on Netflix, Kanopy, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

#3453. Prince William Reportedly Wants to Strip Prince Harry of His Titles

Prince William is reportedly actively considering a plan for a “far-reaching restructuring” of the British monarchy, which he would implement once he ascends to the throne. His brother, Prince Harry, would be at the forefront of these changes: The future monarch reportedly wants only active members of the royal family who carry out duties on his behalf to retain their royal titles and the style of “Royal Highness.” These titles would therefore no longer be an “automatic privilege of birth” but would instead be equivalent to a “job title.”

The plan was detailed by Tom Sykes, a journalist and writer specializing in the royals, in his book Dukes of Hazard, to be published next February, excerpts of which were published by the Mail on Sunday on Saturday, November 21. The author, “a royal authority with impeccable society contacts” as the newspaper puts it, is said to have obtained confessions from friends of Prince William.

“If you are a working royal—going out, touring the country, doing diplomatic work, doing government work, having a public role, pressing the flesh, getting out of bed on a wet Wednesday to go to Sheffield—then you will be an HRH and you will have a prince or princess title. You will also get an allowance, a salary, and a place to live. One place to live,” the associate of the prince explained to Sykes. “If you are not doing those things and you are not a working royal, you will not get to be an HRH, you will not get a free or subsidized place to live, and you will not get any special favors. You will, however, be a private citizen free to get on with your life and make money any way you choose.”

By implementing this measure, Prince William hopes to prevent potential media scandals regarding the legitimacy of certain individuals’ right to retain their titles if they are not prominent members of the Firm (Prince Harry) or if they are under legal scrutiny (Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor). But also, and above all, the Prince of Wales hopes to offer an option to his children, Princess Charlotte, 11, and Prince Louis, eight, who could easily renounce their titles to pursue independent careers. The question does not arise for the eldest child of the Prince and Princess of Wales, Prince George, 13, whose future as heir to the throne is “guaranteed.” In fact, none of the three use their royal titles, preferring simply to be called by their first names and the surname Wales.

Under the rules established by King George V in 1917, the title of prince or princess, along with the predicate, is granted at birth to the sovereign’s children and to the children of the sovereign’s sons, as well as to all the children of the Prince of Wales’s eldest son. Prince William’s children, therefore, received these titles at birth, while Prince Harry’s children, Archie and Lilibet (ages seven and five), did not become prince and princess until King Charles III ascended the throne.

They may have to give them up if Prince William carries out his plan. “Under William’s current plan, the prince and princess titles of Harry and Meghan’s children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, would be legally removed, along with the royal styles and princely titles of Harry and Meghan themselves,” writes Tom Sykes in his book. To do so, according to Sykes’s book, constitutional advisers have told William that he could issue letters patent, an official document authorized by the king. Such a decision could strain the relationship between the two brothers.

Sykes is convinced that Prince William would garner the approval of his subjects and “enormous public support in a country increasingly impatient with the cost and perceived excess of a sprawling royal household,” according to those close to him.

In October 2025, Prince William confided to actor Eugene Levy—whom he was hosting at Windsor Castle for the taping of Levy’s show The Reluctant Traveler—that “there are points when you look at tradition and go, Is that still fit for purpose today? Is that still the right thing to do? Are we still doing and having the most impact we could be having?”

Kensington Palace, however, declined to comment on the rumor. “As a matter of policy, we don’t comment on books or claims made within them.”

Originally published in Vanity Fair France.

#3452. Widow's Bay Season 2 Changes Revealed After Shocking Onscreen Deaths

Widow’s Bay is returning for a second season but the show will look a little different after finding success on Apple TV.

Creator Katie Dippold recently hinted at her plans to shake up the structure, telling Collider that season 1 had scripts that were “longer and pretty dense.” As a result, Dippold will have a different approach for the next installment.

“I spent a lot of time in season 1 having to make cuts, last-minute cuts, and budget cuts for time,” she continued. “And so I’ll just be more mindful of that, because we didn’t need that much.”

Dippold also expressed gratitude for getting more of an idea of each character and the actors who portray them.

“They’re all so naturally funny and have perfect comedic timing, they’re playing it like a drama,” she added about adapting the content for the person bringing each role to life on the hit show.

The Apple TV series, which premiered in April, is set in a fictional New England island town plagued by a centuries-old curse, bringing various supernatural evils to the local inhabitants.

Shortly after the show aired, Matthew Rhys, Kate O’Flynn, Kevin Carroll, Dale Dickey, Kingston Rumi Southwick, Jeff Hiller, Stephen Root, K Callan and more received critical acclaim for their performances in the supernatural comedy.

Rhys, 52, later spoke to Us about the vision for season 2.

“The question I’ve been asking [creator] Katie [Dippold] the most is, ‘What is the curse? The monster? The island? What is it?’” he shared in August. “So I’m so intrigued as to whether it’s something physical and tangible to be reasoned with or something inside us. I have no idea. I just know I’m glad I’m not writing it.”

He continued: “There’s a part of me that wants Hamish Linklater’s character, Richard, to come back. So I kind of want that to be the curse. He keeps knocking on my door and I’m always like, ‘What?’ And he is the curse and always ever present. I think there could be a lot of fun with that.”

Rhys noted he was just as nervous as fans about possible deaths, adding, “[Fans should be] terrified. No one is safe. Anyone can be taken down at a moment’s notice.”

At the time, the actor hinted that nothing was off the table. “The game is wide open for a big shocking death where everyone goes, ‘Oh my God, I didn’t think they would kill off Tom Loftis,'” he teased of his own character. “I have that worry. Present tense.”

#3451. The Best Last-Minute Gifts That Don't Feel Last Minute

This series will help you pick the perfect presents, decor, and activities to make this Christmas the Best Christmas Ever.

We’ve all experienced gift panic—that sinking feeling when you realize you need a present in an hour and you just don’t have one to give. Whether you spent all year chasing the “perfect” gift or simply procrastinated, your time is nearly up. But don’t panic. The clock may have nearly run out, but your options haven’t. Before you resort to re-gifting something from the back of a closet, here’s how to pull off a last-minute gift that is effortless but feels elevated and worthy of the person you’re giving it to.

With the right presentation, even the most last-minute gift can read as thoughtful. Any performer will tell you that the difference between a good show and a bad one comes down to commitment and confidence. The same is true for last-minute gifts: If you act like your gift is thoughtful and intentional, they’ll think it is. The biggest mistake people make is apologizing as they hand over a present—nothing ruins a vibe faster than, “Sorry this is so last-minute.” So give with confidence.

And focus on presentation. A handwritten note that contains a shared memory or personal joke can elevate a present. Use simple but personal wrapping; craft paper and twine, or a reusable gift bag that looks like you planned ahead. Add a small flourish, like a sprig of holly or a fancy bow. Small touches can make it seem like you’ve carefully prepared. What you don’t want are obvious panic gifts that scream, “I grabbed this on the way here.” The goal is effortless, not frantic.

Digital gifts are your friends. You can order something in minutes that arrives instantly online, and with a little thought, will still read as personal and intentional. The trick is choosing a present that speaks to the recipient’s tastes, hobbies, or quirks, and pairing it with a small note to show you remember what they love. From e-books to streaming subscriptions, these gifts hit the sweet spot of thoughtful and last-minute. Here are some suggestion:

When time is running out, gift cards are your secret weapon. They arrive instantly online, don’t require shipping, and with the right presentation, they can feel surprisingly thoughtful. The key is to pick a card that fits the recipient’s interests and add a personal note. The more specific you are, the better. If your giftee is into Italian food, get them an Eataly gift card. If they're a PC gamer, get them a Steam card. If they're into education, a membership to Skillshare is perfect. There's a gift card out there for just about any interest, and all you have to do it google it and email it.

Generic gift cards can be a last-minute lifesaver that can still seem a little personal if you give them the right way.

Pick a theme or design: Many online cards, like Amazon, Etsy, or Starbucks, let you choose designs. The right visual makes the card feel more intentional.

Include a warm, personal message: Even one line can make a digital card feel thoughtful—something like, “I couldn’t pick just one thing for you. Hope this helps you treat yourself.”

Send strategically: Deliver the card by email or text, but consider printing the email or screenshotting it in a small envelope so it feels like a “real” gift.

Sign someone up for a subscription service, write a note explaining you want to keep giving them presents all year, and you're golden. Here are some suggestions:

SnackCrate: This service sends a different snack from around the world every month.

SpiceClub: For the culinary adventurer on your list. A subscription to RawSpiceBar’s Spice Club delivers a curated selection of spices every month.

Mocktail Club: Booze-free fancy drinks delivered once a month? Sign me up.

Thera Box: If you know someone in need of some self-care, this once-a-month box is packed with wellness and relaxation items.

Loot Crate: If your giftee is geeky, consider this monthly surprise box of pop culture treasures.

Cameo is a platform where celebrities, influencers, musicians, and performers create personalized video messages for fans. If someone on your list is a fan of someone on Cameo, you can set up a session, and give a card with a mysterious note like "Keep an eye out for a special message." They'll be delighted with a personal message from wrestling legend Mick Foley or terrified when Chris Hansen appears on their screen; your choice.

I have enough crap in my house, so I love getting experiences instead of things. The challenge with experience gifts is usually timing: Many require reservations or coordination, but there are plenty of options that let your giftee schedule the time, making them perfect last-minute gifts.

Museum membership cards: Many institutions sell digital gift memberships that the recipient can activate whenever they like.

Movie tickets: Your local multiplex probably has a gift certificate you can buy online.

Local attraction passes: Some city attractions offer gift cards or “anytime admission” tickets that don’t expire immediately.

Pair these with a note explaining why you chose the experience, or, if you have that kind of relationship, something like, "I want to take you to the Museum of Modern Art." Just make sure you follow through and actually go.

Sometimes, there’s literally no time to order, wrap, or even think about a gift. If you’re scrambling out the door and need something now, you might be able to fake your way through, even if you're stopping at the liquor store on the way to the Christmas party.

Flowers or a small potted plant: Give a seasonal bouquet or a small indoor plant. Add a handwritten note, even a single line, and it might come off as thoughtful.

Gourmet chocolates or candy: Specialty chocolates from a local shop or grocery store display can feel luxe with a little ribbon or bag.

Wine, craft beer, or non-alcoholic beverage: A bottle with a clean label or interesting packaging immediately elevates your gift. Ask the clerk at the liquor store to help you find something unique.

Lottery tickets: Who wouldn't appreciate a bunch of scratch-off lottery tickets?

Hard cash is the most impersonal gift of all, but the only one you know will be used. This gift really depends on the person getting it, so be aware of whether they're likely to think "Just what I wanted!" or "Wait, I'm not poor." If you give cash, make sure it's crisp bills in a nice card, with a personalized note.

#3450. The Return of Malin Akerman and Brittany Snow’s Twisted ‘Hunting Wives’ Love Story

In 2021, at the recommendation of a film producer, the writer and showrunner Rebecca Cutter read a pulpy murder-mystery novel on a flight from her native Massachusetts to her current base in Los Angeles. By the time she landed, Cutter had finished the book and was already mapping out the TV adaptation in her head.

The plot heavily involved a Texas abortion clinic, and the state had just passed SB 8, one of the country’s most restrictive abortion bills until Roe v. Wade was overturned the following year. As she contemplated bringing The Hunting Wives to life, Cutter saw the political stakes come into focus as well.

“I started thinking about the ‘red state, blue state’ of it,” she tells Vanity Fair ahead of the show’s season two premiere on Thursday. “What if…we really play this culture war?”

“I don’t think I do gratuitous sex scenes,” says showrunner Rebecca Cutter. “I think you always are seeing a power dynamic play out or a plot point play out.”

The result was one of Netflix’s biggest breakout hits in recent years, sent up in a Saturday Night Live sketch as the “straight but lesbian, horny Republican murder drama.” As a show, Hunting Wives amps up the noirish aspects of the suspense thriller written by May Cobb, a native of the East Texas Piney Woods, and adds a heaping dose of MAGA-adjacent camp. Cutter finishes the mix with plenty of sex scenes, particularly between Malin Akerman’s Margo, a femme fatale partly inspired by Melania Trump who is married to a Republican gubernatorial hopeful, and Brittany Snow’s Sophie, a liberal do-gooder who, like Cutter, arrives in town from a blue corner of Massachusetts. (Cutter was raised in Cambridge and graduated from Wesleyan University, the Connecticut liberal arts college known for its progressive politics and pipeline to Hollywood.)

Hunting Wives executive producer Erwin Stoff told Cutter he’d pay for her to go to Texas to meet Cobb and breathe the Piney Woods air herself. She met Cobb’s father and her best friend from high school. She shot skeet with the women—she even got it in three, just as Sophie does in the first season. At a high-end Dallas shopping area where the likes of Gucci can be found, Cutter got a better sense of the hair, clothes, and bodies of her eventual characters. “I understand the notion that Sophie could be amused and entertained and intrigued by these women,” Cutter says, “and eventually seduced.”

Cutter thinks of the show primarily in terms of its tonal mash-up: “I think we managed to wrangle it into one piece of art,” she says, “but there’s comedy, there’s violence, there’s noir, there’s soap, there’s earnest emotion.” To the extent that she assigned any political beliefs to the rich white women of Cobb’s novel, it was in the spirit of grounding her characters in the specifics of their world. Still, as we speak, Cutter decides “to get real with it.”

Cutter on set. She describes Sophie, a fellow native of blue Massachusetts, as a surrogate for her own awakening to MAGA Texas.

“The whole thing was a little bit of a parable, in my mind, of how you could fall for someone like [Donald] Trump,” she admits. “Sophie has her principles, but they only go so far. They end right where something starts to make her feel good.” Cutter was as curious as anyone else from her educated milieu about the quirkier aspects of Trump, like the Diet Coke button he had installed on the Resolute Desk. How liberating must it feel to embrace a movement so openly untethered from the pieties of politics and taste?

“Not that my show is a deep dive on Trump,” Cutter says, “but maybe there is an element that’s sort of looking under the hood.”

The twisted love story between Margo and Sophie entangles all of the wealthy, hard-drinking, gun-toting women in their orbit, and its central killing—one of several propelling the show forward, with a third season slated to begin filming this year—stems from an effort to cover up Margo’s abortion as her NRA-loving husband plots his political ascent. (In this proudly oversexed town, he has his own share of affairs.) Hunting Wives is the rare Netflix soap to receive steady coverage from mainstream national outlets; the fascination undoubtedly has something to do with the impression that, like Yellowstone or Morgan Wallen before it, the show unlocks something about MAGA’s cultural staying power. In a New York Times guest essay this month that evaluated the post-2024 Hollywood landscape, Sharon Waxman, the editor in chief of The Wrap, wrote, “From Melania on Amazon’s streaming service to The Hunting Wives on Netflix to the ever-expanding Taylor Sheridan universe on Paramount+ to Bari Weiss’s being put in charge of CBS News, the vibe shift was visible on all our screens.”

Margo and her politically ambitious husband are partners in subterfuge and debauchery.

Cutter says she had no particular agenda nor any “ultra-evil villain plan of how it was going to be received or how it would be culturally relevant.” But Hunting Wives is sprinkled with enough proper nouns—a Peter Thiel mention here, a Walmart reference there—and distinctly modern aesthetics that she can acknowledge its appeal as something of a Rosetta stone for the moment in MAGA femininity. Even in the ostensibly waning days of the movement, the plastic surgery and soaring heels continue to captivate and horrify coastal elites. Cutter says that Callie (Jaime Ray Newman), another of Margo’s lovers, has a bit of Kristi Noem and Marjorie Taylor Greene in her: that “sort of slightly butch, real gun, real ‘back the blue’ [element]…the toughness of those women.”

The second season of Hunting Wives maintains the slipperiness that keeps the show from veering into moralism; it stands apart from other Trump-era art in its refusal to take sides. “I think I remember, in the pitch, someone saying, ‘But will red-state people like it too?’” Cutter recalls. “I was like, ‘I think so.’” Both Margo and Sophie are awash in their respective red and blue stereotypes, but neither is more admirable than the other. Their sordid union is a testament to the flexibility of both their principles and their preferences. From one vantage, it is, in the end, all about sex.

“Margo is the symbol of freedom and sexuality and feminine power and empoweredness and selfishness that [Sophie] feels she’s lost,” Cutter says, adding that Akerman’s comfort in such a role helped drive her liberal use of physical intimacy. “The audience may disagree with me,” she says, but “I don’t think I do gratuitous sex scenes. I think you always are seeing a power dynamic play out or a plot point play out.” Last year, though, when Netflix acquired Hunting Wives, which was initially ordered by Starz in 2023, Cutter had a more practical concern.

“I literally googled,” she recalls, “‘Does Netflix show boobs?’”

‘Tis the season, and with so many people traveling for the holidays, I've been thinking about the cost of getting everybody where they need to be. Then I was reminded that my travel headaches are nothing compared to Matt Damon's. Hollywood has spent hundreds of millions of dollars making movies about people trying to get this man home. I started adding up four of the most obvious examples, and the total is ridiculous. Somebody, please get him a frequent-flyer card.

Over on Facebook, Cinema Nerd made a pretty great observation and shared a pretty funny reel. Across thirty years and four movies, one thing audiences can be almost sure of when it comes to the best Matt Damon movies—and no, it's not a team-up with his old pal Ben Affleck. What they can expect is a story about a character trekking long distances to make it back home. First, let's start with Saving Private Ryan.

In Steven Spielberg's Saving Private Ryan Damon plays James Francis Ryan, a World War II paratrooper whose three brothers have been killed. Tom Hanks' Captain Miller is ordered to take his squad across war-torn France to find Ryan and bring him home. It's one of my favorite war movies, and a wildly expensive rescue mission.

According to Box Office Mojo, the 1998 film cost an estimated $70 million to make and earned more than $482 million worldwide. Obviously, that budget didn't all go toward locating Ryan, but for this very serious investigation, we're putting the entire amount on the Boston native’s tab.

I still remember watching Christopher Nolan's Interstellar in 2014 and being stunned when Damon popped up as Dr. Mann. His character had been stranded on a distant planet, and for a moment, he seemed like the heroic astronaut everyone hoped to find. Then we discovered how far he'd go to save himself. Let's just say I wouldn't trust that guy with my return ticket.

Interstellar carried a reported $165 million production budget and made about $681 million during its original worldwide run. That wasn't even the Hollywood A-lister's last expensive attempt to escape an inhospitable planet.

Just one year later, he starred in Ridley Scott's The Martian as Mark Watney, an astronaut accidentally left behind on Mars. This time, at least, he was somebody I actually wanted NASA to rescue. Between growing potatoes in Martian soil and McGyvering all sorts of stuff to survive, Watney made a strong case for keeping astronauts supplied with gardening equipment.

The Martian cost approximately $108 million and earned more than $630 million globally. At that point, somebody at NASA should have asked Damon to stop accepting space assignments.

Then came The Odyssey, one of the biggest movies on the 2026 release calendar. Nolan cast Damon as Odysseus, the Greek king trying to return to Ithaca after the Trojan War. Considering how miserable Damon said he was during parts of filming, apparently getting home wasn't much easier for the actor than it was for his character. Monsters, storms, angry gods: no airports or baggage fees, and somehow getting home was still an absolute nightmare.

The epic reportedly cost $250 million to make and has earned a staggering $1.805 billion worldwide. Not too shabby for a page-to-screen adaptation of a text more than 2000 years old. Apparently, the ancient Greeks understood the frustration of a trip home taking way longer than expected.

Here's the grand total of the aforementioned four films: $70 million for Saving Private Ryan, $165 million for Interstellar, $108 million for The Martian, and $250 million for The Odyssey. That's $593 million in combined production budgets. My family's trip to Texas this past summer suddenly looks downright cheap.

For the record, these are entire movie budgets, not actual on-screen rescue costs. The four films have brought in roughly $3.6 billion at the global box office. I understand why executives keep approving these expensive trips.

We actually tallied an even longer list of Damon's fictional rescue missions back in 2015, so this four-film total isn't the complete bill. With the holidays coming up, I only have one wish for his next character: let the man stay home.

Ryan graduated from Missouri State University with a BA in English/Creative Writing. An expert in all things horror, Ryan enjoys covering a wide variety of topics. He's also a lifelong comic book fan and an avid watcher of Game of Thrones and House of the Dragon.

#3447. Nintendo's Black Friday Deals Are Actually Pretty Good

Black Friday is nearly upon us. From now through Cyber Monday, retailers and companies alike are offering deals and discounts on their wares. While I always keep an eye out for Nintendo deals offered by stores like Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart, it seems the company is offering its own discounts this year—and, surprisingly, they're actually pretty solid.

Last Thursday, Nintendo announced its Black Friday discounts. We've already seen Switch 2 sales ahead of the Black Friday season, but now, Nintendo has confirmed an official discount for the console.

Starting Nov. 22 through Dec. 5, you can pick up Nintendo's Switch 2 Mario Kart bundle for $499.00, down $50 from $549.99. That includes the console, a download of Mario Kart World, and a 90-day Nintendo Switch Online Individual Membership.

If you already have a Switch 2 console and/or Mario Kart World, you're not left out of the Black Friday deals here. From Nov. 22 through Nov. 29, Nintendo is also running discounts on several high-profile Switch and Switch 2 games:

Donkey Kong Bananza was one of Nintendo's launch titles for the Switch 2. And while it's been out for over a year, Donkey Kong's first 3D game is still among the best-reviewed titles on the console. Nintendo is taking $20 off the game's MSRP for this promotion.

Kirby Air Riders on Switch 2 is only the second installment in the series. The original launched all the way back on the GameCube, and while the title typically runs for $69.99, Nintendo is letting it go for $49.99.

Metroid Prime 4 arrived last year after an 18-year wait from Metroid Prime 3: Corruption. The game typically retails for $69.99 for a physical copy on Switch 2, but Nintendo is selling it for $49 during its early Black Friday promotion.

Super Mario Galaxy (both the original and the sequel) are beloved by fans. These titles originally launched on the Wii, and Nintendo rereleased both for the Switch. (The company offers a free upgrade to the Switch 2 edition.) Nintendo asks $69.99 for this combo, and while you can find it for under $60, you'll officially be able to pick it up for $48.97 before Black Friday.

Nintendo's latest Mario Party, Jamboree, has a Switch 2 edition with a rather staggering MSRP of $79.99. While it's the version of the game with the most features, it's also the most expensive. You'll be able to buy it for $39.99 for Black Friday, saving up to $40.

Nintendo rarely offers official discounts on some of its biggest titles, especially in this current era. In addition, Nintendo announced a sale on its digital store that runs from Nov. 19 through Dec. 2, though it didn't say which titles would be on sale. Just keep an eye on all these dates: The Switch 2 console promotion runs longer than the physical and digital games discounts, while the digital sale runs longer than the physical sale. Nintendo says that these discounts will be available "at select retailers," as well as its brick-and-mortar locations in New York and San Francisco. You can also buy the Switch 2 bundle through Nintendo's website.

It depends! Its Nintendo Switch 2 bundle deal runs from Nov. 22 through Dec. 5; the select games listed above will be on sale from Nov. 22 through Nov. 29; and digital titles will have discounts from Nov. 19 through Dec. 2.

While we don't know which digital titles will be discounted yet, we do know that physical copies of Donkey Kong Bananza, Kirby Air Riders, Metroid Prime 4: Beyond, Super Mario Galaxy + Super Mario Galaxy 2, and Super Mario Party: Jamboree will be on sale for $39.99 each.

Yes! The Switch 2 alone costs $499.99, so you essentially get the game for free. Mario Kart World is also one of the console's best multiplayer titles right now, so it makes sense to pick it up in this bundle.

#3446. Sell Thy Neighbor: Trump Official Howard Lutnick and the Clandestine Deal to Sell NYC’s Glamorous Pierre Hotel

Here it was, the big reveal. After years of planning and wrangling, after more than $10 million spent on engineers and lawyers and architects, after all of the rumors and headlines and finger-pointing, the long-awaited presentation was ready to be made.

About 42 seconds after it started, things went off the rails. A “shitshow,” as multiple people would later describe to Vanity Fair the two-and-a-half-hour meeting on the morning of July 29.

The setting was the Cotillion Ballroom, the chandeliered 4,000-square-foot event space at New York’s iconic Pierre Hotel, the site of Al Pacino’s blind tango in Scent of a Woman, where the ceilings are 19 feet high, the curtains are golden, and the windows offer views of Central Park’s southeast corner. Seated at round tables were 40 or so of the people with enough disposable income to call the Pierre home, or at least a home: investor Austin Hearst; Tory Burch, the fashion powerhouse; Lois Chiles, the 1970s-era movie star and model. Joining remotely was Michael Eisner, the former Disney CEO, who last year spent $4.3 million to buy a second apartment there and, with it, even more shares in the co-op that owns the Pierre.

In came representatives from the Khashoggi Holding Company out of Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, and the Dorchester Collection, the luxury hotel management firm owned by the Sultan of Brunei. Their proposition was straightforward. Khashoggi wanted to buy the Pierre—the nearly 200-room hotel and all of the apartments too—for $2 billion, less expenses. It was an enormous haul, even for a neighborhood this tony. And it would be all in cash. “The funds are currently available,” a Khashoggi representative promised.

But if the residents with two thirds of the co-op’s shares accepted the offer, everyone would have to move out. Neighbors would be voting, in effect, to force their fellow neighbors from their apartments.

It would be in their best interest, the Dorchester and Khashoggi reps said. The Pierre was a gem, but a tarnished one after 96 summers and thousands of guests. It didn’t have many of the amenities that come standard these days in a five-star hotel. The façade was already undergoing a $22 million overhaul, and there were deeper, systemic problems to solve. The CEO of the company managing the Pierre publicly complained it was something of a money pit. All of that would change after Khashoggi bought the place, the presenters promised. Dorchester would invest more than $1 billion into the Pierre, giving the landmark building a grand new entrance on 61st Street, a pool in the basement, and structural renovations throughout.

When it was done, the residents would be first in line to buy apartments at the all-new, all-modern Dorchester-managed Pierre, ready to last another century.

The response in the Cotillion room was instant and not particularly friendly. Some residents had moved in not long ago. Others had spent millions remodeling their apartments. “How are we going to enjoy all the perks of this wonderfully renewed building when we’re forced to sell at a price you determine and we have to buy reconfigured apartments, not our own, at market prices?” asked Tina Beriro, the philanthropist and longtime resident, in a recording of the meeting reviewed by Vanity Fair. Like many of the residents, Beriro, at 85, was only a few years younger than the hotel itself. “Many of us are going to be dead by the time you finish.”

Christopher Cowdray, Dorchester’s white-haired, Zimbabwe-born president, didn’t have an answer. Nor did he provide much of a response when asked what would happen to the more than 400 people who work at the hotel. “In this case, we are still in discussion at the moment,” Cowdray said, to audible groans.

“Many employees have worked here 30 and 40 years and are just about to hit retirement,” Burch pointed out, per the recording. “I have people in the elevator crying that they feel like their job is on the line.”

The questions kept coming. For years, shareholders had begged—and even sued—to find out more about the sale. But the long-promised detailed plans for the Pierre’s purchase were still weeks away, adding to the tension in the Cotillion room. (One source, very much in favor of a sale, later called the decision to make an elaborate presentation to the shareholders without those specifics “idiotic.”)

“Look, ladies and gentlemen, I’ve been on the board of the Hearst Corporation for over 25 years. Sat on the boards of many corporations, for profit and not for profit. I have never seen anything like this,” Hearst said, his voice cracking. “This is a serious problem that you have presented to the shareholders, and you guys have done a miserable fucking job.”

One of the many lawyers in the room interrupted him, and they started going at it. Cowdray and the other presenters were escorted out. At one point, the wife of Michael Stern, the 88-year-old chairman of the co-op’s board, tried to offer his resignation on his behalf (which he then turned down). Even by the famously hostile standards of New York City’s high-end co-ops, this was nasty.

Ironically, the co-op’s biggest shareholder—the resident with the most at stake in the sale financially—didn’t show up. Howard Lutnick was busy in the Oval Office that day with President Donald Trump in his role as US commerce secretary.

Lutnick had bought the Pierre’s 16-room penthouse, its largest apartment, in 2017 for $44 million. If the sale of the Pierre were to go through, Lutnick would get as much as $100 million for the penthouse, even as his neighbors were forced to sell and hundreds of hotel staffers’ jobs were put in jeopardy. Newmark Group—the real estate services firm hired by the Pierre’s board and controlled by Cantor Fitzgerald, the brokerage house previously run by Lutnick—would earn tens of millions more.

Newmark may have a reputation for shepherding big-ticket sales to completion. But in a letter to the Pierre’s board last year, Beriro called the hiring of the Lutnick-linked firm “a blatant conflict of interest,” an allegation sources close to Lutnick and the board deny. One Pierre resident tells me that Lutnick’s involvement is symbolic of a “culture of corruption” that extends from 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue in Washington to the edges of Central Park in New York. Others imply it is part of a different pattern: the purchase of more and more of America’s most valuable assets by companies and sovereign wealth funds from the Persian Gulf’s petrostates, at times orchestrated by those in and around the second Trump administration. Those shareholders wonder whether Lutnick had personally worked behind the scenes to maneuver the Khashoggi group into place to buy the Pierre, and that speculation spilled onto the pages of The New York Times.

BALL GAMES Guests attend a Valentino party in the Cotillion Ballroom at the Pierre hotel, 1970, New York.

A source close to Lutnick notes that he formally cut ties with Newmark in early 2025 and adds that, since his move to government, Lutnick’s only involvement in the Pierre sales process has been to respond to media reports like this one. A spokesperson for Sabre Park Avenue LLC, Khashoggi’s American holding company, tells Vanity Fair in a statement that “any insinuation or implication that the proposal, the transaction or the parties involved engaged in improper or undisclosed conduct is categorically false.”

I spoke to more than 15 sources and reviewed hundreds of pages of documents related to the Pierre deal, including previously unreported text messages between Lutnick and Khashoggi and a corporate intelligence dossier dropped in my mailbox.

Turns out, the shareholders were right to wonder about Lutnick’s role.

The Pierre for decades was synonymous with New York glamour. At the height of their star power, Audrey Hepburn stayed in the hotel’s suites and Elizabeth Taylor kept an apartment there. The restaurant’s original menu was created by Escoffier. Barbara Walters had a reception for her final wedding at the Pierre (about 10 years after she and my grandfather, the Broadway producer Lee Guber, officially split). Yves Saint Laurent owned a two-bedroom on the 38th floor, which was later bought by Valentino cofounder Giancarlo Giammetti, who then sold it to former Bottega Veneta creative director Tomas Maier.

And yet for 15 years or more, there’s been a growing sense that the Pierre’s best days are behind it, even as the stars continue to use the hotel to get ready for the Met Gala. A 2010 Wall Street Journal article mentions how the Pierre “lost its glory.” By the time Lutnick swooped in to buy the penthouse in 2017, he did so at an $81 million discount off its original asking price.

THE TORY PARTY Fashion designer Tory Burch, in one of the hotel’s elevators, was among the residents opposed to the sale.

Since then, age has continued to take its toll. Scaffolding has surrounded the hotel since at least 2018, according to city records. Exit a multimillion-dollar apartment with a spectacular view of the park and you’re liable to find worn carpets or hallways with the faint odor of mold. Rooms at the Pierre tend to cost much less than they do at the Plaza or the Ritz-Carlton, just around the corner.

Over time, a group of shareholders became particularly vexed with Taj Hotels, which had managed the property since 2005. There were complaints of broken elevators, empty concierge desks, and “slipshod maintenance.” Maier, in an October 2023 co-op-wide email, lamented that Taj delayed long-planned renovations to his apartment for months, citing high hotel occupancy. (A Taj spokesperson said in a statement those concerns “reflected a specific point in time rather than the overall trajectory of the property.”)

What Maier may not have known—and what the residents I spoke to were unaware of—was that the Pierre’s board had already explored the possibility of replacing Taj. The only way to do that, to break the contract with Taj, was to sell the Pierre. In April 2023, the board drafted a memorandum of understanding with the Maybourne Hotel Group, which is primarily owned by members of the Qatari royal family, to buy the hotel portion of the Pierre. “But there was a condition,” a source familiar with the matter tells me. “Everybody had to move out for two years.” The source adds, “You cannot renovate a 100-year-old building with people living in it, right?”

That was a deal killer. So the board decided, in this source’s words, to hire a firm that could broker a “more acceptable” sale. They picked the real estate consultancy Newmark. Lutnick was still chairman of Newmark’s board at that time, though two sources say he had no role in the decision. (The board, through its attorney, declined to comment for this story. But a Newmark spokesperson says its “unanimous” selection was “based on the firm’s experience advising on some of New York City’s most complex and high-profile real estate transactions.”)

From there, “Newmark went out to find another buyer,” the first source adds. Its fee at the time: $50,000 per month, to be counted against any future commissions in the event of a sale. (Eventually that was bargained down to a flat $30 million.) The board retained the high-profile law firm Fried Frank, which had represented Lutnick’s companies before, to assist Newmark in its search.

LONDON'S CALLING Christopher Cowdray, the Dorchester Collection’s president, was part of the contentious presentation to residents in the Cotillion ballroom at the Pierre.

Since Lutnick’s financial firm, Cantor Fitzgerald, owned a controlling stake in Newmark, that gave Lutnick an incentive to see the Pierre sold. He had another: According to the source connected to Lutnick, his 12,000-square-foot penthouse triplex had been uninhabitable since 2021, when a storm had caused catastrophic damage. Lutnick concluded, according to the source close to him, that major repairs wouldn’t make sense if they weren’t accompanied by a larger round of structural renovations to the building. In the meantime, he installed a basketball court in the apartment to make some use of the place.

When the sales process started, the idea was to make a deal for the hotel only. The new owner would likely want to consolidate guest rooms on certain floors. That meant some Pierre residents might be encouraged—strongly encouraged—to sell, but not necessarily everyone.

Brokers approached everyone from Mark Zuckerberg to Michael Dell to the king of Morocco to buy the place. Most of the residents were in the dark. As far as they knew, Newmark was trying to help renovate the building, not sell it off. Nor did they know Lutnick was personally trying to wrangle potential buyers for the Pierre.

On Wednesday, May 8, 2024, Lutnick’s private jet took off from Teterboro, New Jersey, outside of New York. Lutnick was on his way to Paris to meet with the Arnault family who, as part of their dominion over LVMH, run the Cheval Blanc hotel group. The source close to Lutnick mentions he had long admired the hotels and pitched the idea of the Pierre joining the group.

Lutnick’s first stop, however, was in London. After his plane landed, he went to the Dorchester Collection’s eponymous hotel in Mayfair. Shortly after 9 a.m. on Thursday, Lutnick gathered with Cowdray, the Dorchester president, and Motasem Khashoggi, chairman and principal owner of the Khashoggi Holding Company. From the outside, it seemed like an unlikely trio. The Khashoggi family was mainly famous for its wealth, but that was decades ago, back when Adnan, Motasem’s relative, was one of the world’s leading arms dealers. Motasem is recognized internationally today not as a captain of Saudi industry but as the primary legal representative for the Khashoggi family following the brutal 2018 murder of his journalist cousin, Jamal, by the Saudi state.

The source close to Lutnick says he and Khashoggi “met and spoke about a variety of different things” in London, “including: Wouldn’t it be cool if the Pierre was a Dorchester Collection hotel.” Eight days after the London meeting, according to screenshots of WhatsApp messages reviewed by Vanity Fair, Khashoggi texted Lutnick to say that “Brunie”—Hassanal Bolkiah, the Sultan of Brunei, who owns the Dorchester Collection—had “directly” asked him to explore a deal for the Pierre.

Khashoggi then asked Lutnick if he could give one of his kids a summer internship and provided his phone number. (Vanity Fair verified that number, as well as the ones used by Lutnick and the elder Khashoggi in the chats.) Lutnick quickly agreed to the father’s request. “We would be delighted to have your son join us,” he wrote. “I’m excited to invest in and build exciting companies together.”

A week later, Khashoggi sent the chat his greetings “from rainy Frankfurt,” along with a draft letter of intent to the Pierre’s board to begin due diligence for a “potential acquisition of The Pierre Hotel” and a plan to buy up “the remaining residential units.”

Lutnick wrote back on Memorial Day. “I am flying to Europe this evening, Italy and France,” he texted. “I’ve made a few modifications to the letter of intent.” Promise a “complete renovation of the guest rooms, public areas, dining facilities, and amenities,” Lutnick suggested. And be sure to include target prices, both per room and for the whole thing.

Lutnick’s firm, Newmark, was supposed to be representing the sellers in this transaction. Yet here Lutnick was coaching potential buyers, in effect putting himself on both sides of the deal. It wasn’t a cardinal sin in the take-no-prisoners worlds of New York City real estate or MAGA politics, but it wasn’t strictly kosher either.

Lutnick was confirmed as commerce secretary in February 2025; he stepped down from his Newmark chairmanship then and transferred his Cantor Fitzgerald assets to his sons. Lutnick was still listed as a member of the Pierre’s “transaction committee” in March, when the board confirmed in a letter that Newmark was in negotiations with an unnamed “operator.” But not to worry, the board added: “No owner would be required to sell their unit or move to another one.”

Residents scrambled to find out more. All they got back were rumors and whispers. One shareholder’s representative says he heard the chatter but “blew it off,” thinking that nervous residents were being “dramatic.” According to this representative, the attorneys at Holland & Knight, which had represented the Pierre for years, seemed to be in the dark as well. “You can’t sell a co-op. Never happening here,” one of those lawyers told the representative in this source’s recounting. (Holland & Knight declined to comment for this story.)

In June 2025, the New York Post reported that the Sultan of Brunei was in talks to buy the Pierre, along with Essam ­Khashoggi, an older relative of Motasem’s. The board, chaired by Michael Stern, didn’t provide many specifics in a July Zoom with shareholders but emphasized that a sale was in their best interest, according to multiple published accounts. Two months later, according to court filings, four co-op board members—the investor John Levin, former Coca-Cola CEO Douglas Daft, the lawyer and movie producer David G. Johnson, and former KB Home chief executive Bruce Karatz—approved a nonbinding term sheet to sell the Pierre.

On September 16, at a gathering in the Cotillion Ballroom, Fried Frank lawyers broke the news to shareholders. Khashoggi Holding was the buyer, and the sultan’s Dorchester Collection would be the hotel’s managers. The price was astronomical, they said, and would guarantee residents “at least three times the market value” for their apartments, Town & Country reported. But the transaction was different from the one discussed back in March. It was not just for the hotel and selected apartments. It was for the whole building, which meant the co-op owners had to vacate within 12 months. All of them.

BREAKFAST NEAR TIFFANY'S A young woman enjoys room service at the Pierre Hotel, 1943.

An escrow account of $10 million, funded by the shareholders, would be “used for eviction proceedings” for any residents who refused to leave, according to a slideshow presentation delivered by the lawyers that day. And on that happy note, residents were encouraged to open the personalized envelopes that had been given to them at the door, one for each shareholder. Inside were estimates of how much they might get from a sale.

One person who was there says it reminded him of a “game show,” and kind of an insulting one to the ultrarich in the room, for whom a few million dollars either way wouldn’t matter all that much. What was particularly galling, according to sources at the meeting, was the plan for the building’s union employees. Many of them, they said, were like family—to each other and to the residents. The staff would have to begin to go even sooner. Before Khashoggi would be asked to put down a penny, Fried Frank noted in its presentation, the firm “will engage with the Hotel Gaming and Trades Union to negotiate terms for the termination of the Union Contract.”

Employees at the Pierre tend to talk about their tenures in decades. “I only have 12 years here,” one staffer tells me without irony. Some ­workers have jobs that are so old-school, they’re not really jobs anywhere else: elevator drivers, telephone switchboard operators. Housekeeping staff wear black-and-white outfits that wouldn’t have been out of place in Audrey Hepburn’s day. “I’m very used to it,” this employee says, referring to the atmosphere at the Pierre. She means that as a positive.

Like many Pierre staffers, she’s an immigrant. A 2021 New Yorker profile counted “49 languages” spoken by the staff, “including Cantonese, Creole, Danish, Farsi, Greek, Hindi, Japanese, Portuguese, Russian, Tagalog, Tamil, Tibetan, and Twi.” I spoke with employees who are originally from four different continents.

One was a man I’ll call Ray, who has put in more than a quarter century at the Pierre and would very much like to keep going, even if the severance deal written into his union contract is pretty sweet: Ray figures he could live off of it for a year. But then what? He’s still got kids in school. And at the other hotels in town, the competition for open positions is really intense; promotions come mostly from within. “The chances of getting hired [in his particular department] are almost zero,” Ray tells me. “So I wouldn’t want to get a buyout. I don’t want the hotel to be closed.” Just in case, he’s taken a part-time gig elsewhere.

“We’re not like these millionaires, billionaires, the Howard Lutnicks, the Tory Burches,” says another Pierre employee. “Just working people, trying to protect their families.”

The rumors about a sale have been around long enough, and loud enough, that they rattled the staffers I spoke to. Even a renovation could upend staffers’ lives: The remodeling at the Waldorf Astoria Hotel lasted eight years; more than 1,200 union workers were bought out of their contracts. “Most of us, we worry,” a housekeeper tells me.

People move to the Pierre, in part, because of the staff. More than a few residents come to be taken care of, to be treated like five-star hotel guests in their own (second, or third) homes. Room service is available from 6:45 a.m. to 10:45 p.m. Housekeeping comes in seven days a week; the apartments I saw were immaculate in every way, part of the reason why maintenance costs can run tens of thousands of dollars per month. (“I haven’t made a bed since I was a kid,” says one long-term resident.)

My mom for years talked about retiring to a place like this, not that she could’ve afforded it. For older people who can, it’s a way to have the help they need while still living on their own. You see a lot of women who’ve lost or split up with their rich husbands: Beriro, the philanthropist and animal-rights activist; Gale Hayman, the cofounder of Giorgio’s of Beverly Hills; Mimi Sternlicht, the social entrepreneur; Julie Opperman, the prolific author whose late husband started the Westlaw legal-research service.

You could, perhaps, confuse these women for pushovers, one Belle Vivier pump away from assisted living. At the July meeting, Dorchester and Khashoggi brought gifts for the shareholders: bright-red teddy bears. “For little old ladies to snuggle up to in their beds,” one resident laughs at lunch afterward. Then she grabbed my utensils to cut my food.

These ladies were long past cuddly tchotchkes. Over time, several residents, most of them women and most of them over 65, had formed a loose coalition to learn what they could about the deal for the Pierre and figure ways to stop it. “It was a handful of older women,” the resident adds, “banging on the pipes, saying, ‘Listen up, people!’ ”

Some of them, at least at first, were open to the idea of a sale; they had other homes, after all. But the cloak of secrecy around the deal infuriated them. So in the days leading up to the contentious reveal of the Khashoggi proposal in September 2025, Chiles and Beriro and others banded together with Hearst and Burch—relative youngsters—and lawyered up. “We became an informal little group: Tory and a bunch of widows,” one source with direct knowledge of the matter says, tongue a bit in cheek.

ABOVE BOARD Investor Austin Hearst is part of a group of Pierre residents who sued the co-op board to produce more information about the sale of the building.

In November 2025, the group sued the board to force it to produce more information about the sale, with Burch’s LLC as the lead plaintiff: how much the board really knew about the buyer; which third parties might benefit from it. Shortly after, Fried Frank lawyer Michael Keats criticized Burch in a letter to her attorney: “this [her tactics] comes across as completely unhinged.” On at least one occasion, according to a source familiar with the matter, a board member approached Burch to see if she might want to keep her apartment, even while Khashoggi bought everyone else’s. Burch refused. (“The Board never offered anyone any special consideration,” its president and chairman later wrote in a letter to shareholders.)

The suit was quickly dismissed when the board agreed to release some of the information.

A number of shareholders, meanwhile, had found other sources. Some of them enlisted, in the resident’s words, “spies” to ferret out what the sale truly entailed. In March, some shareholders, independently of the board, met with Taj CEO Puneet Chhatwal. People both for and against the deal pressed shareholders for how they were going to vote, like Capitol Hill whips.

In late July, a 41-page corporate intelligence dossier was delivered to my home in an unmarked envelope. Who commissioned it is unclear; the cover page is missing and the report is undated. But it provides a tough assessment of Khashoggi’s corporate expertise.

According to the report, none of Khashoggi Holding’s “eight subsidiaries and associated companies” operate in the “hospitality sector, and none appear to have any international presence or cross-border real estate capability.”

The company’s “most prominent publicly reported investments to date,” it adds, are an approximately $37 million “pharmaceutical investment in Aleppo [Syria] and a cement factory partnership.” Other deals publicly linked to the company and to Motasem Khashoggi are substantial but of a similar size.

In recent years and especially in the second Trump administration, money from the Persian Gulf has backed an attempt to merge two of America’s iconic movie studios, completed a leveraged buyout of one of its biggest video game makers, and purchased some of New York’s most prized office towers. Khashoggi’s deals, on the other hand, “are orders of magnitude smaller than the proposed Pierre Hotel acquisition,” notes the report, which claims that the company’s “registered capital” amounts to “approximately USD 266,000.”

Perhaps it’s just a coincidence that during the July meeting in the Cotillion Ballroom, the Khashoggi and Dorchester representatives received question after question about how Motasem Khashoggi could possibly have the resources to buy the Pierre.

NEIGHBOR VS. NEIGHBOR Michael Eisner, the former Disney CEO, owns two apartments in the Pierre. He has been in favor of finding new ownership for the hotel.

“You mentioned the Khashoggi LLC is the buyer, but who is putting up the money behind the Khashoggi hedge fund?” one shareholder asked.

“There is no hedge fund. This is Mr. Khashoggi. This will be funded in all cash, and it is only him,” was the answer.

“We’re not going to leave you out there with an unfunded buyer,” added Patrick Dowd, a Fried Frank lawyer.

The questions would prove prescient—but it would still be a couple of months before that became clear. In the meantime, the speculation and the finger-pointing continued—splitting neighbor from neighbor—as the possibility of a sale grew closer and residents had taken sides. “They run the hotel, in my opinion, very badly,” Eisner said of Taj in that July Cotillion room meeting, adding that he “would not stay at this hotel” with them in charge.

“Then sell your apartment. If you’re not happy here, leave,” Burch snapped, according to the same recording of the meeting. “You don’t have to force everyone else and fire 700 employees in the process.”

“This is not your home,” Burch said a moment later to a second shareholder, who tried to take Eisner’s side. The decay, the imperfections, they can be a hassle, for sure. But they’re also part of the throwback charm, a necessary side effect to living someplace with so much history. “I don’t need a shiny new hotel,” she added. “People actually love this place, as shabby as it may be.”

Despite the rancor, the board and the Indian hotel operators tried to negotiate a way forward. Or at least a competitive offer to Khashoggi’s. After 10 months of talks, they finally came to what they thought was an agreement. Two agreements, actually: one to buy the hotel portion of the Pierre; the other to extend Taj’s lease, in exchange for a commitment to invest almost $400 million into the building. The idea was to give both options to shareholders, shortly after the Khashoggi presentation.

Then suddenly, with less than a week to go before the Cotillion room meeting, Taj withdrew. The bosses in Mumbai voted not to approve the transactions they had been negotiating.

GLOVES OFF Al Pacino’s blind tango in Scent of a Woman takes place the Pierre's Cotillion ballroom.

A letter from Chhatwal floating the idea of a $300 million investment was rejected out of hand by the co-op board. The heads of the board wrote to shareholders the next day: It’s Khashoggi or the status quo, no other choices.

“Do you want to live here or do you not? Let’s not overcomplicate it,” Burch told the Cotillion room. “It’s going to be down to two options. You either stay with Taj. Or you leave, and then it becomes some fancy hotel that we have nothing to do with.”

About a month later, the board released the details of the Khashoggi deal in a proxy statement sent to residents. It was enormous—more than 200 pages—but perhaps not maximally persuasive. Departing residents were promised five free nights in a suite at one of Dorchester’s other high-end hotels, plus a set of perks. “Priority access to spa treatments” and free breakfast seemed unlikely to move the needle with a crowd accustomed to more elaborate pampering.

The following week, Khashoggi tried reaching out to shareholders directly. “I understand how personal this is,” he wrote. “I sincerely hope that you will welcome me and my family into the Pierre family.”

This personal appeal did not work on those shareholders who were already dug in against the deal. “Where do you get off addressing me by my first name?” one emailed back to Khashoggi.

And with that, the window opened for voting the deal up or down.

The following day, the chairman and president of the Pierre’s co-op board wrote to residents that “a wire transfer instruction has been issued to transmit the $100,000,000 deposit.”

Then something strange happened. Or rather, didn’t happen at all.

Supporters of the sale were baffled. “We are told by all advisers involved that he’s, you know, intending to complete the transaction,” one of those supporters says. “In my business experience, someone who is a wealthy individual who decides that they don’t want to do the deal,” this person adds, “they send you a nice letter or make a phone call and say, you know, ‘I’m very sorry, but circumstances have changed, and I’m moving on.’ ”

That call never came, though. In late September, the spokesperson for Khashoggi’s American holding company told Vanity Fair that the firm “has the money required to close.”

The board gave Khashoggi additional time to come up with the deposit. He failed to do so, and the sale was called off. All of that work, all of those millions spent, all of that rancor—turned out, it was for a lost cause. The Khashoggi deal was dead.

In an interview with the Times, Khashoggi gave a dog-ate-my-homework excuse, blaming the bank for failing to send over his deposit. He gave a shout-out to his “good friend” Lutnick, who had led him to the Pierre deal in the first place and who had been poised to receive as much as a $100 million windfall from it. Then Khashoggi took a shot at the residents he was courting just a few weeks earlier. “They have their building, which I’m sure they know the condition of,” he said. “And I have my money. So I don’t know who’s the bigger loser here.”

At the time of publication, an election for a new co-op board was set for December 1. At least one of the residents who opposed the Khashoggi sale is mulling a run; another of those shareholders is thinking about suing those folks who got them into this whole mess.

But in theory, things at the Pierre will now largely go back to the way they were. Or at least they’ll continue along the same trajectory. Taj has more than 8 years left on its lease, plus an option to extend another 10. Together with the new board, they’ll figure out which of the renovations are a priority. Those costs will then be split with residents. The assessments could reach into the millions for each apartment. The disruptions from the construction could be considerable. No one will be forced to leave their homes in this crumbling old palace by the park. For now, the elevator drivers and switchboard operators get to stay.

The Big Bang Theory Universe has remained alive and well in the years since the flagship series ended. Honestly, it's thriving. This is partly due to the prequel Young Sheldon, which ran for seven seasons and spawned its own spinoff, Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage. The latter is now in its third season on the 2026 TV schedule, and it features some A+ cameos and references to its parent series. However, there’s another cool connection between Georgie and Mandy and Young Sheldon that I had no idea about.

While appearing on The Official Big Bang Theory Podcast, Young Sheldon star Raegan Revord recalled the early days of Young Sheldon as best as they could, given that they were so young. Revord mentioned that they vividly remember sitting right in front of the audience while watching the pilot tape. That's what led to them noting that Georgie & Mandy is filmed on the same stage as Young Sheldon. Speaking about what it's like to see Montana Jordan's new show filmed in the same spot as the old one, the actor said:

It's weird because now Montana's show is on there, and every once in a while, I'll be like, 'Wait a minute, this is the exact same stage.'

Considering that Georgie & Mandy came just months after Young Sheldon ended, I’m not too surprised that they gave the Young Sheldon stage on the Warner Bros. lot to the spinoff. And when you think about it, it also makes sense given that occasionally there are still scenes at the Cooper household from time to time. However, it’s a crazy coincidence to think about, and it really just connects the two shows even more.

Additionally, this connection is even more mind-blowing given the fact that Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage has a live studio audience, while Young Sheldon did not. For some reason, it never occurred to me that even single-camera shows still have places for a live audience. However, in hindsight, it would make sense depending on what was previously filmed on that soundstage.

That is actually not the only stage connection that the Big Bang Theory Universe has. The most recent spinoff, Stuart Fails to Save the Universe, returned to Big Bang’s original soundstage in the wild Season 1 finale, which aired in September, as the episode shifted from a single-camera comedy to multi-cam and went very meta. The show doesn’t actually fully film on Big Bang’s former stage, but it did for the finale, and it made the craziness of the season even better.

Even though Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage references Young Sheldon a lot, and there are a handful of cameos, I do love knowing that there’s another connection that goes even deeper than appearances and references. Now, as the spinoff of the spinoff continues to air, you better believe I'll be looking for more cool Easter eggs.

#3444. South Park's Season 29 Finale Features The Scariest TV Scene Of 2026

"South Park" has been on a roll recently. When the show finally left behind its Mr.-Garrison-as-Trump allegory and stopped doing endless specials (even if most of those were fantastic), it found its stride again in Season 28, which took on AI and deepfakes in the funniest way possible. Then, Season 29 took on everything from the data centers, to "looksmaxxing" and "aura farming" in a hilarious "Backrooms" parody, to club sports in a great "Heated Rivalry" parody, to the US beef shortage, and more.

It's been a funny season, and it's been a heartfelt season at times, particularly when the show killed Kenny (again) and decided to replace him with none other than a kid version of Randy (complete with mustache). It has even been a romantic season, with the Tweek and Craig romance-focused episode. What "South Park" usually isn't, however, is scary. That changed with the Season 29 finale, which delivered the scariest TV scene of 2026 — twice.

In the finale, "City Endings," the town of South Park (renamed this season as South America) is hit with major power outages that disrupt the town's "GTA VI" gametime. It is part of a conspiracy involving secret deals the government made with billionaire weenies. At the same time, there's paranoia involving supposed Chinese spies and possible cyberattacks from that country.

In the middle of all this, Cartman, Stan, and Kyle are also haunted by visions of the late Kenny, who died after being blown up by an e-bike in the season's premiere. Except this is not just Kenny, but a zombified version that haunts the boys in the form of horrific ghouls that even infiltrate "GTA VI," like a spectre out of "The Ring."

"South Park" has toyed with the horror genre before, usually body horror. There was the Michael Jackson parody with Mr. Jefferson slowly rotting away, for example, or the HumanCentipad. The Season 29 finale, however, features one of the wildest and most gruesome eldritch abominations in the nearly 30-year history of the show. It starts with several scenes of Kenny simply standing creepily in the background, stalking the boys as if to try and send a message.

"City Endings" is a legit horror episode, which is rare from the show that spent nearly a decade on a silly weed farm storyline. The image of Kenny just standing in the background, his face obscured by his hoodie but with bright eyes just shining like Pennywise in "It," is already quite disturbing and terrifying. Then, when the boys finally catch up to Kenny, who leads them to the cemetery and to his own grave, he shows off his gruesome zombie face and starts dissolving like that guy in "Poltergeist," in excruciatingly disturbing detail, before exploding in a pool of blood.

It's enough to make your skin crawl, but it's not even the scariest scene of the episode. That climax comes in later, while the boys are playing "GTA VI" at Butters' house. We see the zombie Kenny monster with long spiky teeth, deranged eyes and elongated limbs with claws crawling out of the TV like Samara Morgan from "The Ring." It is the stuff of pure nightmares, and by far the scariest scene in 2026 television.

#3443. 20 of the Coolest Tech Stocking Stuffers for Under $50

This series will help you pick the perfect presents, decor, and activities to make this Christmas the Best Christmas Ever.

What if you make this the year you don't fill all the stockings with candy or gift cards? Both have their place, but if you want to make this the best Christmas ever, you have to shove some tech in those stockings. The good news: Tech gifts don’t have to be expensive to be impressive.

No matter who you're shopping for, there are tons of affordable gizmos that are some combination of cool and useful and that feel pricier than they are. Here are 20 cool tech stocking stuffers to light up any holiday morning, all of which cost less than $50.

If there's an old-school gamer on your list, their Christmas morning will be extra merry if it includes a tiny video game emulator. R36T Retro Gaming Console ($48.98) puts over 18,000 video games in the palm of your hand. It has a 3.5" screen, so whether they like arcade classics or consoles-of-the-past, they can fit 'em all in a pocket.

The Xteink X4 is an e-reader that's smaller than your phone. It uses e-ink like an Amazon Kindle, so you can whip a glare-free screen out of your pocket and start reading anywhere there's a light source. The X4 is a no-frills gadget—there's no lighting, touchscreen, or apps—but if you want a cheap, convenient way to read for around $50, it's perfect.

Those disposable cans of compressed air with the red straws are so 2015. Blow the dust off your electronics with an SDFM Electric Air Duster instead. With an engine that moves at 150,000 RPM, it shoots air such high speeds, the dust doesn't stand a chance. It's also cordless and comes with a variety of cleaning attachments to keep your gear in top shape.

This two-pack retails for $22.99 and contains two headbands with built in speakers you can pair with your phone or other device easily.

Your giftee may have the tech side of their battle station/home office locked down, but I bet they don't have the aesthetics dialed in. Govee Smart LED Light Bars ($54.99, but currently on sale for $34.99) are programmable, colorful light bars that work with Alexa and Google Assistant and can display light effects created from 16 millions colors. My lifestyle doesn't involve cutting down trees, but I still need one of these miniature chainsaws. I mean, it's a chainsaw, and it's only six inches long. This Seeii mini chainsaw ($49.99) is battery-powered, so no one will be accidentally cutting the cord. According to the listing, it's suitable for tree pruning, garden artistry, shrub trimming, forest logging, and wood cutting.

You know what computer fiends are missing in their lives? Knobs. This little $33 gadget lets you assign functions to four external knobs and 12 push buttons, so you can finally have a decent volume control, scrub through video smoothly, skip music tracks with a button push, and control any other function easily and physically. Perfect for gamers.

You could use a tape measure like a caveman, or you could measure things with a frickin' laser that fits in your pocket. This $40 gadget has an LED screen that's easy to read and it doubles as a cat toy. But does it measure things? Damn right it measures things—big things, little things, middle-sized things—it doesn't care what you put in front of it, it will measure the hell out of it! (Up to 98 feet, anyway.)

This compact Bluetooth speaker has an Amazon rating of 4.6 stars out of 5, and it's cheap—just $45. It's waterproof, it sounds great, and it features a built-in light show with six different settings so you can check out cool visuals with your tunes.

A single Apple Airtag makes a great gift to accompany the main gift you don't want someone to lose. Or they can put it on their wallet or your keys, and if they misplace them, they can hit a button and it will play a sound while the FindMy app displays a map that leads to the missing item. Plus, it works in reverse, so you can hit a tag and it will ring your lost phone.

If you want to give the gift of warmth for the holidays, you could do a lot worse than this portable neck, shoulder, and back warmer. There are three temperature settings, a safety shut-off feature, and it heats up really fast, for only $33.

This tiny little vacuum from Odistar will keep their desktop dust-free. It sucks with 1000Pa of suction power for 400 minutes off a single charge, and it's very easy to use: You put it in the palm of your hand and push it around. Cool!

It's not like people need an endoscope camera every day, but if the need for a tiny camera does arise—if they need to see why the engine isn't working or if their wedding ring falls behind the oven—they'll be glad to have this Anykit USB Endoscope Camera.
