If your giftee is carrying their laptop around to coffeehouses like a chump, this is the perfect present. They can connect a foldable mini Bluetooth keyboard from iClever to their phone, and turn it into an ultra-portable productivity device. It even has a little trackpad!

This skinny extra battery charges a phone magnetically or with a USB-C cable. It's fast, too. It can charge an iPhone 16 Pro Max to 37% in 30 minutes via the USB-C port and it's less than three inches wide.

Projectors have gotten really good and really small over the last few years, and they prices have come down massively too. This mini projector costs only $29 and projects a 720p image up to 120" and it weighs only about two pounds.

Most people already have a media streamer attached to their televisions, but in case you're gifting someone who doesn't, the Roku Streaming Stick 4K is a solid choice in the $50 price range. This no-frills device serves up 4K HD video, gives you access to hundreds of free and premium channels, and is easy to setup.

The Twelve South AirFly SE is an ultra-compact Bluetooth transmitter lets you plug into any device with a 3.5 mm jack, like in-flight entertainment systems, gym machines, or TVs, and stream audio wirelessly to your Bluetooth earbuds or headphones. Leave those accursed wired headphone in the drawer where they belong!

This is an essential gift if there's a cyclist in your life and anyone who wants to maintain proper PSI in their car tires. This portable air compressor weighs less than a pound and is a steal at only $40. It's rechargeable, has an onboard pressure gauge, an LED flashlight, and can inflate a car tire in only eight minutes.

I am 100% sure anyone you give this to will be able to use it. This compact, high‑power Anker charger has two USB‑C ports plus one USB‑A, letting you power up your laptop, phone, and tablet all at once, from one plug. Plus it charges fast.

#3442. Jana Kramer Wants to Be in 'Virgin River' Love Triangle After Cast Changes

Jana Kramer isn’t ruling out a role on any Netflix show after auditioning for both seasons of The Hunting Wives — including a possible love triangle role on Virgin River amid the show’s cast changes.

“[My former costar] Ben [Hollingsworth] had made a comment. He was kind of stirring the pot a bit, saying he thought it would be nice to do a love triangle between him and Zibby [Allen]‘s character,” Kramer, 42, exclusively told Us before the release of her new Lifetime holiday movie, Love on the Christmas List.

Kramer confirmed she is “all about it,” adding, “I think the show is great. I’d love to be a part of any kind of love triangle and it brings me back to my One Tree Hill days. So give me a good love triangle to mess things up. It’s great.”

She continued: “I love it for TV purposes. Maybe stay tuned. I don’t know. I did text Ben saying, ‘Hey, let’s figure this out.’ Because I would love it.”

Hollingsworth, 42, also told Us he would love to reunite with Kramer on a new project after they played love interests in a Christmas movie.

“I had such a great time working with Jana. She’s so professional but such a friendly and nice person,” he shared in October. “Our families got along really well. I brought my family out to Nashville when we were shooting The Christmas Ring, and she had us over to her house a couple times.”

Hollingsworth loved the friendship he formed with Kramer, saying, “We just had a really great chemistry right off the bat. So I would love to do something with Jana. You know what? She’s been very vocal about wanting to be on Virgin River. So maybe that’s the play is [to] try and get her on Virgin River.”

The actor showed support for Us‘ idea of having Kramer shake things up by creating a new love triangle with Brady (Hollingsworth) and Brie (Allen).

“That makes perfect sense. I think that would be great,” Hollingsworth added. “New characters come and go on Virgin River, and they change the feeling of that community. But the core of it is still the same: people who show up for each other, who love each other, who support each other, who go through everything together — that’s what makes this show special. So to bring someone like Jana in, of course, would be amazing.”

Kramer, for her part, is keeping her options open with possible TV roles.

“I want to go on MobLand. I love that show. I don’t have a British accent to save my life, so they have to cast an American,” she quipped while discussing her dream roles. “Always cause havoc, those roles are always so much fun. I love those types of shows.”

After previously auditioning for The Hunting Wives, Kramer confirmed she tried again for season 3.

“I have yet to strike one since testing for obviously that one role, but yeah, I auditioned for one other one and didn’t get it either,” she admitted. “So it wasn’t meant to be. It’s OK. My dream is still to get back onto a TV show. I miss it, and so yeah, fingers crossed. There’s some good shows right now, though.”

For now, Kramer is celebrating the release of her new Lifetime holiday movie, in which she portrays Lindsay, an assistant who is on the hunt for the season’s most popular toy to land a promotion. Lindsay crosses paths with a widowed dad as he strives to bring home the toy for his daughter..

“I would say this is very similar to all the moms that are on the hunt for the best toy for their kids,” she teased about the film. “For this movie, it’s about whether you do what you need to do, whether it’s for your job or for your child, and in the middle of that, you might find a little romance along the way.”

Love on the Christmas List premieres on Lifetime Saturday, December 19, at 8 p.m. ET.

#3441. Are the World’s Top Literary Scholars Being Targeted by a Chinese Spy Op?

Stephanie Newell, an English professor at Yale University, was thrilled when she got the email inviting her to be an honorary fellow at the International Institute of Literature & Arts. She had never heard of IILA, but she recognized several prestigious names of fellow big-time literature professors who were listed among its fellows. “I saw Gayatri Spivak and Homi Bhabha, Franco Moretti, and I was like, Oh, finally,” she says.

The letter, signed by one Julian Lee “on behalf of the Secretariat” of IILA, invited Newell to join highly esteemed literature scholars at the Ivies, Stanford, Oxford, and Cambridge. Newell, who has taught world and African literature at Yale for more than a decade, had been inducted into other prestigious societies with many of these same scholars, such as the British Academy.

This one, it seemed, came without strings. “There are no fees or membership dues,” read the letter. “Participation in award reviews, academic meetings, and consultation will be arranged with you in advance and subject to your availability.”

Stephanie Newell, an English professor at Yale University, was initially honored to receive an IILA fellowship.

It seemed like a no-brainer. They’d also given her an award, and she even decided to accept an offer to join IILA’s academic committee. Yale was pleased for her too. The English department posted an announcement congratulating her on receiving the award.

Soon, Newell says, she was listed among IILA’s leadership, even though she’d only agreed to be a committee member. “Please will you remove my name,” she wrote in an email to Lee.

Her concerns compounded when she received a draft of IILA’s bulletin, featuring a perplexingly poorly written biography—not what one would expect from a fancy literary academy. “Please delete my profile from the Bulletin,” Newell asked Lee, “as it contains too many errors for circulation, and is very poorly written.”

While the institute’s membership ranks included many of Newell’s high-profile peers, there were also a number of names on the list that seemed a bit random. Pat Barker, a novelist rather than a scholar, seemed out of place among the critics and theorists. There were, however, about half a dozen Chinese professors (including one who had already died).

“I’ve always been a bit of a doubting Thomas,” Newell wrote in an email to a colleague on the list who confirmed that she, too, had accepted the fellowship despite not knowing who was behind it. “I’m starting to wonder what’s going on and whether we’ve been somehow flattered into something that doesn’t exist!” Newell wrote.

That’s when Newell, who was my professor when I was a Yale undergraduate, decided to reach out to me about “a fake academic institute that has sucked in numerous very high-profile professors.” This was a couple of weeks ago, right after the news broke of Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman US authorities believed to be a Chinese spy. It made sense what China would want from Huang, the CEO of the powerful AI chip maker Nvidia, but could world literature professors really be a target? I started digging, which led me down a rabbit hole that included an entire constellation of shadow academies that former national security officials say have real potential to be part of a Chinese intelligence operation.

The website for IILA, which claims to be based in California, appears to have been registered in China. An IT specialist who reviewed the website for Vanity Fair assessed that it was built using artificial intelligence and riddled with glitches and broken links. The file name of the site’s logo is the Chinese word for “picture.” Registration records list the owner’s location as the Hubei province in central China, whose capital is Wuhan. But a data bug in the site’s administrative code suggests that the computer being used to post news on the site is not in China, but likely in Southeast Asia. The bug leaks the computer’s time zone with every new post saved through the site’s form, and every post carries a UTC+7 offset—the time zone for Bangkok, as well as Hanoi, Jakarta, and Phnom Penh.

Every edit also carries a second fingerprint: The computer saving the changes has an internal clock that runs a few seconds fast. That consistent drift shows that the same machine has been used for every post, which suggests that a single person could be updating the site.

Though IILA says on its website that it is a 501(c)(3), the IRS has no record of it, and it has no California registration. Instead, Colorado records list an “International Institute of Literature and Arts” as a nonprofit corporation registered in August 2025 at the address of a virtual mailbox service in Denver. It’s had a “delinquent” status since late August. (A local Denver newspaper ran a story in May asking why “over 12,000 different businesses all use” this same address.)

Several of the other organizations that use that same Colorado address, including the National Academy of Artificial Intelligence, the International Institute of Film Science & Arts, and the International Institute of Engineering Psychology (IIEP), were the subject of a Nature investigation in September. Nature’s reporting found that these organizations boasted high-ranking academics as their members, oftentimes without their knowledge or consent. According to Nature, the name most frequently associated with these organizations was Michael Chu, whose Chinese name, Chaoyang Zhu, is also listed as the incorporator of IILA in public records.

Yale University boasts one of the top ranked English departments in the world.

Chu’s name was previously listed on IILA’s website where Julian Lee’s name now appears, and his biography, according to another now deleted webpage, recovered through the Wayback Machine, includes a stint at another fake university that appears to belong to the same network, the City University of Colorado.

In response to a request for comment, IILA’s secretariat sent VF a series of unsigned emails, the first of which said the organization’s Colorado address was just an “early transitional filing point” and that a move to a “new regional and national headquarters is currently underway.” The “delinquent” status, they wrote, merely “reflects an administrative transition delay between entities.”

Another email stated that “we don’t know” about the other Chu-linked organizations mentioned in Nature’s report or why they all shared the same address.

“What’s the matter with Michael Chu? He is not working here at present. I can’t contact him at present,” the secretariat wrote, before passing along Chu’s email.

Chu swiftly responded to Vanity Fair in both Chinese and English to “prevent misunderstandings.” “I have no contact with the Chinese government at present” and “I am not related to IILA at present, and I am not responsible for any work of IILA,” Chu wrote. He then went on to speculate about the questions regarding IILA’s legitimacy: “IILA is an organization registered according to law, but because the previous registered agency company said that there was a problem with the agency address, it needs to be re-registered. This may be the reason why some people think IILA is illegal.”

“I think the supervision of the media is good and necessary, but we can’t use the power of the media to deliberately hinder normal academic exchanges,” posited Chu regarding the Nature article, which he says “many professors” he works with called “inexplicable and absurd."

Nature did not respond to a request for comment in time for publication.

Asked to comment on IILA's connection with China, a Chinese embassy spokesperson said, “I am not familiar with the specific situation you mentioned."

Last month, César Pablo Domínguez Prieto, a professor of comparative literature at the University of Santiago de Compostela in Spain, found himself going down a similar rabbit hole after he was invited by IILA to give a talk for an online seminar series titled “New Directions in World and Comparative Literature” and promised an “Outstanding Speaker Award.”

“This solicitation prompted me to review their platform, where I discovered that the names and academic credentials of several of you are currently listed on their website,” Prieto wrote in an email to a group of his peers, which included Cornell’s Jonathan Dwight Culler, Harvard’s David Damrosch, and Shanghai Jiao Tong University’s Wang Ning. “The list includes other colleagues with whom I’m not acquainted.”

Suspicious of the site and the invitation, Prieto dug further, finding those same public records that revealed Zhu’s name and the Colorado delinquent status.

Damrosch, a professor of world and comparative literature, was horrified to learn that his name was still being used by IILA without his “knowledge or permission.” He says he had written to them weeks ago asking for his name to be removed, with no result. (It has since been removed.)

“I suspect it is organized by the Chinese to place Chinese scholars in the company of distinguished Western scholars, but it is all a bit of a mystery,” Culler, a professor of English and comparative literature, tells me.

“I checked, and you’re right! I am a fellow there,” Moretti, a literary scholar, responded when I asked if he knowingly accepted the fellowship from IILA.

Founded in 1896, Shanghai Jiao Tong University is one of China's top public universities.

Yale has since deleted its announcement of Newell’s honorary IILA fellowship amid her concerns about the academy’s legitimacy. Shanghai Jiao Tong University, however, proudly displays comparative literature professor Wang Ning’s honor on its website, congratulating him on his fellowship and on receiving “the Global Laureate Award in Literature and Cultural Theory.” A magazine sponsored and supervised by the Chinese National Academy of Arts under the Ministry of Culture and Tourism similarly applauded Wang’s IILA award in October.

“This organization’s business model relies on unilaterally placing the names of highly respected scholars—such as yourselves—on their website without informed or explicit consent, while using targeted invitations for seminar series like the one I received as a fishing hook,” Prieto alleged in the email to his colleagues. “They use your collective prestige to look legitimate, allowing them to target early-career researchers and charge them annual membership fees ranging from $95 to $175 USD for worthless certificates.” (The membership pricing that previously appeared on IILA’s website has apparently been removed.)

Prieto’s assessment of what might be driving this scam was in line with Nature’s reporting: While the journal said it “has not identified anyone who has admitted paying for” any awards or titles from the academic societies, sources interviewed for that article theorized that they are designed to attract younger professors in China who might be willing to pay to be in the company of more highly esteemed academics.

But experts who spoke to Vanity Fair suggested there might be something else more nefarious at play.

Jeff Fields, a fellow at the UC Berkeley Institute for Security and Governance who spent more than 20 years with the FBI, most recently as the assistant special agent in charge of counterintelligence at the FBI’s San Francisco field office, says he’s familiar with this type of scheme.

“One of the things they like to do,” Fields says of the Chinese government, “is to fabricate these associations that they then use to leverage for more sophisticated operations.”

He has seen Chinese intelligence play such a long game, that it will spend years exaggerating or inventing affiliations in case it ever needs them, whether to lend someone credibility or to reach a particular target. If an agent later wants to get close to a professor who is friends with a certain researcher, for instance, the initial connections are already in place.

Jake Braun, who served as the White House’s acting principal deputy national cyber director under Joe Biden, agrees with Fields’s analysis, citing what’s known as the “thousand grains of sand” theory of Chinese intelligence. Because of its massive population, China has the ability to deploy an extraordinary number of people in its information-gathering techniques. Some might not necessarily be intelligence officers, he says, but each one can collect a single “grain of sand” of intelligence, which, when put together, works as an extremely powerful and effective intelligence apparatus.

Newell says that she was prompted on IILA’s website to create an account using her email address and a password, though once she was logged in, the website appeared entirely the same. Neither Fields nor Braun seemed terribly concerned about the possibility that those passwords could be used by whoever was behind the website to try to hack into the professors’ university accounts or emails.

What’s more likely, says Braun, is that in addition to the long game of network-building for future intelligence operations, IILA may also double as a platform to lend credibility to misinformation and disinformation campaigns by associating them with reputable scholars—another tactic he’s seen used before to influence narratives about China at the West’s foremost universities.

The Chinese professors listed as IILA fellows primarily come from three public, and therefore government-funded, universities, all in Shanghai: Fudan University, Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU), and Shanghai University. In July 2026, the US Department of Defense added Fudan University and SJTU to a list of academic and research institutions deemed “a concern to national security.”

SJTU had already come under scrutiny following a 2023 incident in which five Chinese students enrolled in its joint program with the University of Michigan allegedly photographed military exercises at a National Guard training facility in the state. The students were charged in October 2024 with making false statements and related offenses, months after they left the country following graduation, according to the federal complaint. Three months later, the university announced the termination of its two-decade partnership with SJTU, citing national security concerns. (The partnership is still featured on SJTU’s website, however.)

Fudan University, meanwhile, was involved in the recent high-profile spying case of former Federal Reserve employee John Rodgers, who allegedly funneled classified government information to a spy he met at a conference in China. Rodgers would later send sensitive information to a Fudan professor and become a teacher there himself after leaving the Fed. (In July, he was sentenced to 38 months in federal prison for making false statements to federal investigators about sharing restricted Federal Reserve information with Chinese intelligence operatives.)

Wang Ning of Shanghai Jiao Tong University feels certain that IILA is legitimate.

Still, Damrosch notes that those schools are also home to the leading literature programs in China, so their inclusion on the list does make sense from an academic perspective.

Because of their positions at public universities in China, some of the professors listed alongside Newell and her colleagues on IILA’s list of fellows also have ties to the Chinese Communist Party. Wang, for example, is the dean of SJTU’s Institute of Arts and Humanities, which houses a research hub, jointly established by Shanghai’s municipal CCP publicity department, focused on China’s international image. And, in 2023, he spearheaded the launch of a new cultural research center at SJTU dedicated to China’s “united front” work, which the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission has described as being used “to co-opt and neutralize sources of potential opposition to the policies and authority of its ruling Chinese Communist Party.”

When I reach out to Wang, he is eager to talk, noting that he knows “Vanity Fair is a prestigious popular journal in the United States.” We meet over Zoom, which he joins from an empty room in Beijing with one overhead light.

He tells me he received Prieto’s email, but he believes his colleague is mistaken and feels certain that IILA is legitimate. Wang insists that the members he has nominated from his own university were not asked to pay any fee. He says he’s communicated with both Michael Chu and Julian Lee, and that he doesn’t actually think it matters that he’s never met them. What affords the academy authenticity, says Wang, is its members and their own accomplishments, which are real and impressive—on that part, at least, everyone is in agreement.

“Oh, please let them be Chinese spies, please,” Newell says of IILA’s leadership. “That would be one of the best things ever in my whole life.” She finds the whole thing very amusing, needing to pause in the middle of our interview for a laugh break.

“I love the idea of fooling top academics,” says Newell. “I think it’s hilarious that we’re so famous, that our egos…the fact that none of us questioned getting awards and fellowships and we’re all so eagerly accepting them and letting our universities know how clever we are…I mean, it’s hilarious, and pathetic, and it says so much about the profession.”

#3440. Avengers: Doomsday TV Spot Confirms RDJ's Doctor Doom Has A Scarred Face

Marvel Comics fans know Doctor Victor von Doom is scarcely ever seen without his iron mask — a mask that hides his supposedly horribly scarred face. But with Marvel Studios choosing former Tony Stark actor Robert Downey Jr. to play Doom in the upcoming "Avengers" movies "Doomsday" and "Secret Wars," there's been an expectation that Doom's mask coming off will be a jaw dropping moment.

Now, Chris Evans has claimed that Doom wears his mask for the entirety of "Doomsday." But that could only mean he'll keep the mask on until "Secret Wars." Even then, there's the chance that Doom is so disfigured that his face isn't even recognizable as RDJ. A new TV spot for "Doomsday" does suggest Doom has his scarred face, while also teasing we're eventually going to see exactly what's under his mask ... but not yet.

In this TV spot, Magneto (Ian McKellen) tries to telekinetically rip off Doom's mask — it is made of metal, after all. But Doom does not restrict himself to the laws of science. There's evidently a magical seal on the mask (note there appear to be runic designs across Doom's costume), because glowing green tendrils extend out from Doom's hood and grab the mask, slamming it back onto Doom's face. A brief glimpse of Doom's face, visible through the mask's eyeholes, shows hints of pale macerated skin and scar tissue.

In the "Fantastic Four" comics, it was originally said that Doom suffered his scars during an experiment in college. A machine he built to contact the "nether world" (later revealed to be an attempt to reach his mother's damned soul) exploded in his face, leaving him scarred.

Now, Doom's co-creator Jack Kirby intended that Doom actually only had a thin facial scar — but Doom's ego can't stand even that small imperfection. Later "Fantastic Four" writer/artist John Byrne melded the two ideas. The machine explosion only slightly damaged Doom's face, but then Victor — convinced his face was already ruined — put his freshly forged mask on before it cooled, and that is why he has a horribly scarred face.

The greatest source of Doom's torment is completely self-inflicted. The exemplary 1989 "Doctor Strange and Doctor Doom: Triumph and Torment" goes with Byrne's interpretation. When Doom seeks out the wisdom of the wizard named the Aged Genghis, the sorcerer alludes to Doom's "minor disfigurement." We then see Doom's (barely scarred) face as Victor lashes out at the insult.

It's unclear what origin "Doomsday" will go with, if any of them. Marketing suggests the Marvel Cinematic Universe's Doom will be driven by a lost wife and child, not his mother. What is clear from this TV spot is that Marvel fans can expect to see Doom and Magneto — the two greatest villains of Marvel Comics — clash onscreen. Doom's wizardry here refutes the obvious conclusion that Magneto wins easily because he controls metal and Doom is concealed inside metal armor.

"He is pain, he is extinction," Magneto declares, setting up Doom's famous third person double entendre: "I am Doom!" Ian McKellen's Magneto was the first villain of the Marvel movie boom that kicked off with 2000's "X-Men." Bringing him back to face (and presumably fall to) Doom is some classic carnival barker marketing that would make Stan Lee proud.

"Avengers: Doomsday" is set for theatrical release on December 18, 2026.

If you can believe it, Robert Pattinson put a ridiculous amount of work into getting Batman-ready.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As we approach the end of the 2026 movie schedule, plenty of upcoming superhero movies are worth looking forward to. When I think about actors who have played Batman, I tend to picture guys like Christian Bale and Ben Affleck, both of whom looked like they could probably bench-press the Batmobile. Robert Pattinson's version of the Caped Crusader has a noticeably leaner physique, something fans have debated since Matt Reeves' The Batman arrived in 2022. A resurfaced interview with the actor reveals just how much work he actually put into the role, and his explanation made me laugh.

With The Batman: Part II currently in production, Pattinson's comments about his inability to pack on the weight for a superhero physique are making the rounds again. In a social media post that's been circulating on X, Pattinson's comments about why he turned down Fifty Shades of Grey have resurfaced, reminding fans that his relatively slender appearance wasn't the result of skipping the gym. Speaking with Howard Stern on his SeriousXM series, Pattinson shared how difficult it's been for him to get "jacked." He shared:

I've tried. I've tried. It just doesn't, doesn't happen. I literally, I just can't. I don't understand how people do it.

That's got to sting a little. Especially considering we'd already heard about Pattinson's intense workout regimen for The Batman years before the movie arrived in theaters. Knowing he put in considerably more effort than I would've imagined anyone putting into a role, while also convincing the public that working out was beneath him, is a little sad. Weight training wasn't the only preparation involved. The former Twilight star also trained in Brazilian jiu-jitsu ahead of his Batman debut, which makes sense given how physical Reeves' version of the character turned out.

Pattinson knows exactly where that misconception about his dislike of gym time came from. Back in 2020, while promoting The Batman, he famously suggested that he wasn't particularly interested in the intense workout routines associated with superhero actors. Those comments attracted criticism from fans who expected Bruce Wayne to look considerably more muscular. Now, Pattinson admits he partly caused the misunderstanding, explaining that he was trying to sound cool during interviews.

I have to admit, that's a pretty funny explanation. The guy apparently spent hours training to become Batman, then accidentally convinced everyone he couldn't be bothered to lift weights. I've never been particularly bothered by Pattinson's physique in The Batman. His Bruce Wayne is younger, more isolated, and still figuring out how to operate as Gotham City's vigilante. There's something fitting about a Batman who looks exhausted after spending his nights getting punched in the face.

Besides, the fight sequences in Reeves' movie never gave me the impression that this version of the Dark Knight couldn't handle himself. That brutal hallway sequence alone did plenty to establish how dangerous he is. Pattinson has since set up a home gym to prepare for The Batman: Part II, so he's clearly continuing to take the role's physical demands seriously. He's also acknowledged that filming the sequel's fight scenes has become significantly harder now that he's 40.

I'm curious whether he'll look noticeably different when we return to Gotham. Still, I don't think he needs to resemble a professional bodybuilder to convince audiences he's Batman. What matters to me is whether Pattinson can continue delivering the tortured, obsessive Bruce Wayne that made the first movie so compelling. Based on what we've seen so far, I'm feeling pretty good about that.

Following several production delays and a temporary filming pause, The Batman: Part II is currently scheduled to arrive in theaters on February 18, 2028. In the meantime, you can revisit the original film with an HBO Max subscription.

Ryan graduated from Missouri State University with a BA in English/Creative Writing. An expert in all things horror, Ryan enjoys covering a wide variety of topics. He's also a lifelong comic book fan and an avid watcher of Game of Thrones and House of the Dragon.

#3438. Gemini's New AI Agent Is Surprisingly Useful (If You Use Google for Everything)

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

Google loves a rebrand. What started off as "Spark" is now "Task" in Gemini—not to be confused with Google Tasks, the to-do app. Google took its Spark AI agent, which used to live in a separate tab, and integrated it into the Gemini interface. Gemini Task is available globally, and it’s completely free to use for some. That said, some features are limited to the U.S. and, of course, subject to some pretty strict usage limits. While not exactly a replacement for ChatGPT Dots or Meta Muse, you can think of Gemini Task as a controlled version of an AI agent that can do quite a lot in the background.

To use Task, open Gemini and create a new chat. You’ll see a Task tab next to Chat. Switch to it, and start writing your prompt. (You’ll also see some suggested options here.) Type your task or action and press "Send." The feature works best if you’ve already enabled Personal Intelligence on your Google account, and have connected services like Gmail, Google Drive, and Photos as well. You can then tag “@Gmail” to use your Gmail account, or even a third-party connector. Task natively supports automation, so you can say something like, "run this task once every day," and the AI will add it to your Scheduled Tasks section.

Of course, I did the thing that every AI demo wants you to do: I asked Gemini to create a daily morning briefing for me, highlighting all important emails, calendar appointments, and tasks. And, in my experience, it works really well. It reminded me of this article's due date, that I have a couple of pitches in my inbox to review, that a credit card bill is due soon, and that there are some holidays around the corner.

Gemini is very good at retrieving information from emails and taking action. For example, I created an automation that collects all my coffee orders for the month and presents the data in Google Sheets. I then asked Task to create a subscription manager for me. Instead of paying for a third-party app, it took a few minutes to collate the services I pay for into one list. It even accounted for the currency differences (some subscriptions are in USD, some in INR) and gave me a tally in INR, along with things like average monthly cost, and more.

While Gemini can connect to the open web, it's quite a hostile place right now for an AI bot. Websites are blocking agents from accessing their pages, which hinders their effectiveness. I asked Gemini to create a task that monitors the price of the Sony WH-1000XM5 headphones daily. For this, it asked my permission to spin up a remote browser, and loaded up Amazon, only to be blocked instantly. It did succeed in opening Croma though (a national retailer in India), but it took almost a minute for it to figure out that the price had not dropped below what I asked for. Would it be quicker and less resource-intensive if I did this myself? Yes, but the fact that Gemini can do this every evening like clockwork is the real advantage—as long as the websites comply, that is.

If you're going to try Task in Gemini for free, there are some limitations you should know about. The free plan only lets you run tasks once per day, and you can’t be granular about the exact timing. (Paid Gemini plans have no such restrictions.) You can only run 10 tasks at the same time, while the limit is 50 tasks for AI Pro users. Compute-based usage limits will also apply, based on your plan. The free access is currently live in India, the U.S., Canada, Australia, Japan, and South Korea.

Some features, though, are only for U.S. users. Gemini’s feature that lets you call businesses on your behalf is restricted to the States, as is the ability to forward emails to [email protected] to automatically turn the contents of the email into a task (like adding a college schedule to your calendar). U.S. users can also connect their Google Wallet account to set up payments at supported stores.

Gemini Task is not a proactive agent, nor is it trying to be. You still have to check the work. You have to approve any important steps, and if a website blocks AI models, there’s not a lot Gemini can do about it. For someone like me, who’s all-in on the Google ecosystem, I do see value in Gemini Task. The deep and robust Gmail integration is worth it alone. If you’re on the free plan, set up a couple of background tasks related to Gmail, Google Drive, or background research that run every morning, and call it a day. And if you’re paying for AI Pro, you can get a lot more done.

#3437. Meet the Biggest Ralph Lauren Fan in France

Some people collect works of art; others collect clothes. When I heard about a Parisian who had amassed thousands of Ralph Lauren pieces, my curiosity got the better of me and I wanted to learn more. Séverin Naudet, a former digital adviser to François Fillon when he was France’s prime minister, lives on the fifth floor of a beautiful Haussmann-style building. The tall, dark-haired 50-year-old appears not to age. Since leaving his role with the government in 2012, he has started a digital marketing company and is now also exploring opportunities in luxury and wellness.

At his home, he displays part of his wardrobe, and I realize that the rumors about Naudet are true. He shows me dozens of pairs of sneakers, tuxedo jackets and velvet shoes, pants and shirts, more jackets, and then there are also mugs, books, and pillows. In the bedroom, the linens bear the American designer’s label, while tableware from Ralph Lauren’s Burleigh Collection, carefully wrapped up and placed in a Carrefour bag, is ready to be taken to his house in Brittany, where “more sailboat-inspired” pieces are stored. There are also sorbet-colored swimsuits piled on the plump armrests of a club chair. “About 20 years ago I donated all my other clothes to a charity. Since then, I’ve worn nothing but Ralph Lauren,” he explains, barefoot and dressed in jeans and a Polo shirt, next to a jacket from Denim & Supply, a Ralph Lauren brand that existed from 2011 to 2016 and is now coveted by collectors. Naudet’s Ralph Lauren pieces represent more than just a wardrobe; they embody a way of life that embraces every facet of the American brand founded in 1967—from preppy cool to sophisticated, Gatsby-style chic, and including many nautical pieces that connect to another of Naudet’s passions: sailing.

A selection from his collection of sneakers and dress shoes

But how does one fall in love with a brand to the point of making it part of every facet of their life? “As a teenager, I had body image issues. I had bowlegs, and I didn’t feel comfortable in my own skin,” he explains. Walking into a Double RL store changed everything: “I tried on a pair of Low Straight jeans and it was magical—they were perfectly cut, elegant, and stylish. I almost felt sexy. I had straight legs and a nice butt,” he says with a laugh.

His connection to the American brand speaks volumes about that magic formula that is the goal of retailers around the world: combining storytelling with emotional attachment. “Polo was the cure for a certain melancholy that was the result of a gloomy childhood. Ralph Lauren instilled in me a spirit of joy, where yellows, pinks, and sky blues, stripes and madras fabrics, evoke summer, the sea, and sailing,” explains the man who has amassed several thousand Ralph Lauren items.

As retail experiences increasingly take place online, there’s nothing Naudet loves more than going to a physical store. Walking into one is like stepping into “the family home I never had,” he explains. “A Ralph Lauren flagship store can feel like visiting a house in the Hamptons, a Parisian hotel for a perfect Christmas, or a New York apartment with a view of Central Park.” Ralph Lauren locations are must-visits on the entrepreneur’s itineraries. In Manhattan, he always visits the West Broadway store. He knows, of course, the ones in London and Los Angeles, as well as Manda in Brussels, where he goes in search of vintage pieces. His favorite store, however, remains the one in the mansion on Boulevard Saint-Germain in Paris, where every year he celebrates Christmas at its Ralph’s restaurant.

One might call him a “perfectionist,” but he prefers “meticulous.” He will go to lengths to repair clothes, even if it requires tracking down the original fabrics or finding an expert to repair braided leather straps. He’s also interested in the story behind the brand and how design choices and corporate strategies have made it what it is today. “Ralph Lauren is a marketing genius, and his advertising is never simply advertising. He works instead like a filmmaker; he tells a story. All you need is an image, even without a product. He created a family that we all dream of being a part of by, for example, choosing his wife, Ricky, as his muse. Their marriage has lasted 60 years!” the former adviser shares. And at a time when the world is wondering and worrying about the future, Ralph Lauren and his mythologies are calm and soothing: “In a daily life saturated with screens, images, and now artificial intelligence, Ralph Lauren continues to offer a world that is profoundly real, tactile, and inhabited.” The proof? In a fashion world sometimes tinged with gloom, Ralph Lauren posted a 15% increase in revenue for 2025, surpassing $8 billion for the first time. And in the first quarter of 2026, growth continued strong at 14%.

He quotes from memory Tocqueville’s description of New England in 1835 as “a region left to the dreams of the imagination, which one ought to abandon to the free trials of innovators.” Ralph Lauren is, for Naudet, the brand that stands above the fray, its founder a dreamer embodying “the finest qualities of the United States, from Tocqueville to the present day.” We ask if, as the ultimate embodiment of the American dream, Ralph Lauren, 86, would make a good president? Naudet, an expert on the inner workings of power, smiles: “He possesses at least three key qualities needed to be a good president: He understands the times, he has broad appeal, and he inspires people to dream. The rest is part of the mystery of democracy, and America is a great democracy.”

If the self-made New Yorker has ever wondered who his biggest fan in France is, Vanity Fair has found him. Before our conversation ends, Naudet tells me that recently, as he does every year around this time, he bought two pairs of Heritage Straight jeans, and also spotted a leather jacket lined with shearling that he wanted. It’s “admittedly a bit pricey,” but he’s certain it’ll be perfect once the temperatures drop.

#3435. Landman Star Michelle Randolph's Christmas Movie Is Prime Video's Biggest Streaming Hit

Prime Video has been serving up a feast for romantic comedy fans in 2026. Lili Reinhart's rom-com "The Love Hypothesis" just finished dominating the Prime Video charts, which came in the wake of Ester Expósito's romantic thriller "Drawn Together" becoming a Prime streaming hit. Now, the streamer has added a Christmas-themed romance just in time for the holidays, and this one stars "Landman" actor Michelle Randolph.

The film is called "Clashing Through the Snow" and before you immediately close this window just let me explain. Yes, the name sounds like the result of a "give me a cheesy Christmas rom-com title" ChatGPT prompt, but Randolph alone should pique your interest. The actor has quietly been delivering standout performances in Taylor Sheridan's "Landman" and his "Yellowstone" prequel "1923." The former sees her play Ainsley Norris, the ditzy but determined daughter of Billy Bob Thornton's oil man Tommy Norris. Based on her performances in those shows, Randolph surely has a bright future ahead. While "Clashing Through the Snow" might not be her major breakthrough, it's doing pretty darn well on Prime Video.

Until recently, Nicolas Cage and Christian Bale's sports movie "Madden" was topping the Prime Video charts. But it's now been knocked out of the top spot by this festive romance movie, in which publishing editor Hannah Hendricks (Randolph) is forced to take a road trip with her rival, Ryan Mitchell (Chris Briney). You can see where this is going.

According to streaming viewership tracker FlixPatrol, the film has now hit number two on the United States overall Prime Video chart (which combines TV and films) as of Thanksgiving day, and sits at number one on the movie chart. But Michelle Randolph's comedy is proving popular elsewhere, too. In fact, it's become a global hit. At the time of writing, the film is charting on 61 countries' top 10 movie rankings, which is a pretty good showing. Even more impressive, "Clashing Through the Snow" is number one on the movie charts in 47 of those countries, including the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom.

Meanwhile, the movie has managed to break into the overall chart in 30 countries, taking the top spot in five of them. That means "Clashing Through the Snow" is the most-watched piece of media on Prime Video in Austria, Poland, Portugal, South Africa, and Switzerland. It even managed to hit number one on the overall chart in the U.S. on November 25, 2026. That's a notable achievement, as often films will break into the top 10 movies without making it onto the overall charts. "Clashing Through the Snow" must be good, then...

"Clashing Through the Snow" is a comfortingly familiar rom-com outing that's perfect for the holidays. The film sees Chris Briney's Ryan Mitchell and Michelle Randolph's Hannah Hendricks stranded at an airport during a snowstorm, after which they share a rental car and set out on a cross-country trip to New York. The pair both need to close a deal in order to save their jobs — but wouldn't you know it, they fall in love instead. Along the way there's plenty of romantic Christmas movie moments as the couple stop in charming small towns and overcome mishaps together. Is "Clashing Through the Snow" pushing the boundaries of rom-coms? No. Is it charming? Sure is.

The film is directed by Carlson Young, who made her feature directorial debut with the 2021 fantasy horror "The Blazing World" before directing Sophie Turner in 2025's "Trust." She also oversaw a couple of Prime Video rom-coms before "Clashing Through the Snow," directing 2024's "Upgraded" and 2026's "The Last Sunrise."

Now, she's delivered a major hit with her Randolph-led Christmas rom-com, which has a 77% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. There aren't enough reviews to earn it a critic score yet, but while William Bibbiani of TheWrap found it to be "unapologetically clichéd" he also found the dialogue to be memorable and saw the film as "an efficient delivery mechanism for semi-believable rom and semi-funny com."

If that sounds appealing, "Clashing Through the Snow" is streaming on Prime Video right now.

It was obvious on-screen how much the other wrestlers loved him, and that’s become especially clear in the tributes that have gone out since his passing. Hundreds of both in-ring performers and behind the scenes creatives in the industry have posted really touching tributes to Reed, who worked for a variety of companies before emerging as a breakout star in WWE.

Many time world champion Rhea Ripley, like Reed, grew up in Adelaide, South Australia. You always looked out for me and gave me a shoulder to cry on when I needed it most. Just a genuine teddy bear with an infectious chuckle. You were my wrestling big brother, and it’s really not going to be the same without you around. This breaks my fucking heart.

Many of his friends and colleagues shared similar sentiments about his infectious laugh, his big heart and how much fun he was to be around. Former WWE star Sheamus, who worked with Reed for years and filmed an episode of his Celtic Warrior Workout YouTube show with the big man shared an absolutely adorable video of Reed teaching him how to do the Nutbush Dance, which derives from a Tina Turner song that was a huge hit and turned into a wedding tradition in Australia. I’m sure additional love will come pouring in today as more wrestlers grapple with their feelings and figure out how to pay respect to Reed and talk about how he impacted their lives.

Here’s a post from WWE star Grayson Waller who, alongside Reed and Ripley, also grew up in Australia…

A post shared by Grayson Waller (@graysonwallerwwe)

All proceeds will go directly to his family.

Survivor Series, one of WWE’s biggest shows of the year, takes place tonight. Expect there to be an on-screen acknowledgement and for many to show their respects in their own way during the event.

#3432. Steve Martin And John Candy's Classic Thanksgiving Movie Is A Paramount+ Streaming Hit

John Hughes made some of the most beloved movies of all time in his eight directorial efforts, to the point where it's nearly impossible to rank the films he wrote and directed. Still, there are few movies that reach the specific balance of comedy with such an emotional punch as Hughes does in 1987's "Planes, Trains and Automobiles." This is a goofball movie that borders on the surreal, with some of the most bizarre imagery in a comedy movie, while also delivering some of the most heartbreaking and heartwarming moments that came out of the 1980s.

The film stars Steve Martin as Neal Page, an uptight marketing executive forced to be paired with Del Griffith (John Candy), a goofball salesman with a heart of gold, when their journey from New York City to Chicago is disrupted. What was meant to be just a short cab and plane ride home just in time for Thanksgiving ends up being a three-day odyssey full of shenanigans, attempted murder, and much more.

It's no wonder, then, that "Planes, Trains and Automobiles" is the No. 1 movie streaming on Paramount+ on Thanksgiving Day 2026. After all, there are plenty of movies about Christmas, to the point where it's easy to overlook Thanksgiving, and with good reason. For one, it's not really a holiday outside the U.S. and Canada (and even then, celebrated on different days), and the imagery is not dissimilar to Christmas anyway. Still, the best Thanksgiving movies deliver a very specific tone that's less about holiday magic and more about celebrating what we have despite the horrors of daily life. From the opening minutes of "Planes, Trains and Automobiles," it's clear this movie could not be set at any other time of year except during the chaos and anxiety of Thanksgiving.

The travel chaos that is quite unique to Thanksgiving is the crux of "Planes, Trains and Automobiles." The arrival of snowstorms that plague the East Coast of the continental United States, the huge flux of travelers, and the general anxiety and irritability of travelers around the country add to, well, a very stressful time of year. It's why Steve Martin's uptight businessman Neal is so relatable. The film simply nails the feeling of needing to interact with others and ask for their help while being utterly frustrated with having to deal with anyone at such a bad time. It's also why John Candy's performance is such a tightrope, because his character has to be annoying in addition to being charming. Del's not really someone you'd want as a travel companion, yet he is absolutely the best person you want as a friend.

That tricky balance is what makes the movie so memorable, and why John Candy's best line remains the best Thanksgiving movie quote ever. Neal and Del are forced to not only set aside their differences, but actually recognize the humanity in each other while acknowledging that they themselves are flawed. This is a highly empathetic film that's all about how we should find love and camaraderie even in unlikely companions. That is why the film so perfectly captures the spirit of Thanksgiving, because it's not about estranged family members, but rather complete strangers who must come to learn they need one another and that they should be grateful for what they bring into each other's lives. Togetherness is not just for family members, or even people you like, but also for strangers you come to appreciate despite the ways they annoy you.

#3431. What’s Real and What’s Not in Netflix’s ‘The Altruists’

Even if you followed the news closely in the early 2020s, the sheer audacity of the fraud committed by Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison—as dramatized in Netflix’s new limited series The Altruists, starring Anthony Boyle and Julia Garner—will shock you anew. The show, which follows the stunning multibillion-dollar collapse of the crypto exchange FTX, starts off a bit slow, but accelerates episode by episode until its high-octane finale.

I found the series to be especially striking in the context of last week’s historic Anthropic IPO, which ironically fell on the same day as the premiere. Some of that company’s founders and employees share similar intellectual roots to The Altruist’s protagonists; watching its fictionalized Caroline Ellison, in particular, justify astoundingly reckless behavior with her system of mathematical-optimization-of-everything felt uncannily like watching frontier labs proceed with a seemingly inexplicable appetite for risk.

The Altruists also depicts a surprisingly tender romance between two socially inept, possibly sociopathic adrenaline junkies. (According to people involved with the project, the working title for the project was Untitled Love Story.) But as with any fictionalized account, the series takes some liberties with the characters and plot. If you’re anything like me, you want to know what exactly is fact, and what is fiction.

I spoke with Kevin T. Dugan and Jen Wieczner, two of the reporters who exposed the FTX fiasco in real time, and who consulted on the series. “When Jen and I started working with Graham Moore, the showrunner, he made it really clear that he wanted this to be very character driven. Nobody wants an eight-hour lecture on how the blockchain works,” Dugan tells me.

“The bones of the show are rooted in reality,” says Wieczner. Understanding these flawed and complicated characters helps explain “how one decision leads to another decision and a small oopsies turns into a multibillion-dollar fraud and this huge criminal conspiracy.”

Even if there’s a little fiction in the nitty-gritty, Dugan says that there is one overarching truth he hopes the series will reveal: “That even the prettiest ideas still have to turn into reality through imperfect people, and those imperfect people will end up making mistakes that they cannot foresee.” Here’s what the show ripped from real life—and where it took some creative license.

CAROLINE ELLISON WROTE SEXY HARRY POTTER FAN FICTION

Not quite. In the first episode, Caroline is humiliated when her raunchy writing titled “A Ride on Draco’s Nimbus” surfaces online. And while it’s true that Ellison was a huge Harry Potter fan, there is no evidence she wrote erotic fan fiction herself. Instead, this plot point is likely gesturing toward Ellison’s 2010s-era Tumblr, which was called WorldOptimisation—a reference to a 660,000-word-long work of Harry Potter fan fiction by Silicon Valley philosopher Eliezer Yudkowsky. Yudkowsky’s work popularized the kind of mathematically strategic thinking Ellison applies to love and business alike.

In episode six, Sam Trabucco (played by Alex Lawther) makes the mistake of introducing Sam and Caroline to a hack that proves irresistible: FTX can mint its own coin, FTT, and then allow its crypto trading firm, Alameda, to take out large loans using off-market FTT as collateral. Alameda can then use those loans to place highly leveraged, incredibly risky bets on FTX—which in turn increases the value of FTT. (TL;DR: it’s a perfect loop.) Appalling as it sounds, in real life, this practice is more or less exactly what brought SBF’s empire tumbling down.

“One of the things that led to the FTX bank run,” explains Wieczner, “was the leaked balance sheet that showed that much of FTX and Alameda’s holdings were in FTT, which was FTX’s own coin. So that if that went to zero, it was like a house of cards and things just would’ve fallen apart. And that’s why you see at the end why is everything is falling…you have that kind of death spiral effect.”

As for Trabucco, he and his yacht (yes, it was really named Soak My Deck) didn’t get off unscathed. Trabucco didn’t face criminal charges, but was forced to liquidate many of his assets in order to help return about $80 million to defrauded investors.

True. Caroline chronicled some of her adventures in nonmonogamy on her since-deleted Tumblr. She once wrote, “The only acceptable style of poly is best characterized as something like ‘imperial Chinese harem.’”

Real! In the final episode of the series, SBF presents a last-ditch plan: He wants to repurpose his early stake in Anthropic to cover the losses of billions of dollars in customer funds. Indeed, FTX did use $500 million in customer funds to purchase a 13.5% stake in Anthropic’s Series B in late 2021. Of course, Sam’s plan did not pass muster. Yet if it had, he’d have been in the clear. After the company’s IPO last week, Alameda’s stake would be worth about $35 billion, according to The New York Times—enough to solve the disgraced firm’s liquidity issues several times over. Oh well.

CAROLINE ELLISON CONFESSED IN FRONT OF HER STAFF

True. In the penultimate episode, a visibly cracking Caroline delivers a halting confession amidst fits of nervous giggles to a shocked staff, telling them that she knew about FTX’s shortfall of user funds that would add up to more than $8 billion. I was sure this scene had been invented, but lo and behold: Ellison did admit that she had been aware of the inappropriate transfers between the two firms at a December 2022 all-staff meeting. You can even listen to the leaked recording online.

CAROLINE ELLISON BEARS MORE RESPONSIBILITY THAN SBF

I felt the show tilted towards placing the blame on Ellison, who is portrayed as incorrigibly risk-addicted and the muse behind SBF’s worst decisions. Constance Wang, who is played in the series by Madison Hu, is just one of the former FTX employees who found the show misrepresentative. In a lengthy X post, she rebutted its narrative: Ellison, said Hu, “wasn’t nearly that reckless, and she was never the one pushing to go all in. The idea that she was the mastermind behind everything made us laugh.”

#3430. Everything You Should Know About Black Friday 2026 Sales Before Friday

As is often the case with major sales these days, retailers are increasingly blurring the lines between early deals and the official start of a sale. Black Friday sales have essentially become a month-long event, with early deals appearing in the first week of the month. If you haven't been paying attention, major retailers have already announced their plans and started churning out deals. But you're still in time to make this Black Friday sale a great one. Here's everything you need to know about the big sale.

Black Friday is always the day after Thanksgiving. This year, Black Friday starts at midnight on Nov. 27. Cyber Monday is the Monday following Black Friday, which starts at midnight on Nov. 30.

The major retailers running sales are the usual ones: Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, Home Depot, and many others. Currently, Walmart has publicized its plans already and has early deals available. Best Buy is offering one of the largest Black Friday and Cyber Week sales, with multiple events and early deals. Target has a three-day event. Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Cyber Monday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026.

Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was better for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, do your research, or refer to guides like our Black Friday and Cyber Monday coverage that have done all the vetting for you.

Unlike Spring or Summer sales, Black Friday doesn't focus on specific categories, which means everything is fair game for discounts. In previous years, we've seen tech, tools, fitness equipment, outdoor supplies and furniture, bedding, video games, kitchen appliances, and more. This is one of the best times to make a list of what you need. You're likely to find what you're looking for discounted, and probably at its lowest price it has ever been. If you'd like to avoid having to do all that work, we always vet all of our deals for you. Just follow our Black Friday coverage.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

Yes. Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Home Depot will all have in-store deals, some of which you might not find online, so if you're able to take a trip to your local retailer, keep your eyes open for different deals.

Prime Day and Black Friday are the two best times of the year to get the best deals on most purchases. Of course, depending on what you're shopping for, you might find other opportunities throughout the year, but in general, Prime Day and Black Friday have the best sales.

#3429. Who Died on 'The Hunting Wives' So Far? Breaking Down Every Shocking Murder

No one is safe in Maple Brook — and two seasons in The Hunting Wives hasn’t held back when it comes to killing off main characters.

Based on May Cobb‘s book of the same name, The Hunting Wives introduced Sophie (Brittany Snow), who found herself drawn to prominent socialite Margo (Malin Åkerman) after moving from Boston to an East Texas town. While some became invested in the murder at the center of the series, the show’s first season also provided plenty of entertainment with guns, drinking and steamy onscreen hookups.

Season 1 started off strong with a handful of deaths to set up the show. When the show returned for season 2, however, The Hunting Wives leaned in even more when it came to onscreen deaths.

Keep scrolling for a full guide to each Hunting Wives character who died — and how:

The murder that started it all: teenager Abby (Madison Wolfe) who was killed by Margo before the premiere.

Abby’s mother (Chrissy Metz) met her demise when Jill (Katie Lowes) shot her during a confrontation over Abby’s murder.

After killing Starr, Jill was shot by Callie (Jaime Ray Newman) and Abby’s murder was pinned on her.

Pastor Pete died by suicide after it was discovered he kidnapped two women.

Margo’s brother (Michael Aaron Milligan) was killed when Sophie ran him over with her car and dumped his body in a lake.

Season 2 began with Elly’s body being discovered after she was murdered.

John (Cam Gigandet) was eventually outed as Elly’s murderer — and subsequently killed by Zelda (Dale Dickey).

I've pretty much told everybody I know that Attack on Titan is the greatest anime…OF ALL TIME! This is usually to the annoyance of my other anime friends, who will counter me with shows like One Piece or Full Metal Alchemist: Brotherhood. Hell, I've even professed my love for AoT on this very website.

However, I suppose it's time to eat crow, since I can no longer call Attack on Titan the greatest anime I've ever seen, as I've found a new one that has shown me the light, and that's Frieren: Beyond Journey's End.

So, here's why a show about an over 1000-year-old elf learning about humanity (I'm serious) is now my favorite anime of all time.

One thing I love about Attack on Titan is all of the emotions I felt while watching it. I felt fear, sorrow, anger, and a wide range of what I'll call “uncomfortable” emotions. Now, do you notice how none of those aforementioned feelings were positive? Well, here's the thing when it comes to me: I like ANY form of entertainment that makes me feel something - even if it's “bad” - since most of the entertainment I watch makes me feel nothing.

Sad, but true. That said, when I watch Frieren: Beyond Journey's End, I feel a multitude of things as well, but mostly comfort, and even hope. As alluded to earlier, the story concerns an elf mage named Frieren who has already completed her big adventure.

The first episode actually begins at what would typically be the end of the story (hence the subheader), as the three adventurers Frieren fought alongside - A “corrupt” priest, a warrior, and a hero - have already defeated the big bad and are now going their separate ways. Years pass, and Frieren, who hasn't noticeably aged since she's an elf, meets back up with her former friends, who are all old. One of them even dies.

The story goes on from there, and it's melancholic at times (and exciting toward the later episodes), but also beautiful, and so many other adjectives that really hit me in the heart. It's so good!

Now, here's the thing. Even though I love AoT, I don't think I would recommend Frieren to anybody who also likes AoT, and that's because they're completely different shows. Yes, I love action-oriented stories like The Vermilion Mask, which is a new gem that I recently discovered. But, I also love deep, introspective narratives like This Monster Wants to Eat Me, which is about deep-rooted depression.

Well, what makes Frieren soar is the characters. Frieren constantly has flashbacks of those she journeyed with in the past, but because of her broad perception of time, she didn't realize just how much her previous adventure meant to her until years later when her old friends have mostly passed away. In fact, it's not until Frieren is on her second adventure with a mage apprentice named Fern, and a warrior named Stark, that she actually understands what those previous relationships actually meant to her.

I also love how Frieren still needs to be woken up by her apprentice and is an overall mess when it comes to cleaning up after herself. Her teenage apprentice is almost like a mom to her.

The characters also make me think about my own mortality, but in a good way. A lot of the story is about the memories we make with those in the moment, and how we should enjoy life every second we can, because those moments are what make life worth living. It's honestly such a beautiful story with wonderful characters, and I can't recommend it enough - just know that it's much slower than AoT. You can watch the first season with a Netflix subscription, but you will need a Crunchyroll subscription if you want to watch Season 2.

Rich is a Jersey boy, through and through. He graduated from Rutgers University (Go, R.U.!), and thinks the Garden State is the best state in the country. That said, he’ll take Chicago Deep Dish pizza over a New York slice any day of the week. Don’t hate. When he’s not watching his two kids, he’s usually working on a novel, watching vintage movies, or reading some obscure book.

#3427. 30 Years Later, Jingle All The Way's Funniest Line Is Still The Best Christmas Movie Quote

There are classic Christmas movies like "It's a Wonderful Life" and "National Lampoon's Christmas Vacation," and then there are the Christmas movies that we just watch every year because they're on repeatedly, forcing their way into the holiday zeitgeist, regardless of quality. "Jingle All the Way" is one of those movies.

Remembered as a comedy that glorifies the hollow commercialism of the holiday season, "Jingle All the Way" was far from a critical darling. But Roger Ebert at least had some praise for it back in 1996, writing:

"I liked a lot of the movie, which is genial and has a lot of energy, but I was sort of depressed by its relentlessly materialistic view of Christmas, and by the choice to go with action and (mild) violence over dialogue and plot. Audiences will like it, I am sure, but I have to raise my hand in reluctant dissent and ask, please, sir, may we have some more goodwill among men? Even TurboMen?"

Honestly, we should probably be throwing more praise at "Jingle All the Way." While it might depict the unfortunate side of holiday shopping greed and consumerism, it's hard to deny how much fun it is to watch Arnold Schwarzenegger scramble to find a Turbo Man action figure, while Sinbad taunts and thwarts him at every turn. It's a cinematic masterpiece compared to "Jingle All the Way 2" with Larry the Cable Guy, proving it's a Christmas movie that didn't need a sequel.

But one of the best parts of "Jingle All the Way" comes from the interaction that Schwarzenegger's Howard Langston has with his deceptively thoughtful, sleazy neighbor Ted (the late, great star of "Saturday Night Live" and "The Simpsons," the one and only Phil Hartman). That's where we get one of the best Christmas movie quotes of all time.

Here are some more memorable quotes from "Jingle All the Way," though they might not be as versatile as our favorite:

"I'm not a pervert! I just was looking for a Turbo Man doll!" – Howard Langston

"How about these stupid letters from kids to Santa at the North Pole: 'Dear Santa, can you send me a bike and a slinky?' No! Your father's been laid off!" – Myron Larabee

"I'm gonna deck your halls, bub." — Huge Santa

"They sit there and use subliminal messages to suck your children's minds out! And I know what I'm talking about because I went to junior college for a semester and I studied psychology so I'm right in there, I know what's going on. And then they sit there and they make your children feel like garbage and you, the father, who's working 24/7 delivering mail so you can make an alimony payment to a woman that slept with everybody at the post office, but me! And then when you get the toy, it breaks and you can't fix it because it's little cheap plastic!" – Myron Larabee

"That really was a bomb? This is a sick world we live in! Sick people!" – Myron Larabee

"You know what? Nobody likes you, Booster." – Myron Larabee

"It's Turbo Time!" – Howard Langston as Turbo Man

"Ta-ta, Turtle Man!" – Myron Larabee as Dementor
