#3409. It's 2026, And I Just Watched Daniel Craig's James Bond Movies For The First Time – These Are My Honest Thoughts

We are officially in a new era for 007, with Robert Pattinson recently being announced as the new James Bond, in the wake of Amazon buying the rights to the 64 year-old movie franchise. Before we see what director Denis Villeneuve is cooking, and whether he allows Pattinson to be a little weirdo, this is the time to look back at the franchise so far — what worked and what didn't, and the legacy previous Bond actors have left behind.

As a confession, I have never experienced the James Bond franchise. My only familiarity with it is the N64 game "GoldenEye 007," which I played religiously with friends growing up. I have never watched a single one of these movies before, though I very much enjoy a good spy thriller like the "Mission: Impossible" movies, or the "Fast & Furious" movies when they forget about the drag racing.

So when the editors at /Film asked if I wanted to binge Daniel Craig's James Bond movies and write my honest thoughts about them, I figured I might as well clear a cinematic blindspot on my list. After over 20 movies in the franchise, what did the Craig movies do to keep the Bond franchise fresh, while also competing in the era of mega-budget globe-trotting spy thrillers and action adventure films?

Well, in short, these movies rule. Big shocker, eh? Well, I actually was skeptical at first. My only perception of Bond as a franchise was that of a suave English womanizer who occasionally dealt with ridiculously cartoonish villains in over-the-top sci-fi plots (not that dissimilar to "Fast & Furious," actually). What I discovered was that, sure, but also a lot more.

I must confess that I was skeptical of the Daniel Craig Bond movies at first. Though fun and thrilling, the gadgets of this modern James Bond didn't feel particularly unique, and though cool, his mono-lettered allies like M and Q weren't as purely entertaining to watch as, say, Benji and Luther from "Mission: Impossible," or Roman and Tej from "Fast & Furious." But what does make these movies stand out is their look. In many ways, 007 movies are the prestige TV of spy thrillers. If "Bourne" made them gritty and realistic, and "Mission: Impossible" turned them into sheer spectacle, Bond gave them back a shine and an esteem that other movies don't have. Tapping legends such as Roger Deakins and Hoyte van Hoytema as cinematographers, these movies simply look gorgeous. They are grand and full of spectacle, but without the shine and artifice of a 21st century action-adventure. It's a look that matches the prestige and expense of, well, Bond's car and watch, for instance.

The movies also all have rather unique and different approaches to the spy thriller. Though the Bond formula is rather well established, each movies still manages to feel like a completely unique aspect of Bond's career. That the climax of "Casino Royale" is not some big shoot-out but a simple high-stakes poker game is a testament to the versatility of the franchise. Indeed, though these movies feel big in their scale and thrilling in their stakes, they also feel rather intimate in the way they end up focusing on Bond's efforts to thwart his villain's plots.

Then there is James Bond himself, the undisputed star and focus of these movies, and a completely unique element in the genre at large. No matter how many franchises try to replicate the success of 007, of the archetypical gentleman spy, none can quite nail what makes him work.

Even before "No Time to Die" does what no other Bond movie has done before and delivered a definitive (and quite finite) ending to the main character, Daniel Craig's tenure had already done something unique and special within the spy thriller genre. These movies are the prestige TV of spy thrillers in aesthetics, but also by being serialized. The Craig films tell one complete story of a singular man, following Bond from a rookie 00 agent to a grizzled veteran who is too old for this s**t. It allows the franchise to make Bond more than an archetype, but a full character with an arc, with flaws, with a temper, and with a history. To watch these movies is to fully get Bond (at least this specific version of him): the story of a man that grieves from one movie to the other, and whose years in the service take a toll.

A big reason why this works is Daniel Craig himself, who infuses his portrayal not only with a sense of humor, but with an inner darkness that challenges the idea of Bond as the suave womanizing spy with little to no flaws. Instead, this Bond is a monster, an angry killing machine that hides behind that suave persona, his anger increasing with every loss. The movies, then, become a fascinating arc of him learning to be more human again. By the end, I had become a proper Bond fan.

Disney’s newest animated movie, Hexed, has officially hit theaters, and despite some concerning first reviews, the movie is getting people talking. There’s been lots of chatter around all the Disney-themed Easter eggs hidden in the film, and whether or not Billie is the newest Disney Princess. However, the biggest topic of conversation seems to be around Billie’s eccentric animal sidekick, Beef Roger Crummchuk, and his resemblance to another beloved Disney feline, the Cheshire Cat. However, I couldn’t help but notice the similarities between him and Back to the Future’s Doc Brown.

Now, don’t get me wrong, from an aesthetic perspective, Beef definitely looks like The Cheshire Cat. Both eccentric felines have bushy tails and yellow eyes. Plus, Beef even wears a pink coat that resembles the stripes of the beloved Alice in Wonderland cat. And they both can do weird things with their bodies, like stretching extremely long in Beef’s case. However, that’s really where the similarities end; at least, for me.

Personality and character arc-wise, Beef is a lot more like my favorite eccentric scientist, Doc. Beef might not be a “mad scientist” in the same way that Doc is, but he definitely gives off the same vibe. Beef has potions galore in his trailer-turned-van and always seems to know the perfect solution to get Billie out of a pickle. Sounds a lot like Doc, right? I mean, the entire premise of one of the greatest time travel movies is that past Doc has to help Marty McFly get back to the future.

Beef’s home also feels reminiscent of Doc’s garage turned science lab. Both places are filled with gadgets and potions, and both characters have unusual collections. For Doc, it’s clocks, of course, but for Beef, the collection manifests in the form of porcelain dolls.

Hexed First Reactions Keep Using The Same Adjective, And I’ve Been Waiting For A Disney Movie Like This

Doc and Beef are also both outcasts in their respective worlds, leaving them to lead loner lifestyles aside from their friendships with mischievous teenagers Marty McFly and Billie Doe. And they both have to learn to trust their teenage friends to save the day.

While it’s unclear how much the animators meant for Beef to resemble the Cheshire Cat and even Doc, there’s no denying that the writers were definitely thinking about Doc Brown since Beef quotes the time-travel-obsessed scientist verbatim.

After a tense stand-off between Billie and her grandmother, the ragtag gang finds themselves tasked with finding an all-knowing owl to help them learn a special spell. Safe in Beef’s trailer, which is floating in the water, Billie laments that there’s no road for them to follow to get to the owl. Beef throws on his glasses and says:

And then the trailer’s wheels turn upward, looking oddly similar to the way the DeLorean converts from a car into a flying time machine at the end of Back to the Future.

It could be purely coincidental that Beef utters one of Doc’s most iconic lines, but I don’t think so. I think the writers knew that Beef was going to give off major Doc Brown vibes, and found a clever way to honor more directly. Thankfully, I’m always on the hunt for easter eggs, and it paid off majorly this time.

The only thing that could make the Beef and Doc similarities even better is if Christopher Lloyd had voiced the loner feline. However, that’s not to say I didn’t love Walton Goggins’ performance, because I totally did!

I can’t wait for Hexed to be available with a Disney+ subscription so I can watch it and then immediately watch Back to the Future so I can judge just how similar Beef and Doc are.

A novel solution for connecting to the internet on the go, the TP-Link Roam 7 travel router is now down to $83.49 from $119.99 for Black Friday, marking its lowest price to date. This isn't a full-size home router but, as the name suggests, a compact travel companion that measures roughly the size of a paperback book, with foldable antennas that let it slip easily into a bag.

More about convenience than chasing top speeds, you can use the Roam 7 as a standard router, connect it to public wifi to create a private network, or share your phone's internet through USB tethering. It also supports Ethernet input and USB modems, along with range extender and wireless client modes. That flexibility is particularly useful when you’re juggling a laptop, phone, and maybe a tablet and would prefer not to sign each one into a shaky network separately. Setup is straightforward through the TP-Link Tether app: scan a QR code, choose your connection type, and you’re online in a few minutes.

Once it’s running, the hardware covers the basics, with a 2.5 Gbps port for a wired connection like a hotel’s Ethernet jack, a 1 Gbps port for a wired device, and a USB 3.0 port for a storage drive or phone tethering. And since it draws power over USB-C (5V/3A), a basic power bank can keep it going through a long layover or a camping trip. As handy as it is on the road, though, it’s not meant to replace a full-size home router—even with its 5 GHz band and Wi-Fi 7 support—which will generally offer better coverage and more consistent speeds. Real-world performance also depends heavily on your connection and setup. USB tethering, for example, can feel slower than using your phone directly. It also leaves out features like automatic band steering, so you may end up managing networks yourself. Still, if you travel often or need a portable network hub for multiple devices, you’ll find it holds up pretty well.

#3406. GTA 6's Long Development Cycle Even Made Rockstar Question If It Would Ever Launch

Rockstar's Rob Nelson admitted that some within studio felt like GTA 6's launch day would never come

While Grand Theft Auto 6 is real, out now, and breaking all sorts of records with how well it's selling, it felt like the game might never be released at some points during its lengthy 13-year development. In a recent interview, Rockstar co-studio head Rob Nelson revealed that even those within Rockstar sometimes felt that way about GTA 6.

Nelson, who was one of the lead developers on GTA 6, shared this sentiment in an interview with GamesRadar ahead of the game's release, saying that "it feels surreal" for the highly anticipated game to finally be out. He was also blunt that some people at Rockstar weren't sure the Nov. 19 launch of GTA 6 would ever happen because of how long it took to develop.

"I think a lot of us felt like the day would never come," he explained. "A lot of us, certainly on the senior team, have shipped a fair few games. But it's been a while since we've done one of these and this one took a good chunk of time to sort of figure it out.I think it's surreal, it's a relief – we're very nervous, when you get really close to something maybe your perspective is a little bit compromised. But yeah, we're in a little bit of disbelief and we probably will be until release, and then hopefully it'll become real once people are talking about it and playing it."

A 13-year development cycle is certainly unusual in the video game industry, but GTA 6 was anything but your usual AAA game. It was a sequel to one of the best-selling games of all time and had a scope far greater than most open-world games. The game's development was also elongated, as Rockstar had to focus on finishing Red Dead Redemption 2 before 2018 and then made the tough decision to delay GTA 6 a couple of times after it was officially revealed in 2022.

The wait and long development cycle seem worth it in the end, as GTA 6 has been a massive success. Still, Nelson's comments show that even those at Rockstar felt the pressure and stress that comes with working on such a highly anticipated game for so long.

#3405. 5 Best New Movies And Shows To Stream This Weekend On Netflix, Prime Video, HBO Max, And More (Nov. 27-29)

Thanksgiving 2026 is in the rearview mirror, and whether you woke up after the holiday with a turkey hangover, a regular hangover, or a horrifying combination of the two, you probably just want to lay around and stare at screens for a while. (Because it's a holiday weekend, I won't even judge you for staring at a little screen while your big screen runs at the same time. You do you.) If you can't even bear the idea of putting on pants long enough to drag yourself out to a movie theater to see a new release like "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" (which is pretty good) or "Focker-in-Law" (which is apparently surprisingly funny), don't worry. I've got you covered, because there's plenty to watch from the comfort of your own couch, bed, or whatever lounge spot you prefer.

From a sci-fi series that uses a beloved movie as its basis to the second season of one of the steamiest and campiest shows on TV right now to a buzzy new comedy from a small-screen powerhouse, here are five movies and TV shows new to streaming on Netflix, Amazon Prime, Peacock, and more for you to enjoy on the weekend of Friday, November 27 to Sunday, November 29. Happy bed-rotting!

If you're a longtime fan of Ridley Scott's masterpiece "Blade Runner," you loved the underrated box office bomb "Blade Runner 2049," or both, congratulations: there's a brand new Blade Runner property out in the world, and it's actually great. In his review for /Film, Bill Bria called the new Amazon Prime Video series "Blade Runner 2099" "the best sci-fi show in years," also saying that "showrunner Silka Luisa has put together something that's as unique and bold as it is in conversation with its franchise's past, making it a proud new addition to the saga." If that's not a strong enough endorsement for Blade Runner die-hards, I don't know what is!

The basics are as follows: Oscar winner and international treasure Michelle Yeoh plays a Replicant Blade Runner named Olwen, who's approaching the end of her existence. To try and find a group of evil Replicants, Olwen teams up with a human pretending to be a Replicant, Cora ("Euphoria" standout Hunter Schafer, given a much better role that finally does her talent some justice), and their adventures have a great film noir sensibility while still remaining fun, fresh, and compulsively watchable. Yeoh and Schafer are absolutely fantastic together and are joined by phenomenal supporting players like Daniel Rigby (who's appearing in the forthcoming Harry Potter series on HBO), Matthew Needham (who portrays the slimy Larys Strong on "House of the Dragon"), and Lewis Gribben — so even if you're not a huge Blade Runner person, you should give this show a shot; all eight episodes dropped on Amazon Prime Video on November 25.

I personally loved the first season of Netflix's steamy, silly, and impeccably acted drama "The Hunting Wives," which dropped on the platform in the summer of 2025, so I'm jazzed that the show is returning for a second season and promises to be sillier and steamier than ever. Malin Åkerman and Brittany Snow are back in Rebecca Cutter's adaptation of May Cobb's novel as sapphic star-crossed lovers Margo Banks and Sophie O'Neil, who find themselves drawn to each other in the small, wealthy Texas enclave of Maple Brook after Sophie moves there with her husband and young son. During Season 1 of "The Hunting Wives," Sophie and Margo hook up, murder people, hook up some more, and murder some more people, and they both do plenty of that in Season 2 as well — but it doesn't feel like a simple retread of that inaugural outing.

New additions to the cast of "The Hunting Wives" like Dale Dickey ("Widow's Bay"), Cam Gigandet ("Twilight"), Alex Fitzalan ("The Wilds"), and John Stamos help keep things fresh and fun, and Snow and Åkerman are as delightful as ever as two women who will stop at nothing to be together. "The Hunting Wives" dropped all of its eight episodes in Season 2 on November 26 in the early morning, so queue it up after dinner. Just ... maybe don't watch this one with your parents. Everyone is super naked all the time.

If you were going to sit inside and rewatch all of "Parks and Recreation" this holiday weekend, I have amazing news for you: Amy Poehler and Michael Schur have a brand new show you can try instead. Adapted from the 2023 novel "Excavations" by Kate Myers, "Dig," which premiered on Peacock on November 23, stars Poehler as Elise, an archaeologist working with a team in Greece who all make a discovery that unexpectedly connects this group of history nerds to an international conspiracy. Hugh Laurie joins Poehler as her boss Neville, a professor who just wants everyone to take archaeology as seriously as he does, and the rest of the team is rounded out by Geraldine Viswanathan's Dylan, Antonia Thomas' Clare, and Fina Strazza's Patty.

Schur, as always, also stocks his supporting cast with hilarious people like Dropout's Brennan Lee Mulligan and "What We Do in the Shadows" standout Kayvan Novak as well as his regular collaborators like Jason Mantzoukas, who has appeared in pretty much all of Schur's shows. "Dig" is charming, sweet, funny, and will definitely scratch that "Parks and Recreation" itch ... and the first season is available in its entirety on Peacock.

If you missed the family film "The Magic Faraway Tree" when it released in theaters at August, fret not; it's available on HBO Max as of November 27. Adapted by screenwriter Simon Barnaby from Enid Blyton's beloved children's series "The Faraway Tree," this film stars Andrew Garfield and Claire Foy as Tiny and Polly Thompson, who live in a bustling city with their three young children Beth (Delilah Bennett-Cardy), Joe (Phoenix Laroche), and Fran (Billie Gadsdon), all of whom freak out if they can't look at tablets or phones. When Polly and Tim decide that the family has endured enough technology — inspired partly by Polly's job as an inventor, where she works on a smart fridge filled with secret cameras — they move their furious children to a remote country home.

That's when the adventure really begins. Fran, who normally can't speak, finds herself visited by a fairy and can suddenly talk; before long, Fran starts wandering off on the Thompson's remote property and finds the titular magic faraway tree that transports her to an otherworldly realm. For a modern, Narnia-inspired story and inspired performances from Garfield, Foy, "Baby Reindeer" star Jessica Gunning, and "Absolutely Fabulous" legend Jennifer Saunders, check out "The Magic Faraway Tree" on HBO Max, and sit the whole family down for a treat.

If you want to, uh, relax with a true crime documentary over the holiday weekend, Netflix has just the debut for you: a three-part series titled "The Trial of Karen Read." In 2022, Boston police officer John O'Keefe was killed after attending a party at a friend's house. His girlfriend Karen Read, who claims she dropped him off at said party and returned in the morning to find O'Keefe dead, was ultimately arrested for his murder. Authorities believed that Read was under the influence and hit O'Keefe with her car at some point during their evening, but when she was taken to trial, a mistrial was declared in 2024. She received a new trial in 2025 and received only a single year of probation (for driving under the influence) after being found not guilty.

Naturally, rumors have swirled about Read for years now, so Netflix's three-part docuseries attempts to dig into the couple's relationship and discover the truth. If you're a frequent viewer of this streamer's true crime fare, you know that answers are never really provided, but if you've been following the Read case for this entire time, you might as well check it out; it premiered on the service on November 23.

#3403. Kerry Kennedy on Her Brother RFK Jr.: “We Were Very Close, but He Changed”

Kerry Kennedy is not in Milan on political business, but it’s hard to rein in the enthusiasm of some Americans following the 2026 midterm elections. Democrats won decisive majorities in both the House and Senate, along with 24 of the 36 governors elections held this month. It was a blue tsunami. Kennedy—a lawyer and human rights activist born in 1959 to dynasty Democrats Robert and Ethel Kennedy—is in a celebratory mood.

She’s in town for one night only to attend a charity dinner in support of her foundation, the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center. But first she sits down with Vanity Fair Italia, and over the course of our chat, she takes her beloved poodle, Scamper, for a short walk; sips two cappuccinos (strictly decaf), one of them iced (she apologizes to the Italians present); eats some gianduiotti chocolates; gestures animatedly; and smooths her very blonde hair.

But above all, she never stops smiling: “In America you can only go so far in the attempt to avoid the rule of law and erode democracy,” she says, making clear that her political statements are delivered in her personal capacity, “because at a certain point, even if you’re the most powerful and the richest man there, democracy will bring you down. [The president] made a mess all over the world, but in the end, in America, democracy was stronger.”

From left: Robert Kennedy Jr., Joseph P Kennedy Jr., Tory Kennedy, and Kerry Kennedy on January 1, 1994

Kerry Kennedy: They’re upset about high prices. And they don’t like the corruption.

What do you think will happen to Donald Trump and his associates?

I think that [Representative] Jamie Raskin is now going to be the head of the Judiciary Committee. I happen to know him very, very, very well because Jamie and I studied for the bar together. He’s brilliant, he’s determined, and he hates anything that harms our Constitution. I think that Trump is going to face impeachment. The rumors are that Trump’s going to fire [Pete] Hegseth, but if he isn’t fired, he’ll certainly be impeached.

What will be the repercussions of the blue tsunami for Tehran?

Iran’s leader at the moment, [Mojtaba Khamenei], has seen his father murdered by Trump. His head of state was murdered by Trump. His spiritual leader was murdered by Trump. Now Trump wants to make a peace deal with this guy. The only way to make progress is for the Iranians to think that it’s not Trump but someone else who’s negotiating.

The fact that Donald Trump sold out Western values in Ukraine for a barrel of oil from a mad, thieving, murderous dictator in Russia shocked the American people and shocked people around the world. Congress has the power of the purse, and now it’s going to exercise that power. But…

He’s still the president for two more years. We didn’t get the White House.

Ethel Kennedy and daughter Kerry Kennedy circa 1979

Who is your ideal candidate for the 2028 presidential election?

Do you think [President Barack] Obama played a role in the Democrats’ success?

Obama is beloved. The only person who’s beloved more is Michelle [Obama]. And when I watched his speeches, he was so clear and concise about the differences between the Republicans and the Democrats, with his moral authority and his joy.

You’ve talked about how your mother supported your father. Can you share an example of that?

My father was working for the Senate, and he was investigating organized crime’s infiltration of the Teamsters union, stealing pension funds from the rank-and-file Teamsters. There was a journalist from the New York Post who was also investigating, and somebody threw acid in his face. He was permanently blinded. A few days later, my mother got an anonymous letter saying, “Your children will be next.” She took her three oldest kids, put them in the back of her car, drove them to the Capitol, walked into the hearing room, and sat in the front row while daddy was interrogating Jimmy Hoffa, the head of the Teamsters.

She was saying, “You’re not going to get to me through my children, and you’re not going to get to my husband through me. We are a fortress and we’re coming after you.” I don’t know how she grappled with the trauma.

She needed to be there for us. She was an athlete. And if you feel physically mighty, it’s very helpful when you have to also be psychologically mighty. She would get up and go swimming, then horseback riding, sailing, and after a sail, she would go for a swim. She also had a very deep faith. She went to Mass every day, prayed before and after every meal, and she made us read the Bible out loud at the dinner table every night.

Yes. In December, I’ll step down from being president of this organization. I’ll stay on the board and I’ll be president emeritus and I’ll still be involved, but I want to go to divinity school.

Stephen Colbert and Kerry Kennedy on December 11, 2013

I don’t know. I have to apply and be accepted.

In 2008 you wrote the bestseller Being Catholic Now. What does it mean to be Catholic in 2026?

For Americans, we have had this extremely disruptive, terrifying time for the last two years, and there are existential threats that everybody in the world is facing. And suddenly there’s an American pope who’s saying, “When you feel this is wrong, it is wrong. When this president is allowing ICE agents to go into American cities and start shooting people, that’s wrong. We need to have compassion toward one another. We need to have love toward one another. Every human being is valuable.”

He’s one of the few voices—not one Republican senator has stood up, and other leaders around the world really have not stood up. Mark Carney did from Canada.

Pedro Sánchez [Spain’s prime minister] did a little bit.

Yes, but not much. The pope has been the main person, and I think that’s renewed people’s faith because it’s very simple as a political leader to call on people’s anger and hatred and fury. It’s a simple trick to get elected. But what people really want you to do in the end is call upon their better angels and say, “You’re good. I see that the God in me sees the God in you.” That is the alternative message, and that’s the spiritual message. I think that it’s created a revival of faith. My daughter Cara is 31 years old, and every Sunday night, she and all of her friends go to church and it’s packed.

What lesson did you learn from your parents?

When we were kids, when we would have a battle, and there were lots of battles, my father always did the same thing. He would bring two of us into a room. My brother had to be silent, and I would tell my father what happened and all the horrible things my brother did. And then I’d have to be silent, and he would tell his story. And then it would be clear that neither of us was completely innocent. We would have to kiss and make up and go to our rooms to read for an hour. His message to us was his message to our country, which is: You have to stop thinking of your adversary as your enemy and think of them as your brother and sister.

Your brother, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., currently the secretary of health in the Trump administration, is known for his anti-vax views. You’ve often said, “I love him very much, but I don’t agree with him.”

We were very close, but he changed and went way over there. And that’s where he is today. But we have much more in common than not.

Robert F. Kennedy Jr and Kerry Kennedy on May 20, 2015

I’m not going to go talk to him about vaccine policy. That’s not going to change him, and he’s not going to change me. So when I’m with him, I want to talk about, how are his animals? How are his children? His daughter, who is my goddaughter, Kyra, lives here in Milan, and she’s getting married to an Italian, and I’m so happy for her. There are many things to talk about besides vaccines.

Your shared past also includes the assassination of your father. Who told you that news?

We were all together in the Ambassador Hotel in Los Angeles and we were watching the returns, but I was eight and I went to sleep. I woke up very early the next morning because I was still on East Coast time, and I went into the living room area of my hotel room. I turned on the TV to watch Bugs Bunny. That’s how I learned.

Did you guys see a therapist when you were little?

Of course not. It was 1968. If it happened today, every kid would get their own therapist; back then, you dealt with it.

Other students were reading Charlotte’s Web, and I was trying to figure out if somebody was going to kill someone in my family. What happens if Mommy dies? Are they going to split us up? Who could take 11 kids? Houses aren’t big. Where do we go? Would we see each other on Christmas?

Were you a happy little girl before that day?

When I was a child, my parents really didn’t separate my father’s life and work from our home. So Daddy would call my mother and say, “You know what? There are three or four of us. We’re trying to work out this [policy] issue. Could we come home for lunch?” Sure. And then he’d call back half an hour later. “Actually, now we’re 12.”

They sat at the dining room table, and there would be three or four kids doing homework and eating peanut butter and jelly sandwiches and asking them to pass the milk. And then they would be talking about these issues. My mother would come in and say, “Time to play football.” And everybody would get up and go out. For us kids, it felt like we were part of something bigger.

Your latest book, which has just been published, is a biography of your mother: Ethel Kennedy: The Extraordinary Life and Bold Legacy. What kind of person was she?

My mother loved men. If you’re a woman, you’re great, and you’re her friend. But when a man was watching, it was incredible. Her whole life, that’s the way she was. When she was 96 and her mind was kind of in and out, I called her from my hotel in Milan and I said, “I’m here. Can I bring you anything? Do you want some limoncello or a bag of that beautiful spaghetti that they sell at the airport? What can I bring you from Italy?” And she answered, “An Italian boyfriend would be nice.”

#3401. 44 Years Later, E.T.'s Most Famous Line Is Still The Greatest Spielberg Quote Ever

Steven Spielberg entered the summer of 1982 as a bona-fide blockbuster machine. Aside from "1941," a chaotic comedy that was not a commercial wipeout (popular belief to the contrary), he was Hollywood's preeminent hit-maker on the strength of "Jaws," "Close Encounters of the Third Kind," and "Raiders of the Lost Ark." He had complete cachet, and he was ready to let it ride with two original movies — the Tobe Hooper-helmed "Poltergeist" and "E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial" – that would test his ability to palpably connect with moviegoers.

It's important to note that Spielberg and Hooper's suburban haunted house flick was a managed risk, as was the former's tender science fiction film about a stranded and scared alien. Still, contrary to Spielberg's track record, pictures like "Rocky III" and "Blade Runner" (which paired Han Solo with the director of "Alien") were expected to be the major players of the summer.

"E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial" premiered at the 1982 Cannes Film Festival, and the reviews that flooded out of that screening were rapturous. Clearly, Spielberg had pierced the hearts of critics who were lamenting the rise of the blockbuster era that garroted the New Hollywood age. They were none too pleased about the influx of VFX-heavy genre films (see Vincent Canby bashing that year's "The Thing" as a "moron movie" for The New York Times), but Spielberg's delicate sci-fi tale of young Elliott Taylor (Henry Thomas) was undeniable.

Within weeks of its release, "E.T. the Extra-Terrestral" was being hailed as Generation X's "The Wizard of Oz." By the end of the year, it was the top-grossing movie ever at the time. Truly, Spielberg's film was an all-ages happy tear-jerker. And there was one line, what writers call an "I want" moment, that brought it all, well, home.

Our long-necked extra-terrestrial's epiphany arrives via the assistance of beer, which, due to his telekinetic bond with Elliott, leaves both inebriated. Hence, Elliott gets unexpectedly drunk at school, leading him to free live frogs that were about to be dissected. Meanwhile, as E.T. keeps guzzling suds at the Taylor homestead, he figures out how to use kids toys and home appliances to contact his family. Just as vitally, he learns how to tell Elliott exactly how he can help him: "E.T. phone home."

Steven Spielberg lets us share in Elliott's epiphany, which peaks with E.T. raising a finger toward the sky in front of venetian blinded windows. I cannot unsee this scene. The mission is clear. This is an inverted "The Wizard of Oz." Elliott must return Dorothy to Kansas. But in the process, this child of divorce will lose the best friend he's ever had.

Spielberg was clearly tapping into his childhood with "E.T" (which was written by the great Melissa Mathison). I love Elliott's older brother and his friends ordering a pizza under the assumed name of "Papa Ooh Mau Mau" and Elliott hurling "penis breath" as an epithet. "E.T." has New Hollywood élan, particularly in its overlapping dialogue. But Spielberg never went down that road again, which is a shame because he's one of the best to do it (every bit the equal of Robert Altman and Hal Ashby).

You can and should savor every bit of dialogue in "E.T." It's one of the greatest movies ever made about a broken family. Just remember the line that encouraged us to commit an empathetic feat and hoped to hell that people would follow Elliott's example. Phone home. And if home is a bad deal, your own home will do just fine.

"Elliott, I don't think he was left here intentionally, but his being here is a miracle, Elliott. It's a miracle and you did the best that anybody could do. I'm glad he met you first." — Keys

"Okay, I just hope we don't wake up on Mars or something surrounded by millions of little squashy guys." — Michael

"Here he is. The man from the moon. But I think you've killed him already." — Gertie

"I taught him how to talk now. He can talk now." — Gertie

"Damn it, why don't you — grow up and think how other people feel for a change!" — Michael

"You must be dead, because I don't know how to feel. I can't feel anything anymore." — Elliott

I write a lot about e-readers and e-ink tablets for Lifehacker, and one issue I'm constantly grappling with is how to write informatively about a bunch of devices that can be quite different in some details, like build or native firmware, and pretty much identical in others, given that literally all e-ink devices use display technology produced by the same Chinese company. (It's called E-Ink.) The best way to do this is to include more video in my articles, but I've lacked a good way to film hands-free so I can easily demonstrate a device's look and feel—until recently.

I recently got an offer to try out a magnetic neck mount from Telesin, a low-cost option to turn my iPhone into a wearable so I can keep my hands free while filming. It's a pretty basic concept, but well-executed: The band that goes around your neck is made of rubber with a firm but flexible core, so you can easily position it to be longer or shorter or at an angle, and the phone mount is on an extending arm with three joints to give you additional options.

I haven't had a chance to film anything for public consumption quite yet, but my testing has already given me some great ideas for how I can use it to show off, say, what it's really like to use a micro-reader in comparison to a full-sized Kindle, as I'll be able to wear it to give a more accurate user's point of view. And right now is a good time to pick one of them up, as many of Telesin's phone and camera accessories (including similar models built to handle an action camera like a GoPro) are discounted for Black Friday; the one I tested is down to $17, or 15% off.

This won't be the right device for every filming scenario. Though MagSafe holds my iPhone fairly securely, I found that I would accidentally detach it every time I tried to adjust the shooting angle—once even leading me to drop it. That's potentially bad news, as using it may require you to take the phone out of its case if it isn't MagSafe-compatible. (Mine isn't.) But if you're just looking for an inexpensive way to shoot hands-free video in a controlled environment, it could be exactly what you need.

#3399. 58-Years Later, 'Blade Runner' Finally Adapts Philip K. Dick’s Weirdest Idea From the Book

Silka Luisa shares the joy of expanding on Philip K. Dick’s writing

Philip K. Dick’s writing has inspired numerous sci-fi movies and TV series including The Man in the High Castle, A Scanner Darkly, and Minority Report, but those adaptations rarely capture just how strange his works truly were. Case in point: Ridley Scott used the basic plot of Dick’s 1968 novel Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? for his 1982 cyberpunk classic Blade Runner, following Rick Deckard (Harrison Ford) as he is tasked with retiring rogue androids that appear human, but he left out a big section of the book dealing with Mercerism, a new religion whose followers use technology to experience the pain of a man being pelted with stones while trying to climb a mountain.

More than half a century later, that detail finally made it to the screen in Prime Video’s Blade Runner 2099. Hints of Mercerism pop up early on signs and billboards in showrunner Silka Luisa's sequel series. But episode six fully delves into the concept as Cora (Hunter Schafer), a human fugitive pretending to be a Replicant Blade Runner, returns to the abandoned Mercerite monastery where she grew up in search of a memory hidden by her mother Helena (Sheila Atim). There she encounters a Mercerite looking to spread the faith by restarting the broadcast of Mercer’s ordeal.

Wilbur Mercer is a martyr, and his followers use an “empathy box” to feel his pain, sharing that experience with others using the technology. The act is meant to distinguish humans from unfeeling androids (the term Replicant wasn’t introduced until Scott’s film). Blade Runner 2099 uses it to explore those same themes as the Replicant Olwen (Michelle Yeoh) is forced to use the empathy box by a Mercerite who wants to see if its power is strong enough to reach her.

“I just love Mercerism as a concept,” Luisa tells Polygon. “Philip K. Dick’s mind was so incredible and so rich to be able to look so far in the future. The idea that there is a religion based on technology for people that are lonely, looking to connect and create empathy – how relevant is that for today? It was just something from the book I was always curious about. What does an empathy box look like? What kinds of people practice this? What does Mercer walking up a mountain look like? As a fan, you just get the pleasure of being able to pick all the stuff that you wanted to explore and magnify it.”

But while Luisa was able to resurrect some abandoned ideas from Dick's original novel for Blade Runner 2099, she also had to invent entirely new ones to show how this world has continued to evolve from Scott’s vision of 2019.

Part of expanding on Dick’s book and the Blade Runner films involved imagining a far future where Replicants have seized control of Earth. Instead of hunting rogue Replicants, Blade Runners now arrest humans using hoods that intubate them and cut off their airflow.

“I’ve seen someone be intubated and it’s just a really horrific, visceral event,” she says. “The idea was to create a device of terror where you could do it in the middle of the street, and it would really stay in people’s minds. Sound design is such an important part of it, because you really want to have an iconic sound that everyone, even if they were a block over, would hear it and be like, ‘Oh my God, I know what’s happening over there.'"

Costume designer Helen Huang based the striking look of the hoods on the work of French comic artist Jean Giraud, better known as Moebius. It was a challenge to create a version that was safe for the actors to wear.

“They’re sort of the tool of oppression without falling into the sort of cliches of fascism,” executive producer Jonathan van Tulleken says. “It was really difficult to find our own language.”

Blade Runner 2099 also found a new language for vice. While Blade Runner included a strip club and Blade Runner 2049 featured a prostitute, Blade Runner 2099 borrowed the design of a ‘70s New York peep show for a place where Replicants can try on prosthetics to make them feel human.

“Even though Replicants have more agency, that doesn't change the fact that there's components of the human experience that they still want,” Luisa says. “You always want what you can have. They can't get pregnant. They can't grow old. They want to experience that. Wouldn't you? They're surrounded by humans that can still do that. This is a place that instead of selling sex, it sells what they can’t have.”

Blade Runner 2099 is streaming on Prime Video.

#3398. 21 Best Thanksgiving Movies to Stream This Week

Sandwiched between the kitschy horrors of Halloween and the commercialized merriment of Christmas, Thanksgiving is often unfairly overlooked as a cinematic main course. But while there might not be a feast’s worth of Thanksgiving movies, there is undoubtedly an appetite for Thanksgiving fare in film. Look no further than the inclusion of the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in Miracle on 34th Street or Wednesday Adams’s sinister (if historically-accurate) re-enactment in Addams Family Values for proof that audiences love turkey’s least favorite holiday. Of course, Thanksgiving tends to get a better treatment on TV, inspiring canonical episodes of Gossip Girl, Friends, Master of None, and, of course, A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving.

Nevertheless, we’ve collected 21 Thanksgiving movies (and Thanksgiving-adjacent movies) that capture the spirit of the holiday—turkey-trotting, tossing the pigskin, carb-loading, fighting with your family, and then overheating in a gorgeous cashmere sweater. Here’s to finding post-meal common ground with one of the titles on this list.

This isn’t known as the quintessential Thanksgiving movie for nothing. You know the story: Steve Martin’s uptight marketing executive, Neal, just wants to travel from New York to Chicago for turkey with his family. His plans for an uneventful trip are foiled again and again by John Candy’s boisterous shower-ring salesman, Del, who’s eager to make friends with Neal during their wayward journey. We will never look at pillows—or rental car agents—the same way again.

Don’t let the word Christmas in the title scare you away. This 2016 ensemble comedy starring Danny Glover, Kimberly Elise, Mo’Nique, and Gabrielle Union has undeniable Thanksgiving vibes. Produced by Will Packer and originally sold to Universal Pictures under the title A Meyers Thanksgiving, Almost Christmas follows the dysfunctional Meyers family as the family patriarch, Walter Meyers (Glover), tries to get through his first holiday season after the death of his wife. While it isn’t exactly about Thanksgiving per se, most of the best moments in Almost Christmas—including Elise chasing Romany Malco away from the table with a shotgun, or the whole table having to pretend to like Mo’Nique’s terrible food—take place during large family gatherings around the dinner table. What could be more Thanksgiving-coded than that?  With an all-star cast of Black actors that also includes J.B. Smoove, Nicole Ari Parker, Omar Epps, and Gladys Knight, Almost Christmas feels like a homecoming full of your favorite uncles and aunties. And, to be fair, isn’t Thanksgiving almost Christmas?

The turkey isn’t the only thing getting carved up in this holiday slasher. Starring Patrick Dempsey and Tik Toker turned recording artist turned film actress Addison Rae, Thanksgiving begins with a Black Friday sale gone horribly awry in Plymouth, Massachusetts, leading to the death of multiple customers. The following year, a murderous slasher wearing a John Carver mask is wreaking havoc in Plymouth, and targeting Rae’s Gaby and her friends. If you’re not feeling warm and gooey on over the holiday, you might want to throw on Thanksgiving and watch Rae and Dempsey’s Sheriff Eric Newton try and track down and escape the clutches of a grisly murderer.

In Jodie Foster’s comedy, Holly Hunter plays Claudia Larson, who returns home for Thanksgiving after losing her job and learning that her daughter (My So-Called Life–era Claire Danes) plans to spend the holiday with a boyfriend. The family she returns to is filled with colorful performances from Anne Bancroft and Charles Durning as her eclectic parents, Robert Downey Jr. as her misanthrope brother, and Dylan McDermott as a semi-mysterious dinner guest.

Fantastic Mr. Fox isn’t technically about Thanksgiving, or even really about humans. And yet, Wes Anderson’s 2009 stop-motion film, featuring the voices of George Clooney and Meryl Streep, has been labeled a Thanksgiving must-watch. Perhaps that’s because the film, based on Roald Dahl’s classic children’s novel, is all about animals trying to escape the tyranny of farmers—something every turkey not lucky enough to be pardoned by the president wishes it could do around Thanksgiving time. Beyond the war between animals and farmers, Anderson’s rustic color palette filled with burnt orange—and the massive feast that brings a diverse array of animals around a dinner table after they successfully joined forces to steal food from their nemeses—are full of the spirit of Thanksgiving.

At times, the titular April’s (Katie Holmes) fate feels as if it rests on whether she’ll successfully cook a turkey in her crowded Lower East Side apartment. As April prepares to host her suburban Pennsylvania family, the high-stakes nature of spending a day hunkered down with relatives—played by Patricia Clarkson, Oliver Platt, Alison Pill, and John Gallagher Jr.—rushes in.

Sometimes getting families together over the holidays is fraught. In this 1997 moody drama directed by Ang Lee, two affluent Connecticut families unravel over Thanksgiving break as their secrets come to lights. The ensemble cast includes stalwart actors Kevin Kline, Joan Allen, Sigourney Weaver as messy parents, and, at that point, up and comers, Tobey Maguire, Elijah Wood, and Christina Ricci as their even more troubled teens. The Ice Storm, which won best screenplay at Cannes Film Festival, is rife with adultery, substance abuse, as well as surprising turns from a host of talented actors and a sharp early film from one of cinema’s most celebrated directors.

Nothing feels more nostalgic during Thanksgiving than watching Snoopy whip up a makeshift meal with jelly beans, popcorn, and mountains of buttered toast for all of his Peanuts pals. And Vince Guraldi’s timeless score makes for a perfect soundtrack to your own festivities.

A Thanksgiving flashback provides key context for the complicated dynamics amongst this group of recently-reunited college friends, played by Glenn Close, Kevin Kline, Jeff Goldblum, Mary Kay Place, and William Hurt. Lawrence Kasdan’s film earned three Oscar nominations, including best picture, original screenplay, and supporting actress for Close.

While not a Thanksgiving-themed film, protagonist Nola Darling (Tracy Camilla Johns) invites all three of her potential suitors to a tense dinner on that very holiday, making her memorable decision between them from her head-of-the-table vantage point. This was most of the world’s introduction to Spike Lee, both as an actor and director, and the electricity is still palpable. And if you’ve gotta have more? You can always stream the 2017 Netflix original series of the same name, starring Lee and DeWanda Wise as Nola Darling.

Rian Johnson’s whodunnit has all the trappings of a Thanksgiving movie, without ever mentioning the holiday. There’s family infighting, Chris Evans in a cable-knit sweater, foggy fall weather, and even a political allegory about the treatment of people of color. Also not about Thanksgiving, but worthy viewing for the full family: Glass Onion: A Knives Out Mystery, which hit theaters last November.

The same year that Merriam-Webster acknowledged Instagram captions everywhere by adding “Friendsgiving” to the dictionary, a movie of the same name was released. True to its titular tradition, a group of friends convenes for a meal that inevitably devolves into chaos.

While not an outright Thanksgiving movie, 1997’s ensemble dramedy contains some of the most sumptuous shots of food ever committed to film. After the death of their family matriarch, a group of disparate relatives must put aside their differences and reconvene for a weekly Sunday dinner. Starring Vivica A. Fox, Vanessa Williams, and Nia Long, Soul Food captures the bonding powers that plates of cornbread, catfish, and collard greens can bring.

This 1976 best picture Oscar winner stars Sylvester Stallone as the eponymous down-on-his-luck boxer, whose fate begins to change with the meeting of his future wife, Adrian (Talia Shire). “To you, it’s Thanksgiving. To me, it’s Thursday,” Rocky tells Adrian as he whisks her away from a disastrous family feast minutes after her brother Paulie (Burt Young) hurls her turkey into the nearby alley. As fans of the franchise, which has debuted several films over the Thanksgiving holiday, know, their Thanksgiving meet-cute will stand the test of time.

Thanksgiving isn’t always about bickering with your blood relatives. Spend Thanksgiving with Instant Family, which stars Mark Wahlberg and Rose Byrne as Pete and Ellie Wagner, an unwitting couple who, overnight, become parents to three foster children. Their decision to become parents happens over  a tense Thanksgiving dinner where Ellie’s family shares they don’t think that Pete and Ellie were ever really cut out to be parents. In an effort to prove them wrong, the Wagners wind up biting off more than they bargained for as they become foster parents to three children, the eldest played by Madame Web star Isabela Merced.

Before Greta Gerwig forced Noah Baumbach to write Barbie with her, there was Mistress America. Written by the real-life couple who helmed the billion dollar blockbuster, this 2015 Sundance favorite centers on the unlikely friendship between Lola Kirke’s Tracy, a first-year college student alone in New York, and Gerwig’s Brooke, the Times Square-living twentysomething who will soon become her stepsister. Conflict between the pair gets resolved on Thanksgiving at New York City’s Veselka, a Ukrainian institution where pierogis stand in for the traditional bird.

Greta Gerwig must really love Thanksgiving. The auteur’s Oscar-nominated take on the Louisa May Alcott classic is brimming with cozy, Thanksgiving-esque vibes. Set largely in the weeks before Christmas, the March sisters (Saoirse Ronan, Emma Watson, Eliza Scanlen, and Florence Pugh) and matriarch (Laura Dern) battle wits, trot through the snow, and stage living room plays in a film that feels reminiscent of many a-family gatherings.

“First, let’s give thanks to our families not being here. It’s always easier without the family,” Adam Sandler’s George Simmons, a stand-up comedian who has been newly diagnosed with cancer, says to a group of new friends. In Judd Apatow’s 2009 dramedy, George attempts to revamp his fledgling career in the eleventh hour with the help of aspiring comic Ira Wright (Seth Rogen). At one point, he  joins the younger talent’s friendsgiving festivities, where the table is surrounded by stars including Jonah Hill, Jason Schwartzman, Aubrey Plaza, and Bo Burnham.

In one of the newer entries to the turkey day canon, Stephen Karam adapts his 2015 Pulitzer finalist play of the same name, exploring the long-held resentments and deeply-rooted admiration that live in an East Coast family. Jayne Houdyshell reprises her Tony-winning role as Deirdre alongside a stacked ensemble, including Richard Jenkins, June Squibb, Beanie Feldstein, Steven Yeun, and Amy Schumer, all gathered in a drab Chinatown apartment for Thanksgiving.

Prisoners finds Hugh Jackman and Jake Gyllenhaal teaming up to find a pair of missing girls who were abducted after Thanksgiving dinner in Conyers, Pennsylvania. EGOT recipient Viola Davis also stars in the thriller as the mother of one of the kidnapped girls. Directed by Dune’s Denis Villeneuve, Prisoners is an unconventional and unsettling Thanksgiving film.

Another unconventional choice, Sam Raimi’s Spider-Man is arguably the only superhero movie that doubles as a Thanksgiving movie. While the central action follows Tobey Maguire’s Peter Parker, there’s a pivotal scene set at Thanksgiving dinner that directly follows a heated battle between Spider-Man and the Green Goblin (a.k.a Norman Osborne, played by Willem Dafoe.) Parker and Osborne have Thanksgiving dinner together with MJ (Kirsten Dunst), Harry Osborne (James Franco), and Aunt May (Rosemary Harris). During the meal, Osborne comes to the stunning realization that Peter Parker is, in fact, Spider-Man. Others have already made the case that the first Spider-Man film deserves to be included in the Thanksgiving canon. The way Dafoe carves the turkey is also both sinister and iconic, as is Maguire apologizing for his tardiness because he “had to beat an old lady with a stick to get these cranberries.”

#3397. Dune 3 Will Set A Box Office Record For The Franchise (But It Can't Compete With Doomsday)

One of the most epic sci-fi trilogies in recent memory is reaching its conclusion. "Dune: Part Three" will bring director Denis Villeneuve's take on the saga of Paul Atreides to a close in December, and it's going to be a big hit — so much so that it's going to set a record for the franchise. However, it's still going to be no match for "Avengers: Doomsday." All the same, "Dune" round three is going to be a resounding success on its own terms.

As of this writing, Warner Bros. and Legendary's "Dune: Part Three" is expected to pull in between $91 and $115 million domestically when it opens on the weekend of December 18, per Box Office Theory. That will set a new high bar for the franchise. The box office debut for "Dune: Part Two" was twice the size of the first movie, pulling in $82.5 million on its opening weekend en route to $715 million worldwide. With an even bigger opening in the cards, that bodes very well for this star-studded trilogy capper.

The new installment is set nearly two decades after Paul Atreides (Timothée Chalamet) seized control of the Imperium at the ending of "Dune: Part Two." Now a ruthless Emperor, Paul must face the consequences of his reign. Haunted by visions of Imperial collapse and the reappearance of his long-lost love, Paul is drawn into a sweeping conspiracy with Chani (Zendaya) at the heart of the mystery.

Meanwhile, presales show a clear winner between "Avengers: Doomsday" and "Dune: Part Three," with Marvel's latest on track to break the record for the biggest opening weekend ever, possibly north of $400 million. There's no real competition here, but we don't have to lower one project to raise the other, either.

The fact of the matter is that we could be looking at a combined $500 million-plus opening weekend to help close out 2026, which is absolutely bonkers. Dunesday will blow Barbenheimer out of the water at the box office, which is pretty darn crazy. This is one of those "everybody wins" situations, especially when we look at it on a slightly longer timeline.

January is a pretty dead month for theaters, meaning that December blockbusters often leg out for weeks on end. That's how James Cameron's "Avatar" became the biggest movie of all time, and why the sequels were also massive, record-breaking hits. So, assuming critics are on the side of "Dune 3" (and there's no reason to think they won't be), the movie should be able to parlay that big opening weekend into a leggy run well into February and into awards season. If all goes really well? We could be looking at a $1 billion global hit when all's said and done.

One thing that "Dune" has going for it is IMAX. Warner Bros. locked down those screens well in advance, meaning that "Avengers: Doomsday" has to go without them. IMAX has proved that it's more important to the box office than ever before, as those higher ticket prices can add a lot to the bottom line. And for cinephiles, few cinematic events justify those higher prices than a science fiction epic from Denis Villeneuve.

So no, "Dune" may not be able to compete with "Doomsday," but that also doesn't matter in the grand scheme of things. This trilogy is going to go out on a high note, and that's all that really matters.

"Dune: Part Three" hits theaters on December 18, 2026.

There's quite a bit of variety here, too, from battery-powered projectors you can take camping or move between rooms to more powerful 4K models designed for a dedicated movie-night setup.

The Soundcore Nebula P1i is down to $299 from $399, while the Nebula P1 is $699.99, down from $799. Both offer 1080p resolution and Google TV, but their speaker setups are what make them interesting. The P1i has two 10W speakers that flip out and rotate to direct sound toward your seating area, while the P1's speakers detach completely and can run wirelessly for up to 20 hours. The P1 is also brighter at 650 ANSI lumens versus the P1i's 380, though you'll need a power outlet for either projector since neither has a built-in battery.

Small enough to slip into a bag, the Nebula Capsule 3 and Capsule 3 Laser are worth considering if you want something you can easily take on trips or move around the house. The standard Capsule 3 is down to $399 from $529, saving you $130, while the Laser version is $649.99, down from $749.99. If you're ready to move beyond 1080p, the Nebula Cosmos 4K SE at $1,099.99 (originally $1,299.99) offers a more affordable way to get 4K resolution. You also get Google TV and automatic image adjustments for easier setup, though it doesn't have a built-in battery, so you'll need a power outlet nearby.

At the premium end of Nebula's lineup, the X1 and newer X1S are designed for a more serious home theater setup. The X1 is down to $2,299 from $2,999, saving you $700, while the X1S is $2,799 from $3,299. Both use triple-laser technology with 4K resolution, Dolby Vision, and optical zoom, but the X1S has a considerable advantage in brightness, reaching up to 6,000 ANSI lumens compared with the X1's 3,500. That extra brightness is useful in rooms with some ambient light, but the tradeoff is louder fan noise.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

The best thing you can do is compare the prices with other retailers that have Black Friday sales. If that seems like too much work, you can just follow our Black Friday coverage (we're already doing all the searching and vetting for you). Some other tips are making sure you're not being sold an older or cheaper version and always reading reviews.

Since McKenna Grace was cast as Maysilee for Sunrise on the Reaping, she's been showing her love for the franchise in true Panem fashion. Grace has been dropping a bunch of Hunger Games looks and dressing like Jennifer Lawrence during the 2026 movie release's promotional tour. The I, Tonya actress’ latest fashion choice was an amazing Mockingjay winged dress, and unfortunately for anyone looking to cosplay the fit, the designer confirmed it’s very pricey expensive.

One of the best ways that actresses have been promoting a movie they’re proud of is through method dressing, which has become a key aspect of celebrity fashion. As part of McKenna Grace’s fashion journey to channel The Girl on Fire, she showed up at the New York City premiere of Sunrise on the Reaping wearing a winged dress that took me back to Catching Fire. Take a look at The Hunger Games and Grace’s IG joint post of the beautiful, winged gown below:

A post shared by The Hunger Games (@thehungergames)

Looking like a true Mockingjay right there! Wearing a custom Pamela Rolland gown, the Scream 7 actress looked incredible in the navy blue, bedazzled dress, which shone at the premiere. Of course, the dress’ standout feature has to be those gigantic custom wings, which look similar to the ones worn by Katniss in Catching Fire (which is streamable with a Hulu subscription) during her tribute interview.

While Claudia Martin was the visionary behind the red carpet look, the stylist we have to thank for Grace's amazing wings is Molly Dickson. She’s the talented artist responsible for many of the Gifted actress' Hunger Games-inspired outfits, including Katniss’ famous white wedding dress. But, according to People's exclusive story about the look, designing that custom-winged fashion piece wasn’t cheap, and Marin estimated that 20% of her business income went into the materials alone.

With the custom wings costing customers between $1,500-$3,500, Claudia Marin said she had to make these custom wings herself, as, of course, the ones from the dystopian flick were CGI. So, that meant taking matters into her own hands and replicating those massive feathered wings herself. With pricey wings like these, I don’t think this would be a go-to cosplay costume for even the biggest fans (unless they believe these wings are worth every penny).

The process that went into designing Grace's wings started with patterning the wings' base out of foam and fabric so it’s shaped around Grace’s arms. Then, Marin sewed the fabric structure and added boning channels to thread wire for more support.

Finally, the designer hand-dyed batches of goose and silver pheasant feathers in different shades of blue, sewing and gluing each feather into place. While the final product of the winged gown looked absolutely eye-popping, Marin made it clear that designing it was anything but easy:

Then I had a small panic attack, and then I just kept sewing and gluing feathers with the reference photo next to me until it was done.

Considering how expensiveness of this fashion endeavor, I can understand Marin being “terrified” that she’d run out of feathers while placing each feature in the right position to match both sides. Still, since Grace’s designer put in the grunt work, her recent red carpet outfit serves as an ode to sheer craftsmanship.

The “bird” may be becoming a new red carpet trend, but I can’t picture cosplayers spending thousands to wear McKenna Grace's custom-made wings. Even though we all can’t look like the Mockingjay, we can still appreciate the artistry that came with an incredible look that takes flight on the red carpet. You can watch Mckenna Grace, her co-stars as well as plenty of incredible costumes by checking out The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping in theaters now.

#3394. An Iconic Hollywood Actor Inspired The Look Of Marvel's Tony Stark

Tony Stark as played by Robert Downey Jr. is distinguished by his goatee, but historically in the "Iron Man" comics, Tony has stuck with only a pencil moustache. It's the same facial hair worn by, as just one example, famed inventor Howard Hughes (whose life was told onscreen in 2004 by Martin Scorsese and Leonardo DiCaprio in "The Aviator"). Stan Lee would later claim he modeled Tony Stark's character on Hughes; Tony is a tycoon and adventurer, and where Hughes had airplanes, Tony has his suit of armor. Tony Stark's father canonically being named Howard also fits into the narrative that Iron Man is Howard Hughes as a superhero.

You might think, therefore, that Tony's physical appearance, pencil moustache and all, was taken from Howard Hughes. But, in fact, artist Don Heck had a different model in mind. Designing Iron Man was a team effort. The (initially, bulky gray) armor was designed by Jack Kirby, and Tony Stark himself was designed by Don Heck. Drawing Tony's face, Heck decided to make him an "Errol Flynn-type."

Born in Australia, Flynn was one of Hollywood's biggest stars in the 1930s. Partnered with director Michael Curtiz, Flynn starred in the 1935 pirate film "Captain Blood" and then 1938's "The Adventures of Robin Hood." Flynn's Robin remains the baseline for Robin Hood in cinema: the green tunic, the bycocket hat, the mustache and chin beard, etc. Whenever there's a Robin Hood homage or parody, whether it be Disney's "Robin Hood" movie featuring talking animals or the "Star Trek: The Next Generation" episode "Qpid," Flynn's Robin Hood is the source material.

In the biography "Don Heck: A Work of Art," Heck recounted that comic artist Alex Toth often drew his heroes looking like Errol Flynn. Heck decided to do the same for Iron Man.

"Captain Blood" and "The Adventures of Robin Hood" remain some of the best swashbuckler movies ever made. Likewise, Errol Flynn endures, decades on, as the go-to image of what a swashbuckler is: a confident, chivalrous hero who rescues fair maidens and defeats foul villains with his sword, all without ever losing a smile. There's undeniably some of Errol Flynn's cocky Robin Hood in Robert Downey Jr.'s Iron Man. (Flynn, in his private life, was known for hedonistic substance abuse and womanizing, which also mirrors less flattering chapters of Iron Man's history like the famous "Demon in a Bottle" arc.)

Iron Man does not stand alone among Errol Flynn-inspired superheroes. Nightcrawler/Kurt Wagner of the X-Men is an in-universe fan of Flynn's swashbuckler movies. As a superhero, often acts out his childhood fantasies of being Flynn, down to fighting with swords like Captain Blood.

Speaking to Syfy, "X-Men" writer Chris Claremont discussed writing Kurt as a swashbuckler and arguably the most well-adjusted X-Man, even though he looks the most like a mutant. Claremont's thinking was that Nightcrawler has lived with his appearance (blue skin, a tail, etc.) all his life, so he's made peace with it — especially as a man of faith. So instead of wallowing in torment, he seeks the fun out of life. "Being a young, impressionistic kid in a circus, who does [Kurt] fall in love with? Errol Flynn!" Claremont explained.

DC's Green Arrow/Oliver Queen debuted in 1941 and the concept for his character was essentially "modern day Robin Hood." "The Adventures of Robin" was still on people's minds then, and Green Arrow's costume resembled Flynn's Robin Hood — same color, same hat, and of course the same bow.

Robin Hood was famed for stealing from the poor to give to the rich, so many stories give Green Arrow a liberal bent. The "Hard-Traveling Heroes" arc of the 1970s paired Oliver opposite the more conservative Green Lantern, while the new "Absolute Green Arrow" series depicts Green Arrow as a slasher targeting billionaires.

With "The Adventures of Robin Hood" now a distant classic, modern "Green Arrow" stories have depicted Oliver Queen as, like Nightcrawler, an in-universe fan of Errol Flynn. While Kurt goes for swords, Oliver took up archery because he literally wanted to be Robin Hood. As Green Arrow, that's exactly who he becomes, but it takes some learning to get there.

In 2007's "Green Arrow: Year One" by writer Andy Diggle and artist Jock, Oliver — still a spoiled rich kid and not yet Green Arrow — splurges $100,000 on a bow once owned by archer Howard Hill, who performed Flynn's archery stuntwork in "The Adventures of Robin Hood." When Oliver gets stranded on a deserted island, his archery skills help him survive, while the humbling experience teaches him to mirror Robin's charity, not just his swashbuckling.

Hawkeye/Clint Barton, as another archer hero, is often considered Marvel's counterpart to Green Arrow. He's got Errol-Flynn-as-Robin-Hood's wit, just like Oliver Queen does. Long time Marvel fan George R. R. Martin has expressed annoyance that the movies sapped out Hawkeye's (Clint Barton) funny side.

Discussing Hawkeye brings us right back to Iron Man, because Hawkeye debuted as an Iron Man villain in "Tales of Suspense" #57 (by Stan Lee and Don Heck). I'd like to think Lee and/or Heck noticed the amusing parallel that Tony Stark, a hero with Errol Flynn's face, was fighting an outlaw archer in Hawkeye.

Apple says the Series 12 checks your heart rate variability 24 times more than the Series 11, and your background heart rate 60 times more frequently than the Series 11. Powering the new heart rate monitor is the S11 chip, Apple's latest processor for the Apple Watch. The S11 isn't only responsible for these new heart rate features, however. #3392. Persona Studio Director Wants Younger Developers To Help Shape Persona 6

Kazuhisa Wada hopes future generations of developers can give Persona 6 and other titles 'their own spin and their own flavor'

P-Studio chief director Kazuhisa Wada shared his hopes for the future of the Persona series, including Persona 6, in a new interview with IGN. After reflecting on his own journey as a developer, Wada voiced his openness to letting Atlus and P-Studio's next generation of developers influence the direction of Persona 6 and the future of the popular RPG franchise.

When asked by IGN what the Persona series needs to do to keep growing and evolving ahead of Persona 6, Wada pointed out that game development takes longer and happens on a much larger scale than it ever has before. While smaller teams of experienced developers led previous Persona games, Wada wants a younger generation of game developers to be much more involved in the direction of Persona 6 and future titles in the series.

"Since this is no longer an individual kind of process and is more of a team situation, we want to make sure everybody at our company shares the basic vision for the future of Persona. Everybody gets to have a say," Wada explained. "We get to share the direction we want to go in, get feedback, have conversations with everybody we're working with. And we want to make sure we bring in the younger generations of game developers into the process as well so that they have a voice and they have a way to show their own creative incredible-ness to the world."

Ultimately, Wada hopes that his generation of developers can "pass that identity" of the Persona series that they established to the next generation of game developers, and from there they can "give it their own spin and their own flavor." While the remake Persona 4 Revival will be the next game in the franchise to come out, it seems like Persona 6 will be the first real showcase of this approach to development in action.

We still don't know much about Persona 6 right now, as it has only gotten a couple of teasers at Xbox and Nintendo showcases. It doesn't have a release window, but we know it'll eventually come out across Nintendo Switch 2, PlayStation 5, Windows PC, and Xbox Series X/S.
