#3391. Ingrid Bergman and Roberto Rossellini: The Affair That Outraged America

The whole situation had become such a mess that their marriage had to take place by proxy, through lawyers thousands of miles away. The romance between actor Ingrid Bergman and director Roberto Rossellini was one of the great scandals of the 20th century. They were two married people who had fallen in love and embarked on an adulterous relationship—nothing that hadn’t been seen before, especially in the film industry—but something about their particular situation sparked a wave of international outrage with an intensity that’s rarely seen. There were condemnations from the Vatican, proclamations from the US Senate, insults of every kind, and an avid and destructive interest from the press and the public. There were also some glorious moments, erupting volcanoes, and even plates of spaghetti used as weapons.

I saw your films Open City and Paisan, and enjoyed them very much. If you need a Swedish actress who speaks English very well, who has not forgotten her German, who is not very understandable in French, and who in Italian knows only “ti amo,” I am ready to come and make a film with you.

This now legendary letter above has become part of film history. It’s no surprise that two artistic sensibilities of the caliber of Bergman and Rossellini would connect through the latter’s films—masterpieces of Italian neorealism that Bergman connected with emotionally and intellectually. “The realism and simplicity of Open City were heart-shocking,” she recalls in Ingrid Bergman: My Story. “No one looked like an actor, and no one talked like an actor. There was darkness and shadows, and sometimes you couldn’t even see it. But that’s the way it is in life…. You can’t always see and hear, but you know that something almost beyond understanding is going on.” Bergman left the movie theater where she had just seen the film on a spring night in 1948 deeply moved. She didn’t know it, but her life had just changed forever.

The world 80 years ago was very different from today, of course, and the actor had a hard time tracking down the director. When she finally did locate him, they began an exchange of letters filled with deep admiration, during which they agreed to collaborate on a screenplay that Rossellini was working on which would eventually become the film Stromboli. The involvement of someone as famous and talented as Bergman should have, in theory, made it easier for Rossellini to raise funds for another film. She was Sweden’s most successful export since Greta Garbo, the Ilsa of Casablanca, and an Oscar winner for her performance in Gaslight. She was admired worldwide for her naturalness and beauty. She was so popular that there was even a reported surge in women choosing to become nuns after the release of another film she starred in, The Bells of St. Mary’s, much to the chagrin of many parents. For his part, Rossellini might not have been well-known in the US, but his revolutionary ability to capture the realities of life on film had earned him a Palme d’Or at Cannes and the admiration of cineasts. He had also starred in various encounters with Italy’s fledgling paparazzi. Married for over a decade, he maintained a relationship that was an open secret, with his lover and muse, the spectacular actor Anna Magnani. Together they were a tumultuous and popular couple—that is, until Bergman appeared on the scene via her letter.

Their relationship was long limited to correspondence, but there was clearly some passion in those letters because, upon arriving at the Hotel Luna Convento in Amalfi with Magnani, Rossellini requested that any telegram or letter from England be delivered to him with the utmost discretion. (Bergman was, at the time, shooting Under Capricorn at the Elstree Studios outside London.) The staff assumed this didn’t apply to his well-known partner, and when they were in the hotel dining room, a waiter approached him and said, in full view of Magnani, “I was instructed that if a telegram arrived for you from England, I should give it to you in private. Here you go.” Magnani had already begun to hear rumors about the relationship between Rossellini and the famous Swedish actor, whom he was said to be planning to offer a role that had been written specifically for her. “Now, is this all right—eh, Roberto?” she asked kindly as she served herself more spaghetti with tomato sauce. “Ah, yes, yes, grazie,” he replied distractedly.

“Good. Here, you can have it,” and she tossed the heap of spaghetti straight into Rossellini’s face.

Magnani’s intuitions were right. When Bergman first arrived in Rome to then travel through the south of the country on her way to Stromboli, the island in the Aeolian archipelago where the film was to be shot, she and Rossellini became lovers: “I fell in love with him because he was so unique. I’d never met anyone like him, so free. He brought new dimensions to life, new boundaries, new emotions, and new horizons. And he gave me a courage I’d never known before.” She had been married for over 10 years to Petter Lindström, a doctor who was her first love, but she hadn’t been happy for a long time—neither in her relationship nor in Hollywood. In fact, she’d earlier asked him for a divorce; he refused to grant it, and since they had a young daughter, Pia, and their cohabitation was proceeding smoothly enough, they continued to live together under the same roof. In the eyes of the world, they were still husband and wife. But shortly before meeting Rossellini, Bergman had had a romance with another tormented artistic figure, the photographer Robert Capa. Since that affair had no major consequences, Lindström turned a blind eye. The story with Rossellini would be completely different. He represented a way out of a marriage and an industry in which she felt trapped. “I think I was just waiting for someone to come along and help me out of that marriage because I didn’t have the strength to go. That was over three years before I met Roberto Rossellini.” What she didn’t realize was how much her decision would turn her world upside down.

Italy would be a revelation for Bergman. Rossellini introduced her to his circle of friends, including figures such as Federico Fellini, and served as the best possible guide on her journey to Naples, Amalfi, Sorrento, and Messina. In Amalfi, the actress decided that this was more than just a passing fling; it was a love intense enough for her to end her marriage and leave the United States. She wrote to Lindström from the very same Hotel Luna Convento where Magnani and Rossellini had their confrontation, telling him that she had fallen in love and was staying in Italy. He refused to accept the news, and his denial would give rise to much of the drama that was about to unfold.

Meanwhile, the new happy couple drove along the country’s roads, which still bore the visible scars of World War II, through one of the most spectacular landscapes on earth. Everywhere the film crew went, crowds cheered them, delighted that the world’s most famous actor had decided to make a movie in their country. At one of the simple hotels where they stayed, Bergman had to leave her room to use a bathroom on a hallway. Fans cheered her on both on her way there and back.

It soon became clear that their partnership was more than just a creative one. Life magazine photographed them holding hands, and the images went around the world. By the time they arrived on the small island of Stromboli, the shoot, with its many ordinary people recruited to perform in the film, was swamped by press from all over the world eager to capture images of the lovers at the foot of the island’s volcano. The role of a refugee who agrees to a loveless marriage in order to be released from an internment camp and then ends up trapped in an unfamiliar world that is as oppressive as the one she escaped came naturally to Bergman. It reflected her emotional state: She was caught between the joy of being in love, the guilt of leaving her husband, and the doubts and pain regarding her 10-year-old daughter, Pia, who remained in the United States. In Ingrid Bergman: My Story, Bergman recounts, “It was absolute hell. I cried so much that I thought there couldn’t be any tears left. I felt the newspapers were right. I’d abandoned my husband and child. I was an awful woman.”

There are images from the shoot in which Bergman is seen in close-up, and behind her are several women in mourning, an oppressive and threatening presence. They evoke exactly what happened to her. The world exploded in anger against its once favorite star. She was portrayed as a lost woman, if not a whore, and an insult to every sense of propriety. Much of the intensity of the reaction was related to Bergman’s previous popularity and her nearly flawless, pristine image. She was seen as an embodiment of a strict Lutheran morality, a sincere and honest woman. (Lindström would later say she was, in fact, a heavy drinker and smoker, promiscuous, and cared only about her career, not her family.) That this almost angelic figure would give up everything to run off with an unattractive, tempestuous Italian director seemed like an unfathomable mistake. Added to this was the intrigue that she was now his new muse, following the landmark films shot with Magnani. And there was also, of course, Pia’s complicated situation. Rossellini prevented Bergman from returning to the United States, fearful that if she went, she wouldn’t come back to Italy, while Lindström refused to let their daughter travel to Italy. The divorce and custody battle became bitter, filled with mutual accusations and animosity. As a result, mother and daughter went two years without seeing each other. And then, after that, another six. This is how Pia, the main casualty of this love story, would recall those times: “I stayed with him [her father], and my mother left. She was offered a dramatic life, full of excitement, with romantic, wonderful love affairs. It was magnificent for her. But not what came of it. I didn’t experience the splendid side of the situation. In other words, I was left behind. That’s why I see things differently. I was part of what was left behind.”

As if there weren’t enough elements to this scandal already, it soon emerged that Bergman was pregnant. Senator Edwin C. Johnson referred to her in the Senate as “a powerful influence for evil.” Some of her friends, however, came to her defense. In 1961, she told Lillian Ross of The New Yorker: “When I gave birth to little Roberto, the whole world started to throw stones at me. But I knew I had friends when I received a letter from Ernest Hemingway saying he wanted to be the baby’s godfather. And when I came to New York to accept the New York Film Critics award for Anastasia, Hemingway said, ‘I’ll come with you and punch the first one in the nose who says anything bad to you.’”

The night Ingrid went into labor coincided with the Italian premiere of Volcano, a film with a plot similar to Stromboli—created by Anna Magnani to compete with her ex’s film and directed by a German émigré to the United States, William Dieterle. Midway through the screening, the press began to leave the theater upon learning that Bergman had gone into labor and been admitted to a clinic. Magnani resigned herself to the situation, knowing that her film could not compete with Bergman’s baby in terms of media interest. Volcano was a critical and commercial failure. And so, in 1950, the boy, whom they named Robertino, was born. The press hounded the hospital relentlessly: One photographer passed off his pregnant wife as a woman in labor by adding padding to her belly; another crawled through a drainpipe to reach the actor’s balcony; others tried to bribe nuns at the hospital with a million lire; and still others, resigned to not being able to get a photo, created montages with Bergman’s and Rossellini’s faces and published them.

The baby’s birth presented a tricky situation. Legally, Lindström could have claimed custody because his divorce from Bergman hadn’t been finalized, which infuriated Rossellini, so they registered the child under Rossellini’s name and that of a “mother whose identity would be revealed later.” Eventually Lindström’s and Bergman’s divorce would be finalized in a Mexican court, where Bergman also decided to get married to Rossellini by proxy. A producer and a lawyer, friends of the couple, stood in for each of them while, on the outskirts of Rome, the real couple stopped into a small church near the Via Appia. “I knelt down and Roberto held my hand and then we went home and told all our friends that now we were married and drank Champagne.”

The couple settled in an apartment on Viale Bruno Buozzi in Rome and spent their summers in Santa Marinella, a town on the coast about an hour by train from the capital. After years speaking a mix of broken English and French, Bergman managed to learn Italian. The twins, Isotta Ingrid and Isabella, were born in June 1952, and the young family enjoyed a period of intense happiness. But their challenges were not over yet, of course. Bergman’s eldest daughter was becoming a teenager and her relationship with her mother was conducted solely through letters. Living with Rossellini wasn’t easy either. At the height of the tension with Lindström, the director had threatened to kill himself by either shooting himself or crashing one of his sports cars into a tree. Moreover, he was jealous, domineering (he let Bergman work only with him), and at times violent. This was all behavior that Bergman appeared to excuse as simply part of his Italian temper. This is how she describes one episode: “Things were flying through the air, I rush up and I took him in my arms and I started to say…and bang, he threw me against the wall so hard I almost broke in pieces. Well, I mean, I couldn’t do anything. Even to get near him was to risk your life.”

And then there was the matter of money. Rossellini, who had grown up in affluence, was used to living the high life, but every single movie he made with Bergman was a commercial failure. In 1956, director Jean Renoir approached Bergman to offer her a role in Elena and Her Men. Rossellini admired Renoir so much that he allowed his wife to work on the film, which finally put an end to the frustrating professional slump she had been stuck in for years. After that, she was offered the lead role in a French adaptation of Robert Anderson’s Tea and Sympathy. This is how Bergman recounts what happened: “Tea and Sympathy is the story of a young boarding-school boy who is afraid he is homosexual. Roberto was always disturbed by any sort of homosexuality. When I wanted to send Robertino to a Swiss or English boarding school, he blew up. ‘What!’ he screamed, ‘That’s where it all starts, in those boarding schools.’…The whole theme was too distasteful to him. It wasn’t the writing or the writer; he just hated the general theme. He also hated the fact that in the play I was going to prove to this boy that he wasn’t a homosexual, lead him into sex. The whole part disturbed Roberto immensely.”

Rossellini tried to forbid his wife from performing in the play, but she ignored him, arguing that she had signed a contract and that she loved the script. He fought back by emphasizing that people would laugh at her and that it would be a flop. On opening night, he snapped at her, “Be prepared when the first intermission comes for half of them to walk out.”

That’s not what happened. She was greeted with a thunderous ovation. “The house went wild. You couldn’t stop them. They were standing up and screaming, standing up and applauding, and the ‘bravos’ never stopped. Then I took my solo bow in the center of the stage, and as I bent over, I turned my head and looked at Roberto. Our eyes met. We looked straight at each other. I knew then my marriage was over even though we might stay together.”

He, for his part, stated: “I separated from Ingrid Bergman because it was impossible for me to continue. We loved each other very much; we had three children…she could return to the industry, but I didn’t feel comfortable in the role of the man whose wife brings home the money. We decided to separate, and that’s why I went to India, as far away from her as possible.” In India, Rossellini began a romance with the wife of his film’s producer, Sonali Dasgupta. Bergman wasn’t outraged when she found out; instead, she calmly proposed a divorce. He insisted on two conditions: that the children never travel to the United States and that Bergman never remarry. She laughed at the absurdity of the requests and refused, saying, “That was just Roberto.” (Shortly thereafter, she began a relationship with the Swedish theater producer Lars Schmidt, whom she married in 1958.)

The custody battle over the Rossellini children was also contentious, almost as much as the one involving Pia. There were mutual accusations of kidnapping and bad faith, and in the end, Bergman ceded custody to Rossellini. The children split their time between Rome and Paris, and Bergman frequently traveled to both cities to be with her children. The couple never completely drifted apart; they remained connected by Isabella’s health issues, including a back operation that nearly left her paraplegic, and the emotional bond that tied them together.

The world changed very quickly, and the former persona non grata won her second Oscar in 1957 for her role in Anastasia, which was accepted on her behalf by her friend Cary Grant. Bergman heard the news on the radio while taking a bath at her hotel in Paris, where she was staying while performing in Tea and Sympathy. She cried tears of joy in front of her son, Robertino, and soon returned to the United States to resume filming. Her rehabilitation within the industry was complete. She became one of the most respected names in cinema across various countries and languages—a living legend. In 1972, an apology was read into the Congressional Record for the attack against Bergman that had taken place in 1950. At the time she stated, “When I left for Italy, there was a senator in Washington who made a speech against me, and he ended by saying that out of Hollywood’s ashes will grow a better Hollywood.” Bergman didn’t realize her mistake, saying “Hollywood’s ashes” instead of “the ashes of Ingrid Bergman” until she later heard a recording of her comments. She laughed and laughed. “A line I had been waiting 22 years to deliver, and I mess it up!”

Vengeance was never a part of Anna Magnani’s plans after her separation from Rossellini, beyond that infamous plate of pasta. She continued her career working with Italy’s top directors and even won an Oscar a year before Bergman won her second statuette. When she was diagnosed with cancer, Rossellini sent her flowers despite the years that had passed. She wrote to him asking him to come see her, and from then on they saw each other regularly. Bergman recalls, “When I found out, I called her to tell her I was happy about what she was doing. The circle had closed: She had the man she had loved above all others close to her again.” When Magnani died in 1973, Rossellini agreed to have her buried in his family crypt, and she still rests there alongside him. (He died in 1977.)

Petter Lindström remarried in 1956 to Dr. Agnes Ronavec, with whom he had four more children. He continued his career as a renowned brain surgeon and died in 2000 at the age of 93.

Over time, Bergman would also be reunited with Pia after many years apart. At age 20, following a failed marriage, the young woman—feeling lost and unsure of what to do with her life—moved to Paris to live with her mother and Lars Schmidt. “I came to see Mom in a new light and fell in love with her. Few young women have such an extraordinary, cheerful, fun-loving mother—always ready to go out and do things, see this or that, go to the movies and the theater, dine out, run around, get up early, and go shopping. She had boundless energy. It was amazing.” Shortly after that, the grandmother of her half-siblings—Isotta Ingrid, Isabella (who would go on to become an acclaimed actor), and Robertino—passed away. Pia decided to go to Rome without speaking a word of Italian and take charge of the household, with a cook and a governess, to get to know them as well as find herself. “That way I’d be doing something and mattering to someone. I spent three years with them. Mom sent me money; I paid the salaries and took my siblings to the dentist, horseback riding, and to their lessons. It was a wonderful experience that, in a way, I needed. I didn’t have a specific place in the world; I couldn’t imagine a profession I felt called to; I felt lost. I needed to put down roots, find a place to live, convince myself that I was useful, help someone, and do something that wasn’t just for the sake of doing it.” Rossellini would visit them at lunchtime, talk on the phone about business, movies, and money, and leave after giving everyone a kiss. Pia continued: “I liked Italy. I was happy to be there. I was glad to have met them and to get to know Roberto firsthand, without relying on other people’s opinions or ideas about what he was like; I’m glad to have met Sonali and everyone else, because it helped me observe and understand everything that was happening, to get a sense of how things had come to be.”

Bergman concludes in her biography: “Someone wrote somewhere about my life with Roberto that I had found a world that for me was probably better than most of us ever attain. And that is true. I did have marvelous happiness with Roberto as well as deep troubles. But trouble is part of one’s life. If you have never had any trouble, if you have never cried, if you have never been really miserable and thought that you could not go on, what kind of understanding would you have for other people who are in trouble?…I think a person who is always happy would be a big bore. And Roberto was never a bore.”

Originally published in Vanity Fair España.

#3390. John Carpenter Tried To Remake This Classic '60s Sci-Fi Horror Movie, But It Backfired

If you were a studio executive in the 1990s looking to remake a black and white alien horror movie from a few decades earlier, getting John Carpenter to handle it would probably seem like the easiest way to score a win. He was, after all, the director who took 1951's "The Thing From Another World" and remade it as 1982's "The Thing," creating what is still regarded as one of the greatest horror movies of all time (even though it notoriously flopped when it hit theaters).

Surely he could do the same thing with 1960's "Village of the Damned," especially with a stacked cast that includes Christopher Reeve and Mark Hamill. Superman, Luke Skywalker, and the guy who made "Halloween" all teaming up for a terrifying tale of creepy kids with psychic powers? There's no way that could miss, right?

Unfortunately, it did miss. When Carpenter's "Village of the Damned" hit screens in 1995, it was an absolute bomb.

Like the 1960 version, Carpenter's "Village of the Damned" was based on John Wyndham's 1957 novel, "The Midwich Cuckoos," which told the story of how the eponymous English village was taken over by a bunch of creepy kids. After a strange event where everyone in town fell unconscious, 61 women woke up to find themselves unexpectedly and inexplicably pregnant.

All of the babies that were born as a result had platinum blonde hair and golden eyes, and as they grew up, developed telepathic powers that — in case anyone hadn't yet figured out something really weird was going on — indicated that they were alien imposters sent to infiltrate the Earth.

The original British film was a hit that turned a pretty considerable profit in 1960, and still has a 93% rating on Rotten Tomatoes over six decades later. As a black and white horror classic that had a relatively small budget and a pretty brisk runtime of only 77 minutes, it made a pretty obvious candidate for a big-budget American remake in the '90s. And yet, despite the star power in front of and behind the camera, it tanked, losing money at the box office and receiving a thorough beating from critics who called it "mediocre." And those were the nice ones.

Considering that Carpenter changed very little of the story other than relocating it from an English village to a small town in California, we're left wondering why the original succeeded and the remake failed. It may be that the idea just wasn't as fresh anymore. The 1960 "Village" hit screens long before other famous creepy kid movies like "The Omen" (1976), but by the time the remake made it to theaters, the idea of a sinister youngster had been around long enough to be a cliche that audiences just weren't that into.

Maybe it was that the film is just unpleasant, and not in the way that a horror movie should be. In the years before a movie like "Saw" and "Hostel" — a movie Carpenter famously didn't care for — would show that people were actually pretty into seeing horror movie victims mutilate themselves, audiences clearly didn't want to see Kirstie Alley dissect herself with a scalpel or watch kids force a woman to boil her own hand in a pot of pasta. Also, no matter how creepy they are, having the hero of your movie kill a bunch of children by bombing a school is just not a great look. It may not be Carpenter's worst film, but it's still pretty far from his best.

Although Bari Weiss has been the editor-in-chief of CBS News for over a year now, the past several months have truly served as the test of her editorial prowess. That’s especially the case where 60 Minutes is concerned, given Season 59 is airing in the aftermath of her major behind-the-scenes changes. In recent weeks, the show has reportedly seen ratings setbacks, and series alums haven’t been holding back. Now, one former producer is weighing in on how Weiss and her colleagues have already “failed” the show.

Weiss and 60 Minutes executive producer Nick Bilton parted with a number of series veterans on May 28, which is now said to be known internally as “Black Thursday.” Among the people to be let go was Guy Campanile, who worked with CBS News for 34 years before being fired. The veteran journalist recently spoke with The Wall Street Journal about the news magazine show’s new era. In Campanile’s estimation, the show has lost its “sizzle,” and he also believes there’s a key indicator of that:

If it's Wednesday, and you can't remember what was on the show on Sunday, you failed.

That wasn’t all that was said by Campanile, who served as 60’s managing editor by the time he was let go. He also opined that Weiss was spearheading “the destruction of the most prestigious news program on American television” and creating unmemorable coverage as a result. Weiss herself recently responded to concerns about the show, stating that it had been doing “tremendously well” and that she’d been aiming to block out the noise surrounding it. Nevertheless, the numbers remain a major topic of discussion.

Last week, as part of the WSJ’s same story, the news outlet reported that with nine 60 Minutes Season 59 episodes that aired between September 9 and November 16, the show averaged 8.3 million viewers. That number marked a 16 percent drop from last season, and there’s further nuance to this decline as well. What’s been specifically noted is that the news program has seen a 25 percent decrease in the ever-so-crucial 25-54 demographic.

Why 60 Minutes Veteran Lesley Stahl Is Supposedly Unhappy With CBS News’ Bari Weiss

As previously alluded to, Guy Camanile isn’t the only series veteran to have weighed in on this new era of the show. Months before the season began, fired correspondent Scott Pelley criticized Bari Weiss’ leadership and argued that CBS News needed “adult supervision.” For another fired employee, veteran correspondent Cecilia Vega, it “hurts to watch” the show carry on as it has. Vega also admitted to still finding it “disturbing” that she still didn’t know the exact reason why she was fired.

Insiders have made a plethora of claims about Bari Weiss, with some most recently claiming that the Free Press founder entered CBS like a “conquering hero.” Despite that, it’s alleged that times have changed due to the ratings struggles that have reportedly impacted shows like CBS Mornings and CBS Evening News as well. Reports still indicate, however, that Skydance chief David Ellison still has considerable confidence in Weiss’ ability to lead the Eye Network’s news branch.

For now, the viewing public will just have to wait and see whether the situation for 60 Minutes improves and what moves Bari Weiss makes next. It’ll also be interesting to see which other former CBS employees choose to weigh in on the matter. Viewers, meanwhile, can check out the show when it airs on Sundays at 7 p.m. ET on CBS amid the 2026 TV schedule.

#3388. If You Loved 'The Good Daughter,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

There are plenty of reasons Peacock’s The Good Daughter is so damn watchable. The performances, for one—Rose Byrne and Meghann Fahy are terrific as estranged sisters Sam and Charlotte Quinn. But it’s also a great story, tracing the corrosive effect of a years-ago trauma on the women and their lawyer father (Brendan Gleeson) amid the slow revelation of many extremely dark secrets. If you want more of that flavor of trauma-driven drama with a tight focus on family bonds, there’s one movie you should watch: 2015's Dark Places.

You want buried secrets? Dark Places has seriously buried secrets. Adapted from the Gillian Flynn novel, the film follows Libby Day (Charlize Theron), who survived the mass murder of her family in 1985. The crime is blamed on her brother Ben, a moody loner whose conviction was based in large part on Libby’s own testimony. For a long time, Libby is financially sustained by donations from people who sympathize with her plight, but three decades after the murders, the money has dried up, and Libby is desperate—so desperate, she agrees to help out a “true crime” club that believes her brother is innocent and is working toward his release.

Like The Good Daughter, Dark Places is anchored by a sibling relationship reshaped by the impact of horrifying violence. Libby and Ben’s experience mirrors Sam and Charlie’s in many ways, including in the way both Libby and Ben carry secrets for years after the terrible events that took family from them. The stories are also both compelling mysteries, slowly revealing the shocking truths behind one horrific night, and ultimately allowing the characters to better understand one another.

Dark Places also explores the insular, suffocating nature of small-town life, and how rumor and gossip become a poisonous presence in people’s lives. Libby, Ben, Sam, and Charlie all have to deal with others' assumptions and revelations that they've been betrayed by those closest to them, leading to powerful resolutions. If you loved The Good Daughter, you’ll love this movie. Stream Dark Places on The Roku Channel or Kanopy, or rent it on Prime Video.

Want more stories about family dynamics around secrets, violence, and explosive emotional confrontations? Here are a few more movies fans of The Good Daughter are bound to enjoy.

There’s no violent crime at the heart of this slow-burn drama—just an explosive chaos agent named Kym, played by Anne Hathaway. If your favorite aspect of The Good Daughter was the relationship between sisters Sam and Charlie, then this movie is perfect. Released from rehab to attend her sister’s wedding, Kym is self-hating, angry, and haunted by a terrible event from her childhood. Her sister, Rachel (Rosemary DeWitt), is welcoming, but has never truly forgiven Kym, and the simmering tension between the sisters and the rest of the family drives a drama that you won’t be able to look away from. Stream Rachel Getting Married on Apple TV or rent it on Prime Video.

If you really vibed on the Southern setting, the slow-burn mystery, and the exploration of flawed justice in the modern age depicted in The Good Daughter, check out Where the Crawdads Sing. It’s a slower, dreamier rumination on rural life, violence and its cost, and small-town justice, but it hits the same sweet spot in its story about a woman named Kya (Daisy Edgar-Jones) who was raised in an isolated house in the swamps of North Carolina. Accused in 1969 of a murder, Kya’s story stretches back to her childhood, when she’s slowly abandoned by her entire family, leaving her at age seven to survive on her own. Ostracized as the “swamp girl” by the town, Kya fights to live her life and be loved while facing the unwanted—and violently persistent—attention of the murder victim. It’s about broken families, deeply buried secrets, and what we do to survive. Stream Where the Crawdads Sing on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

The Good Daughter is about life in a small, Southern town, family trauma, and the legal system—which makes A Time to Kill the perfect movie to watch when you finish the show. When a Black man’s daughter is sexually assaulted in Mississippi and her attackers—local members of the Ku Klux Klan—look likely to go free, he violently and publicly murders them. Local lawyer Jake Brigance (Matthew McConaughey) takes on the case, assisted by law student Ellen Roark (Sandra Bullock). They face violent opposition, withering racism, and an unfair legal system that echoes the environment in The Good Daughter in ways fans will appreciate. Stream A Time to Kill on YoutTube or rent it on Prime Video.

The Dry might be as close as you can get to The Good Daughter in terms of tone and story. Although set in Australia instead of the American South, The Dry is a story driven by past crimes and buried secrets in a rural setting just like the show. Twenty years ago, Federal agent Aaron Falk (Eric Bana) fled his hometown when he was suspected of the murder of his girlfriend. When his childhood friend, Luke, appears to have murdered his wife and young son before killing himself, he returns to investigate. The slow revelation of two mysteries—one in the past and one simmering in the drought-stricken present—makes this an ideal companion film to the show. Stream The Dry on The Roku Channel, Kanopy, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

Set in Boston instead of the South, and focused on male friendships instead of a sisters’ bond, Mystic River nevertheless nails the same atmosphere of dread as The Good Daughter. In 1975, boyhood friends Jimmy, Dave, and Sean are traumatized when Dave is abducted and assaulted by two men. In 1990, the three men remain connected in their Boston neighborhood—Jimmy (Sean Penn) is an ex-convict still connected to local crime, Sean (Kevin Bacon) is a State Police detective, and Dave (Tim Robbins) is a blue-collar worker still haunted by his experience. When Jimmy’s daughter is found murdered and Dave seems implicated, Sean and Jimmy launch investigations from either side of the law, with Dave’s fate hanging in the balance. The ending is powerfully brutal, but this story of secrets and suspicion will resonate with fans of the show. Rent Mystic River on Prime Video.

#3387. Marlon Brando and Anna Kashfi’s Wedding: A Brief Romance and a Son Convicted of Manslaughter

Two years of marriage were enough for Marlon Brando and Anna Kashfi. After marrying in October 1957, the couple—the renowned actor and the up-and-coming actress—divorced in April 1959. But after the divorce decree, another long and dark journey would begin, one that would eventually end in tragedy. To understand the end of the story, however, it’s best to go back to the beginning. The couple first met at the Paramount Studio commissary in October 1955. That was the beginning of a doomed romance in which the 33-year-old movie star would get Kashfi, 10 years his junior, pregnant. When she said “I do,” she was two months pregnant.

At that time, according to Sarah Broughton, author of Brando’s Bride: The Incredibly True Story of Anna Kashfi and Her Marriage to One of Hollywood’s Greatest Stars, Brando had a known preference for women of Asian appearance. He had first gotten engaged to Kashfi almost a year earlier, around Thanksgiving 1956, but the relationship had had its ups and downs, and there had been no firm wedding plans made until they reconciled while he was filming The Young Lions, from June to mid-September 1957. After that, they decided to get married almost immediately.

It was a sunny day. On October 11, 1957, the couple celebrated their wedding at the Eagle Rock home of Betty Lindemeyer, Brando’s aunt, with an intimate gathering. Kashfi wanted a Buddhist ritual, and Brando, a Zen one. They ended up with neither and instead settled on a Protestant ceremony. It was the first wedding for both of them (others would follow). They had everything planned out; days earlier, they’d had a photo shoot, and as soon as their wedding reception ended, they would leave for their honeymoon.

The groom had worn a navy blue suit and a large opera cloak, which he soon had to take off because he wasn’t very adept at handling it and kept bumping into chairs, lamps, and potted plants, according to Broughton. On this momentous day, the bride wore a sari (some media outlets of the time described it as powder pink, while others described it as sea green) and a simple, sleek updo. Her choice of outfit may have been motivated by the fact that she had introduced herself to the American actor as a successful Indian film star. Just 24 hours after that “I do,” the British media revealed that the story wasn’t entirely true.

Kashfi’s résumé included very few films; she hadn’t been in Los Angeles very long when she met Brando. Now, after their wedding was a headline story around the world, a man named William O’Callaghan, who lived in Cardiff, Wales, claimed that she was his daughter, Joan (in other reports, Johanna or Joanna) O’Callaghan, and that she was not Indian. She had indeed been born in Calcutta but, he said, into a British family, and she had spent much of her life in Cardiff (she was 13 when the family left India). Before moving to Hollywood, she had worked as a cashier at a butcher shop. While the families of both of Kashfi’s parents had a long history in India, they were not Indian but British workers on the Indian Railways system. Kashfi did not have any Indian films to her name, and her only feature film experience was in a Spencer Tracy movie shot in 1955 and three other films in which she played supporting roles.

On May 11, 1958, Christian Brando, the couple’s only child together, was born, but the actor never forgave his wife for lying to him about her background, nor did he commit himself to their marriage. The relationship grew increasingly turbulent and ended in divorce in April 1959. While their marriage ended at that point, a tumultuous and public decline, including a bitter custody battle, followed and was extensively covered in the press. The young British woman would come to regard her encounter with her ex-husband, who had won custody of Christian by claiming she abused alcohol and barbiturates, as a curse. “Marlon ruined my life,” she told the South Wales Echo. “The world may be mourning the loss of a brilliant actor, but personally he was a monster.”

It was well-known at the time that Brando had had a turbulent childhood and adolescence, with a dysfunctional family life. He went on to get married one more time, to Movita Castaneda, and had a 10-year relationship with Tarita Teriipaia. He had a total of 11 children, and in 1976 he told biographer Gary Carey, “Like a large number of men, I, too, have had homosexual experiences, and I’m not ashamed.” In 1991 his son Christian went to prison for killing Dag Drollet, the boyfriend of his half sister Cheyenne Brando, one of Marlon’s daughters with Teriipaia. Christian stated that Cheyenne had told him that Drollet had abused her, so Christian decided to confront him, drunk and armed. After a struggle, he shot Drollet. Christian pleaded guilty to voluntary manslaughter and was sentenced to 10 years in prison (he would serve five). Cheyenne would die by suicide in 1995. Christian died in 2008, at age 49, from double pneumonia, following a life marked by drug and alcohol abuse. Marlon Brando had already died four years earlier, in 2004. At Christian’s sentencing hearing, he stated, “Perhaps I failed as a father. There were things I could have done differently…I did the best I could.”

Originally published by Vanity Fair España.

#3386. Roger Ebert Named This Panned Nicolas Cage Thriller One Of The Best Sci-Fi Action Movies Ever

Most critics hated Alex Proyas' 2009 film "Knowing," and I haven't heard much mention of it in the years since its release. At the same time, it was something of a box office hit, and it even had Roger Ebert in its corner. Awarding the film four stars (out of four), Ebert called it "one of the best science fiction movies I've ever seen." Ebert was famously a sci-fi aficionado who often gave perfect ratings to unexpected examples of the genre, so his review is high praise indeed.

Looking over the premise, one might be able to intuit why so many critics rejected "Knowing." It's an ambitious and somewhat gonzo sci-fi thriller about John Koestler (Nicolas Cage), an astrophysics professor who finds a 50-year-old string of numbers that, when interpreted correctly, seemingly point to future disasters and cataclysms. Koestler tries to prevent said cataclysms, but he's unsuccessful. In other words, he bears the weight of knowing about the future, yet he's powerless to prevent it.

This is especially depressing when Koestler finds that the numbers predict the end of the world. But then, there's a twist leading to an ending that will likely catch most folks off-guard. I won't spoil what happens, but the movie's final shot is not one you would be able to predict.

As for Ebert, "Knowing" was philosophical catnip. "The plot," he wrote, "involves the most fundamental of all philosophical debates: Is the universe deterministic or random?" Heady stuff.

To offer a few more story details: The prophetic numbers in "Knowing" were written on a sheet of paper in 1959 by a young girl named Lucinda (Lara Robinson), and the paper was then buried at her elementary school, tucked into a time capsule. Eventually, in 2009, the capsule is dug up, and the prophetic papers find their way into the hands of Caleb (Chandler Canterbury), John Koestler's nine-year-old son.

When John looks at them, he finds that the numbers represent global coordinates, dates ... and death tolls. He lines up multiple lines of Lucinda's "code" with real-life disasters like 9/11 and Hurricane Katrina. And then additional disasters begin happening in line with the code, including a harrowing and predetermined plane crash.

John also finds that the papers are incomplete, discovering later that Lucinda's final numbers are scratched into the interior of a cabinet at Caleb's school. The final predicted death toll on the page reads "EE," which John takes to mean "everyone else." Shudder.

Roger Ebert, as mentioned, was impressed with the themes of "Knowing," writing that, "For Koestler, [the code] leads to a rejection of what he has always believed, to his acceptance of the paranormal." He added:

"With expert and confident storytelling, [director Alex] Proyas strings together events that keep tension at a high pitch all through the film. Even a few quiet, human moments have something coiling beneath. Pluck this movie, and it vibrates. Even something we've seen countless times, like a car pursuit, works here because of the meaning of the pursuit, and the high stakes."

More than anything, Roger Ebert felt that "Knowing" was thought-provoking. The film, after all, is a sci-fi thriller about the philosophy of predetermination, which is no small thing. As Ebert put it:

"You may have guessed from the TV ads that something very bad is unfolding for planet Earth, and you may ask, not unreasonably, how these two nice parents and their lovable kids can possibly have any effect on it. Ah, but that would be in a random universe, and 'Knowing' argues that the universe is deterministic. Or does it? Your papers will be due before class on Monday."

As mentioned, though, other critics really disliked "Knowing." Anthony Quinn, writing for The Independent, argued that "Alex Proyas directs with maximum portentousness, and [Nicolas] Cage pulls many angst-ridden expressions as he realizes doom might be at hand."  Quinn added that the special effects were unconvincing and "the big shock-and-awe finale is a throwback to the days of 'Deep Impact," (which, as one can guess from context, is meant to be a negative thing).

Basically, most critics felt "Knowing" was implausible, silly, and smacked of unearned portentousness. It was only a viewer like Ebert who loved the portent and the philosophical underpinnings therein.

Personally, I'm more on Ebert's side. "Knowing" has a few wild images in its climax, but I admire its hugeness. If one is going to tell a sci-fi story, why not fold in enormous themes of predetermination, Biblical prophecy, and the ultimate fate of humankind? There's no reason why sci-fi movies can't juggle big-picture questions, following their premises to logical extremes. "Knowing" does that, and it's fair to say it has a lot on its mind.

#3385. Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave’s Fan-Favorite Hero Is Definitely a Secret Vampire

Ever since the release of Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave back in September, fans of the series have been arguing about which of the Four Flame Lords they like best. For my money, it’s Dietrich. That’s mostly because his route features the best supporting cast (i.e. Fabio and Esmeralda) and includes the most lore that connects to Three Houses. I also prefer Dietrich because I’m 100% convinced that he is a vampire, even if Fortune’s Weave never comes out and says so explicitly. In honor of Polygon’s annual Fangsgiving extravaganza, here are five reasons why Dietrich is totally a vampire.

[Ed. note: Minor spoilers ahead for all of Dietrich’s Act One storyline.]

Dietrich has alabaster skin and flowing silver-gray hair. He consistently wears only black clothing (though with occasional purple, gray, and silver accents). When Nintendo gave players their first in-depth look at Fortune’s Weave back in August, viewers were quick to point out that the character bears a strong resemblance to Alucard, the son of Dracula in the Castlevania series. (Get it? Alucard is Dracula spelled backwards.) Both Dietrich and Alucard share the same flowing locks, dark clothing, and delicate, pale features. If this guy isn’t a bona-fide bloodsucker, he’s certainly a fan of cosplaying as one.

Though Fortune’s Weave never shows Dietrich chomping down on someone’s neck or drinking goblets of human blood, he sure does talk about the stuff a lot. Whenever he has a particularly strong level up, he will say, “My blood thunders.” Whenever he defeats an enemy, one of his zingers is, "My path is soaked in blood." For Dietrich, battle is inextricably linked with sensuality, indulgence, and blood. To him, the most challenging combat represents the ultimate pleasure.

This guy just loves killing people, like an accomplished composer loves music. We learn about his zeal for fighting in the route’s opening moments, and his motivation throughout Act One changes very little, with the exception of a dramatic twist in Chapter 12. But in Acts Two and Three, he’s back to his same ol’ shtick of thirsting for blood on the battlefield.

Dietrich’s bloodlust is explicitly connected to being a member of the Lamine family line. It’s an inherited curse he shares with Jeritza from Three Houses. That’s because the Crest of Lamine traces its origins back to the blood of a Nabatean dragon during the War of Heroes. In other words, you can’t talk about House Lamine without talking about blood.

Many of Dietrich’s unique combat skills involve words like, “blood,” “beast,” and “shadow,” all terms strongly associated with vampires. His highly useful Blaze Art, Moving Shadow, allows him to cover additional spaces on the battlefield, letting him close the gap with enemies quickly. Though it’s not a universal rule, there are plenty of pop-culture examples of vampires having superhuman speed, like in the Twilight movies and The Vampire Diaries.

What’s more, one of Dietrich’s passive abilities, Ever Vigilant, restores a small amount of HP every time Dietrich defeats an enemy with a critical hit. Given his high dexterity and critical rate, this is an ability that triggers quite often. In any given battle, Dietrich is frequently restoring himself with the blood of his foes.

In addition to being cursed with unquenchable bloodlust, descendants of House Lamine are notorious for being really, really attractive. Though almost every character in Fortune’s Weave is conspicuously good-looking, everyone Dietrich meets is completely stunned by his beauty. Young, old, male, female — nobody is immune to this man’s charms.

Vampires combine forbidden desire, danger, and intense pleasure in a way few other monsters do. They live forever, or at least substantially longer than normal mortals. They could offer immortality to you, too, but you have to be willing to submit to their unholy desires. Vampires are intrinsically sexy in a way that supernatural creatures like ghosts or goblins simply are not. The fact that people are consistently thrown off-balance by Dietrich’s good looks is our best evidence that he is, indeed, a vampire.

During one of their support conversations, Fabio offers to change to a different body if Dietrich would prefer it. (Fabio is an Agarthan, a descendant of a super-advanced interstellar civilization in the lore of Three Houses and Fortune’s Weave, and they can just do stuff like that.) Dietrich dismisses the idea, telling Fabio, “The things I esteem are strength and purity. Nothing else. What form they take is irrelevant. Man or woman… it is the same to me.” Throughout the game, Dietrich develops a romantic closeness to both Fabio and Esmeralda. Though the two rivals bicker over who he prefers, Fortune’s Weave allows both relationships to coexist.

Of course, not all vampires are bisexual. But a lot of them are, especially after Anne Rice’s hugely influential Interview With the Vampire franchise. Ever since Victorian times, all that ambiguity about blood drinking as a metaphor for sex has made space for queerness. There are several reasons for this. Vampires are very attractive to pretty much everyone. They also have a lot of time to kill, being immortal and all. Living forever gets pretty dull, so why not try something new? In other words, Dietrich’s nonchalance about the gender of his paramours might be surprising in the context of a Nintendo Switch game, but it’s also perfectly in character.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

A Survivor 51 Castaway Is Not Pleased With Jeff Probst And Called Him Out On Social

Survivor changed the TV world forever when it debuted back in 2000, and it's still going strong to this day. The Open Era is officially here as we watch the whopping 51st season on CBS (and streaming with a Paramount+ subscription), but fans are already looking to Season 52 in the spring. Namely because the competition series is extending each episode to 2 hours long moving forward. If I'm going to be forced to dedicate this amount of time on a weekly basis, there are a few major changes that I think need to happen to make it work.

While fans constantly wonder how much Survivor contestants make, I haven't seen the fandom very excited for Season 52 to give us 2-hour-long episodes. As a superfan myself, I think there are a few ways that future seasons might be able to win folks over and make the new runtime worth the watch. Hear me out.

I think the most obvious change that the competition series needs to make for these 2-hour-long episodes is to extend how long the game lasts. During COVID, the show went from 39 days to just 26, presumably to accommodate the quarantine period that the cast, crew, and production team needed to go under after arriving in Fiji. Jeff Probst made it clear that this change would be permanent, meaning that basically every single day of the game has a challenge and a trip to Tribal Council.

Longtime fans have been complaining about this format change for years. Namely because it's much harder for contestants to form real bonds when they're subjected to a constant barrage of twists and Tribals. Days off allow for new plans and alliances to form, and can also help the contestants properly whip the votes ahead of time. If we're getting longer episodes every week, why not extend the game's length as well? Even if it's not a full 39 days, I'd love if it even went up to 30. Let's split the difference, Jeff.

I'd also love to see more Reward Challenges, separate from the ones where contestants fight for Immunity. More challenges mean more losses, which can often create drama or inspire a change of strategy during the pre-merge part of the game. Having reward challenges can also make way for the return of beloved ones like the gross food challenge or the Survivor auction, which used to happen every single season during the best Survivor seasons.

Personally, I think that it's about time that we saw the return of the Loved Ones' visit as well. The Family Visit created tons of memorable moments during the show's heyday, and it usually ended up making me cry (and creating drama) in the process. This has also been missing since the New Era, and I think that the 2-hour episodes could free up time to include them.

Finally, I would like to see more of camp life on Survivor. With so many twists and turns happening every single episode, we get way less of this in newer seasons. I want to see which contestants are getting on each other's nerves, and some interpersonal drama outside of actual gameplay. After all, the show started largely as a social experiment.

Survivor airs new episodes on Wednesdays on CBS as part of the 2026 TV schedule. Fingers crossed that some changes are coming to the game starting in Season 51, because two hours is a ton of time to fill.

#3382. December 2026 Movie Releases: Avengers: Doomsday, Dune: Part Three And More

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Looking back, 2026 has been a relatively strong year for movies, from indie darlings to the occasional well-crafted blockbuster. The best movies of 2026 so far represent a wide diversity in stellar cinematic output that have thrilled audiences worldwide. Of course, the year isn't over yet, and there are plenty of eagerly anticipated movies set to premiere throughout December 2026. We're taking a look ahead at the widely hyped and most exciting movies set to debut in the final weeks of 2026, each looking to end the year strong.

Some of the most ambitious movies of the whole year are set to make their wide theatrical release in December. We've gathered them up along with the smaller production titles that still have people buzzing ahead of their premiere. We're providing all the major details that we know about these movies so far, why we're excited, and when you can expect to see each of them.

These are the biggest December 2026 movie releases, including "Avengers: Doomsday", "Dune: Part Three," and more.

If you were hoping Pedro Pascal to get more dramatic movie fare to dig into than his usual lead roles, "Behemoth!" gives his truly juicy material to work with. Pascal stars as Alex Serian, a celebrated cellist who arrives in Los Angeles to record movie scores. This leads to Serian contemplating his life, particularly his family and the various women that he's been involved with in his life. The movie, which explores the perspective of a tortured creative figure, is written, directed, and produced by filmmaker Tony Gilroy.

Pedro Pascal finds his perfect star role in "Behemoth!," really showcasing what he's capable of dramatically when the movie had its premiere at the New York Film Festival. While Alex Serian may be an emotionally detached figure on the surface, Pascal imbues his character with an enormous depth that eventually bursts free. Gilroy punctuates this introspective story with flashbacks that allow us to see what it is that makes the protagonist tick. A mature, character-driven look at the musical side of the entertainment industry, "Behemoth!" features a strong pairing between Gilroy and Pascal that audiences should see with the movie's wide release.

After partnering up with Netflix, filmmaker Brad Bird is set to deliver a stylish neo-noir animated movie with "Ray Gunn." A longtime passion project for Bird, the movie's eponymous protagonist, played by Sam Rockwell, is a private detective in an alternate 1939 with extraterrestrials living among humanity. Gunn is drawn into a mystery involving pop star Venus Nova (Scarlett Johansson) that escalates to scandal and murder. The movie features sweeping Art Deco cityscapes along with retrofuturistic technologies as Gunn uncovers a larger scheme.

"Ray Gunn" technically had its premiere on October 10 at the BFI London Film Festival, where it was heralded as a heartfelt, visually dazzling marvel. Following this, the movie will open in select theaters on December 4, before becoming available to stream on Netflix on December 18. The movie showcases Bird's penchant for mid-century retro sci-fi with a moodier quality than his Disney and Pixar work. One of the most eagerly anticipated animated movies of the year, "Ray Gunn" is right in Bird's creative wheelhouse.

Four years after its 2022 release, "Violent Night" has become a violent action movie must-watch on Netflix. Its sequel "Violent Night 2" is shaping up to double down on the brutal yuletide carnage as Santa Claus (David Harbour) learns he's been placed on the naughty list. With his wintry magic taken away, Santa has to fend for himself as he contends with a local mob boss (Jared Harris). Fortunately, Santa is not alone, with Kristen Bell and her big sword coming to save Santa as Mrs. Claus this time around.

After making his feature directorial debut with 2022's "When You Finish Saving the World," Jesse Eisenberg's third movie that he's helmed is "The Debut." A musical comedy that Eisenberg also wrote and produced, the movie centers on amateur actor Mona Friedman (Julianne Moore). After being cast in a local theater production in a supporting role, Mona lets the role gradually overtake her life as an unassuming New Jersey housewife. Pushing Mona in the production to work on her performance is renowned theater director Jerry Blankenbuehler (Paul Giamatti), driving this instability.

"The Debut" had its premiere at Telluride Film Festival this past September before landing its wide theatrical release on December 11. The movie itself offers a deflating approach to the transformatively self-important world of actors, particularly within the realm of local theater productions. With Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti headlining the ensemble, the production is a showcase for its impressive cast. Featuring Eisenberg at his most winkingly self-deprecatory towards the craft, "The Debut" is a sharply performed good time at the movies.

British filmmaker Danny Boyle examines tabloid journalism, a term that we use loosely, with his latest movie "Ink." The movie has editor Larry Lamb (Jack O'Connell) hired by Rupert Murdoch (Guy Pearce) to revamp the newspaper The Sun to drive up its readership in the 1960s. Lamb assembles a team to help with this transformation and resorts to increasingly more underhanded methods to break stories. This informs the trajectory of mass media consumption for decades to follow, for better or worse.

After premiering at the Venice International Film Festival this past September, "Ink" will open in select theaters on December 11. After its theatrical run, the movie will become available to stream on Netflix on January 8, but this is a story that deserves to be seen on the big screen. "Ink" is an industry origin story that will make you feel sick, as it delves into its lurid tale of lies, sex, and other forms of bad behavior. A deep dive into the media's own heart of darkness, "Ink" follows bad people doing bad things for public consumption.

Given that "Spider-Man: Brand New Day" was distributed by Sony, the only other Marvel Studios movie release of 2026 is "Avengers: Doomsday." The culmination of the Marvel Cinematic Universe so far, the movie has universes collide as the multiverse comes under threat. Based on the promotional materials seen so far, including official "Avengers: Doomsday" concept art, Fox's X-Men are set to meet two different Avengers squads and the recent MCU Fantastic Four. The movie also fully introduces Doctor Doom (Robert Downey Jr.), who is poised to be the greatest supervillain any of these teams have ever known.

After a string of lackluster Marvel Studios projects and diminishing box office returns, it feels like the MCU is betting it all on "Avengers: Doomsday." The movie boasts one of the largest MCU casts assembled for a single project yet, with many of the details still tightly held under wraps. Reportedly, "Avengers: Doomsday" test screenings praise Downey's Doctor Doom, so we're cautiously optimistic about the grandiose production. With a wide U.S. release set for December 18, "Avengers: Doomsday" will prepare audiences for its 2027 follow-up "Avengers: Secret Wars" and the future of the entire MCU.

The only other major studio movie set to open directly opposite "Avengers: Doomsday" is "Dune: Part Three." The conclusion of filmmaker Denis Villeneuve's trilogy, the movie adapts the 1969 novel "Dune Messiah" by franchise creator Frank Herbert. Picking up from Paul Atreides (Timothée Chalamet) seizing control of the Imperium in 2024's "Dune: Part Two," the sequel has Paul brutally assert his control over the cosmos. As Paul contends with his bloody legacy, he finds himself reunited with familiar faces and a sweeping conspiracy threatening his rule.

"Dune: Part Three" confirms Paul Atreides was the villain all along, set to make the movie the darkest of the trilogy. The film boasts an all-star cast, like its predecessors, including more prominent roles for Florence Pugh, Anya Taylor-Joy, and the return of Jason Momoa. The movie is also expected to bring plenty of sci-fi spectacle, with its trailer teasing fierce rebellions and rain-soaked battles. Poised to bring a moody, epic finish to Villeneuve's ambitious adaptations, "Dune: Part Three" will hopefully stick the landing to a heartily entertaining trilogy.

It's been a minute since the Angry Birds crossed the silver screen, but somehow the video game property has returned after a seven-year hiatus. "The Angry Birds Movie 3" reunites the main voice cast, including Jason Sudeikis and Rachel Bloom as the red and silver birds, respectively. Red and Silver are now the proud parents of three birds who are growing up quickly. As the couple try to raise their children as they progress into their rambunctious teenage years, they must contend with a new threat to their world.

"The Angry Birds Movie 3" is one of those movies that feels like a safe holiday season release, with a dose of wacky humor. There may be fans who have been waiting for a new movie in the series for the past seven years and they're sure to be thrilled. Looking back at its predecessors, the past movies in the series have been occasionally inspired and generally tolerable. Hopefully, "The Angry Birds Movie 3" can continue that trend as it brings back its avian adventurers for a more family-focused story.

Another biopic following a polemical figure coming out in December is "Artificial," which focuses on Sam Altman. With Altman played by Andrew Garfield, the movie traces the rise of OpenAI, where Altman holds the role of CEO. The company's rise has Altman butt heads with OpenAI's co-founder Ilya Sutskever (Yura Borisov) over the safety and risks associated with artificial intelligence. Other pivotal figures in the legacy of OpenAI appear throughout the film, including co-founder Elon Musk, who is played by Ike Barinholtz.

"Artificial" premiered at the New York Film Festival this past October, and after being ditched by its initial distributor, Amazon MGM Studios, it has been picked up by Neon. Directed by Luca Guadagnino, the movie is poised to become this generation's "The Social Network" in a year that also saw the release of a disappointing, flat sequel to the 2010 film. The movie already appears to be making several of its subjects uneasy with its depiction of them, to say the least. That controversy alone certainly has our curiosity piqued to see how Guadagnino depicts the rise of AI.

We're not sure how many people were anticipating another "Jumanji" movie, but we've got another installment in the action-adventure comedy franchise coming to theaters. Opening on Christmas Day, the movie reunites the main cast from the revival trilogy that began in 2017. Picking up from the ending of 2019's "The Next Level," "Jumanji: Open World" has the video game avatars enter the real world. This leads the human characters who previously inhabited the avatars in the game to try to find a way to return them to their digital homes.

Look, if you're a fan of the preceding entries in the revival trilogy and enjoy the comedic pairing of Dwayne Johnson and Kevin Hart, "Jumanji: Open World" is for you. Beyond those two, it's genuinely nice seeing Jack Black and Karen Gillan back in action as the other video game avatars. The reverse fish-out-of-water premise also provides a fresh twist to the usual gaming antics that these movies provide while retaining its goofy sense of humor. More of a comfort watch for fans than anything else, "Jumanji: Open World" is the safe, family-friendly viewing option this Christmas.

As he had with 2024's "Nosferatu," filmmaker Robert Eggers is set to provide audiences with a very different kind of Christmas movie this year with "Werwulf." The werewolf movie reunites Eggers with collaborators Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Lily-Rose Depp, Willem Dafoe, and Robert Ineson for more monstrous mayhem. Set in 14th century England, Eggers heightens the historical authenticity by having his cast speak in Middle English. To build the unsettling mood, Eggers strives for a darker and grainier cinematography compared to the more operatic presentation in "Nosferatu."

Based on its first trailer, "Werwulf" looks like a perfect companion piece to "Nosferatu" and its stylish scares. The movie retains Eggers' penchant for heavy atmosphere but with an even grimmer tone than much of his past work. Though plot details are still being quietly withheld ahead of its premiere, the movie is set to take full advantage of its medieval setting. The release of every Eggers movie still feels like an event and "Werwulf" is looking to continue that horrific trend.

#3381. I Tried Coros' New 'Expedition-Focused' Smartwatch, and I'm Impressed

Coros has unveiled the Vertix 4, an “expedition-focused” update to the Vertix 2 and 2S. Coros says it pairs the brand's brightest display yet with long battery life, and after unboxing it myself, I can definitely say it has a more refined feel that could indeed suit the office as well as the summit.

This watch is being marketed as a major step up from the Vertix 2S, with an AMOLED display, a more refined design, satellite maps and, for the first time on a Coros watch, a built-in flashlight. The Vertix 4 will be available to buy starting on Black Friday, Nov. 27, but it won't exactly be at a discount: It costs $799, a $100 increase over the Vertix 2S.

That price does still undercut the latest Garmin Fenix 9 line-up, which starts at $999, though some rivals are cheaper still. For instance, the Suunto Vertical 2 steel model costs $599, and the Garmin Fenix 8 is currently on sale for $749.99 at Amazon.

I've only just started testing the Vertix 4 and haven't even had enough time to get through its substantial battery life, but I can share some first impressions, particularly in how it compares with the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro that launched earlier this year.

Built-in flashlights have become a must-have feature on premium sports watches, and now the Vertix 4 is the first Coros watch to get one. Coros has departed from the usual layout, though. Garmin, Suunto and Amazfit put the light on top of the watch, but Coros places it on the side, between the digital dial and the back button.

Previous Vertix watches used a memory-in-pixel (MIP) display. MIP has advantages, most notably longer battery life, but I know I much prefer the vibrant display on AMOLED screens, like on the Vertix 4. It is the biggest visual change and a large part of why the watch looks more premium than its predecessors.

Coros claims up to 30 days in watch mode, or 10 days with the screen always on. It also quotes 48 hours of multi-band GPS tracking with the screen always on. I haven't had time to test these claims properly, so stay tuned.

Coros watches are high-quality sports watches, but don't expect to find all the little lifestyle features you've come to expect on a more traditional smartwatch:

Music: It can store tracks, but only files you drag and drop onto the watch. It doesn't pair with streaming services.

Payments: There is no NFC payment support.

Watch faces: Customization is more limited than on rivals.

On paper, the Vertix 4 looks like a significant upgrade: a better display, a more attractive design, a flashlight and satellite maps, at a price well below the Fenix 9 line-up. The $100 increase and cheaper alternatives like the Suunto Vertical 2 and discounted Fenix 8 will matter to some buyers, as will the limited smart features.

#3380. Shrek 5 Teaser Officially Reveals New Look, and Fans Are Divided

It seems Shrek 5's animation style isn't for everybody

Shrek 5 was announced in the summer of 2024 and initially scheduled to release in July 2026. After a couple of delays, DreamWorks settled on a summer 2027 launch for Shrek 5. With only a few months to go until its release, fans are eager to learn more about how life has been treating the inhabitants of the swamp.

In previous trailers, we got to see the main cast, including Shrek, Fiona, Donkey, and the triplets, alongside secondary characters such as Pinocchio and Gingerbread Man. Many fans weren't happy with the tweaks made to these classic characters in favor of a more modern animation style. While the redesign has grown on some, it's still a divisive discussion among the community. Shrek 5's latest teaser, which provided a first look at even more characters, only made matters worse.

In the new Shrek 5 teaser, Shrek arrives at the swamp in the iconic onion carriage. As it comes to a stop, several characters jump out, namely Fiona, the triplets, Pinocchio, Big Bad Wolf, the Three Little Pigs, the Three Blind Mice, Gingerbread Man (accompanied by two Gingerbread Ladies), Dragon, and Donkey. It included several characters that had remained unseen until now.

Fans immediately ran to the comments section to discuss the redesigned appearance of these returning characters. While some noted that the new animation style had won them over, others couldn't get past it and pointed out how strange the characters looked.The Big Bad Wolf and the Three Little Pigs were the main focus of discussion. The wolf's fur has a different texture and color; he has a hunchback, and his snout is considerably slimmer, making him somewhat look like Death from Puss in Boots: The Last Wish. As for the pigs, their skin is a much brighter pink, and their stomachs are huge, giving them a completely different appearance. Although the changes are less noticeable on the mice because of their small size, they have larger stomachs and ears, and their legs are barely noticeable.

It's evident that there was a major time jump between Shrek Forever After and Shrek 5; the last time we saw the triplets, they were toddlers, and now they're fully grown teenagers. Therefore, it's possible that the difference in appearance isn't only because of the new animation style but also because the characters have aged significantly.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3379. Cowboy Bebop's Co-Creator Directed This Underrated Blade Runner Anime Short Film

Japanese filmmaker Shinichirō Watanabe is one of the most acclaimed directors in the field of animation, especially for directing "Cowboy Bebop." Watanabe was one of the co-creators of the series, with the creation credited to Studio Sunrise's shared pseudonym Hajime Yatate. His eclectic inspirations from film noir to science fiction made "Cowboy Bebop" a glorious lightning in a bottle.

Watanabe's other directing credits include historical road trip series "Samurai Champloo," the sci-fi comedy "Space Dandy," and futuristic spy thriller "Lazarus" (boasting action designed by "John Wick" director Chad Stahelski). One of Watanabe's more obscure works took him into the "Blade Runner" universe.

In 2017, ahead of "Blade Runner 2049" arriving in theaters, three short prequel films were released showing key moments in the 30-year time lapse after the original "Blade Runner." Watanabe's short, the only animated one, depicts the "Blackout" — the electro-magnetic pulse that hit Los Angeles in 2022, destroying most digital records (such as the identities of replicants) and leading to a temporary termination of replicant production. The short, titled "Blade Runner Black Out 2022," is available to watch on the Warner Bros.' YouTube channel.

"Blade Runner Black Out 2022" follows two Nexus 8 replicants, Iggy Cygnus (Jovan Jackson) and Trixie (Luci Christian), who orchestrate the Blackout. The short runs about 15 minutes long, but in that time it explores the plight of the replicants while still saving room for Watanabe's trademark martial arts-inspired action. The score, composed by Flying Lotus, blends the sweeping synth of "Blade Runner" with the jazzier music typical of Watanabe's anime.

The short comes with an introduction from "Blade Runner 2049" director Denis Villeneuve, who says he asked artists he admired to make the three shorts. Watching "Blade Runner 2049," it does feel plausible that Villeneuve is a "Cowboy Bebop" fan.

Many viewers have noted how the ending of "Blade Runner 2049" mirrors the famously ambiguous ending of "Cowboy Bebop." Agent K (Ryan Gosling) lies down, possibly dead, on a stairwell just like Spike Spiegel does in the last scene of "Cowboy Bebop." Both men are probably dead but the scene stops just short of outright confirming that.

Rendering the world of "Blade Runner" in anime fits because there's a lot of Asian influence in this cyberpunk future. There are giant billboards showing geishas, neon signs written in Japanese, Rick Deckard (Harrison Ford) eats at a noodle cart, etc.  Los Angeles 2022 is so culturally intertwined there's a whole new dialect, Cityspeak, mixing together Japanese and various European languages. In "Black Out 2022," returning character Gaff (Edward James Olmos) briefly talks in Cityspeak.

Watanabe directing a "Blade Runner" anime is also recursive, because he's cited the original "Blade Runner" film as one of his influences for "Cowboy Bebop." You can tell he's a fan with how "Black Out 2022" goes about recreating "Blade Runner." There's the same Los Angeles skyline with the Tyrell Corporation's pyramids, the same dark and smoky LAPD office filled with blue light peeking in through the window blinds, etc. Speaking to IGN in 2017, Watanabe explained "Blade Runner" hit very big in Japan.

"When it was released in the 80s in Japan, 'Blade Runner' was actually a series that influenced the Japanese media very much so. I assume that everyone in the anime industry has seen 'Blade Runner' at some point. Pretty much all of the special effects style sci-fi movies or series out there starting looking a lot like 'Blade Runner.'"

Indeed, the future of "Cowboy Bebop" resembles "Blade Runner"; both are noir/sci-fi hybrids.

There's no androids in "Cowboy Bebop," but as in "Blade Runner," humanity has begun colonizing other worlds because Earth isn't in great shape anymore. The result in both is an Asian-heavy cultural melting pot. The Bebop crew are bounty hunters similar to Rick Deckard. The lead villain of "Cowboy Bebop," ruthless gangster Vicious, carries himself in a similar way to Roy Batty (Rutger Hauer), and even has white hair. Except, amusingly, the replicant Batty has much more of a human soul than Vicious does.

In his interview with IGN, Watanabe said his first idea for a "Blade Runner" anime was a short focusing on Roy Batty, but "the owner of the whole entire franchise wanted to have something that connects the first and second films, and because Roy dies in the first movie, I wasn't able to pass that through. It was a rejected idea." Thus, his short became "Blade Runner Black Out 2022."

"Cowboy Bebop" shares its philosophical side with "Blade Runner." Compare Batty regretting that all his memories will be lost like "tears in the rain" with Spike's dying lover, Julia, telling him, "It's all a dream." Just as "Blade Runner" leaves its big questions open (especially whether Deckard is an unknowing replicant), "Cowboy Bebop" makes its viewers fill in most of the blanks about its characters' pasts.

"Black Out 2022" squeezes in some similar musing when Trixie asks if replicants get to Heaven when they die. Even in a movie shorter than a single "Cowboy Bebop" episode, her silent yearning hits hard. Watanabe would later produce a 13-episode anime, "Blade Runner: Black Lotus," but if you want a bite-sized experience of what he can do in the "Blade Runner" universe, watch "Black Out 2022."
