We just witnessed a profound moment in the Percy Jackson series, and I have chills. The latest episode marks the official halfway point in Rick Riordan’s original five-book arc where our characters really have to grow up, and I think the series nailed it. Of course, I’m talking about the death of Bianca di Angelo (played by Olive Abercrombie) in the Junkyard of the Gods. CinemaBlend had to talk to the cast about filming the emotional sequence, and they offered some poignant thoughts on the subject.

Percy Jackson actor Walker Scobell admitted filming the scene, for him anyway, was “quick” because the production was “running out of time” that day. As he recalled:

The weirdest thing happened where I couldn't, like, fully process it because I've never done anything like that before. I hope that it works, but I literally couldn't cry or feel that sad. I was just really thinking about how it's kind of my fault and then I promised Nico and, it was just... I don't know. I was just kind of in shock and then I pumpkined, and then I went right home. So, it was a really weird day for me.

The scene is a particularly difficult one for his character, Percy Jackson, because he’s the one who Nico specifically asked to keep her safe. But there’s nothing he could do because Bianca chose to risk her life to save her fellow quest mates. This is the first time in the series where a major character has died, and she’s just 12 years old. It’s certainly a moment that we just know is going to inform the rest of the season.

In our interview, Tamara Smart, who plays Thalia, echoed my own thoughts when she commented that Scobell’s own experience with the scene is “apt” because it’s probably similar to how Percy experiences the death himself. Smart added that Abercrombie became a “true part of the group” during the couple of weeks it took to film the episodes prior to her character’s death. So, it was hard to lose her on the show even though the actress came back to visit. In Smart’s words:

I think it was just a heartbreaking day, and we ended up taking selfies later in the day, which I'll post at some point because they're hilarious. But she was brilliant. She was so, so good, and it was so sad in the best of ways.

She was a woman of her word, too. You can check out the selfie on the third slide of her latest Instagram post. It sounds like the cast had time to make light of a rough day – as they should. However, they were really affected by Abercrombie’s performance that day. Scobell said he felt like he was watching Bianca try to live and then “accept” her fate. Then, Smart brought this up:

I mean, also in the books, we don't find her ever. And so, that was a huge change that I found out personally from Dan [Shotz], and I was very upset about, because I was like, ‘This is traumatizing to all of us.’ It's far easier for someone to just disappear and be sad about it than to watch someone wither away in front of you. It's incredibly upsetting. And I think that just really solidifies the darkness this season.

The Percy Jackson series has had a lot of notable changes, many of them for the better, such as getting to see Annabeth’s journey this season. As Smart shared, she was actually “upset” with the decision for the group to witness Bianca’s death. In the book, it’s a lot more PG because they never find her body after she saves the group.

Personally, I think Percy Jackson has earned a scene like this, and just as the Harry Potter movies got darker as the kids got older, it feels like the right time for the show to up the stakes – including through Percy and Annabeth’s “slow burn” romance. I’m on the edge of my seat about how Nico and the rest of the characters are going to move forward after this scene. It was absolutely heartbreaking, and I’m in awe of how this show pulled off this emotional yet beautiful sequence.

The next two episodes of Percy Jackson and the Olympians are slated on the 2026 TV schedule to drop next Friday, December 4.

#3377. ‘All of a Sudden’: Why Does an 11-Minute Scene Centered on a Whiteboard Lecture Work So Well Onscreen?

It is an unorthodox sequence. In the middle of “All of a Sudden,” Mari (Tao Okamoto) pulls out a whiteboard and markers to diagram the principles of nature vs. capitalism for her new friend Marie-Lou (Virginie Efira). The scene lasts 11 minutes and digs into material you would expect in a university seminar, not the latest cinematic achievement from the Oscar-winning director of “Drive My Car,” Ryūsuke Hamaguchi.

While a guest on this week’s Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Hamaguchi acknowledged the whiteboard is not what we generally consider to be cinematic, but then again neither is the three-hour-and-17-minute film about two women who form a powerful bond by talking about life, their life’s work, and the ever so sexy topic of eldercare for dementia patients. Related Stories ‘Odyssey’ Cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema Was More Interested in the Intimate Than the Epic Forget Photorealism: How ‘Wildwood’ Made Its Handmade Digital Artistry Visible

And yet “All of a Sudden” blew away the world’s toughest critics at Cannes. Now, its distributor, Neon, heads into this weekend’s holiday theatrical release believing it has a legit shot at winning over the more commercially oriented Oscar voters — and becoming one of the (increasingly common) foreign-language Best Picture nominations. Neon similarly released “Sentimental Value” and “The Secret Agent” to Best Picture nominations the year before.

The whiteboard scene is not an extraneous aside, but a critical turning point in the women’s relationship. We asked the film’s writer/director why it not only works, but was deemed vital to the film.

“In trying to answer why this somehow works, I think there’s a few layers to it,” said Hamaguchi while on IndieWire’s Filmmaker Toolkit podcast. “And one maybe is because it really is something that is far removed from what is generally considered as cinematic. Perhaps because of that, it brings about a certain suspense, where you wonder, ‘OK, what is this for? What is this actually going to do?’ And there’s a certain sense of wondering that happens.”

The scene comes a little over an hour into the film. Neither woman wants their magical evening to end. Mari follows Marie-Lou to her job as director of a nursing home, where she struggles to implement her passion project, “Huminitude,” a patient-centered care method based on touch and eye contact, which Mari sees in action. What prompts Mari’s whiteboard seminar is an attempt to help her new companion put into perspective the resistance she faces in implementing Huminitude and open the door to problem-solving.

“I think the second part [of why the scene works] really comes down to the efforts of the actors that are performing this scene,” said Hamaguchi of Okamoto and Efira, who shared the Best Actress Prize at Cannes. “For Tao, I think it was an incredibly difficult scene to perform because first of all she really needed to understand all of the concepts that she was describing here and to really understand everything intellectually. And so in her preparation she did read a lot of the relevant books to really understand what she is talking about.”

Hamaguchi believes the key to his dialogue-driven film is not necessarily how the words are spoken, but the performance of the listening and how the words are received. In Efira’s whiteboard scene, we see a shift from determined frustration to open enthusiasm that changes the direction of the film itself.

“The attitude of listening that Virginie portrays in this moment, I think, is very important and really supports this scene,” said Hamaguchi. “She’s not uninterested in what is going on, but in fact she feels that this is something that she should really be exploring together and she’s there and very much present. And I think this attitude of interest and curiosity really starts to work on the audience as well. And so in that sense I think ultimately this scene really works because of the actors’ performances.”

One topic that comes up in most post-screening Q&As is that both actresses were not working in the native language. Hamaguchi himself had to work with an interpreter to direct his leads. This is not the first time Hamaguchi has worked this way. On the podcast, he said that, in his experience directing the play inside “Drive My Car,” the language barrier was less of a hindrance and could even aid actors in listening to one another, as shown in the whiteboard scene.

“I felt that, in fact, this kind of difficulty that exists can in fact provide an environment for even more heightened concentration than you might have if you were speaking the same language,” said Hamaguchi. “ I think that actually when you can actually hear a lot and get a lot of information from somebody’s voice, you can, in fact, precisely feel just how concentrated the person is when they’re saying something by listening to their voice.”

Asked if any of his collaborators or producers ever questioned the whiteboard scene after reading the script, Hamaguchi said no, and speculated why: “Because it’s so unusual, I think people understood that this is something that I really wanted to do.”

“There were some questions around, ‘This section feels a little long. Is there anything we can do about that?’” recalled Hamaguchi, adding that he made a concerted effort to cut his four-hour script to a three-hour, 16-minute running time.

“For me, I was ultimately trying to bring in the shortest version that I felt was accurate for this moment. But ultimately, there is this understanding that this moment is a very important turning point within the film, and so I believe that the producers also understood this.”

“All of a Sudden” is now playing in select theaters.

#3376. These Are the Best Black Friday 2026 Deals on Kindles and E-Readers

Score the year's biggest savings during the Black Friday sale on the best e-reader deals as they launch in real time. Follow our Black Friday Live Blog for live coverage of the absolute best deals, flash sales, and tech savings. For a deep dive into top-rated offers, expert buying guides, and exclusive discounts, explore our Best Black Friday Amazon Tech Deals page.

Amazon's Black Friday sale is in full swing, which means it's a good time to score some of the year's best prices on e-readers. Timing your purchase is now a bigger deal than ever (so to speak), as Amazon recently raised the price of basically every Kindle by $50 or more due to the ongoing RAM crisis.

Because of this, the prices aren't nearly as low as they were last year, but now is still the time to get a decent discount on a Kindle Paperwhite or Colorsoft—but if you'd rather read differently, you can also save big on a few worthy Kindle alternatives. Here are your e-reader best bets in the lead-up to Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

The Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition is the best e-reader for most people. An upgraded version of the basic Kindle, the Paperwhite adds a larger screen, temperature-adjustable lighting, water resistance, and better battery life—and if you opt for the Signature Edition, you also get double the storage and no lock screen ads. Earlier this year, it jumped in price to $250, even before the company introduced a new model—but you can get the 2024 model for $179.99, 28% off the new list price.

If you want a great Kindle but you don't care about paying extra for more storage or getting rid of lock screen ads, the non-Signature Edition of the Kindle Paperwhite is also a great buy right now. The 2024 model has been discounted to $129.99 from the list price of $199.99. It's available in standard black, Jade, or Raspberry colors.

If you don't need the bells and whistles of the Paperwhite, you can also pick up the standard Kindle. It's still a very capable device, with good lighting, 16GB of onboard storage, and the ability to hook up your Bluetooth speakers to listen to Audible audiobooks. The standard Kindle, which now retails for $150, is marked down to $119.99, making it the cheapest Kindle option. Though I think it makes more sense to spend $10 more on the Signature Edition, this is the way to go if you want the cute Matcha color.

If you like to read comics or you just appreciate looking at your book covers in full color, the 2024 Kindle Colorsoft is also at a strong 41% discount for Black Friday, bringing it down to around $170. For $10 less than the Paperwhite Signature edition, you get all the same perks (including an ad-free experience) and a color e-ink screen that's great for reading magazines, graphic novels, and manga. Color e-ink isn't for everyone, but if it's for you, the Colorsoft has the best color screen on the market. For an extra $10, the Colorsoft Kids Edition adds a case, a yearlong subscription to Kindle Kids+, and an extended warranty.

If you're looking for a combination e-reader and e-notebook, the Kindle Scribe is a great option. With a larger screen than Amazon's other e-readers, it offers all the benefits of the Paperwhite but adds support for the excellent Premium Pen stylus, allowing you to take notes in your Amazon e-books or create handwritten documents that you can later convert to text using the onboard AI tools. The 32GB black-and-white version of the Kindle Scribe is currently $349.99, while the Colorsoft version will run you $449.99. Both of these are the newest models, released in 2025.

The new Kindle Scribe Colorsoft has all the same great features of the black-and-white version discussed above, but adds a full-color e-ink display. Combined with the large 11-inch screen, this makes it a great device for reading comics or magazine articles as they were meant to be read, or marking up PDFs using the included Premium Pen. This device usually costs a hefty $630, but the current Black Friday sale cuts $180 off of that price.

If you want to step outside of the Amazon ecosystem, the Kobo Libra Colour is a good bet. Discounted $30 to $229.99 at Best Buy, it's currently pricier than the Kindle Colorsoft, but you get a bit more for your money. While most of the specs are similar (they both use the same Kaleido 3 screen and offer 32GB of storage), the Kobo supports a stylus, so you can jot down notes in your books or keep a digital journal. It also has physical page-turn buttons, which the Colorsoft lacks.

If you don't want to be tied to the Amazon ecosystem and/or you're looking for a device that's a bit more portable, consider the Viwoods AiPaper Reader, currently marked down to $200, its lowest price ever. It's got a 6.13-inch screen, so it's the same size and shape as your phone, and it has a crisp e-ink screen with a strong (if not temperature-adjustable) front light and 128GB of onboard storage. The best part is, it runs on an open Android system, so you can install multiple reading apps, including Kindle, Nook, Kobo, and Libby, and keep all of your books in one place. (Check out my review of the Viwoods AiPaper Reader for more—it's a nifty little device.)

If you don't have a large Kindle library, you're moderately tech-savvy, and you praise portability above all else, I can't recommend Xteink's line of e-readers more highly. The 4.3-inch Xteink X4 Classic is at its lowest price ever, coming in at just under $55, around $34 off the list price. Meanwhile, the smaller 3.7-inch Xteink X3 is about a dollar more; that's a less-generous 19% discount. I own both, and while the Classic is definitely worth the current sale price, I actually prefer the form factor of the smaller X3 (currently $55.72), which is about the size of a library card.

For about $30 more than the X4 Classic, you can upgrade to the Xteink X4 Pro, which happens to be Lifehacker's e-reader Gift of the Year pick. It offers all the perks of the other Xteink devices, with two critical quality-of-life upgrades: A touchscreen for easier navigation, and a temperature-adjustable front light so you can read it in a dark room. (Less obviously, it also has a slightly faster processor that makes the whole thing feel a little snappier.) Right now, the X4 Pro is at its lowest price ever when ordered directly from Xteink: $84, or around 15% off the usual $99 price.

If you're feeling tentative about trusting a seemingly no-name Chinese tech brand, read more about the devices in my review, or listen to the collected wisdom of the tens of thousands of people in the bustling r/xteink Reddit group.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

For the majority of products, the deal from Black Friday will be the same one on Cyber Monday.

#3375. 10 Games With Permadeath That Are 10/10 Masterpieces

There’s something reassuring about knowing you can pick up some extra lives in a video game, ever since the days of Super Mario Bros. and Pac-Man. When your character dies, the action resumes right where you left off — or pretty close to it. You don’t lose much progress. Things can continue largely as they were.

Some games don’t offer that safety net. The best of them are better for it, building on the limitation to produce a truly unique experience. They’re often challenging, but it goes beyond that. With the difficulty comes the sense that the stakes are real. If the thought of permadeath gets your heart racing in all the right ways, here are 10 games with that mechanic that you should seek out as soon as you can.

Available on: Switch, PS4, PS5, PC, Xbox One, Xbox Series X

In the original Rogue Legacy, players assume the role of a whole line of heroes, all of them exploring a dark castle in search of a cure for an ailing king. Each time a family member dies, their child takes up the hero’s mantle. That child has advantages that might allow them to finally succeed where their ancestors failed, but they may also suffer from unexpected new limitations that make the task more difficult. Every new run builds the family fortune, which grants new resources that should eventually lead to success. But you have to wonder: by the time you reach the end of the game, what will success even look like, and how many innocent lives will have been lost? 2022’s Rogue Legacy 2 revisits the concept with additional polish and a much deeper narrative to make it all practically irresistible.

Available on: 3DS, Switch, Wii U, PS4, Vita, PC, Xbox One

Released in 2011, The Binding of Isaac is a game from Edmund McMillen (Mewgenics) and Florian Himsl about a little boy named Isaac who flees to the basement after his God-fearing mother turns homicidal and goes after him with a kitchen knife. Fearing for his life, he battles all sorts of nightmares while negotiating a seemingly endless series of mini-dungeons populated by nightmarish creatures determined to put an end to him. He gathers loot and resources along the way to survive showdowns with powerful foes. It all makes for a dark but strangely compelling experience. A significantly expanded package, The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth, was released in 2014 to provide players with new collectibles and features to justify many, many more runs. But they all end the same way when I’m in control: with Isaac losing his life.

Canabalt was made to be played with one hand, if it suits you. Actually, you can play it with just a single button: the one you press to make your character jump. As your sharp-dressed hero sprints across city rooftops, leaping between crumbling structures or to clear obstacles, his urgency steadily increases and so does his speed. Eventually, it will all come crashing down. But before it does, your goal is to get as far as possible before turning into “a fine mist.” Your score is the distance traveled before disaster finally strikes.

The Fire Emblem games have famously incorporated permadeath since the very beginning. You can play pretty much any of them with that mechanic enabled, though later ones do make it optional. Not everyone likes to sink many hours into their character’s development, only to lose that connection forever when a battle goes horribly wrong. The Divine Pulse ability, which you can use to rewind your previous actions, provides a welcome chance to set things right. You might well find yourself taking advantage of it, because Fire Emblem: Three Houses makes a loss even more difficult to bear than usual. You might become close to some of your characters while clearing the slice-of-life events between battles, and having to go without seeing their smiling face for the remainder of your adventure can be a bit much to take. There’s always a trade-off.

Available on: Switch, PS4, Vita, PC, Xbox One

An ancient evil slumbers beneath your ancestral home, and only you can put an end to it. That’s the idea in Darkest Dungeon, a turn-based RPG that lets you send a band of adventurers on what might well prove a suicide mission. First you deploy them to surrounding dungeons, where they can find the loot necessary to rebuild the local town and upgrade its facilities. Then you send them to their doom, equipped with powerful new weapons and armor but probably not prepared for the eldritch horrors they will encounter. With determination and enough heroes lost, you might gain the knowledge necessary for your latest band of adventurers to conquer great evil. Or they might all die once again. It’s alright, though; that’s a risk you’re willing to take.

In Heavy Rain, you play as a man whose young son goes missing at a park. From there, you launch an investigation to find him and bring him back home, whatever the cost. You already lost one son, years earlier, to a car crash. You’re determined not to lose another. Along the way, you’ll meet a cast of strangers who are also investigating for reasons of their own. You’ll control each of them along the way, learning about their motivations as the twists keep coming. Just how much you learn by the end is up to you. Along the way, pretty much anyone can die. And if they should happen to perish, the story doesn’t come grinding to a halt. It keeps right on going, without a key character to make the connections you might desperately need to get to the truth. It’s a unique experience that invites experimentation, even after you know some of its darkest secrets.

Originally planned for the PlayStation 3, but eventually released on the PlayStation 4 instead, Until Dawn is a slasher-inspired horror game that follows several young friends who have reunited at a remote lodge where terrible events transpired one year prior. On that fateful evening, two sisters fell off a cliff while fleeing from a stranger with a flamethrower. As the friends gather to mark the anniversary, a new nightmare begins. During the events that follow, any or all of them might become the next victims and pay a permanent price for their shortcomings. The game saves automatically at various points, so any bad decisions you make cast long shadows that impact the rest of your experience. Sony also published a remake in 2024 for the PlayStation 5, but the original version is the one that really brings the horror home.

Available on: PS4, PS5, PC, Xbox One, Xbox Series X

Take Until Dawn, but set it in an idyllic summer camp. That’s the idea behind The Quarry. Developed by Supermassive Games, it’s the ambitious spiritual successor to the team’s earlier success story. This time around, cinematic inspiration comes from slashers like Friday the 13th and Sleepaway Camp. Players once again are tasked with making sure the young characters live to see the next day. Along the way, there are plenty of reasons things might go awry. Should the worst occur, those characters are gone for good, at least on your initial trip through the game, victims of a fate they could never have imagined. Not every story has to have a happy ending.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

Don’t Starve has a title that suggests there will be a lot of starving, which is appropriate. It drops players in a hostile wilderness environment without directions and leaves them to find a way to survive. Three meters monitor their hunger, health, and sanity. If any of those meters drop too low, it’s a problem. You’ll spend daylight gathering the resources necessary to survive the night, and you’ll spend your evening hours huddled near a fire, hoping the shadows outside your line of sight don’t converge on you and end you. The longer you survive, the better your resources become, but you’ll face harsher weather and greater danger with the passage of time. The game has multiple modes, and one of them is endless. If you prefer, there’s also an Adventure Mode with more restrictions that can eventually let you roll credits. You just have to make sure your character stays alive that long.

Available on: Switch, PS4, PS5, PC, Xbox One

In 2017’s The Long Dark, you are Will Mackenzie, a bush pilot who crashed his airplane while taking his ex-wife to meet one of her patients in the Canadian wilderness. Unfortunately, he picked a devil of a time to go down. Earth has just fallen victim to a geomagnetic storm, and electricity doesn’t function as it once did. Will must now prove he has the will to survive harsh elements, where a task as simple as securing clean drinking water might spell the end of him. He’ll monitor cold, thirst, hunger, fatigue, and general health. Looting local buildings for supplies will buy him time, but he might lose everything if he runs into a wild wolf or bear, even if he survives the encounter. And when Will finally succumbs to the elements, there’s no coming back from it. The game deletes your sandbox and you get to start fresh. In 2024, the developers added an option that lets you keep going even after an event that might formerly have been fatal, but you’ll lose something along the way. Maybe it’s your maximum health or some precious gear. And you still only get a few chances before you finally have no choice but to face Will’s death. It’s dark stuff, but how long it lasts is mostly up to you.

Zero Company, Fortune’s Weave, and more spearhead a genre renaissance

#3374. Superman Star Christopher Reeve Headlined A '90s Remake Of A Classic Alfred Hitchcock Thriller

"Rear Window" is one of, if not the best Alfred Hitchcock movie, which automatically means it's one of the best films of all time. As such, "daunting" doesn't quite seem to cover the prospect of remaking it. But that didn't stop Superman star Christopher Reeve from doing just that with a 1998 TV movie that marked his final lead role.

2024's "Super/Man" was one of the most powerful, emotional, and inspiring documentaries ever made. The film told Reeve's life story with a focus on the years after the actor became paralyzed from the neck down in a 1995 horse-riding accident. During that time, not only did he throw himself into advocacy work and strive to overcome his spinal cord injury, he also continued to work. Reeve made his directorial debut with the 1997 HBO film "In the Gloaming," which received positive reviews and five Emmy nominations. After that, he returned to the screen in "Rear Window." Unfortunately, this remake of Hitchcock's 1954 classic wasn't — as you might imagine — quite as well received.

Thankfully, Reeve came out of it unscathed. The actor delivered an affecting performance that, at times, is actually quite tough to watch — especially in the wake of "Super/Man" which gave us a candid look at Reeve's personal life after his accident, and an insight into how much the actor believed he would one day walk again. He might not have accomplished that goal, but he did somehow manage to ensure a "Rear Window" remake wasn't entirely redundant, which is a superpower in and of itself.

In 1944, crime writer Cornell Woolrich published his short story collection, "After-Dinner Story" under the pen name William Irish. It included the story "Rear Window" which was previously published in a 1942 issue of Dime Detective Magazine as "It Had to Be Murder." This, alongside some real-life murders, was the basis of the 1954 film, in which James Stewart's photographer L. B. "Jeff" Jefferies witnesses what he believes to be a murder from his window.

It's a bold move, remaking "Rear Window." That's probably why many filmmakers paid tribute to the thriller without actually remaking it. Brian De Palma made obvious reference to the film (alongside other Hitchcock classics) in 1984's "Body Double," and Variety called Phillip Noyce's 1993 thriller "Sliver" "little more than a high-tech homage to 'Rear Window.'" Then there was "The Simpsons" episode, "Bart of Darkness," which parodied Hitchcock's film and introduced an entire generation to it in the process. Christopher Reeve and director Jeff Bleckner, however, decided to go one better and deliver a full-on remake that aired on ABC in 1998.

Bleckner had overseen several features and TV movies in the '80s, and also had plenty of credits on well-known shows of the era, including "Remington Steele," "Hill Street Blues," and "Knots Landing." His version of "Rear Window" is, on its surface, much different to its 1954 counterpart. For one thing, Hitchcock's film takes place almost entirely within Jefferies' apartment, while the 1998 version finds Reeve's divorced architect, Jason Kemp, recovering in hospital after a car crash that has left him quadriplegic. But as the film goes on you see how closely the two stick to Woolrich's original story, and therefore how alike they are.

Christopher Reeve's "Rear Window" is, believe it or not, never going to be considered the quintessential on-screen version of Cornell Woolrich's story. But that doesn't mean it isn't without its charms — the most obvious being Reeve himself.

After returning to his loft apartment following his accident, Reeve's Jason Kemp spends his nights watching the apartment block opposite, which, as he jokes, "goes from a PG-13 to a hard R" after dark. While spying on his neighbors' R-rated exploits, he witnesses sculptor Julian Thorpe (Ritchie Coster) seemingly beating his wife Ilene. The next night, Kemp hears a scream, after which Ilene goes missing. Kemp tries to convince his colleague, Claudia (Daryl Hannah playing an analogue of Grace Kelly's glamorous Lisa Fremont) of Thorpe's guilt. But the killer soon becomes aware of Kemp and what he knows, putting Reeve's architect in mortal danger.

Reeve is easily the best thing about this remake. Hitchcock famously thought actors should be treated like "cattle," but the former Superman star makes the film his own. Aside from his naturalistic performance, the fact Kemp is a quadriplegic adds an extra element of danger, as unlike James Stewart's L. B. Jefferies, Kemp is completely unable to defend himself when Thorpe comes for him. Reeve was also nominated for a Golden Globe and won a Screen Actors Guild Award for his performance in "Rear Window," and was even praised by critics who otherwise rightly called out the redundancy of the whole exercise.

If you're interested in seeing Reeve's final lead performance, you can see the movie for free on one of the best streaming services available, Tubi.

#3373. Will Ferrell Golf Comedy ‘The Hawk’ Canceled at Netflix After Just One Season

“The Hawk,” a Will Ferrell golf comedy that debuted just this summer, has been canceled by Netflix and will not return for a second season, an individual with knowledge told IndieWire.

Ferrell co-created the series in which he plays a former top golfer who is now trying to return to the tour. And while it figured to be a tentpole series for Netflix, one that carried possibly the most expensive budget for a comedy series on Netflix and reunited Ferrell with his “SNL” co-star Molly Shannon and co-creator Harper Steele, it didn’t connect with critics or audiences.

“The Hawk” spent just three weeks on Netflix’s Top 10 when it debuted back in July, topping out at #2 in its second week on Netflix with just 6.2 million views. Ferrell’s vulgar, loudly-dressed golfer with a personalized visor and big mess of bleached blonde hair played a lot like some of Ferrell’s other string of sports comedies throughout the years. But even our critic was perplexed by the series’ tone that makes it sometimes play like a “bizarre addiction drama.” Related Stories ‘The Hunting Wives’ Review: Season 2 Reloads Without Slowing Down in Netflix’s Delirious Soap ‘The Lowdown’ Season 2 Finale Hinges on Two Monologues — Let Ethan Hawke and Sterlin Harjo Break Them Down

Steele, in a recent appearance on “Late Night with Seth Meyers,” tipped her hand a little that the show was likely ending when she let slip that, “I was working on a short-lived but probably the best show ever, ‘The Hawk.’”

The cancellation comes in the wake of a changing of the guard at Netflix, with Peter Rice taking over for veteran creative chief Bela Bajaria. Our critic also recently wrote about the challenges Netflix is facing right now in getting audiences to discover new series in the ways they used to.

But at the same time, Netflix has already renewed a couple of other comedy series that even premiered after “The Hawk” later this year, including “Nobody Wants This,” “A Different World,” “Tires,” “Big Mistakes,” and “The Four Seasons.” Netflix is also still working with Ferrell’s Gloria Sanchez Productions on three new series, “All the Rage,” “Prep,” and another scripted series from Nikki Glaser.

#3371. Steven Spielberg's Unmade 2020s Horror TV Series Had A Wild Idea Behind It

Steven Spielberg was once going to make a Quibi series. Seriously. The gimmick? It would only be available late at night. "Spielberg's After Dark" never came to be, however, because Quibi died a hasty death.

To provide a little context, I may have to remind readers what Quibi was all about. Back in 2020, executive Hollywood bigwigs Jeffrey Katzenberg and Meg Whitman launched Quibi, a $2 billion streaming service that was to be chock full of nothing but original TV shows and feature films. Unlike other streaming services, though, Quibi was only going to be made available on mobile devices, and shows were shot to be consumed in an upright, vertical fashion. Quibi, short for "quick bites," presented movies and TV shows in seven-to-ten-minute chapters, intended to be consumed on the go.

At the time, Quibi was roundly mocked, with many people tittering over the idea of reducing the art of cinema to a vertical, short-form, small-screen serial. As /Film described in our Quibi post-mortem, the service only lasted seven months, running from April to December 2020. A big reason the service failed was likely because it was launched in the middle of COVID-related lockdowns, and no one wanted a short-form service intended for consumption in public. 2020 was the time for long-form TV on bigger home screens.

Most notably, though, Quibi attracted a lot of high-end talent, and many, many notable stars to appear in their shows and movies. Katzenberg's DreamWorks co-founder Steven Spielberg was even roped into the service, and his horror show, "Spielberg's After Dark," was poised to be one of the service's bigger hits. Sadly, it never came to pass. Because of Quibi's unique tech, the series would only be made available after midnight, wherever you happened to be watching from.

Jeffrey Katzenberg told Variety that "Steven Spielberg came in, and said, 'I have a super scary story I want to do' [...] He's writing it himself. He hasn't [written anything in a while] so getting him to write something is fantastic." Variety noted that Spielberg had already penned "five or six" chapters of a show that was to run 10 to 12 episodes total.

The story of "After Dark" was not revealed, but Spielberg revealed that he only wanted his show to be made available between midnight and sunrise, local time. Because Quibi had to be watched on phones, the service would be able to access a user's clock and unlock "After Dark" after dark. Once the sun rose, the series would vanish from the service.

This sort of thing was very doable with Quibi. As one of the world's only regular Quibi users, I can personally attest to the slickness of the service's tech. There were never any slow-downs, the images were always crisp, the ads were brief and never lagged, and the aspect-ratio flips always worked perfectly. It was also easy to find any titles you might be looking for; by contrast, services like Netflix can sometimes present their content in a seemingly random fashion. I have every faith that "Spielberg's After Dark" would have worked just as perfectly. I would have even tried to watch an episode right before dawn to see if it cut off mid-episode right when the sun rose.

In wanting to offer a wide variety of TV shows and movies right from the jump, Quibi was no stranger to horror. One of the service's launch titles was "50 States of Fright," a horror anthology series kicked off by director Sam Raimi. Each story took place in a different state, and Raimi co-wrote and directed the three-episode short "The Golden Arm" with Rachel Brosnahan. Quibi also offered a stalker thriller with Dane DeHaan and Maika Monroe called "The Stranger" and a "Rosemary's Baby" riff called "The Expecting." A horror series from Steven Spielberg would have slotted into the service's ethos nicely.

Sadly, the whole Quibi project crashed and burned before "After Dark" could find purchase. As reported by Variety in 2021, Roku ended up buying the Quibi library and broadcast a lot of its shows and movies as traditional programs. Variety noted that "After Dark" might move to Roku, but that seemed to be mere speculation. As of this writing, nothing has been spoken of about "After Dark" for about five years. The series still has an empty entry on the Internet Movie Database.

"After Dark" would have marked one of the rare moments when Spielberg wrote one of his own movies. Of the films he has directed post-1960s, Spielberg is a credited screenwriter only on "Close Encounters of the Third Kind," "A.I. Artificial Intelligence," and "The Fabelmans." He also has a story credit on "Disclosure Day."

"After Dark" would have also seen Spielberg making a rare sojourn into horror. Apart from "Duel," "Jaws," "Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom," "Jurassic Park," and arguably "War of the Worlds," Spielberg has stayed away from directing proper horror. I wish "After Dark" had come to be.

#3370. What Are Local Movie Theaters Showing for Thanksgiving 2026?

One of the great things about going to the movies by yourself is that, technically speaking, you’re not alone. Even if you’re the only person in the auditorium, somebody thought about what you might like to watch, put it on the calendar, and made sure there was a place for you to sit.

That’s something worth being grateful for this Thanksgiving.

Earlier this month, IndieWire surveyed the programming at independent movie theaters across the United States on Election Night. Continuing that exercise over Thanksgiving weekend reveals another delightful cross-section of American film culture — albeit with considerably more cannibalism. Related Stories ‘Odyssey’ Cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema Was More Interested in the Intimate Than the Epic Forget Photorealism: How ‘Wildwood’ Made Its Handmade Digital Artistry Visible

At the Music Box Theatre in Chicago, where audiences have spent more than two decades celebrating Thanksgiving by singing along to “The Sound of Music,” moviegoers can also catch Ruggero Deodato’s “Cannibal Holocaust” late Friday night. It’s hard to imagine the Von Trapps sticking around for that one, but there’s something lovely about a neighborhood institution accommodating both crowds.

In Seattle, the Beacon is observing its own Thanksgiving tradition with “Blood Rage,” the gloriously ridiculous slasher that made cranberry sauce an enduring point of reference for a certain subset of horror fans. For a somewhat more realistic depiction of the horrors of going home for Thanksgiving, SALA Event Center in Los Alamos, New Mexico, is showing Jodie Foster’s “Home for the Holidays.”

In Cambridge, Massachusetts, the Brattle Theatre is celebrating Black Friday with a double feature of “Chopping Mall” and “Night of the Comet.” If you’d rather watch people die in a shopping mall than go to one yourself, that’s certainly an economical alternative. Meanwhile, Minneapolis’ Trylon Cinema is spending the biggest shopping weekend of the year celebrating the work of documentary filmmaker Barbara Kopple, screening her Oscar-winning “Harlan County, U.S.A.” and “American Dream” as part of a series dedicated to class struggle.

Thanksgiving also marks the 50th anniversary of the Band’s legendary farewell concert, held at San Francisco’s Winterland Ballroom in 1976. At Film Streams in Omaha, Nebraska, audiences can spend Friday morning watching Martin Scorsese’s “The Last Waltz.” That half a century later, people are still getting together to experience a concert most of them weren’t alive to attend speaks to one of the more miraculous things movies can do.

And in Portland, Oregon, stop-motion animation studio LAIKA is expressing its gratitude to its hometown audience by offering free screenings of “Wildwood“ on Sunday at theaters across the area, including the historic Hollywood Theatre. Considering how many thousands of hours of human labor go into making a stop-motion animated feature, there’s something especially sweet about giving people whose real home served as the setting a chance to enjoy the outcome together.

Of course, what Americans celebrate on Thanksgiving — and whether they celebrate it at all — varies considerably. On Wednesday, California Indian Nations College is presenting a free screening of “People of the West,” a documentary series examining the history of California’s Indigenous peoples from Indigenous perspectives, in Palm Desert. At the historic Raymond Theatre in Raymond, Washington, a free Saturday screening of a documentary about the Qwayat Canoe Society’s journey to Nisqually offers an opportunity to learn more about a living Indigenous tradition.

And for anyone navigating a particularly painful holiday season, a film festival in Magnolia, Texas, is making a different kind of space. Presented by the nonprofit My Grief Angels, Grief Fest is hosting an in-person community screening on Black Friday, with films also available to watch virtually throughout Thanksgiving weekend. Dedicated to exploring loss and healing through cinema, the festival recognizes just how complicated an invitation to celebrate can be.

There are innumerable ways to spend a long weekend like this, and movies aren’t a substitute for the people we wish we could spend it with. But the wonderful thing about indie exhibition is just how much of it depends on random people thinking about other random people. Someone has to remember that a certain movie exists. Then someone else has to think it might mean something to you. And finally a different person has to care enough to bring it all together.

Whether you’re somebody who spends every Thanksgiving with the same people or a cinephile whose traditions are still taking shape, consider making a little time for your local movie theater this weekend. Thank the person who takes your ticket, and tell the programmer when you love something they booked. Maybe even invite that friend you’ve been meaning to catch up with.

There are so many extraordinary works of art to see in this lifetime and never quite enough time to see them all. How lucky we are to get to watch some of them together.

#3369. Every Eevee Evolution, Ranked From Worst To Best

Eight Eeveelutions. One impossible decision

​Eevee, the adorable Normal-type Pokémon first introduced in Pokémon Red and Blue, has become something of an unofficial second mascot for the franchise, thanks to its supreme cuteness and near-ubiquity throughout the mainline games. Beyond that, Eevee's ability to evolve into a whopping eight distinct forms (or Eeveelutions, as they're affectionately known), each with a different typing, makes it something of a blank canvas for exploring different battle styles and strategies.

Of course, the video game aspect of Eeveelutions is just one reason why people adore them. Eeveelutions are also hot commodities in the Pokémon TCG, with some of the most valuable Eeveelution cards ranking among the most beautiful and coveted chase cards in the game's history.

Ultimately, though, what is the definitive order of the best Eeveelutions? As you might expect, such a list is deeply subjective, as one person's favorite might be another's least beloved. Just know that there are no wrong answers, as each of Eevee's evolutions is a precious angel that should be protected at all costs. Since ranking them is the name of the game, though, let's get to it.

Each Eeveelution is its own special snowflake, and when referencing the Ice-type Glaceon, that's quite literal. One of Eevee's evolutions had to be ranked last, and in this case, Glaceon's elegant design and formidable 130 base Special Attack stat weren't quite enough to save it from drawing the short straw (or icicle).

Glaceon debuted in the Generation Four Pokémon games (Diamond, Pearl, and Platinum), where it could only be obtained by leveling up Eevee near an Ice Rock, conveniently located south of Snowpoint City on Sinnoh's Route 217. Thankfully, later games simplified the process, with an Ice Stone doing the trick in more recent entries like Pokémon Legends: Z-A, as detailed in Polygon's Eevee evolution guide.

The choice between Glaceon and Leafeon is more or less a coin flip, as both have their merits. In fact, Glaceon might be the more formidable offensive Pokémon thanks to its towering Special Attack stat and reasonable bulk. However, this writer simply prefers Leafeon and "thinks they're neat."

Leafeon, alongside its Generation Four compatriot Glaceon, has also been featured on a number of gorgeous full-art Pokémon TCG cards. Notable standouts include the Alternate Art Leafeon V from Evolving Skies, as well as the Galarian Gallery version of Leafeon VSTAR from Crown Zenith.

The first Kanto Eeveelution arrives pretty early on this list, but Flareon has always been the weakest and least interesting of Eevee's original three evolutions.

While its original Pokémon TCG Jungle printing boasts inarguably the best artwork of the three, Flareon has historically struggled to distinguish itself in the video games. Even its monstrous 130 base Attack stat can't quite overcome its middling Speed and frequently underwhelming movepool. Beyond that, its design simply isn't as distinctive as either Eevee's Water- or Electric-type evolution (or its Generation Two additions, for that matter). Sorry, Flareon.

The most recent Eeveelution debuted in the Generation Six Pokémon games (Pokémon X and Y), bringing the then-new Fairy typing to Eevee's ever-expanding evolutionary repertoire. Pixilate FTW.

While Sylveon's evolutionary method has, ahem, evolved over the years, the gist is that Eevee needs to adore its trainer and know a Fairy-type move when it levels up. Originally, that meant raising its affection through Pokémon-Amie, while newer games rely on high friendship instead. Meet those criteria, and you'll be the proud trainer of (debatably) the most objectively adorable Eeveelution in Pokémon history. Those flowing ribbons and baby-blue eyes certainly make a compelling case. Again, no wrong answers on that front, either.

Smack-dab in the middle sounds just about right for Vaporeon, which boasts a lofty 130 base HP stat combined with a respectable 95 base Special Defense. That combination makes it one of the bulkiest Eeveelutions, capable of soaking up considerable punishment while dishing out plenty of its own.

Seeing as Water is the most populous typing in Pokémon, it makes perfect sense that Eevee would have an aquatic evolution. Resembling an elegant fox-mermaid hybrid, Vaporeon's design is wonderfully simple, yet distinctive enough to establish its place among Eevee's iconic original trio.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

The fastest Eeveelution is the very definition of a glass cannon, capable of outrunning countless opponents and delivering devastating blows with its 110 base Special Attack stat. The trade-off? Wafer-thin physical defenses, including a laughably low 65 base HP stat.

Despite that fragility, Jolteon's spiky, electrically charged design is tremendous, and battling with Eevee's Electric-type evolution remains a thoroughly enjoyable experience. Just make sure to keep some healing items readily available, because Jolteon isn't particularly fond of taking a hit. Also, Jolteon Gold Star is surely a thing of beauty.

The Generation Two Pokémon games, Gold and Silver, introduced two new Eeveelutions to Eevee's branching evolutionary tree. Perhaps the more immediately intriguing of the pair was Umbreon, which boasted the then-new Dark typing and could be obtained by leveling up a highly friendly Eevee at night.

Umbreon's sleek black design, glowing yellow rings, and impressive defensive stats make it a perennial fan favorite. While its relatively feeble offensive capabilities can make battles a prolonged affair, its remarkable staying power and plethora of support options still provide an intriguing battle style in-game.

Umbreon's popularity also extends directly into the Pokémon TCG, where it stars on some of the most coveted modern grails. These include Evolving Skies' iconic "Moonbreon" (Umbreon VMAX Alternate Art) and Prismatic Evolutions' striking "Sunbreon" (Umbreon ex Special Illustration Rare). Both cards command prices well into the four figures, even ungraded, with pristine graded examples fetching considerably more.

Indeed, the obsession with Umbreon cards has reached rather extraordinary heights. One collector even traded a $130,000 car for a collection of miscut Evolving Skies cards featuring an unusual Umbreon VMAX. That's quite a premium for Eevee’s fetching Dark-type evolution.

Eevee's Psychic-type evolution, Espeon, boasts arguably the most elegant and striking design of the entire Eeveelution family. It's also a fearsome special attacker, with its 130 base Special Attack tied with Glaceon for the highest among Eeveelutions, while its impressive 110 Speed allows it to dispatch many opponents before they can retaliate.

While Umbreon certainly boasts a gorgeous design, formidable defenses, and a cool typing, its more supporting role in battle isn't quite as satisfying as Espeon's sheer offensive prowess. Espeon can hit hard and fast, and its combination of speed, special attacks, and the always-useful Magic Bounce ability makes it a delight to deploy in-game.

In the Pokémon TCG, Espeon's chase cards aren't quite as famous as those of its nocturnal brethren, but stunning pieces of cardboard like Espeon ex from Unseen Forces and the Holo Aquapolis Espeon certainly make it a notable grail subject for collectors. The latter shares a set with the magnificent Crystal Lugia, which recently tied its $360,000 auction record, further demonstrating the enduring appeal of the TCG's early e-Reader era.

Eight evolutions, eight devoted fan clubs, and absolutely no chance everyone agrees. Who knew one little Normal-type could cause so much disagreement?

Ranked from best to very best, like no one ever was

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3368. Beats' Newest Over-Ear Headphones Are Down to a Record-Low $249 for Black Friday

While you can find plenty of deals on older headphone models during Black Friday sales, it’s rare to see a record-low price and a nearly 30% discount on newer, highly rated models from top brands. That’s exactly why this deal on the critically praised Beats 360 headphones should be on your radar. They’re now down to $249 (originally $349.99) in Amazon’s early Black Friday sale.

With a design that looks like the love child of the AirPods Max and the Beats Studio Pro, these have an adjustable telescoping frame and a unique modular design that lets you mix and match ear pad colors. The color-swapping bundle isn’t currently on sale, but it’s reassuring to know you can replace the ear pads as they wear out.

They’re controlled by two buttons on each earcup and powered by a dedicated Beats chip, with support for both Android devices and iPhones. You can switch noise modes and, on an iPhone, activate features like Personalized Spatial Audio in Settings. They last up to 32 hours with ANC on, which is longer than both the more expensive Sony WH-1000XM6 and AirPods Max 2.

According to Beats, the 360 offer up to 1.75 times the noise cancellation of the Beats Studio Pro. PCMag’s review, which gave the headphones an “Excellent” rating, was impressed by how well they blocked out everything from plane engine noise to café chatter. The noise cancellation falls short of pricier models, and PCMag found the Sony WH-1000XM4C slightly better in that respect.

The PCMag review says the headphones deliver “nice, deep bass, reasonably crisp highs, and a more neutral tuning than you might expect for a pair of Beats headphones.” If you’re after long battery life, rich audio, and plush earcups you can swap for a pop of color, $249 is a great price for the Beats 360 headphones.

#3367. 8 Action Movie Heroes Who Could Beat Alan Ritchson's Reacher In A Fair Fight

Alan Ritchson's Reacher has yet to meet a foe he couldn't punch out of existence - but these action movie heroes might stand a chance in a fair fight. Non-readers couldn't quite understand what was so controversial about Tom Cruise being cast in Jack Reacher, but while he gave a good performance, he was just wrong for the part.

The Jack Reacher books follow a 6-foot-5, 250-pound demigod of a man, which is a description that fits actor Alan Ritchson much better than Tom Cruise. Ritchson was perfect casting on so many levels that it's hard to imagine anyone else playing the role, and the show has struggled to pit him against villains who could stand a chance against him.

The Reacher vs Paulie brawl from Reacher season three remains the best fight for this reason, as it feels like a fair match. Still, it's fun to think about how other action heroes might actually pose a threat to Reacher. For the sake of fairness, superheroes or cyborgs are omitted from this mental exercise.

The John Wick movies have done an impressive job painting Keanu Reeves' titular hitman as both a borderline supernatural force - and as a very squishy, vulnerable human being. In addition to Wick's impressive shooting and martial arts skills, it feels like his biggest superpower is his sheer resilience and overcoming pain.

Time and again, he gets beaten up, shot, exploded, stabbed, thrown off roofs, etc, yet he keeps coming. That would naturally make him a strong candidate to take on Jack Reacher, in what would surely be a bruising fight for both men.

It would be over quite fast if Wick just chose his classic headshot tactic, but as his bouts with stocky foes like Scott Adkins Killa prove, he has to earn his victory in a mano a mano clash. A fight with Reacher would surely see him collect more scars, but since Wick is always the last man standing, Jack would be in for a bad day too.

Escape from New York propelled Kurt Russell from a teen Disney actor to a full-blown movie star, and in Snake Plissken, he portrayed one of the all-time great antiheroes. What should be noted about Plissken is that he's not all that tough, as both of his movies highlight.

In the original film and its sequel, Escape from L.A., Snake isn't some ripped action guy who effortlessly beats all-comers. By the end of both films, he has been beaten up and betrayed many times over, but what makes him so dangerous is that he will do anything to survive. That's what would make a fight with Reacher so intriguing.

Plissken wouldn't beat Alan Ritchson's drifter via sheer brute force, and would need to get creative. This could involve the use of improvised weapons or holding out until Reacher himself is exhausted. The fight between Plissken and Slag (Ox Baker) in Escape from New York shows how Snake can take on a physically much tougher opponent and emerge the winner - and that doesn't end well for Slag.

Now, claiming a Tom Cruise character could realistically take down one played by Alan Ritchson is already playing with fire. That would be especially true if it was Cruise's version of Reacher in this entry, but when it's Mission: Impossible's unstoppable Ethan Hunt, matters are a little different.

Across eight Mission: Impossible movies, Hunt constantly overcame, well, impossible odds. His combination of brawn, smarts and often sheer luck saved the day on many occasions. While Hunt rarely battles against a truly hulking foe, his fight with Henry Cavill's Walker in Fallout provides a good framework to judge a potential clash with Reacher.

That's a vicious fight against somebody who is clearly bigger and stronger, but Hunt uses his resourcefulness to prevail. Like John Wick, Hunt has often proven himself unkillable, so while he might end up with a nasty concussion, he would find some way to bring Reacher down.

Not only did Mad Max: Fury Road rev up the franchise after a 30-year break, it also introduced another iconic character in Furiosa (Charlize Theron). This one-armed wasteland warrior gave Theron one of her best roles, and the character proved so popular she even earned a spin-off with 2024's Furiosa: A Mad Max Saga.

Now, tough as Reacher is, he has never had to live through a post-apocalypse. That would not only impede his hobbies like traveling around America or drinking coffee, he would also need to improve on his weaknesses, like driving. Furiosa, on the other hand, learned to survive the wasteland the hard way, and is so tough that she once severed her own arm to survive.

As her nasty brawl with Max (Tom Hardy) underlines, Furiosa is willing to fight hard and dirty. Max is no weakling himself, and he just about prevailed in that scuffle, meaning Reacher would have an equally unpleasant time.

The Raid movies became instant classics for their gruelling, relentless action sequences, with poor protagonist Rama (Iko Uwais) having just a miserable time of it. In the original Gareth Evans film, Rama has to employ his silat training to fight his way through a seemingly limitless horde of killers armed with machetes.

He just about lives through that nightmare - only to go through an even harder time in The Raid 2. Aside from Uwais' innate charm and likability, what makes Rama such an easy hero to root for is that he always on the edge of losing. At any moment, his exhaustion threatens to overwhelm him, and it's only sheer willpower that keeps him going.

Outside of maybe John Wick, it feels like Rama would have the most credible chance against Alan Ritchson's Reacher. The Raid proved his talent for wearing down his opponents gradually, and his graceful martial arts skills would be a good counterpoint to Reacher's brute force approach.

Now, if this entry was focused on the war machine that John Rambo (Sylvester Stallone) transformed into in later sequels, he would just blast Reacher with a bazooka and be done with it. However, the more human version seen in First Blood (or even 2008's fourth instalment Rambo) would make for a more compelling fight.

The First Blood take on Rambo is someone who doesn't want to fight - but is still exceptionally skilled at it. War is second nature to him, and from hand-to-hand combat to laying traps or using firearms, Rambo has few weaknesses. Thanks to his time in the army, Reacher himself has similar gifts, but even he would struggle with Rambo's inherent gift for violence.

The Lee Child books highlight that Reacher is kind of useless with blades, so he would struggle in a knife fight with Rambo. Also, while Reacher may see himself as a nomad who doesn't belong in society, Rambo is a borderline feral creature, and there are few things he won't do to survive.

It has been said time and again that James Cameron is uniquely good at writing female action roles (see also Ellen Ripley in Aliens), but Sarah Connor remains his greatest. Across the first two Terminator movies, Linda Hamilton's Sarah went from an innocent, regular waitress into a hardened guerrilla fighter.

The Judgment Day version of Sarah is motivated first and foremost by survival and keeping her son safe. From using her brains to break out of her confinement in an asylum to coming real close to killing the T-1000 (Robert Patrick) by herself in the finale, Sarah would be a genuine threat to Reacher in combat.

In all likelihood, Sarah would want to end things fast, so knives or improvised tools would be the order of the day. All in all, Reacher might prefer his odds with the T-800 instead.

One of the fun things about the Jack Reacher novels is that they take a standard murder mystery formula, and then inject a muscle-bound, square-jawed 1980s action hero into the lead role. Now, what was so refreshing about the original Die Hard movie is that Bruce Willis' John McClane was intended as an antidote to the invincible Stallone/Schwarzenegger action heroes that dominated that decade.

Instead of brawn, he had to think his way around problems, and he typically ended every entry very bloody and exhausted. He wasn't much of a fighter either, which would make a bout with Reacher a challenge. Even so, as his scuffles with Karl in the original or Targo in Die Hard with a Vengeance show, John can take an almighty whopping and still come out on top.

In a full-on punch-up with Reacher, McClane would be left with injuries that would kill a lesser man, but he would also figure a way to win. Given the pragmatic nature of both men, they would probably just call it a tie and go grab a burger instead.

Without a phone and traveling light, former military police officer Jack Reacher drifts between American towns, embroiling himself in local crimes and bringing justice in his wake. Based on the series of novels by Lee Child, Reacher's journey offers him an intimate understanding of the nation he once served.

#3366. Danielle Brooks Shares Insights from the Indie Success of ‘If I Go Will They Miss Me’

“I’m not one of those people that try to act like I don’t want the thing. I want the thing. I’m excited about the thing,” said recent Academy Award nominee Danielle Brooks. “I know how much it has impacted little Dani when I’ve watched Oprah Winfrey or Whoopi Goldberg or Viola Davis or Halle Berry receive [Oscars], and listened even to the speeches now, [from Emmy winners] Niecy Nash-Betts and Sheryl Lee Ralph. They push you to continue to work hard.”

Though her 2023 role in “The Color Purple” cemented the Grammy winner’s status as a performer who has at the very least been nominated for each letter of EGOT, the real reward the recognition among her peers has brought is the opportunity to executive produce and star in projects like the Walter Thompson-Hernandez film “If I Go Will They Miss Me,” which premiered at Sundance 2026 to rave reviews. “Yes, I have the desire to be receiving awards one day,” said Brooks, “but at the end of the day, I get to do that with my work. I get to do that with stories like ‘If I Go,’ where my goal is for people to feel seen.” Related Stories ‘Odyssey’ Cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema Was More Interested in the Intimate Than the Epic Forget Photorealism: How ‘Wildwood’ Made Its Handmade Digital Artistry Visible

The coming-of-age drama set in Watts, California sees the actress play a mother named Lozita doing her best to hold her family together while there’s inscrutable tension between her partner, recently released from prison, and their imaginative 12-year-old son. “I started out in theater, so to me, it’s never been about a paycheck,” joked Brooks. “It’s always been about the story and what you’re putting out into the world. And so, when I watched [Thompson-Hernandez’s] short, I was like, ‘Yo, this is different. I ain’t never seen nothing like this.’ And it was captivating just the way he was shooting it.”

Expanding on what drew her to the project, which came to her during her time bouncing between Los Angeles awards press for “The Color Purple,” and the New Zealand set of “A Minecraft Movie,” Brooks said “They handed me the script and it was really the conversation, sitting down with Walter, his passion for his community, hearing about the real Lozita who had unfortunately passed away from cancer two years prior, hearing about the Compton Cowboys, just getting to talk to him about relationships between kids and their parents and the complications that it can bring.”

She said, “I like the balance. I got to have a little comedy, but I got to do some drama and it does my heart well.” While “Minecraft” brought her “laughs all day with Jack Black and Jason Momoa,” “If I Go” brought Brooks “purpose.” “I’m excited that we get to share stories like this where people are really dealing with their personal issues and healing and all of that stuff,” she said.

Having screened the film in Los Angeles the night before, Brooks said “You can feel the energy of everyone feeling super represented and feeling a sense of ownership. It’s cool hearing the audience be like, ‘Yeah, yeah,’ When you talk about the planes passing by, or the story about the fuel engines falling on elementary schools. People remember and know that to be a part of what has happened in LA, and the fabric of LA.”

One job that was foundational to how she approaches projects like “If I Go” happens to be Brooks’ breakout role as Taystee on “Orange Is the New Black.” Coming out of the prestigious Julliard School, her mind was more so on “how am I going to make my money for the subway and pay for my college tuition and how am I going to pay for this PB&J sandwich?,” when she booked the role on the series for the then-nascent streaming service Netflix. “I didn’t know what I was stepping into at the time. ‘Orange’ was looked at as a webseries, so nobody knew what this was about to be. But once we got into the work, I was like, ‘Oh, this is deeper than that.’ I remember talking to people who’ve been incarcerated, and I remember even doing a clothing drive for women who have just come out of prison so that they could have clothes for job interviews and stuff like that. We were really invested in the community and giving back,” said Brooks.

“We had that as a group, as storytellers, but then individually, I was watching my co-stars have a point of view, have something to say. And so, I [was] just learning that being an artist is also a form of activism,” she said. “That was one of the beginning seeds planted in my head once I was in the industry, because I’ve always known that what we do is about service, that’s number one. But I hadn’t experienced that on this level.”

Since then, Brooks’ goal has been to tell at least one story a year that incorporates a bit of activism, and with “If I Go,” the actress and producer has been more active than ever. “I’ve deemed us the little engine that could, because I really believe that we can take this far. My goal is that we just get as many eyeballs on it as we can. But the truth of the matter is nothing moves like money does. And that’s what I’ve learned is you’ve got to get really creative and strategic about how you can push a movie into the face of the people when you don’t have the money.”

“If I Go Will They Miss Me,” distributed by Rich Spirit, has truly been an indie success story, making over $1 million at the box office from the humblest of beginnings. As Brooks noted, that haul has been hard fought, with her, Thompson-Hernandez, and her co-star J. Alphonse Nicholson touring as much of the country as they can to screen the film, and even abroad. “I’m going to Africa this week, I got invited, but then I learned there’s a film festival in Africa. So, I’m like, ‘Can we take the film to Africa?’ And they said, ‘Yes.’ So now, the film’s going to be in the festival there,” said the actress.

She continued, “It’s even in the form of fashion. People pay attention to what you’re wearing and then they’re like, ‘Why you got that on? Oh! She had a premiere.’ Boom. It’s insane how many tricks I have been working to get people to pay attention to this film that is worth paying attention to.”

One of the more beautiful aspects of this “If I Go” experience has been the way in which her community has shown up for her and the film. Snoop Dogg and Ava DuVernay have Instagrammed about it, while Helen Hunt and André Holland have even hosted talk backs for the film. But in terms of creativity, one marketing strategy takes the cake. “Issa Rae, even at her restaurant, she did a menu dedicated to ‘If I Go’ where it was a discount, 15 percent off or something if you bought a ticket,” she said. “People understand the importance of this,” said Brooks. “If the film wasn’t good, I wouldn’t be doing all this.”

On the awards front, the challenge is still getting the film in front of the steak eaters who still make up a good chunk of the awards body, and maybe do not immediately think they identify with the material. “The Academy is working really hard to change that narrative by who is allowed to vote. The voting party is shifting, but that’s what I’m experiencing right now,” said Brooks.

But regular filmgoers have a role in getting smaller, truly independent films awards recognition too. “The general audience plays a huge part because the culture tells the voters where to look, what is important,” said the actress. “The people, we have a voice in this too. I think we make it very clear what we want to see, but it’s a weird cycle.” Studio films have a budget for billboards, commercials, advertisements, and more. “When you are a small independent film, you have to be that big machine on your own to get it out there. And that’s a lot of work, and that’s a lot of time, and that’s a lot of smarts,” said Brooks. “You’ve got to have a lot of faith and hope too. You’ve just got to believe that what you’ve created is strong. And I do know that we all do, myself, J. Alphonse, Walter, MACRO, Rich Spirit, we believe in this film wholeheartedly.”

“Movies like these are worth telling, and I think they do reach who they need to reach, and they do lock in with the world on a larger scale when they’re supposed to,” said Brooks, reflecting on the fruitful journey “If I Go” has already had so far. “This is the thing I’m most proud of in my whole career because just the fact that people are having conversations, hard conversations with their loved ones, and they’re finding ways to heal.”

“If I Go Will They Miss Me” is now available to rent on all platforms.

Black Friday deals start showing up long before Black Friday actually arrives, and it's easy to shop most sales online without ever having to set foot in a store. But if you are willing to go early, stand in line, and navigate the crowds, you may be able to get some free stuff for your effort. Here are the freebies on offer this Black Friday.

The first 100 shoppers in line at Target on Black Friday will receive a gift card worth $25, $50, or $100, and one shopper at every store will get a $1,000 gift card. Stores open at 6 a.m., and tickets redeemable for free gift cards will be handed out starting approximately an hour before. Shoppers must exchange their tickets for their gift card within the first hour after doors open.

The first 200 shoppers at every Kohl's store on Black Friday will get a voucher for Kohl's Cash worth $5 to $100. Doors open at 5 a.m. If you show up on Saturday, Nov. 28 instead, you're eligible for a Sephora at Kohl's coupon (also worth $5 to $100).

If you're a MyLowe's Rewards member and you show up early on Black Friday, you could get one of several free buckets filled with products and coupons. The first 50 loyalty program members in line will receive a Black Friday Mystery Bucket, and four of those individuals will win one of the following grand prizes:

The next 100 members get a Golden Mini Bucket, which contains $5 in MyLowe's Monday and a 20% off coupon, among other things. The loyalty program is free to join, and doors open at 6 a.m.

The first 250 shoppers at Bass Pro Shops and Cabela's locations on Black Friday will receive a promo card worth between $10 and $500. The cards are valid Dec. 4 through 26, so you can't use them to shop that day.

JCPenney is running scheduled giveaways in stores throughout the day on Black Friday, so you could get free products even if you aren't there when doors open. If you line up at 5 a.m., you will get a peel-away card that is good for $10 off, $50 off, or $500 off your purchase, as well as a free Harry Potter mini snow globe. Additional giveaways will take place at 9 a.m., 1 p.m., and 5 p.m. for those in line.

Michaels is giving away 500 Countdown to Craftsmas advent calendars in stores on Black Friday while supplies last. The calendars come with store coupons, and some include other freebies and cash prizes up to a $100 gift card. One winner will receive a $10,000 nationwide grand prize.

Academy Sports is distributing bonus cards worth $20, $50, or $100 to the first 100 customers in line on Black Friday between 5 a.m. and 6 a.m. CT. Prize amounts will be randomly awarded among entrants. Academy Sports has locations across more than 20 states.

Best Buy's Black Friday promo isn't strictly free, but members of the My Best Buy rewards program (including the free tier) can purchase a $100 gift card for $60. There is a limit of one per person while supplies last, and cards can be used immediately, so you can take advantage of sales.

The first 30 shoppers at Golf Galaxy locations on Black Friday are eligible for instant prizes, including products, gift cards, and in-store services. One person per location will win a swag bag worth more than $500. Doors open at 7 a.m.

If you're among the first 500 shoppers at Fleet Farm when doors open at 5 a.m. on Black Friday, you'll receive a plush eagle toy. The company has also been running an "Orange Friday" event with in-store giveaways, though these have passed at most locations.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.
