#3364. Opinion: 'Godzilla Minus Zero' Features the Wrong Godzilla Monster

Sorry, King Ghidorah, but you didn't make much sense

Life is all about the choices you make. On Nov. 19, I chose to go to the cinema to watch Godzilla: Minus Zero instead of playing GTA 6. I regret it. I expected a sequel to Takashi Yamazaki’s somber, tragic reflection on loss, trauma, and violence in Godzilla: Minus One. Instead, I got the next entry in the Monsterverse franchise.

Godzilla: Minus One is a masterpiece. Director Takashi Yamazaki won me over with his modern retelling of the King of the Monsters’ first appearance. And I’m a longtime Godzilla fan who loves Hideaki Anno’s Shin Godzilla and was resentful that the Evangelion creator didn’t get a chance to make a sequel (although I hope that might still happen).

However, Godzilla: Minus Zero squandered all that goodwill by stepping into the pitfall that ruins every Godzilla sequel: It’s not a movie about Godzilla. Instead, most of the film focuses on Ghidorah, one of Godzilla’s most iconic foes but also a monster that has very little to offer to this sequel, besides a few spectacular action sequences.

However, there is another character in Godzilla’s massive rogues' gallery that would have been a perfect fit for Godzilla: Minus Zero, given the themes that the movie tries to present to its audience: Biollante.

The reason why, 72 years after Godzilla’s roar first echoed on the silver screen, we are still talking about a giant lizard with an atomic breath, is that Godzilla is a monster in the true sense of the word. Like Dracula, Frankenstein’s monster, or the Xenomorph from Alien, Godzilla is a catalyst: an abhorrent presence that provokes a reaction in the humans around it. Through that reaction, good monster fiction can reveal and analyze the deepest aspects of human nature.

In its first appearance, Godzilla was an allegory for post-World War II trauma in Japan. The bombing of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, American occupation, coming to grips with the past while struggling to build a future: all these themes and more come to life in a giant, walking disaster.

Godzilla: Minus One was a fantastic movie because it went back to that original concept, making post-war Japan the real protagonist. The story of Koichi, a former kamikaze pilot who suffers from post-traumatic stress disorder and struggles to rebuild his life along with other survivors, is one of the two pillars of the movie. The other is Godzilla.

Yamazaki shows the monster from the perspective of the tiny humans whose lives it’s destroying. Godzilla is always an imposing, almost impossible presence, majestic in the most dreadful way possible, something that the director achieves by shooting the monster from below in most of the city-destroying sequences. It felt like watching a god walk among mortals, with all the disaster that follows.

In the first seconds of Godzilla: Minus Zero, a monster pops up on screen, but this time it’s Ghidorah. There is no dramatic tease of the creature’s arrival, no buildup, no mystique. The movie begins in the middle of the monster attacking a town, setting the tone for the rest of its runtime.

Godzilla himself shows up mid-movie in the much overused ship-sinking sequence. The creature had supposedly been killed at the end of the first movie, but its return is treated as almost an afterthought because everyone is focused on the three-headed dragon spreading chaos and destruction all over Japan. As a result, Godzilla becomes completely demystified, undoing all the first movie's achievements.

This becomes quite significant in the scene where Koichi learns of Godzilla’s return. The pilot had nearly given his life to kill the monster in the previous movie. Ryuunosuke Kamiki, who plays Koichi, perfectly portrays the anguish and desperation of the character in the 30 seconds he’s given to react to the news — and then the movie moves on. By the end, I even had the impression that Koichi and his wife Noriko looked at Godzilla with sympathetic eyes.

Godzilla: Minus Zero isn't really about Godzilla at all. The movie spends most of its runtime showing Ghidorah’s progression from alien goo inside a meteorite into a dragon into an even scarier three-headed dragon, along with the efforts of the Large-Scale Disaster Response Bureau to kill the beast.

However, Ghidorah bears no significance besides being a new, scary monster. It’s not a metaphor for anything (except maybe: if you find alien goo in a rock, destroy it immediately!), and its actions in the movie don't serve as a catalyst to reflect on human nature, as Godzilla originally did.

The only glimpse we get of something more profound than “monster smash” is Professor Murakami, a survivor of the Hiroshima bombing who secretly plans to lure Godzilla to the U.S. to exact his revenge. While Yamazaki's visceral depictions of both the devastation of Hiroshima and Murakami's vengeful fantasy of annihilating New York City are remarkable for their raw violence (and earned the film a rare R-rating), the revenge itself is mostly squandered and reduced to a somewhat cringey sequence of Murakami laughing like a maniac in his study.

This might have worked in a more absurdist Showa era Godzilla movie, but it's totally out of place in the grounded "Minus" movies.

Still, the Murakami subplot made me realize Godzilla: Minus Zero would have worked much better if it had featured another, less famous monster from the franchise: Biollante.

Making its debut in the 1989 Toho movie Godzilla vs. Biollante, Biollante is a plant-kaiju-human hybrid created by scientist Genshiro Shiragami. After his daughter was killed​​​​​​​ in a bombing sanctioned by an American corporation, Shiragami spliced her DNA with that of her favorite flowers (roses)​​​​​​​, creating a breed with latent telepathic abilities. When these roses were threatened by a volcano’s eruption, Shiragami spliced the plant with Godzilla’s DNA in the hope of granting it regenerative abilities. The plan worked, but the plant gained full sentience and the ability to evolve, ultimately becoming a giant monster.

All the elements of this plot are present in Godzilla: Minus Zero, just in a different form. Murakami lost his wife, daughter, and niece in the Hiroshima bombing, and his desire for revenge against America is the only thing that keeps him going. Instead of Ghidorah, the movie could have featured Biollante, or any other kaiju created by a human scientist like Murakami as a consequence of the United States’ actions during the war. This would have tied together the movie’s various plotlines, thus making the featured monster a more meaningful presence.

Unfortunately, Biollante isn’t nearly as popular as Ghidorah among franchise fans. Moreover, having Godzilla fight a giant plant, no matter how scary, wouldn’t have been nearly as cinematic as the clash with Ghidorah, which is probably the best part of the movie.

The first Godzilla movie told viewers about the danger of unregulated science. Shin Godzilla showed the dangers of bureaucracy and ineffective government. Godzilla: Minus One was about survivors’ guilt and finding hope under the rubble of disaster. What is Godzilla: Minus Zero trying to say? I have a hard time answering this question.

At first, it seemed that the movie’s main theme could have been the American occupation of Japan after the war. In fact, the U.S. military's plan to use Godzilla as a weapon emerges at the end of the movie as the film’s big moral question, but it’s a rushed, poorly explained subplot, dragged down by paper-thin American characters.

Overall, Godzilla: Minus Zero did what all the Godzilla sequels did: It turned into a monster movie. It’s an inevitable downturn in quality. One giant monster born of nuclear experiments can be a metaphor for humankind’s fears. Add a second one, and it becomes a spectacle.

The seven Godzilla movies of the Heisei Era (1984–1995)​​​​​​​ are an exception. Coming after the franchise’s long Shōwa Era (1954–1975), which shifted the original movie’s dark tones into family-friendly monster team-ups, the Heisei Era movies felt like a return to form. Godzilla is back to being a destructive force of nature, and its monstrous foes, while still somewhat wacky, represent the dangers of unbridled science and the weapons race.

Godzilla vs. Biollante is a great example of the Heisei Era, and I wish Yamazaki had drawn more inspiration from this underrated entry instead of falling victim to the biggest trap in kaiju cinema.

Looks like Godzilla will be taking another bite out of the Big Apple

#3363. 10 Greatest Sci-Fi Series With Perfectly Executed Time Loops, Ranked

The time travel subgenre of science fiction has delivered several of the greatest and most beloved sci-fi shows in history. Then again, there are many ways to make a time travel show, and one of the most entertaining is the time loop subgenre, which is built around a period of time repeating itself over and over again. Throughout history, many shows have made use of perfectly executed time loops.

Whether we're talking about a show that's entirely built around a time loop, such as Russian Doll, or one that only features a perfectly-executed time loop somewhere in its run, such as Star Trek: The Next Generation, there are a few noteworthy cases of series that definitely understood the assignment when it came to crafting a time loop that's compelling, logical, and fun.

After Gene Roddenberry's Star Trek: The Original Series revolutionized sci-fi television back in 1966, fans began clamoring for a new Star Trek show. That long-awaited follow-up finally came with 1987's Star Trek: The Next Generation, one of the most masterful space sci-fi shows of all time, and arguably the best piece of Star Trek content to date.

The show's time loop episode is "Cause and Effect," where the whole Enterprise is caught in a time loop that ends with its collision with the USS Bozeman. Featuring a guest appearance by Kelsey Grammer, it's far and away one of the best-ever episodes of Star Trek television, a true ticking-clock thriller that keeps raising the stakes with every passing minute.

This is not the first time that Doctor Who, a real cornerstone of British pop culture, has been on hiatus; but since the show has never been canceled outright, it's technically still the longest-running sci-fi series the small screen has ever seen. And like many time-travel sci-fi show masterpieces throughout history, it features no shortage of storylines featuring some kind of time loop.

From the Third Doctor's "The Claws of Axos" to the Twelfth Doctor's "Heaven Sent," Doctor Who has been executing time loop stories masterfully since the '60s. That's because most of the time, these time loops are built to explore nuanced themes or the Doctor's complex psychology, rather than just being cool narrative tricks. What's more, the show is so open to playing around with its rules that no two Doctor Who time loops feel exactly the same.

Summer Time Rendering, based on the manga series written and illustrated by Yasuki Tanaka, is a standout example of an entire show being built around a time loop narrative. It's the story of a young man who, upon returning to his remote island hometown for a funeral, discovers a death-based time loop and must outsmart memory-stealing doppelgängers in order to save those he loves.

The result of such a premise is one of those modern anime where every episode's a masterpiece, arguably one of the most underappreciated sci-fi anime series of the 2020s so far. Where many time loop stories anchor their protagonist to a single moment every time the loop resets, Shinpei dying in Summer Time Rendering sends him to shifting points in time, lending freshness and excitement to every reset.

Since its conclusion all the way back in 2010, many mystery shows have tried to replace Lost; and even though no show will ever be able to replicate that modern classic's unique magic, shows like the British gem The Lazarus Project at least come close in terms of quality. In it, a man who can remember time resets is recruited to prevent global extinction, until personal tragedy tempts him to break the rules.

What makes The Lazarus Project feel so delectably unique is that, whereas most sci-fi shows treat time loops as traps to escape, this series treats them as an institutional emergency response system. This, combined with the way the show integrates the time loop mechanics into its protagonist's arc, makes for a show as intellectually compelling as it is emotionally engaging.

Based on the novel written by Tomihiko Morimi and published in 2004, The Tatami Galaxy is one of the best anime miniseries the small screen has ever seen. It follows an unnamed and disillusioned Kyoto University student who repeatedly rewinds his college years to join different campus clubs in pursuit of an idealized life, only to have his plans derailed each time.

The Tatami Galaxy isn't really concerned with the intricacies of its time loop mechanics at all. Instead, it treats its time resets as a character-building plot element, reflecting the protagonist's feelings of regret, self-sabotage, and yearning for connection. People who love time-loop stories are character- and theme-driven are bound to absolutely love The Tatami Galaxy.

Steins;Gate is based on 5pb. and Nitroplus' 2009 visual novel of the same name, and it follows a self-proclaimed mad scientist who, after accidentally building a time-traveling text-message device, must leap across shifting timelines to save his friends from fatal consequences and a shadowy organization. It's far and away one of the most universally beloved and acclaimed sci-fi anime series of the 2010s.

Steins;Gate is also one of those anime thrillers that are perfect from start to finish, and even though it's primarily a time-travel show, it features loop-like elements that are downright perfectly executed. With intelligently constructed internal mechanics that make the show lean quite satisfyingly toward hard sci-fi, these loop-like elements make every shifting timeline feel like it's adding to an emotional, narrative, and thematic domino effect.

It's an absolute tragedy that ABC canceled Day Break before its full first season had even finished airing, because this is one of those sci-fi thrillers that absolutely had the potential to become something far greater. In it, an LA detective framed for murdering an Assistant District Attorney is trapped in a time loop, trying to clear his name and uncover the conspiracy around him in order to protect his loved ones.

It's such a forgotten 2000s gem that it may feel like a deep cut, but it's a truly essential part of the conversation when talking about the best-executed time loop narratives in television history. Heavily serialized and deeply connected with its conspiracy thriller genre elements, Day Break's time loop elements may have never come full-circle due to the series' cancellation, but they show incredible promise.

Based on Twelve Monkeys, the '90s sci-fi cult classic film directed by Terry Gilliam (which itself was based on the experimental short film La Jetée by Chris Marker), Syfy's 12 Monkeys is one of those intense sci-fi shows you need to watch twice to fully understand. It's about a time traveler from a plague-ravaged future who journeys to the past in order to stop the release of a deadly virus that will wipe out humanity.

It's a familiar enough premise within the field of time travel and time loop sci-fi, but 12 Monkeys elevates that premise with some of the most intricate plotting that any sci-fi show of this kind has ever seen. From beginning to end, everything about this loop makes perfect sense rationally and is deeply hard-hitting emotionally, resulting in an absolute masterpiece of a 2010s sci-fi series.

Netflix is no stranger to making absolutely masterful sci-fi shows involving time loops. Case in point: Russian Doll, a dramedy co-created by and starring Natasha Lyonne. It follows Nadia, a game developer who keeps dying and reliving the same night in an ongoing time loop, leading her to find someone else in the same situation.

On top of the razor-sharp writing and Lyonne's unforgettable lead performance, Russian Doll benefits from having some of the smartest time loop writing of any sci-fi series in history. The loop works on multiple levels, serving as the fuel for the show's narrative momentum, sense of humor, character depth, thematic complexity, and emotional core.

It's not every day that you see a streaming platform get something right on their first attempt, but it just so happens that Dark, Netflix's first-ever German-language series, is also one of the streaming giant's best shows to date. It's set in a small German town where children suddenly go missing, leading four intertwined families to uncover a multi-generational time-travel conspiracy binding their fates across decades.

It's one of those sci-fi shows that get time travel right, and even though its approach to deterministic time loops and cyclical time travel is quite unconventional within the field of time loop series, it works. Each beat of Dark's multi-layered three-season run was carefully plotted and outlined from the start, making it so that all of its time travel elements—time loops included—work flawlessly from start to finish.

#3362. ‘The Lowdown’ Season 2 Finale Hinges on Two Monologues — Let Ethan Hawke and Sterlin Harjo Break Them Down

[Editor’s Note: The following review contains spoilers for “The Lowdown” Season 2 Episode 8, “The Tower” — including the finale’s ending.]

“I saw the structure of the episode as these kind of waves that crash upon Lee,” Ethan Hawke said in an interview about “The Lowdown‘s” Season 2 finale. “The way life works, it’s not like, ‘Oh, this one thing happens and then you change.’ It’s usually a series of things that happen, and the walls of your defenses come down.”

Lee’s walls were certainly up when “The Lowdown” Season 2 began. Untethered by the acclaim for his Season 1 exposé on Dale Washberg (Tim Blake Nelson), Lee reacts with vehement defensiveness. He mocks the journalists who named him Tulsa’s Journalist of the Year during his acceptance speech. He alienates his friends and embarrasses his daughter. Related Stories ‘Cliff Booth’ Brings Back a Fan-Favorite ‘Once Upon a Time in Hollywood’ Face ‘The Hunting Wives’ Review: Season 2 Reloads Without Slowing Down in Netflix’s Delirious Soap

He’s a mess, and when Ginger (Betty Gilpin) walks into his life with a tantalizing new story, he’s lucky — not because she’s the woman of his dreams carrying his drug of choice (a “truthstorian’s” next crusade), but because grounding forces are on the way in the form of his estranged father, Lee Raybon Sr. (Tommy Lee Jones), as well as a few clear-eyed, full-throated friends. Over the course of a riveting, revelatory Season 2, they all help to bring Lee back to himself, one wave at a time.

The finale’s first swell comes as quite a surprise — two surprises, really. When Lee pulls up to the funeral home, prepared to pay a terse goodbye to his departed dad, so, too, does his former business partner and best friend, Wendell (played by Peter Dinklage). Wendell tells Lee he’ll “always be grateful” for Senior’s guidance when they were younger, and it’s immediately clear he’s not about to take the man’s final tribute as lightly as his son may have hoped.

“When Tommy’s character dies and there’s a funeral, we’re all like, ‘Well, wouldn’t Wendell be there?’ I mean, they’re really great friends,'” Hawke said. “I called Peter up and I was like, ‘Is there any way you’d come down for one day to be just at this funeral?’ And Peter was shooting in London and flew in and flew right back. He came in and made it happen for us.”

But Dinklage’s return was no mere cameo. Creator Sterlin Harjo knew better than to let the opportunity go to waste.

“I think there was a Shakespeare monologue in it first, and it was beautiful,” Harjo said. “Then Peter suggested the Dylan Thomas. […] I can’t imagine a more exciting way to have Peter be in your show than doing this Dylan Thomas poem that’s a gentle poem, but he does it with this rage — how it’s supposed to be read. It’s amazing.”

Volunteering to speak when Ray (Michael Hitchcock) gets overwhelmed, Wendell spends a few seconds scrolling to find the right poem (“Do not go gentle into that good night”) and then tears into it with vigor. Dinklage’s recitation is more of a resuscitation — powerful enough to wake the dead, it wakes Lee up, snapping him into the present and bringing him back to life.

“When he’s doing the poem, he came in at a 10,” Harjo said. “The only direction I gave him was, ‘What if you build to that?’ And that’s what he did, and it was just unbelievably great.”

“That one is violent and abrupt,” Hawke said. “It’s a friend shaking you up.”

In Hawke’s case, Lee’s friend was his real friend. He knew Dinklage “loved poetry,” and he even knew a little bit about what his fellow actor would bring to this poem.

“This is where collaboration is really mysterious about how it works and when it works really well,” Hawke said. “I’ve been friends with Peter Dinklage since, I don’t know, 1990. […] We both arrived in New York around the same time, and we used to sit around and tie one on and try to flirt with girls and read poems. We used to geek out about how much we loved the ways people would read poems in the old days. If you hear Dylan Thomas read a poem or you hear Orson Wells read a poem, they weren’t afraid of feeling or emotion or a theatricality. They weren’t afraid of passion — actual passion — and caring and looking foolish.”

“We’re living in an age of irony and cynicism and detachment, and this definition of cool being that you don’t care. Whereas the definition when I was growing up was Bob Marley and John Lennon and Miles Davis and those guys cared a tremendous amount. They weren’t detached. They were completely attached. So for me to watch Peter bring that to his performance was like, ‘Let me show you kids how to do a poem!’ [laughs] ‘You got to do it like your life depends on it.'”

“The key to that scene is the interaction between him and Lee,” Harjo said. “I love that he’s watching Lee the whole time. It’s like there’s no one else in the room and he’s doing it for Lee. I love that.”

“The camera does pick up subconscious,” Hawke said. “A lot of times I’ll see work that might be good, but it has no subconscious to it. I can tell there’s no secret sewn into the filmmaking. And Sterlin loves — you can call it poetry, you can call it whatever you want — but [he loves] when there’s multiple layers happening. […] And so for me, I’m not just sitting there with an actor doing this scene. I’ve known this guy for 30 years and I know what this poem means to him, and he knows me.”

“If there was an Academy Award for Best Single Scene, I would give it to Peter Dinklage in our show.”

While Dinklage may have to settle for an Emmy, Harjo had to write the other big finale monologue for an actual Oscar winner. At the reception, Lee’s daughter Francis (Ryan Kiera Armstrong) reads a passage from her grandfather’s journal, written shortly after Lee Jr. was born, as a way to honor her ancestor. Then, as Francis speaks Senior’s words, Senior appears seated behind her, and Tommy Lee Jones takes over the scene.

“The bigger thing about that monologue is I knew it was coming,” Harjo said. “I was like, ‘Oh shit, I got to write this thing for Tommy Lee Jones.’ I kind of had Tommy Lee Jones dialed in through the whole season. I felt like I could really write his voice. But when it came to that monologue, I’m like, ‘God, he’s already known for one of the best monologues in the world at the end of ‘No Country for Old Men,’ and I can either try to do a fancy monologue that isn’t like that at all, or I could lean into the fact that Cormac McCarthy and the Coen brothers did this really well already, and there’s no way that I don’t know that as a filmmaker. So I’m going to lean into it and almost give homage to that speech.'”

“Not to toot my own horn, but I feel like I nailed it,” he said, laughing. “Of course, it filters through Tommy Lee Jones and all of a sudden it’s like this fucking amazing thing that he does. It was wonderful being on set. Just watching him give that, it was unbelievable. I could have used any take and it would’ve been amazing in a different way.”

Throughout the monologue, Lee sits in thoughtful silence. He’s not only absorbing what his father wrote and remembering who he was; he’s also recognizing his shifting role as a son who’s now a father. There’s a connection across generations. Yes, his responsibility to his daughter means avoiding repeating his dad’s mistakes, which Lee is well-aware of, but it also means honoring his father’s better intentions, like the ones he voiced in that journal and Francis is voicing again now.

“Lee’s adamant that he’s nothing like his father,” Hawke said. “The first thought I had is, ‘All right, this is why Lee Raybon is obsessed with the truth: It’s that his father was a chronic liar.’ If you grew up in a house where your parent was really comfortable lying to you, you would get obsessed with people in power misleading you, and that would really drive you.”

“But then as we played the scenes deeper, I realized that Lee was lying to himself; that he was just as manipulative as his father is. He just does it in the name of truth. All this bad behavior that he was in denial of, he’d actually internalized it, and he was so much like his dad that he was completely blind to it, which is behavior I’ve seen in so many friends. It’s amazing. But I had to live through it. I didn’t get it when I was reading it. I got it when I was playing it, and that was very powerful for me.”

One way Harjo & co. illustrate Lee’s development over the course of Season 2 is simple: He listens. Instead of shouting, pontificating, or generally causing chaos, Lee spends much of the finale hearing what everyone around him has to say. Even when he’s up his own ass or annoying the hell out of folks, he has a community who cares about him, and their steady presence in his life is what eventually breaks down his defenses.

“The first [wave] is Peter reading that poem, and then the second one is gentle and persuasive where my daughter is revealing to me that my father did love me,” Hawke said. “Part of the thing you learn watching this show is that Lee feels like he has to conquer the world to be worthy of self-respect. His daughter is saying, ‘It’s right here for you, and it always has been.'”

While another monologue played a significant role in how the episode plays out — Ginger’s speech to Francis, outside the bookstore — that moment wasn’t about Lee. (“The whole idea was Ginger and Francis don’t really get to hang out, but they are alike,” Harjo said. “Ginger immediately recognizes it and probably also knows that she had a father that was a lot like Lee.”) So his final wave comes from a curious source.

“The third one is just this final little moment that happens with Vickey (Abbie Cobb) when she tells him his fortune is bad and he sees it as a good thing. He understands that everything is point of view, and for him, towers coming down would be good.”

“Those are the three steps that I think are designed to get Lee back on his feet again,” Hawke said. “That push him to be like, ‘All right, you know what? I’m not quitting. I’m going to keep being me, and I’m going to be a better version of me.'”

How he’s feeling when Season 3 starts is anyone’s guess, and that assumes a renewal that’s yet to be announced is still in the offing from FX. But one thing’s for sure: If Lee comes back, he’ll be a changed man — and he won’t be alone.

“The Lowdown” is available on FX and Hulu.

#3361. 10 of the Best 'GTA 6' Cheat Codes, and How to Use Them

Cheat codes have long been a part of the Grand Theft Auto video game franchise, and the tradition continues with GTA 6. Not only does GTA 6 support cheats, but it also has a menu that lists all of them as well as instructions for unlocking them. However, you cannot fire up the game and start using cheats from the beginning. In fact, it requires quite a bit of work on your part. Here's how to unlock cheat codes in GTA 6, how to see the list of cheats, as well as the 10 best cheat codes in GTA 6.

Gone are the good old days when you could fire up GTA, enable god mode, unlimited ammo, no reload, spawn a jetpack, and run around the entire city destroying things at will. In GTA 6, you'll need to complete the main story to unlock the ability to use cheat codes. On top of that, you'll have to complete challenges of various difficulty levels to access specific cheat codes. Some of these cheats unlock the moment you finish the main story. Others, however, are quite challenging or time-consuming. For instance, unlimited reload requires you to win 25 gold medals at shooting ranges.

Once you complete the main story in GTA 6, just go to in-game settings, and you'll see a new Cheats tab. This lists all 61 cheats and how to unlock them. You'll see the actual button combo for each cheat right after you complete the unlock requirement.

Unfortunately, there are some serious gameplay ramifications to using cheat codes in GTA 6. For starters, you can't save the game once you input even one cheat code. That's why it's best to save before you start using cheats, to avoid losing progress. Using cheat codes will also disable trophies and achievements in GTA 6.

To start using cheat codes in GTA 6, you'll have to get your character to pull up the smartphone by pressing the up arrow on the D-Pad. Then, hold L1+R1, and press the cheat's key combination on the D-Pad.

While there are a lot of cheat codes in GTA 6, these are 10 of the best, listed with the right key combination, and the condition to unlock them:

This cheat unlocks the moment you complete the main story in GTA 6. To use it, press up, right, down, left, up, left, down, right.

You unlock this cheat code after losing a three-star wanted level 25 times. The key combination is left, down, right, down, up, down, up.

Lose a three-star wanted level 50 times to unlock this cheat. The key combination is left, down, right, down, up, right, up.

This cheat unlocks the moment you wrap up the main story. Press this to unlock: down, up, up, down, up, down, up, down, up, right.

This is the third cheat that unlocks when you finish the main story. When you shoot or punch/kick characters, this cheat will launch them in the air. The key combination is: down, up, left, right, down, down, up, down

If you win 25 silver medals at shooting ranges, you can unlock infinite ammo in GTA 6. The key combination is: down, up, right, down, left, left, up, down, down, down.

To stop needing reloads, you need to win 25 gold medals at shooting ranges in GTA 6. The key combination is: down, up, right, down, left, left, up, down, down, up.

If you complete 100 workouts during your GTA 6 playthrough, you'll unlock the cheat that lets you instantly obtain body armor. Press this key combination to make it work: down, up, left, up, up, up, up, up, down, down.

This GTA 6 cheat allows you to change the weather at any time, and it unlocks when you finish the main story. Press this key combination to toggle it: down, right, up, down, right, up, right.

To spawn this cool emergency vehicle, you just need to discover the MTL Pumper in the game's progress menu. Use this key combination to spawn one: left, up, right, down, left, left, up, left.

#3360. GTA 6: Should You Buy Eddie Acosta's NFT Or Kill Him At The Rooftop Party?

There's a random Grand Theft Auto 6 encounter with an NPC named Eddie Acosta, who is an annoying crypto enthusiast who Jason first meets at the Y Hotel bar during the "Pool Day" mission at the beginning of Chapter 4. A few in-game days after this interaction, Eddie will send you a text inviting you to a rooftop party at Heathcliff Heights in central Vice City.

You can attend the party as either Jason or Lucia, though you'll have to go without your partner. After meeting Eddie in the lobby, he'll spend the elevator ride hyping up his latest cryptocurrency venture. However, once you step onto the rooftop, Eddie will lock the door behind you, revealing that there isn't actually a party at all.

Eddie demands that you invest a whopping $20,000 in his scheme before he'll let you back inside, leaving you to decide whether to fork over the cash or find another way off the rooftop.

If you decide to give in to Eddie's demands and invest $20,000 in his blockchain art project, he'll happily unlock the door and join you on the rooftop. Eddie will send a picture of your newly acquired NFT to your phone, and you'll be free to leave the building without any further complications.

Unsurprisingly, Eddie's NFT is completely worthless, and there is no way to recoup your investment. Despite his enthusiasm for the project, Eddie doesn't have any follow-up missions, and purchasing the NFT won't unlock any additional content or provide any long-term benefits. You'll effectively have spent $20,000 on a glorified digital picture and the privilege of taking an elevator back downstairs.

If you refuse to invest in Eddie's NFT, you'll be stuck on the rooftop and will have to find your own way down. You can kill Eddie if you're particularly annoyed by his little scheme, though doing so won't solve your immediate predicament. Either way, you have two options for getting off the rooftop without spending $20,000.

You can parachute down to street level or use the bicycle on the other side of the rooftop to jump the gap between buildings, allowing you to access an elevator and make your way downstairs. If you choose to leave Eddie alive, you'll have the opportunity to confront him afterward and call him a loser. You'll walk away with all your money intact and have the satisfaction of knowing you didn't fall victim to his ridiculous NFT scheme.

You should absolutely refuse to invest in Eddie's NFT, as there's no tangible benefit to spending $20,000 on his ridiculous scheme. However, as tempting as it might be to kill Eddie after he essentially holds you hostage on the rooftop, it's ultimately not worth taking the negative hit to your criminal profile.

Getting off the rooftop is relatively easy, especially if you're comfortable using a parachute or doing an easy bicycle stunt. Sparing Eddie also gives you the opportunity to insult him afterward, which is arguably a more satisfying conclusion to the encounter. Considering the money you save and the unnecessary consequences of killing Eddie, walking away without investing is easily the best outcome in GTA 6.

#3359. 2026's Best Silksong Replacement Is Officially A Hit On Steam

Well Dweller is a must-play for Metroidvania fans

After a long, long wait, Hollow Knight: Silksong finally launched a year ago, and we're already getting DLC soon with December's Sea of Sorrows expansion. But you shouldn't let your anticipation overlook one of the best Metroidvanias of 2026: Well Dweller, from developer Kyle Thompson. Following its September release, Well Dweller is currently sitting at 98% "overwhelmingly positive" reviews on Steam based on more than 2,000 reviews.

In Well Dweller, you play as a bird, Glimmer, living in a kingdom where birds are hunted down on orders from the queen... so she can kill them personally. Glimmer's family is captured by the hunter, who leaves a menacing "You're Next" message behind for Glimmer. What's a bird to do but set off on a fairy-tale adventure to try to save his family?

Though Glimmer is no doubt a cutie — he's got big, almost googly eyes — the world around him is certifiably not cute. Skeletons dot its landscape, plant life protruding from the hollows where eyes once belonged. Glimmer and his family even live inside of a skull at the bottom of a well.

This is a dark fairy tale, one where gravestones pop up after you defeat a boss. The first boss is The Groundskeeper, a monstrosity with a Joker-like smile that's just two arms and a head protruding from a circular body. He's a creep, and the game's first true challenge. While you'll likely have no problem with Well Dweller's common rabble, its boss fights will pose challenges. Not to worry, however, as Well Dweller gracefully has difficulty options, something we wish Silksong had.

Exploration is just as essential to a Metroidvania, and Well Dweller has plenty of biomes, hidden areas, and shortcuts to explore. Glimmer gradually uncovers new exploration-focused skills, like the ability to use his matchstick as a springboard and the ability to fly on gusts of air.

While it feels like some games take ages to come out — like, ya know, Silksong — developer Kyle Thompson puts out a new well-received Metroidvania every two years. Well Dweller is his latest after Sheepo (August 2020), Islets (August 2022), and Crypt Custodian (August 2024). Though they're all Metroidvanias, they each have a unique identity; if you want something a little more colorful, Islets might be the way to go, while Crypt Custodian is for players who want more games to star charming cats.

Well Dweller is a much more bite-sized experience than some Metroidvanias, like Silksong, where you might need 50 hours to scour everything it has to offer. According to stats on Howlongtoeat, Well Dweller is around 11 hours long, much like the developer's previous Metroidvanias. Like January's Mio: Memories in Orbit, Well Dweller won't wear out its welcome on its way to becoming one of 2026's must-play Metroidvanias.

As anyone who has ever shopped at The Home Depot (or any hardware store) knows, power tools are expensive. That’s why Black Friday at The Home Depot is so important: It’s the perfect opportunity to get the tools you’ve been wanting at some pretty steep discounts. And the best deals even give you a free tool if you purchase a starter kit from one of the major tool brands (Ryobi, DeWalt, Makita, or Milwaukee).

Here’s how this year's “buy one, get one” (BOGO) deal works: Pick out a starter kit from one of the brands, add it to your cart, and you’ll be presented with a list of available tools you can add (they’ll be marked “FREE,” so you can’t get confused). When you go to check out, the price of the tool will be listed as “SAVINGS.”

Here are the starter kits you can choose from:

Ryobi ONE+ 18V Starter Kit (includes one 4.0Ah and one 2.0Ah battery and charger). Cost: $99.

DeWalt 20V Max Starter Kit (includes 6.0Ah and 4.0Ah batteries and charger). Cost: $199.

Makita 18V LXT Starter Pack (includes two 5.0Ah batteries and a rapid charger). Cost: $199.

Milwaukee M18 FUEL Combo Kit (includes a brushless, cordless hammer drill and an impact driver). Cost: $399.

Note that the Ryobi, DeWalt, and Milwaukee offers include 14 free tools to choose from, while the Makita offer only includes 8. Also, note that while the Ryobi starter kit is your cheapest option for a free tool, the batteries included are weaker. The DeWalt or Makita batteries cost more, but offer more power and flexibility.

Some of the deals go beyond just getting a freebie. For example, if you choose the DeWalt Starter Kit for $199, you can get an Atomic 20V Max impact wrench that normally costs $239 for free, which is a significant savings even if you already have batteries and a charger and don’t really need those items (plus, you can never have too many batteries).

The Home Depot is also offering deep discounts on just about everything in the store. Some of the most notable tool deals include:

50% off this DeWalt Cordless Brushless Oscillating Multi Tool, including battery and charger

33% off this Ryobi Combo Kit, an incredible deal for a circular saw, reciprocating saw, and a power drill/driver plus two batteries and a charger; the batteries are small, but this is a great deal on a starter kit.

42% off this Combo Kit from Milwaukee, including a Packout toolbox, a hammer drill, an impact driver, a grinder, and a reciprocating saw, plus two batteries and a charger—a massive deal for anyone who needs to tool up rapidly.

45% off this Brushless Cordless Impact Wrench Kit from Ryobi, which includes a battery and charger.

That only scratches the surface—if you’ve ever needed anything from Home Depot, Black Friday is the day to run out and get it.

Of course, Black Friday can be a little chaotic, so here are a few tips to maximize your savings and experience:

Check online and in-store. Some deals are in-store only, and some items (especially BOGO tools) may not be available at your nearest location—make sure you enter your ZIP code when you’re checking out to ensure you won’t have any problems.

Consider whether you need more batteries and chargers. Depending on your existing collection of batteries and chargers, buying more to get the discount may or may not make sense.

There's no price matching or rain checks. Remember that the store won’t honor price-matching or offer rain checks on Black Friday items.

Cyber Monday will have deals, too. More deals will be rolled out on Cyber Monday (November 30), which may include items you want but don’t see on sale for Black Friday. But keep in mind that Black Friday prices probably won’t go any lower—so snap up what you need as soon as you can.

Sign up for text alerts to save a little more. Home Depot offers a $5 coupon (off a purchase of $50 or more) when you sign up for email or text alerts, which you may be able to apply to your Black Friday purchase for a little extra savings.

Home Depot isn’t the only store offering free tool giveaways:

Like Home Depot, Lowes is offering BOGO tools with the purchase of starter kits from major tool brands.

Tractor Supply Co. has a wide range of BOGO tool offers during its Black Friday Event.

If you’re looking for outdoor equipment, note that Bass Pro Shops and Cabela’s aren’t offering a BOGO deal this year, but the first 250 customers at each physical store will receive a free “mystery promo card” valued between $10 and $500. If you’re going to go for this, plan to line up early—250 cards are going to go fast.

The best early deals on tools right now are at Home Depot, where you can get up to 65% off on select Milwaukee tools, 50% off on DeWalt tools, and 30% off on Ryobi tools. They also have several offers for over 50% off on hand tools..

Home Depot and Lowe’s often compete with each other for seasonal sales, so it’s always a good idea to check both sites before buying. Right now, Home Depot has the best deals on DeWalt and Milwaukee cordless tool sets, but Lowe’s has a better deal on Craftsman hand tool sets.

The best prices of the year on tools are during the holidays in November and December. This is because of the holiday shopping push, as well as making space for new tools that come out in the spring. The second-best time to buy tools is in May and June during Father’s Day sales.

#3357. Roku Is Officially Removing Its Best Feature

Erielle Sudario is a Collider News and Feature Author from Australia and has worked in the journalism industry since 2018. She has a passion for entertainment and pop culture news and has interviewed YouTubers, voice actors, film directors, and musicians throughout her career. When she's not writing, you can see Erielle building keyboards, reading a good book, playing video games, and creating content on social media.

Streaming platforms have ways to make themselves stand out. Netflix has a long history as the first platform on the market, Crunchyroll hosts the largest anime library, and Prime Video has the "X-Ray" feature that pulls up information about the content viewers are watching. Unfortunately, one of this platform's standout features will be removed next month.

Roku is a streaming platform owned by Roku Inc. and has over 100 million users, according to the company's April 2026 press release. The platform boasts a large content ecosystem, with over 500 free live linear channels in the U.S., thousands of on-demand titles like Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, and the #5 streaming app in the country. In June 2026, it was announced that Fox Corporation planned to purchase Roku, and in November 2026, the acquisition closed for $22 billion. As a result of this deal, one of Roku's standout features will leave the platform.

Cord Cutter News reported that the iconic fish tank screensaver will no longer be available on Roku next month. Known in the app as "Aquatic Life," the screensaver's creator, Jim Sachs, made the decision after learning that Fox was acquiring the platform. Users were reportedly notified about the screensaver's removal but will be able to choose other options, like the "Jungle Screensaver," "Nautical Screensaver," and more. Users who haven't made the switch will automatically see the "Roku City" screensaver. Users have expressed disappointment about "Aquatic Life's" removal, opting to share their opinion on the platform's decision through social media, especially the YouTube video version of said screensaver.

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

Ars Technica spoke with Sachs about his decision to remove the screensaver from the platform in an interview. He explained that he "can't be part of the Fox World," noting the outlet's controversial status and its biased reporting. He also noted that Roku asked to restore the license, which he declined. He said he would consider restoring the license if Fox reversed its business model.

“I’m assuming that Fox will not be reversing their whole rage-based business model and take responsibility for all the harm it has caused. I’d be happy to restore the license under those circumstances. They could even have it for free.”

Sachs has noted that his decision will financially impact him as the Roku deal was his main source of income. He revealed the licensing agreement he had with the platform, offering Roku either $80,000 per year for exclusive rights to all set-top devices or $60,000 per year for non-exclusive rights, and that the platform opted for the first option. While Sachs knows his decision won't have any meaningful impact, he hopes another platform will offer to license his work.

[Editor’s note: This interview was originally published on April 24, 2026, when “I Swear” was released in American theaters. Aramayo recently won Best Actor in a Film at the BAFTA Scotland Awards. The film and his performance are eligible for this year’s Oscars, and “I Swear” is now streaming on Netflix.]

When Robert Aramayo signed on to play Scottish Tourette’s activist John Davidson in filmmaker Kirk Jones’ biopic “I Swear,” he could scarcely imagine where the film would take him.

A hit in the UK, the film netted Aramayo a pair of BAFTA wins earlier in the year, as the British actor won both the vaunted Rising Star Award (previous winners include James McAvoy, John Boyega, Tom Holland, Tom Hardy, and those are just some of its biggest names) and the Best Actor trophy (beating out Timothée Chalamet, Leonardo DiCaprio, Ethan Hawke, Jesse Plemons, and eventual Oscar winner Michael B. Jordan). Related Stories ‘Odyssey’ Cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema Was More Interested in the Intimate Than the Epic Forget Photorealism: How ‘Wildwood’ Made Its Handmade Digital Artistry Visible

But that’s hardly all that happened at the February awards show, which was instantly and forever marred by a number of loud, racist outbursts from Davidson himself that were directed at “Sinners” stars Jordan, Delroy Lindo, Wunmi Mosaku, and more. The fallout from the incident was both swift and prolonged, and will likely impact the domestic release of “I Swear,” which is rolling out in stateside theaters now.

Aramayo’s performance in the film is indeed star-making and awards-worthy, as he brings sensitivity and great courage to his portrayal of Davidson, following him from his earliest symptoms through his current passionate activism. Hopefully, viewers can see and appreciate the work on its own merits, and get to know Aramayo much better, though he has previously appeared in plenty of projects recognizable to American audiences, from “The Empty Man” to “The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power” to a little thing called “Game of Thrones” (young Ned Stark!).

Ahead, Aramayo tells IndieWire about his deep research for the role, everything BAFTAs, and what he hopes will come from more people seeing the film and, hopefully, understanding Tourette’s all the better.

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

IndieWire: When I saw the film at TIFF in September, I did my due diligence before I reviewed it, and learned that John is a huge figure in the UK, but relatively unknown in America. How much did you know about him before this film?

Robert Aramayo: John’s made a lot of documentaries, but the big one that probably had the most impact was “John’s Not Mad,” and that was in 1989. So if you speak to people who were around then, they have a lot of very personal stories about watching that documentary and being like, “Wow, is this Tourette’s? What’s Tourette’s?”

So when you get the script, are you someone who then wants to do more research into him, or do you feel like the script is the thing?

The production team and Kirk were so gracious, and they gave me so much time. I think they were like, “Oh, yeah, take a couple of months or something to research and stuff.” I was really thankful for that. The first thing that I did was to meet John; I met him very quickly. And then I went away for a month, and I spent that time gaining as much knowledge as I could about Tourette’s and what it is. That was through watching the documentaries, watching YouTube videos, and reading books.

I based myself in Galashiels and spent weeks with John, just following him around and spending as much time with him as I could. And also traveling through Scotland, meeting people, mainly through [support organization] Tourette Scotland, who lived with Tourette’s as well. I wanted to have, I don’t know, a more expansive view of Tourette’s than just John. Obviously, John was my main focus, though.

When you’re getting ready to meet John, what were you expecting and anticipating? What were you nervous about?

I don’t know what I felt, really. I was so filled with anxiety about, oh my word, am I going to do this? I wanted John to like me. I was already feeling, God, this is going to be a really big challenge. And I met him within days of saying yes.

But then, when I met him, one thing that struck me straight away was his knowledge. He’s got a really amazing knowledge about, obviously, Tourette’s, but also a lot of neurodiversity and how it lives, other conditions that exist with Tourette’s, and stuff like that. He’s got a lot of thoughts about how we can do better and help young people and things like that. He’s very forthcoming with it.

He’s got so much heart. He’s such an amazing, welcoming, supportive man that I was just like, wow, this is a really impressive person that I’m meeting here. Of course, then your anxiety and the responsibility meter have gone through the roof.

Just watching the film, I learned so much about what Tourette’s can entail and the very wide spectrum of symptoms that people can have. What was the most unexpected thing you learned about it during your research?

A couple of things really that had a really big impact on me straight away, and that sort of broke my perception of what I thought Tourette’s was, that anything can be a tic, and that it’s so singular to the person. So if you’ve met one person with Tourette’s, someone said to me, you’ve met one person with Tourette’s. That was a big thing.

And also the fact that there’s a lot of tics that you just don’t see. There’s tics that you don’t see as tics because anything can be a tic, or there’s tics that exist only in somebody’s mind, and things like that, tics linked with OCD. Just the complexity of it was massive.

I learned some statistics recently, which I found really interesting: One in 50 kids in America live with persistent tic disorder, and one in 160 live with Tourette’s, so it’s unbelievably common, it’s everywhere. We have met people with Tourette’s, we meet them all the time. It was part of the experience of the film as well, we met loads of people who were living with Tourette’s undiagnosed. 50 percent of people who live with Tourette’s in the U.S. are undiagnosed, and that was true for us in the UK as well in our experience. Maybe the thing is that we don’t know that that’s what’s happening. That made me think, wow, there’s a real educational piece to this as well.

You are playing someone who is a real person who has been captured on film for many years. People know what he looks like, they know what he sounds like. How do you find the line between impersonation and impression in your performance?

I never wanted to impersonate John. I think I would’ve gone the wrong way if that was what I was thinking. You have to, at a certain point, take ownership of the character and try and make him your own. I was lucky because there was so much that I needed to learn, so for so long, I wasn’t thinking about performance or playing him at all. I was just trying to immerse myself as much as I could in everything, anything that I could get my hands on. Then, at certain point, I moved to thinking about how I was going to try and play my version of John.

In a [narrative] film, you get the opportunity to maybe show a little bit more [than a documentary]. A documentary film crew comes into somebody’s life and they can capture what they can capture, but we could capture way more intimate moments throughout the whole film that John had spoken to.

We could show the moments where he is on his own, whether there’s been an impact or how he’s feeling or his emotional life, how things change over time and stuff like that, and hopefully try and do it with truth and authenticity.

You attended Juilliard, which always seems a little, “Oooohhh, he’s Juilliard-trained.”

But now that you’re a few years out of school, what are the pieces of training that are proving to be most useful to you?

I think that acting teachers and drama school is vocabulary, really. At the time, certain things that teachers would say to me had a massive impact on me and really opened me up to other ways of looking at things, and other things are only impacting me now, as I keep working and as I get older. I think that’s the beauty of drama school, you get flooded with all of this stuff, and then you’re going, “Oh, that’s what they were talking about.” And then there’s things that my teachers would consistently say, “You’ve got to work on this, you’ve got to work on this,” and I’m still working on it. It’s like a toolbox, and every now and again you go, “Oh, yeah, that’s what I need.”

They also made us do liberal arts which — I’m from Yorkshire, I don’t even know what liberal arts meant — but I’d encounter Nietzsche and Plato and all this stuff. I had no time at all to digest anything, but I’d read it and be like, “I don’t really know what’s going on here, but I think this is going to be important one day. I think I’m going to reread this one day!”

What was the morning of the BAFTA nominations like for you?

I knew it was happening that morning. I remember talking to my agent, and we just didn’t speak about it, but we both knew that they were coming out that morning or whatever, so we had a really chill conversation about something else. [Laughs] I put it on in the background, because I thought we had a chance at, I don’t know, something, and then I heard that Peter had been nominated and I was so happy for him. I was elated for him.

So, I was just in that, and I was doing the dishes, and I was like, “Wow, that’s so cool. I can’t wait to go text him.” And then they said my name, and I just absolutely couldn’t believe it. My agent called me back straight away and was like, “Oh, my God.” It was an amazing feeling, but it was really unexpected because I was still really, really sort of overwhelmed by the Rising Star thing.

You genuinely looked so surprised when you won Best Actor at the show. I feel like I would black out in that moment. Do you remember what that moment felt like?

Yeah, because I almost did! I had this weird physical reaction where I sort of went back [pantomimes sitting way back], and I think somebody grabbed me. I think I would’ve just kept going. I would’ve fallen off my chair or something.

I honestly couldn’t believe it. I’m honestly not sure I still can believe that that’s something that happened to me, because for someone like me to be in that group of people blew my mind. I felt like, “Wow, and there I am, that’s my name.” To me, that was the thing that sort of really, really, really, really blew me away. When it happened, yes, it all just becomes a blur, and I’m running down the stairs, and I don’t know what the hell I’m going to say.

Obviously, other things happened at the awards show involving John. As someone who had seen the film, I felt like I had a greater grasp on what was happening; I had that context. Now that the film is coming out in America, what hopes do you have for people seeing the film and how that might impact that conversation?

I think lots of people watch the film, and they feel like their education around Tourette’s has improved and increased, and that would be amazing [if that continued]. I think it’s important to acknowledge that … Tourette’s has an impact on a person who’s ticcing, and the same tic obviously has an impact on the person who’s receiving the tic or impacted by the tic. And it’s important to acknowledge that, because that is what it is. Coprolalia, which is the tic that John has, that tic, it’s not saying what you think, it’s saying the worst thing imaginable. That’s how it was described to me.

I hope people watch the film. And I hope people watch the film and think, “Oh, I’ve learned something about Tourette’s.” I hope that people watch the film from the community, because that’s been an amazing thing as well. People watching it who have lived with Tourette’s or lived with another neurodiverse condition have reached out and said, “I see myself in this.” You want people to go to the movies and enjoy the film, but if people go home and Google “John Davidson” or Google “Tourette’s,” that’d be amazing.

The film is going to introduce you to a much larger audience, but you’ve also been in some massive hits before this one. Which is a fun way to ask: Do you know that “The Empty Man” has a huge cult fandom?

[Laughs] I’ve been told this. What an experience. I loved making that film. It was a long journey with it, and I learned a lot. And it was my first movie that I’d done with James Badge Dale, and I did another one with him as well. And I really, really liked working with him. He’s a really nice guy, and he’s a really talented actor. And the director, David [Prior], was wonderful. I learned a lot on that film. I love that people love that film.

You are also in the “Lord of the Rings” world as well. Are you going to be turning out to see “The Hunt for Gollum”?

I’m so excited. I can’t wait. I’m a massive fan of the Peter Jackson films. I can’t wait to see what they do with it. It’s a really interesting story. I’m glad that they’re doing it and doing it properly.

Now that you’ve had what feels like a big breakthrough, what sort of things are you pursuing next?

What do I want to do next? I don’t know! I feel lucky to just be an actor, to work. I’ve been lucky enough to work with some incredible people on “I Swear,” to work with Kirk and Peter and Shirley and Maxine. People like that, you learn, you grow, you get better. And so if I can just keep doing it, I’ll be happy.

That Rising Star Award feels like a lot of pressure!

I just feel really, really grateful for everyone who voted for me. It’s such a cool award that the public, the British public, vote for you. I feel so grateful for everyone who voted for me. I just feel very, very grateful for the whole thing, for everything, and mainly that people hopefully watch the film and talk about it.

For more information about Tourette Syndrome and access to free resources and support, visit the Tourette Association of America right here.

#3355. 5 Anthologies Better Than Black Mirror

There's no question that Netflix's Black Mirror is something exceptional. The anthology series, created by Charlie Brooker, debuted on Channel 4 in the UK, but it didn't take long for it to blow up on streaming. Now, Black Mirror has seven seasons and counting, yet it still manages an impressive 83% critic score on Rotten Tomatoes, as well as an 80% audience score. This is a series built for binging, but that doesn't mean it's easy, mindless watching by any means. The whole point of Black Mirror is to wake you up and get you thinking.

Each standalone episode of Black Mirror is set in what is imagined to be the near future. Just enough time has passed for technological innovations to change mainstream culture, and this often comes with less-than-ideal social development. These are cautionary tales about entirely conceivable developments that have a haunting and twisted impact on humanity's darkest impulses. Perhaps the best thing about Black Mirror is that, as it has carried on over the years, real-world technological development has added further fuel to the fire, increasing the show's relevance.

Of course, no TV show is perfect, or even unique. Black Mirror isn't the first anthology series of its kind, and it won't be the last. There are plenty of others for those who love this series to discover, many of which take the central concepts and formats of Black Mirror and do them even better. Don't get us wrong—Black Mirror is truly singular in many ways. Still, with so many intriguing concepts to explore outside the "technology is bad" foundation, it's hard to deny that other anthologies have gained an edge.

Guillermo del Toro's Cabinet of Curiosities served as Netflix's revival of classic TV anthologies such as Alfred Hitcock Presents or Rod Serling's Night Gallery. In these projects, hosts served as the central axis of the series, evoking a sense of bedtime stories or campfire haunts. Continuing this throwback approach, Cabinet of Curiosities features distinct horror subgenres in each episode. We get some H.P. Lovecraft, body horror, gothic architecture, and so on.

The quality of Black Mirror and Cabinet of Curiosities is certainly comparable. These are both great series that take a different approach to the anthology format. While Black Mirror centralizes near-future social commentary, Cabinet of Curiosities has a much broader scope. The series isn't boxed in by any specific theme, which means each episode can stand far more independently within the genre. This concept is ensured by the individual directors who take control of their own episodes. Each one brings their own visual style, allowing the series to function as a collection of art.

The British dark comedy anthology series Inside No. 9 did the impossible by remaining both alive and successful for 10 years, from 2014 to 2024. It's created by and stars Steve Pemberton and Reece Shearsmith, while each episode features guest cast members that pack an additional punch. While the various stories are completely self-contained and unique, with individual settings and themes, each features the number nine in some way, whether it's a house number, shoe size, or anything in between.

Choose the movie with the higher Rotten Tomatoes score.

Sign in to claim your place on the leaderboard!

This is another series that shines because it doesn't carry the burden of centering each episode around an overarching premise. There is plenty of focus on human nature, but the whole idea is complete unpredictability, which certainly can't be said for Black Mirror. That comedy element is a real asset as well, and, combined with tight 30-minute episode runtimes, Inside No. 9 makes for an easy watch without compromising on thrills. The proof is in the pudding with this one, as the show holds a perfect 100% score on Rotten Tomatoes​​​​​.

The year 2017 brought Philip K. Dick's Electric Dreams, a 10-episode anthology sci-fi series featuring standalone short stories inspired by the author. Each episode is about an hour long, and the adaptation process is handled by a different British or American writer each time. The cast of Electric Dreams is where the show really shines, with names like Bryan Cranston, Steve Buscemi, Greg Kinnear, Anna Paquin, Timothy Spall, and more. Philosophy is the name of the game in this series, and that's how it ultimately shines over Black Mirror.

The race is certainly close, but the philosophical depth of Electric Dreams allows it to stretch a bit further thanBlack Mirror​​​​. Each episode presents a sort of existential question, but without the frequent forced nihilistic cynicism that other psychological anthologies often lean on. There is certainly plenty of tragedy, but these instances aren't used just for shock value. Instead, there is genuine nuance and some subtle glimmers of hope that break up the tone of Electric Dreams.

The original The Twilight Zone, created by Rob Sterling in 1959, is the benchmark for the broader sci-fi fantasy anthology format. The lens of this series is beyond vast, as the many episodes explore social issues, yes, but it goes far beyond that. The human condition, morality, and psychological responsibility are explored and challenged in a variety of thrilling, suspenseful ways. The Twilight Zone is tonally diverse while still centralizing a very specific impact on viewers' nervous systems.

Black Mirror is often considered a spiritual successor to The Twilight Zone, but the prize must go to the original masterpiece here. The 1959 TV show is a breathtaking example of versatility. There are plenty of profoundly bleak episodes, but they are balanced by instances of whimsy, hope, and humanism. There is even a bit of dark comedy woven through here and there. The Twilight Zone can sometimes serve as a cautionary tale, but the overall takeaway is more generally enlightening and bittersweet insight. Add in that classic retro quality and it just really doesn't get any better.

With Tim Miller and David Fincher at the wheel, it's no wonder that Love, Death & Robots is something so spectacular. The series is an adult-animated sci-fi with episodes that run between 3 and 17 minutes long. As the title implies, this is another anthology largely set in the sci-fi genre, but there is plenty of fantasy, horror, and dark comedy as well. There's little question when watching Love, Death & Robots that the project is approached first and foremost as art, and this allows each episode to really shine as something special and unique.

Love, Death & Robots feels extremely experimental compared to Black Mirror, and while that wouldn't always be considered an asset, it truly works in this situation. The different artistic styles, themes, and episode lengths allow viewers to feel as if they are being carried along for the creative process. There is absolutely no narrative drag in this series, with each and every moment serving to capture the episode's central concept. It's all style and variety, which have come together to earn Love, Death & Robots 100% scores on several of its seasons.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3354. PS5s Are in Short Supply for Black Friday, but You Can Still Buy One

There may be a ton of Black Friday deals on electronics, toys, and gadgets out there, but don't get your hopes up if you're looking for a PlayStation 5. Not only are they not discounted, but the combination of international chip shortages, high demand caused by the release of Grand Theft Auto 6, and the general holiday shopping frenzy has also made it nearly impossible to purchase a new, unbundled PlayStation 5 at any price—nearly impossible, but not impossible.

Whether you're looking for a PlayStation 5 Digital Edition, a PS5 with a disc drive, or the flagship PlayStation 5 Pro, you won't find them at major online retailers. PlayStation Direct lists all three consoles as "currently unavailable." Best Buy suggests making an account with them to "improve your odds" of getting one. I can't find a listing for a new PS5 on Amazon either.

You still have some options for obtaining a PS5, but none of them are great. Many refurbished PS5s are selling for well above the list price of a new unit. There are some bundled, special editions available, but you'll likely be paying a ton for those. If you're willing to get your hands dirty by dealing with the wild west of Facebook Marketplace, you might be able to track down a used PlayStation 5 at a reasonable price, but approach with extreme caution.

If you're looking for a refurbished PlayStation 5, the best way to avoid a headache is to focus on who did the refurbishing. Buying refurbished electronics directly from a manufacturer is generally safer than buying from a third party, and in this case, it's cheaper too. PlayStation Direct is offering a "Certified Refurbished PlayStation 5 Console" for the relatively reasonable price of $519, while a refurbished Slim sells for $499. But if you're in the market, I'd lock it in quick: PlayStation Direct is already out of refurbished PS5 Pros.

Amazon's Renewed program has some strict requirements for third parties to stay in the program, like keeping defect rates under 0.8%, but refurbished PlayStation 5s are going for a premium on Amazon at the moment. A quick look at the site reveals that the price of a refurbished PlayStation 5 is hovering near $900; a refurbished PS5 Slim will run you somewhere around $750, and the current average price of a refurbished PS5 Pro has ballooned to over $1,700. These are well above the retail prices of $649 for the standard version, $599 for the digital version, and $899 for the flagship Pro version of the PlayStation 5.

There are some bundled versions of the console listed for sale online too. If you buy one of these, you're getting a new console and some other piece of hardware or a game, but there's a ton of upcharge at the moment. They're generally more expensive than the original price and more expensive than refurbished units as well. Here are some examples:

Best Buy lists this PS5 Pro with PlayStation Portal Remote for $2,134.99.

GameStop lists a Ghost of Yotei Gold Limited Edition PS5 bundle for $769.99 ($731.49 for GameStop Pros).

Best Buy lists a PS5 Slim with an external drive for $979.99.

By far the largest used market for anything in the U.S. is Facebook Marketplace, including PlayStation 5s. I checked out my local Marketplace, and there are a lot of listings for the console within a 40-mile radius of Los Angeles. The average price of used PS5 consoles here is hovering between $300 and $500, which seems fairly reasonable. But with Facebook Marketplace, the number of potential red flags rises with the demand for the product.

I've bought and sold a fair number of things on Marketplace with no problems beyond the occasional flaky person, and I've written a list of hacks for the service, but I wasn't covering a "shortage buying" situation like this. Scams tend to rise with demand, so when I see a listing for a $150 PS5 console (that contains the text "$250 or best offer"), I'm suspicious. It could have been posted by someone who doesn't know what they have, but I wouldn't count on it. If you're buying a PS5 on Marketplace, check the model and generation details very carefully against the actual item. Make sure the seller is offering what you want and not a PlayStation 4 with PS5 games. Verify how it was stored and the condition it's in. But it ultimately can come down to vibes: Don't let your desire to score a PlayStation 5 get in the way of your gut check about the seller or situation.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.
