#3353. How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?

[Editor’s note: The following story contains minor spoilers for “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.”]

A few years ago, Quentin Tarantino was set to direct one last movie to fulfill his self-imposed ten film limit before riding off into the sunset. And while he was open about his desire to stay creative in other mediums, not even the most outside-the-box thinkers would have predicted that his next big screen project would be a Netflix movie he wrote for David Fincher. “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is an unlikely miracle that emerged for a few distinct reasons: Tarantino’s hesitance to commit to his final directing effort, Brad Pitt‘s determination to play Cliff Booth again and his longtime friendship with David Fincher, and of course, the collapse of Tarantino’s planned film “The Movie Critic.” Related Stories ‘Odyssey’ Cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema Was More Interested in the Intimate Than the Epic Forget Photorealism: How ‘Wildwood’ Made Its Handmade Digital Artistry Visible

Given that “The Movie Critic” was also reportedly set in 1970s Los Angeles, and Pitt had signed on to reprise his “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” role, there was always going to be speculation about that script turning into “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.” Tarantino pours gasoline on that flame in the new film when Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki), the Hollywood manager who serves as both a foil and love interest to Booth, reveals that she used to be a film critic before moving into talent representation. The revelation is not crucial to the plot, though it does provide some clever character development as she explains her view that all movies are the culinary equivalent of hamburgers: enjoyable, but not worthy of serious analysis. Yet the inclusion of those lines kicked off a treasure hunt for fans of a director whose unmade movies are almost as legendary as the ones he actually shot.

A definitive answer to the question of “How much of ‘The Movie Critic’ made it into ‘Cliff Booth?'” is going to be hard to come by. Tarantino scripts are some of the most closely guarded secrets in Hollywood, and even the attached actors are often kept in the dark about scenes that don’t concern them. (In an interview with IndieWire, Debicki denied knowing anything about “The Movie Critic,” and everything we know about Tarantino’s process suggests that she was telling the truth.) Beyond that, reports about “The Movie Critic” suggest that the project was constantly changing, even as it neared the planned start of production. It’s impossible to know about every iteration of the project that may have existed at one point or another, but we can use the history of on-the-record quotes and credible reporting about “The Movie Critic” to make an educated guess about where it ended and “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” began.

Cinephiles spent much of 2023 and 2024 receiving piecemeal updates on what was supposed to be Tarantino’s farewell effort. When the project was first reported in March 2023, all we had was the title and a rumor that it was based on legendary New Yorker film critic Pauline Kael. But two months later, Tarantino began to reveal plot details that suggested it was actually inspired by an unnamed film critic who wrote for a magazine he stocked in the porn theaters that he used to work at.

“All the other stuff was too skanky to read, but then there was this porno rag that had a really interesting movie page,” Tarantino said in a May 2025 interview with Deadline. “He wrote about mainstream movies, and he was the second-string critic. I think he was a very good critic. He was as cynical as hell. His reviews were a cross between early Howard Stern and what Travis Bickle might be if he were a film critic. Think about Travis’ diary entries.”

Tarantino went on to say that the movie would take place in Los Angeles in 1977 (just like “Cliff Booth” eventually does) and would take inspiration from the critic’s real life, though the porno rag he wrote for would be fictionalized as The Popstar Pages. The director explained that he had done research on the largely unknown writer’s life, saying that “He wrote like he was 55 but he was only in his early to mid-30s. He died in his late thirties. It wasn’t clear for a while but now I’ve done some more research and I think it was complications due to alcoholism.” He also added that the role would have gone to an American man in his mid-30s, with rumors that Paul Walter Hauser was up for the part.

Tarantino said that the film, which was set up with his “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” backers at Sony, was set to begin “pre-pre-production” in June 2023, and the film secured a California tax credit to shoot the following year. But by April 2024, Tarantino officially scrapped the project. A blockbuster report in THR detailed the many creative changes that “The Movie Critic” went through during its tumultuous year of pre-production. Pitt’s involvement was never in doubt, but the report says that Tarantino looked at multiple ways of incorporating stars of his previous films like John Travolta and Jamie Foxx. He reportedly considered introducing the concept that his movies like “Pulp Fiction” and “Django Unchained” were real ’70s films that existed in this universe, possibly shooting new sequences from movies-within-movies or having his stars show up as the actors who played those characters. There was also an idea that they would interact with a teenage movie theater usher who would be a Sammy Fabelman-style stand-in for a young Tarantino.

None of which happens in “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.” Debicki’s character says that she wrote movie reviews for a grocery store circular, not a porno rag, and she has far more Pauline Kael than Travis Bickle or Howard Stern in her. And it’s hard to imagine that her and Hauser are ever up for the same parts. The only returning Tarantino characters are Booth and Margot Robbie’s Sharon Tate, who appears in a commercial for his signature fake brand Red Apple Cigarettes. But it’s not hard to see how this film could have emerged from the ashes of that one.

When you put all of the reporting about “The Movie Critic” together, it appears that the only constants were Tarantino’s desire to revisit the vintage L.A. world of “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” bring back Cliff Booth, and illustrate how working in a movie theater and watching ’70s cinema shaped his worldview and his future. The project collapsed because he couldn’t settle on a story that would incorporate all of those elements while containing enough gravity to serve as his directorial mic drop. But regardless of how many specific plot details from “The Movie Critic” survived the transition to “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,” all of those elements are present in the movie opening this week.

The film opens with a movie-within-a-movie, a fictional blaxploitation effort starring Yahya Abdul-Mateen II. From there, we see that Cliff is working as a projectionist at the New Beverly Cinema, where he also conducts some of his shadier business after hours. He does tell two of his teenage concession stand workers that their young age means it’s time to clock out — if you squint hard enough, that might be considered an Easter Egg about Tarantino’s youth and his possible inclusion in “The Movie Critic,” but the brief encounter hardly makes them seem like stand-ins for a man who loves to memorialize himself.

In a recent interview with Empire, Fincher said that he and Pitt each played a role in cutting 60 pages from the 230-page script that Tarantino initially turned in, resulting in a movie that took place in his sprawling world but was shaped by the type of movie that his two collaborators wanted to make. Looking through that lens, a plausible story for how one movie turned into another begins to take shape.

If you believe all of the reporting, it seems clear enough that Tarantino scrapped “The Movie Critic” because he had more vibes than plot. And “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” provides those exact vibes in droves. We’ll never be able to truly know how many elements were carried over unless Tarantino ever releases or novelizes his “Movie Critic” script (and even then, we won’t be able to fully trust that he didn’t make changes over the subsequent years.) But the safest guess is that he took the idea of Brad Pitt wandering through a darker, sleazier version of L.A. than the hippie paradise he inhabited a decade earlier and simply replaced the plans to make a grand statement about cinema with a pulpy crime plot that could have been ripped from one of his beloved Elmore Leonard novels. And the film still devotes plenty of time to showing scenes from fictional ’70s movies and TV shows, so Tarantino still had a chance to indulge that impulse.

The only other factor that can’t be dismissed is the possibility of self-referential trolling. Tarantino might love talking about movies more than he loves watching them. His insistence on retiring after ten films has nothing to do with his own enjoyment of the filmmaking process — in his own words, he simply doesn’t want anyone studying his future filmography to declare that he got washed up at the end of his career. Anyone who factors the opinions of future podcasters into his own major life decisions is deeply aware of what people say about him, and it’s possible that he simply included the lines about Karen’s career as a critic to add to the mythology about one of his legendary unmade movies. For all we know, the fact that IndieWire published this essay and you read it could be the exact reaction he wanted. In that case, well played, Mr. Tarantino.

“The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is now playing in IMAX theaters. It will be available to stream on Netflix starting Wednesday, December 23.

#3351. 7 Great Movies That Are Hard To Watch Today

Plenty of great movies are timeless, working as well now, or even better, than they did when they were first released. This is not a list of those movies. This list is for those great movies that were once showered with acclaim but are now hard to watch. Some are products of their time, featuring offensive stereotypes or character behavior that should never have been acceptable but may have been commonplace in the era they were made. Others have become hard to watch not for anything on the screen, but because of the off-screen behavior of those associated with them.

When it comes to debates about viewing older films from a modern perspective or separating art from the artist, there can be a surprising lack of nuance, at least in many online spaces — film appreciation isn't binary. These films can be appreciated for their strengths and acknowledged for their flaws without condoning or ignoring one or the other. It's up to the individual to decide whether they want to watch them or not, and all of them are still readily available. No movie is perfect or beyond criticism, even the great ones, and there's no denying that these ten movies can be hard to watch now.

Gone with the Wind is the poster child for hard-to-watch films once considered masterpieces. It was, and in many circles still is, considered a foundational Hollywood epic and sweeping romance that has had an enduring legacy and influence. It was nominated for thirteen Academy Awards and won eight, including the first for a Black actress, Hattie McDaniel. It was among the first films selected for preservation by the National Film Registry in 1989 and is often ranked among the greatest American films ever made by various publications. It's also a film that helped perpetuate racial stereotypes, blatant historical revisionist theories that have been embraced by white supremacists, and romantic depictions of sexual assault.

The film was immediately criticized by many members of the black community when it was first released. That criticism was just drowned in a sea of praise from the predominantly white critics and Hollywood elite. Gone with the Wind has always been problematic. Even McDaniel's achievement, often cited as a major progressive milestone, is tempered by the fact that the actress had to attend the Academy Awards in a segregated section. Every so often, the film becomes a catalyst for debate between film historians and activists, but it has never fully disappeared from the cultural conversation. It's a piece of American history, and all the ugliness that comes along with it.

The Western genre as a whole has a long history of problematic depictions of other cultures and ethnicities. When attempting to depict the violence and conflict that defined those chapters in American history, many of the earliest films in the genre took a reductive approach that relied on stereotypes rooted in decades of historical bigotry. John Ford's The Searchers is often noted as one of the earliest films to offer a more nuanced portrayal of the conflict between its white settlers and indigenous characters, though it still falls woefully short.

John Wayne, a man with his own complicated legacy of personal bigotry, plays Ethan Edwards, a virulently racist man who is just as violent as the "savages" he purports to hate. The character is far from heroic, and his hatred is not portrayed as aspirational by Ford. The film equates the prejudice and violence of men like Ethan to that perpetrated by the Comanche in the film as part of an endless cycle of hate, but it still affords far more humanity and innate heroism to its white characters. The influence of The Searchers on filmmaking cannot be overstated, but its revisionism of American myths certainly can be.

Much like The Searchers, Orson Welles' iconic film noir Touch of Evil seeks to contend with racial bigotry in a battleground defined by moral corruption and characters who operate in shades of grey rather than strictly moral black and white. The villain of the film, played by Welles himself, is a bloated, vile racist, and the hero is a Mexican officer of the law. Unfortunately, that Mexican hero is played by the very white Charlton Heston.

White actors playing characters of color in film has been a longstanding issue that isn't limited to bygone eras of Hollywood, contributing to a larger issue of cultural appropriation. Heston's character in Touch of Evil is portrayed as a morally just hero in a world of corruption. The fact that he's played by the definitively American Heston while all the other Mexican characters, played by actors of varying ethnicities, are depicted as far less savory, makes it harder to accept the film on a thematic level. Noir films often exist in realities where no one is morally clean, but when they try to engage with racial themes, a greater level of nuance is needed — Charlton Heston in brownface is not nuanced.

The entire James Bond franchise is problematic — it's just one of the things that fans of it have to accept. Its overall treatment of women and the misogynistic behavior of its spy protagonist have plagued it since the very beginning, and even more recent efforts to correct these issues have often been awkward at best. These issues are most apparent in the early films starring original Bond actor Sean Connery, but perhaps none more so than his most iconic, Goldfinger.

Often recognized as the most influential Bond film where every essential element of the franchise was crystallized, it is also rife with some of the most blatantly sexist and repulsive content of the entire series. Connery's Bond treats women like sexual trophies long before one is painted to literally resemble one, and his conquest of the unsubtly named Pussy Galore pushes far past playful innuendo into definitive sexual violence. The contributions of the franchise to rape culture are far too messy to untangle in one entry here, but the worst individual moments of one of the best Bond films are some of the hardest to watch.

Chinatown is often considered the greatest neo-noir ever made, with one of the most perfect scripts ever written and incredible performances by Jack Nicholson and Faye Dunaway. It's not what's on-screen that makes the film so hard to watch but rather the events that occurred off-screen. It was Roman Polanski's last Hollywood effort before he was indicted for sexual assault of a thirteen-year-old girl in 1977. Polanski fled the country and never returned for fear of imprisonment. It was not the last time the filmmaker would face allegations of sexual assault, though his career has continued in Europe mostly unimpeded, and he was awarded an Oscar for The Pianist in 2003.

Polanski's crimes have been relitigated several times in the court of public opinion over the years, but they've never resulted in any substantive change in the availability of his films. Conversations about separating art from the artist are common, but the issue becomes even thornier with Polanski and Chinatown, since the sexual assault of a minor is a major plot point. Some viewers may be able to distance the abhorrent actions of the director from those in his film, but it's impossible not to consider them at all. Chinatown can be hard to watch based on its content, but it's even harder to watch because of the dark man who made it.

At the very least, the assault in Chinatown is rightly treated as a horrific event. Manhattan, Woody Allen's romantic comedy love letter to New York City, though not depicting anything technically illegal, still gives a serious ick, especially in the wake of the allegations that have been leveled at its director/star. In the film, Allen's middle-aged character is dating a seventeen-year-old high school student, played by the then legitimately teenage Mariel Hemingway. Though the age gap is referenced in the film, and even treated as a source of humor, it doesn't lessen the discomforting effect it has.

Age gap relationships in Hollywood films and in general raise greater questions of power dynamics and grooming. Many older films and more modern ones still feature these kinds of dynamics, but regardless of the era of a film, it's an issue that should never be disregarded. Even though most reviews of Manhattan from the time it was released didn't raise the issue, and the allegations against Allen have never been brought to a court of law, there's no denying it makes many of his films hard to watch, Manhattan most of all.

Many '80s comedies have aged like milk thanks to their problematic depictions of sexual content. Some were never that good in the first place, like the genuinely revolting Revenge of the Nerds, while others are of actual quality, like most John Hughes ​​​​​​​films from the decade. Then there are those that somehow still completely work in spite of how unhinged they are. The entire plot of Back to the Future is predicated on a teen's own mother having the hots for him, but it is still a charming and beloved comedy.

Big is similarly beloved, but it does make one mistake that Back to the Future didn't. The premise, where a thirteen-year-old boy wishes to be an adult and wakes up with Tom Hanks' body, is ingenious and works because of Hanks' Oscar-nominated performance. Naturally, the film gets some solid comedic mileage out of the idea of a young boy in a man's body maintaining a relationship with an adult woman, played by Elizabeth Perkins. It also makes the insane narrative decision to have them consummate the relationship. The woman is completely unaware she's sleeping with a magical manchild at the time, but she doesn't have a complete mental breakdown upon later learning that, which is more than a little disconcerting.

#3350. GTA 6 Has Multiple Vice City References, Here's How Far It Goes

Fans have been enjoying Grand Theft Auto 6 for some time now and, unsurprisingly, have already begun to uncover its wealth of secrets. There are plenty of cool cars to find in GTA 6, new outfits, hidden areas, surreal and almost paranormal NPCs to fight and be killed by, and so much more. Most of this is slowly making its way out of the woodwork, with various GTA 6 guides showing fans how to find it all for themselves now that the hard part is done.

However, one hidden GTA 6 secret fans likely weren't expecting was an exciting reference to Grand Theft Auto: Vice City. Sure, the game is absolutely packed with references, from clothing, little lines of dialogue, and even a handful of locations. Yet, this particular easter egg goes above and beyond the expected and delivers a reference that is so unbelievably ridiculous that fans have to see it to believe it. Fortunately, the solution to unlock it has already, and rather miraculously, been discovered, leaving just a handful of somewhat simple steps for players to follow.

It turns out that Grand Theft Auto 6 has a secret hidden portal to the original PlayStation 2 version of Vice City nestled within Leonida. As first discovered by user Memeio and later shared on their X, this portal sees whichever character you're playing as leap into GTA: Vice City's Malibu Club. That isn't all, however, as it also transforms either Jason or Lucia into a pixelated, PlayStation 2 version of themselves, as well as the entire environment around them.

Furthermore, to leave the Malibu Club and return to GTA 6's world, you'll need to talk to the iconic Vice City character Kent Paul, which will trigger the exit portal to open. It's an impressive and immersive easter egg to the legendary Grand Theft Auto: Vice City, but the way one uncovers it is perhaps even more intriguing. The portal to the Malibu Club isn't simply sitting around somewhere in Leonida. Rather, you'll need to go through a series of complex steps to open it, all of which relate to a cheat code from the original Vice City video game.

After going to the Badger Radio Tower in Key Lento, flicking a lever and then pressing a button, players will find, scattered across GTA 6's LPL substations, a series of letters that spell out the Vice City cheat code, "LIFE IS PASSING ME BY." Additionally, in the aforementioned radio tower is a poster with the phrase "LOSE TRACK OF TIME," which is also a Vice City cheat code. By pulling the levers in these various substations that correspond to the letters in this cheat code, you'll officially open the portal, revealing the PS2 Malibu Club world inside.

If you're interested, there's a full breakdown of how to unlock the Malibu Club in Grand Theft Auto 6 in Memeio's original Reddit post. Should you succeed, you'll unlock Tommy Vercetti's iconic shirt and bike.

It is rather miraculous that Memeio even managed to find this in the first place, especially as numerous users have reported that using the RydeMe app, taking public transport, swapping characters, getting busted or wasted, and auto-driving all reset the process. However, thanks to the determination and ingenuity of Memeio, we now know about this incredible reference and can replicate it ourselves. It is impressive that Rockstar went to such lengths to include references to Vice City within Grand Theft Auto 6, and who knows how many more remain hidden.

#3349. ‘The Hunting Wives’ Review: Season 2 Reloads Without Slowing Down in Netflix’s Delirious Soap

Amid all the sex and murder in “The Hunting Wives” Season 2 — and there is a lot of sex and murder — the riskiest scene suspends itself between the two. Sophie (Brittany Snow), an East Coast liberal out of place in the conservative Texas town of Maple Brook, and Margo (Malin Åkerman), the mysterious local matriarch who can wrap just about anyone around her finely manicured fingertips, are confronted with a fresh dilemma. For spoilers sake, I won’t get into specifics, but the issue is urgent and impacts them both, without being serious enough to warrant what turns out to be their first-thought fix:

In the moment, their lethal instinct seems reasonable. Margo already shot a pregnant teenager in the woods, and Sophie committed vehicular homicide against Margo’s brother (which invited suspicions about Sophie’s past, considering its eerie similarities to a deadly “accident” back in Massachusetts). Their friends, neighbors, and even a youth pastor met their maker, too — just in the first season! So what’s one more body to bury? Go on! Kill ’em! Get yours! Related Stories ‘The Lowdown’ Season 2 Finale Hinges on Two Monologues — Let Ethan Hawke and Sterlin Harjo Break Them Down Will Ferrell Golf Comedy ‘The Hawk’ Canceled at Netflix After Just One Season

But before their bloodlust gets the best of them, their better angels make one last plea. Margo hesitates. Sophie follows suit. The gears start turning as they stare into each other’s wide, worried eyes: Are they really prepared to take another life? Are people that disposable to them? What does their initial response say about how they’ve changed? What does it mean about who they’ve become?

No need to spoil what happens next. The pause makes all the difference. “The Hunting Wives” has always been self-aware, but Margo and Sophie’s recognition of slaughter as their default response to trouble is a critical moment in a second season that reloads without slowing down. Creator Rebecca Cutler knows her Netflix soap is careening past the point where its central couple can reasonably return to lives lived between Margarita Mondays and Sunday church. Killing again, so quickly and carelessly, puts them on the precipice of becoming Bonnie and Clyde Bonnie — known fugitives who are only out for each other. Taking a beat lends the series a critical perspective — a vantage point from the top of the roller coaster, right before the big drop, where you can appreciate for a few brief, fleeting seconds the insanity to come.

Then you’re flying. You (and Margo and Sophie) are convinced it’s better to just move forward. Heck, this crisis isn’t going to fix itself!

Margo and Sophie’s breakneck pace to break necks is mostly a feature in Netflix’s surprise hit. The high-key camp comedy and low-key conservative satire moves quickly, sure, but where its characters are often flustered and panicked, it’s decisive in a way that exudes confidence. Progress is fast but assured. The drama is elevated but mindful. Characters don’t ask for permission or forgiveness; they just go after what they want, what they need, or what they feel they have to have, creating a propulsive viewing experience that zips by in a (muzzle) flash.

It’s a welcome change from prestige dramas that regularly feel like they’re stalling for time. While other shows tout firearms around for so long it’s like they’ve never heard of Chekhov, the hunting wives pull the trigger like they’re expecting money to come out — or lovers. Before you can think, “Wait, are they gay, too?” the person in question is already bending their same-sex partner over a desk. Even Season 2’s in-media-res opening lasts only a few seconds — like it’s flipping the bird to streaming TV’s favorite plot device — giving just the briefest glimpse of cop cars racing up to a giant cabin where Margo is (supposedly) being held hostage and Sophie is (supposedly) with her, holding a gun.

The opening tease only gets funnier as you find out how much unfolds between the start of the season and the flash-forward, especially considering its implication — that Sophie would threaten Margo’s life — makes sense from the start. Sophie begins Season 2 trying to repair her marriage to Graham (Evan Jonigkeit) and distance herself from Margo. The former goal sees her going to counseling sessions (where she comically compares her family to a box she wants to be trapped in), running errands, and playing the dutiful housewife.

The latter goal is harder and, arguably, more important. Margo doesn’t know her brother is dead. He’s not answering her calls or texts, but that’s hardly unprecedented behavior, so Margo ignores it — until the leader of a motorcycle gang (Dale Dickey!) shows up, claiming Kyle owes her, and if he doesn’t pay, she’ll take what she wants from Margo.

There’s never a good time for angry bikers to roar up your driveway demanding money, but it’s a particularly bad time for Margo. She’s in the doghouse with Jed (Dermot Mulroney) over the whole “a high schooler got me pregnant and then I had an abortion” issue, but a) that means she’s living in the pool house, not the poor house, and b) he’s really only mad because it’s a potential threat to his run for governor, which is gaining steam. Margo tries calling and texting Sophie, but she’s not answering. She wants to believe she doesn’t need Margo, love Margo, that she maybe even hates Margo. But a few cleverly laced connections make it clear she can’t.

Outside our core couple, Season 2 introduces plenty of plotlines that could pull them together and/or tear them apart. Callie (Jaime Ray Newman) doesn’t see why welcoming a camera crew to film her friends for a reality show (“Married Justice”) could lead to problems, even when the flirty producer warns participants that they should assume they’re “always on camera.” Her husband and co-star, Sheriff Jonny (Branton Box), is just as foolishly carefree, despite Deputy Wanda (Karen Rodriguez) investigating another dead girl in the woods — aka giving Callie a reason to ask questions about the last dead girl in Maple Brook, aka the aforementioned pregnant high schooler Margo killed.

Speaking of people Margo would prefer to forget, her former boy-toy Brad (George Ferrier), is having a hard time at Baylor. He can’t get over the recent murder of his mother, and his lonely boy coping mechanisms (playing acoustic guitar) soon attract the wrong kind of attention: a predatory music mogul named Chase (John Stamos) who promises to make Brad forget all his worries by turning him into a star (right after he loads him up with booze and drugs).

How Cutler shifts the puzzle pieces around to exert pressure proves just as engaging as before. There are plenty of big, loud laughs to go along with a steady supply of sly jokes and juicy melodrama. Anyone tuning in for the soap should be satisfied, just as anyone eager for some edgy satire should find it.

So long as they’re as open as these characters. “The Hunting Wives” may don MAGA drag to tell its story, but it’s a savage critique of conservative values. There’s Brad’s holier-than-thou father, Reverend Clint (Jason Davis), whose over-reliance on Old Testament discipline masks a hands-off parenting style that feeds his desperate son to the wolves. There’s Jed’s hypocritical right-wing politician, who’s more than OK with a little murder if it helps his campaign (knowing his constituents wouldn’t hold it against him) but can’t abide by his wife’s emotional outbursts in the pursuit of personal independence.

Then there’s the fun fact that everyone is gay (or bi or curious). So much of the show’s tension stems from secret trysts that only need to stay secret because of Maple Brook’s pervasive intolerance. That goes double for Sophie and Margo, whose continued pursuit of their repressed desires manifests in bigger and bigger risks. They get a small taste of what their lives could be like if they could just follow their hearts, sans consequence, forever, and then someone comes along to remind them why they can’t. It so often feels like there’s no real hope for the life they want that they fight like hell for whatever sliver they think they can sustain.

That fight gives the series its heart and its haste, but not everything fares better at a high velocity. By season’s end, Margo and Sophie’s individual interiority is rooted in too many questions and not enough answers, while their relationship feels more symbolic than genuine. Perhaps that’s the point. Perhaps the couple isn’t fated to be together as much as they’re fated to go further alone. Perhaps their relationship is more of a means to an end; a reminder of how far off track they got when they were isolated, and how hard it is to get back on track when the world is working to keep them apart.

Either way, it’s good drama. Either way, they’re going to discover new sides of themselves. Either way, the coaster is already racing ahead. Maybe it jumps the tracks, maybe it doesn’t. Maybe after all that, they really should just keep killing.

“The Hunting Wives” Season 2 premieres Thursday, November 26 on Netflix. All eight episodes will be released at once.

In a way, much of it feels familiar to recent Disney Animation Studios fare: A secret world of wonder and magic awaits just around the riverbend and/or through a magic portal, accessible only by imbuing one’s inner spark with “witchification.” But there is still something fundamentally broken about that magic world that our protagonist is positioned to make happen. And by “something,” “Hexed” Celeste (Jodie Foster), the queen of the hidden realm of Hexe, who is waiting to complete a moonlit ritual that will change the world forever.

According to Miller, the “Hexed” team differentiates this world from the magic of others in the Disney Vault through character design. “ If you look at Billie, you look at Alice, and you look at Celeste, I think we see their personalities come forward,” Miller told IndieWire. “With Alice in particular, she wears this impractical, tight, fitted skirt suit. For me, that was always indicative of the way she is trying to control everything around her, including herself. Even the way she does her hair, she is trying to make sure that her world is safe and contained.”

But the world isn’t safe or containable, and that’s part of the character design, too. Billie doesn’t just have a sparkle in her eyes — he has a crescent moon, hinting at the importance she may hold in completing Hexe’s magic.

“The crescent moon was something that was done in Vis Dev, and then the lighting department told us, ‘We can track that all the way through,” Veerasunthorn told IndieWire. “[It hints at] something special and witchy about Billie, even though she doesn’t know that about herself yet. The way that you see her hair curled in the same shape of the crescent moon, too, is speaking to someone who is looking to fulfill her potential.”

Billie’s design, from the reflection of the moon in her eyes to the color and shape of her hair to the natural elements woven into her clothes, hints at her tendency toward witchiness — and toward belonging in a world she doesn’t even know she belongs in. “We as the audience, we can be like, ‘Girl, figure yourself out!’” Veerasunthorn joked.

Both Billie and Alice are designed in stark contrast to Celeste, who perhaps has too much figured out in terms of witch magic and her silvery, flowing, regal appearance. “[Celeste’s] magic is elegant and powerful, very controlled,” Veerasunthorn said. “The color of Alice’s magic is in between these two extremes, and we wanted to get the sense that there’s something broken about her magic that we don’t quite understand yet. There’s a lost-and-found quality, and hopefully subconsciously we’re hoping that she can put her magic back together.”

“What was a challenge was that it’s this world of magic, a world of witches, and we’ve seen that a lot in media,” Trinidad told IndieWire. “We were trying to find our unique take on that world and how we could be modern and fresh and also sort of pay homage to our own Disney legacy.”

One key way “Hexed” speaks to that Disney tradition is by having a powerful queen who blurs the line between what’s best for her and what’s best for the world. Celeste is also [SPOILER] Alice’s mother and Billie grandmother; there’s a long and proud Disney tradition of very complicated abuelas to outright villain grandmothers, which Bush himself has contributed to in the past.

“The worst part is that my own mother, who’s absolutely lovely, is a grandmother now to my three boys, and she is deeply offended by my choices,” Bush joked to IndieWire about what he has against grandmothers, anyway. “I think the only grandma I’ve written that’s been undeniably loving nonstop is Grandma Tala [from ‘Moana’] — and she didn’t survive the movie.”

But Celeste is a collection of influences from the writers’ lives, the Disney storytelling tradition, and wider pop culture — and not least the actor who ended up voicing her. “We were trying to figure [Celeste] out, and the second that Jodie said yes to the role, it changed the entire character. Because, to be honest, when you’re writing for Jodie Foster, that’s nerve-wracking,” Bush said. “We better get this right. We better make this character interesting and layered.”

Bush and Miller’s writing intended to create space between Celeste’s polished appearance and the roiling jealousy and insecurity she’s buried underneath. “She’s a real villain in a way that’s icky and, for me, that’s a really fun thing to write. On top of the fact that she’s this person trying to take power and maintain power any way that she can, she’s also weirdly vulnerable and needy at the same time. It’s this really uncomfortable combination of characteristics that was really fun to write and to see what Jodie would do with it.”

Leaving space in the writing for animation and performance, the collaboration between story and animation teams is a core part of the writing for “Hexed” and all other Disney Animation Studios films. “We sit down with our story artists and with our animators, and we say, for instance, ‘the premise is we’re going to a weird place with a bunch of reject familiars. What could happen there?’ And everyone spitballs, and great ideas rise to the surface,” Bush said. “More than anything, what I love doing is trying to find a fun sandbox and then being really willing to go wherever the great ideas go.”

Bush, Miller, Veerasunthorn, Trinidad, and Hand all told IndieWire that this openness to great ideas is what makes Disney animation so special, and can make even familiar storytelling territory feel fresh and exciting.

“Maybe we’re coming for granddads next,” Bush said.

#3344. Princess Donut's Pivotal Dungeon Crawler Carl Moment Hits Different Thanks To Jeff Hays

There's no question that Dungeon Crawler Carl's massive success is at least partially owed to the incredible audiobook adaptations on Audible from voice actor Jeff Hays. His ability to seamlessly transition between dozens of wildly different character voices is impressive enough on its own, but the emotional depth he brings to Matt Dinniman's characters truly elevates the experience.

From the unhinged delivery of the System AI's announcements to the subtle cracks in Carl's voice as he struggles to maintain his composure, Hays adds an entirely new layer of drama to the story. His comedic timing is impeccable, but arguably his greatest strength is his ability to capture the emotional weight of Dinniman's most heart-wrenching moments.

There are several instances throughout Dungeon Crawler Carl where a particular scene just hits way differently in the audiobook than it does on the page. However, there's one scene involving Princess Donut that stands out as a prime example of why the audiobooks bring a whole new flavor to the experience.

When I first read Princess Donut's iconic scene in Book 5, The Butcher's Masquerade, where she performs her hit song, "All Eyes On Me," I actually laughed out loud at the absurdity of the lyrics. While it was certainly described as an emotional enough moment for the character, it didn't jump off the page as a particularly deep look at Princess Donut's character. I read it much more as a reflection of Bea's character more than anything, but listening to the audiobook version of this scene completely changed my conception of what was going on.

In Jeff Hays audio version, he actually sings a beautiful adaptation of the song over an acoustic guitar, and the song comes off as a melancholic folk ballad that absolutely tugs at the heart strings. For a moment that I was laughing at on paper, I wasn't really expecting it to land so differently when listening to the audiobook, but I was nearly brought to tears at how much the song itself reflects Donut's feelings toward her former owner.

The song itself captures a certain feeling of loss and longing that I simply did not experience when reading the ridiculous lyrics on the page, largely because the song is completely off the wall and makes no real sense. You can listen to the audiobook version of the song below.

While the brilliance of Dungeon Crawler Carl's story is obviously all Matt Dinniman's, it's difficult to imagine the series having quite the same impact without Jeff Hays. The audiobooks have accumulated over 140 million listening hours on Audible alone, and for a substantial portion of the franchise's fan base, Hays' interpretations of these characters are the only versions they've ever known.

Dinniman himself has acknowledged how instrumental the audiobooks have been to his success, even revealing that he hears Hays' voice in his head when writing new characters. There's something special about the creative relationship between the two, with Hays having an incredible understanding of the nuances of Dinniman's characters and the series' delicate balance between absurdist comedy and existential horror.

Perhaps the biggest testament to Hays' talent is that many readers who finish the physical books will subsequently purchase the audiobooks to experience the story all over again. Despite knowing exactly what's going to happen, hearing Hays perform some of the series' most memorable scenes can be an entirely different emotional experience.

It's also incredibly encouraging that Hays is officially involved in Peacock's upcoming Dungeon Crawler Carl television adaptation, reprising his role as Princess Donut. Of all the creative decisions surrounding the adaptation, casting Hays was arguably one of the most important. His involvement suggests that the people behind the show understand what made Dungeon Crawler Carl such a phenomenon in the first place, and hopefully, they'll be able to capture some of the magic that makes the audiobooks so exceptional.

#3343. 10 Greatest Thriller Series of 2026, Ranked

2026’s thriller television landscape has been marked by high-concept hits, major returning shows, and a mix of critical acclaim and commercial ups and downs. Some of these shows have redefined how far the genre can be expanded and elevated, with several matching the quality and prestige of their big-screen counterparts.

One of the major highlights of thriller TV this year has been the long-awaited return of Tom Hiddleston’s The Night Manager, which returned with a second season after a decade-long hiatus. Later in the year, Crystal Lake took fans back to the origins of the Friday the 13th franchise, delivering nostalgia and thrills at the same time. Between returning favorites and new shows, miniseries, and spin-off hits, here’s our ranked selection of the top 10 greatest thriller shows of 2026.

A series adaptation of Alice Feeney’s mystery novel created by William Oldroyd, His & Hers follows Anna (Tessa Thompson), a former news anchor who returns to her hometown in Georgia, where a series of murders have left locals tormented. As Anna starts investigating, she clashes with local detective Jack (Jon Bernthal), who’s also her ex-husband, and a further mystery brews between them.

When it premiered, His & Hers earned mixed reviews from critics but became a major genre hit and one of Netflix’s top miniseries of the year. The narrative blends crime noir, small-town murder mystery, and Southern Gothic tropes into a tense and twisty miniseries that genre fans would love to binge. While the show is a bit lacking in terms of plot development, it makes up for it with the leading cast’s strong central performances.

A series adaptation of Patricia Cornwell’s best-selling crime novels, Scarpetta revolves around forensic pathologist Kay Scarpetta (Nicole Kidman), who uses her brilliant medical skills and the latest forensic technology to solve crimes. The first season of Scarpetta is based on the books Postmortem and Autopsy. Jamie Lee Curtis, Bobby Cannavale, Simon Baker, and Ariana DeBose play other main characters.

Even though the show is designed like a procedural, Scarpetta is essentially a heavy psychological thriller that explores the protagonist more than the criminal investigations she undertakes. Despite receiving mixed reviews and criticism for its departures from traditional procedural storytelling, Scarpetta is still among the best new crime shows of the year, with a stacked cast and magnetic performances by Kidman and Curtis.

A series adaptation of the 1989 film by Joe Dante, The ‘Burbs reimagines the Tom Hanks-starrer with a newly married couple, Rob (Jack Whitehall) and Samira (Keke Palmer), who move into Rob’s childhood home in the suburbs. When a new neighbor moves into an old Victorian home across the street from them, tied to a mysterious incident from decades ago, it stirs up old secrets in the seemingly peaceful neighborhood.

Though technically a remake, Celeste Hughey’s series adaptation is much more lighthearted than the chaotic, absurdist black comedy classic from the '80s. But it is just as bizarre a murder mystery and even spookier and funnier, successfully engaging the viewer from start to finish. Released in the spring of 2026 and renewed for another season, The ‘Burbs has earned critical acclaim for Palmer’s crackling comedic chops and its fresh take on the original with a broader setting and quirkier characters.

Britain makes more detective television than any country has any business making, and somehow almost all of it is good. Here is the one you belong in, what it says about you, and the case for it being the best of the four.

You want the tea, the gossip and the vicar behaving oddly. Midsomer is a county where the scenery is beautiful, the fete is on Saturday and the murder rate is roughly that of a small war, and absolutely nobody involved thinks this is strange.

You feel other people's grief as if it were handed to you personally. Broadchurch is less a whodunnit than a study of what a small town does to itself when it finds out that the answer was always going to be somebody everybody already knew.

You go through things rather than around them. John Luther is the best detective in London and a liability to everybody who works with him, and the show is completely honest that those two facts are the same fact.

You say the thing and you do not dress it up. Vera Stanhope turns up in a hat and a mac, is rude to almost everybody, and is the only person in the room prepared to ask the question that the family has been waiting years for somebody to ask.

Bruce Miller returns with a follow-up to his award-winning The Handmaid’s Tale with The Testaments, a series adaptation of Margaret Atwood’s novel that is set in the same dystopian universe of Gilead. Set four years after the final chapter of The Handmaid’s Tale, the new series follows Agnes (Chase Infiniti), the 16-year-old daughter of a commander (and June Osborne’s biological child), who begins to question the system after she befriends a newcomer named Daisy (Lucy Halliday), who arrives from the outside.

The Testaments revisits the grim world of Gilead from a coming-of-age perspective, centering on a new generation of young women and exploring their girlhood, survival, and friendships within Gilead’s oppressive social structure. The series has been critically acclaimed for its visual style and terrific acting by the young cast, and was renewed for a second season. Since its premiere, The Testaments has become a critical and fan favorite, ranking among the most engaging shows you can stream on Hulu right now.

Developed by Brad Caleb Kane, Crystal Lake is a slasher miniseries prequel to the Friday the 13th franchise, revealing the origin story of Jason Voorhees and his mother, Pamela. Set seven years before the events of the first film, the movie explores the events that take place in the titular town after a young Jason (Callum Vinson) apparently drowns in the lake. When bodies start turning up in the woods, Pamela (Linda Cardellini) finds herself on a dangerously desperate path to get her son back.

Crystal Lake is a perfectly crafted spin-off prequel for a franchise that is equally good and bad, successfully expanding the Friday the 13th mythos. While retaining the brand’s classic campy and gory slasher style, the show elevates the narrative to the level of a high-concept psychological thriller. The eight-episode series is primarily anchored by Linda Cardellini’s riveting performance, which is the show’s biggest strength, as well as a period-perfect production that takes you back to the world of the original film.

Nick Antosca’s latest psychological thriller, Cape Fear is a series adaptation of John D. MacDonald’s 1957 novel The Executioners and takes inspiration from the book’s film adaptations from 1962 and 1991. It follows a vicious ex-convict named Max Cady (Javier Bardem), imprisoned for 17 years for murdering his pregnant wife, who gets released and seeks revenge on his former lawyer, Anna Bowden (Amy Adams), who represented him 17 years ago.

Cape Fear revitalizes the original crime classic with a reinvented plot and complex character motivations, veering more towards a chilling psychological thriller with modern updates rather than a conventional revenge story. The series builds on its earlier screen versions’ cinematic legacy, especially Martin Scorsese’s adaptation, and is as violent and vicious as the 1991 film, with Bardem’s menacing performance ranking at par with Robert De Niro’s maniacal murderer.

Two years after its first season premiere, the hit Netflix original spy thriller Black Doves returned this year with a brand-new and more thrilling season, with Keira Knightley and Ben Whishaw returning as Helen and Sam, spies working for the titular spies-for-hire agency. In Season 2, Helen faces more challenges after her husband becomes the Prime Minister and her agency is thrown into chaos after their handler, Reed (Sarah Lancashire), mysteriously disappears. Ambika Mod, Neve Campbell, Babou Ceesay, and Samuel Barnett join the second season as new characters.

Black Doves Season 2 became an instant hit among critics and fans, who praised its faster pace, higher stakes, and sharper comedy, all of which are balanced with deeper explorations of the harsher side of espionage and the friendship between the two leads. The second season has even surpassed the success and critical acclaim of Season 1 and easily ranks among the best spy shows of the 2020s. However, fans have also criticized the unrealistic plotlines and lack of crime-noir-style atmosphere as the main drawbacks of the second season.

One of the most hotly anticipated sci-fi shows of the year, Star City is Ronald D. Moore, Ben Nedivi, and Matt Wolpert’s follow-up to their highly acclaimed For All Mankind, exploring an alternate history of the Cold War-era space race between the Soviet Union and the US. Set in 1969, the story revolves around a group of scientists at the titular facility, where rocket engineer Sergei Korolev (Rhys Ifans) drives ambitious missions amid political paranoia and intense state scrutiny.

A thrilling combination of high-stakes espionage, alternate history, and sci-fi drama, Star City is undeniably one of the most elite sci-fi thrillers of 2026, joining the ranks of Apple TV’s prestige sci-fi library. Packed with tension, political intrigue, and human drama, the show reinvents history in a narrative that feels as compelling as reality. Since its May 2026 premiere, Star City has been widely acclaimed, earning praise for its stunning visuals and excellent storytelling.

Created by Steven Conrad, DTF St. Louis follows Clark (Jason Bateman) and Floyd (David Harbour), both lonely men undergoing a midlife crisis, who join the titular dating app to spice up their lives. But when Floyd is suddenly discovered dead, indicating foul play, his wife, Carol (Linda Cardellini), becomes the prime suspect. When Detective Donoghue Homer (Richard Jenkins) and special officer Jodie Plumb (Joy Sunday) investigate, the evidence points to something much darker than they first imagined.

Headlined by terrific lead performances, DTF St. Louis​ is thrillingly unpredictable and reveals an incisive psycho-social thriller under its dark comedy veneer, completely taking the audience by surprise and breaking all expectations. Simultaneously sharp, sardonic, and humanistic, DTF St. Louis has been critically acclaimed for its touching narrative about isolation, loneliness, and midlife crisis, and became one of the top Emmy winners of 2026.

Among all the returning shows of 2026, the second season of The Night Manager has been the most anticipated and long-awaited since its first season 10 years ago. Tom Hiddleston returns as British spy Jonathan Pine, who now gets himself entangled in a high-stakes international arms deal to thwart his old nemesis, Richard Roper (Hugh Laurie), who resurfaces in Colombia years after his presumed death with the help of a rising young entrepreneur named Teddy Dos Santos (Diego Calva).

The Night Manager Season 2 is not an adaptation of any book and expands on John le Carré’s original novel with a completely new story. In Season 2, Hiddleston’s Jonathan Pine is not only more mature, but also exhibits more depth as a character who has aged for a decade since we last saw him. Perfectly complemented by his equally compelling villains in Calva and Laurie, the second season of The Night Manager might not be as gritty as Season 1, but it hits harder emotionally and morally than the last.

#3339. ‘Cliff Booth’ Brings Back a Fan-Favorite ‘Once Upon a Time in Hollywood’ Face

”The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” stands on its own as a beautifully written (by Quentin Tarantino) and directed (by David Fincher) Los Angeles noir that both invites and earns comparison with 1970s classics like “Night Moves” and “The Long Goodbye,” but its rewards increase exponentially the more familiar you are with its predecessor, “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.” Although Fincher and Tarantino have both argued that the movie is less a sequel than simply another Cliff Booth adventure, the movie has quite a few fun Easter eggs to reward fans of Brad Pitt’s first time playing the laid-back stuntman.

Perhaps the most delightful callback to “Once Upon a Time” is the reappearance of two of cowboy actor Rick Dalton’s (Leonardo DiCaprio) collaborators on the “Lancer” pilot that took up a good section of the middle third of Tarantino’s earlier film. Co-star James Stacy (Timothy Olyphant) makes a brief appearance alongside “Lancer” director Sam Wanamaker, played once again by Nicholas Hammond, whose exuberant turn as the real-life actor-director in “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” was one of that film’s greatest pleasures. Related Stories ‘Odyssey’ Cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema Was More Interested in the Intimate Than the Epic Forget Photorealism: How ‘Wildwood’ Made Its Handmade Digital Artistry Visible

Hammond’s part is, like the other returning faces from “Once Upon a Time” (aside from Pitt, of course), essentially a blink-and-you’ll-miss-it cameo, but he was delighted to return to Tarantino’s world and to share the screen with Olyphant once again. He first heard rumblings that Wanamaker might return for “Cliff Booth” well over a year ago, when the assumption was that Tarantino would direct the script.

“Quentin has his team, and it’s the same crew that works on all his films,” Hammond told IndieWire. “I’d gotten to know them on ‘Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,’ and a couple of the guys from the crew sent me emails saying, ‘Hey, it’s great we’re going to be working together again.’ Everyone had an ironclad NDA, so no one could tell me anything about the film, but that was my one little clue. Then, of course, when Quentin dropped out, and it looked like the movie was not happening, I thought, ‘There goes that chance.'”

Hammond was elated, therefore, when Pitt resurrected the movie by giving the script to his friend Fincher. “Timothy and I knew that we were coming in basically as an Easter egg,” Hammond said. “It was a tiny scene, and we knew that, but we were just thrilled that we were asked to come back, that Quentin thought it would be cool to have those characters back in the movie again. Let’s face it, he can get any actor he wants in the world to do anything, so it was an honor and a joy even though it’s a tiny little moment in the film.”

When Hammond played Wanamaker in the first film, he saw an opportunity to pay tribute to all the talented, hardworking directors and actors who work in the industry without necessarily becoming A-list names — a category that includes himself. “Your career ebbs and flows,” Hammond said. “You do a lot of small roles on television or small roles in movies, and then you get your own series, or then you get a big movie, and that’s the life of most actors in Hollywood. Even people like Leonardo and Brad say they have tons of friends who were as good as them when they were all starting out, but so much of it depends on if the right role comes along at the right moment.”

Hammond noted that for a lot of actors that moment never comes, but Tarantino has always recognized that that doesn’t make someone any less of an actor. “Most people think that if you’re good, you’re going to become a star. Quentin realizes there are a hell of a lot of very good actors out there who don’t become stars — that there are so many stars that have to align in the universe for that to happen. He admires and celebrates actors like Michael Madsen and Bruce Dern who have been journeyman actors their entire lives with moments of success, or flares of global recognition.”

Hammond experienced one of those flares as a teenager, when he played one of the Von Trapp kids in Robert Wise’s classic musical “The Sound of Music,” and again several years later when he played Peter Parker on the CBS television series “The Amazing Spider-Man” — the role that made Tarantino a lifelong Hammond fan. “I’m fortunate in that way,” Hammond said. “I feel luckier than most actors in my situation, because I’ve had a few goalpost roles that the world is aware of.”

60 years after he made it, Hammond still runs into “Sound of Music” fans all the time. “I was on a plane yesterday flying to Sydney, and a stewardess crouched down next to my seat and said, ‘Nicholas, I just have to let you know that my family watches ‘Sound of Music’ every year,'” Hammond said. “‘When my grandmother was ready to pass away, she said the last thing she wanted was for all of us to gather around the TV together as a family and watch that movie.’ I don’t care how rich you are or how many movies you’ve been in, how many actors get a chance to be in a movie that has that kind of effect on people?”

Hammond says that, having lived through the eras “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” and “Cliff Booth” recreate, he knows Tarantino got that period of L.A. history completely right—something he attributes to the writer’s encyclopedic knowledge of his own work and that of all his peers. “There are very few people who could capture the 1970s as accurately as Quentin does,” Hammond said. “It’s his era. He grew up watching me as Peter Parker in ‘Spider-Man,’ and he watched all the episodes of ‘Gunsmoke’ I did, and all the episodes of ‘The Waltons’ and ‘The Brady Bunch.’ There’s not a show I was on that he didn’t see and know about.”

In “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” Hammond honored the directors of those episodic series whose names the public has forgotten, though Wanamaker, as an actor, was probably better known than many. When he got the part, Hammond was intent on playing Wanamaker with respect while still delivering on all the comic potential of Tarantino’s conception. “One of my fears when we were doing the film is I did not want Zoe Wanamaker to think we were making fun of her father, because we definitely weren’t,” Hammond said. “He was a very serious actor and a serious theater person.”

Hammond took a deep dive into Wanamaker’s life and career for the part. “Quentin’s office sent me a stack of DVDs of movies that Wanamaker had directed, and movies that he had appeared in,” Hammond said. “I got quite familiar with him. The Globe Theatre exists in England today solely because of him. If it weren’t for Sam Wanamaker petitioning and raising money and basically forcing the British government to authorize the building, the Globe wouldn’t be there. They wanted to build public housing there, and he managed to get a groundswell of support. And now, of course, it’s a huge tourist attraction, and in his honor the smaller studio theater within the building is called the Sam Wanamaker Theater.”

Hammond says he knew he was a part of something special when he saw “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” at its Cannes world premiere. “I’ve been lucky enough to be in three really significant films: [Peter Brook’s] ‘Lord of the Flies,’ ‘The Sound of Music,’ and ‘Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,'” Hammond said. “With three very significant directors. So I’ve had a very fortunate career, and I still get excited just seeing my name on the call sheet. And when you’re working with people like Leo or Timothy Olyphant who are right at the top of their game, they’re the best of the best. I’m on the New York Yankees now, and when I get up to the plate, I better deliver.”

Despite starring in several classics, Hammond is less interested in looking back than in whatever he’s working on now. “I absolutely love being an actor, and I love being on stage. I’ve done a great deal of stage work, and I’m always asked, ‘Which do you like better?’ And the answer always is, whatever I’m doing right then. When I walk into the stage door of a theater, I get exactly the same charge of excitement that I do walking onto a sound stage at a studio. I just feel like I’m home. I feel these are my people. These are the people that I’ve always been the happiest being with since I was 10 years old, and I that will never change.”

Hammond looks to his “Sound of Music” costar Christopher Plummer, who did some of his best work late in life, as a role model. “I’ll do this as long as I possibly can. I’m of the Christopher Plummer philosophy that way,” Hammond said. “The word retirement doesn’t really exist. What would I do? Give up the thing I love the most in the world to play golf? I’m not doing that.”

Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd held a press conference after the Thanksgiving Day shooting, detailing what the police know so far.

Judd said the violence erupted as a result of the online "Girls Gone Wild" ad that brought about 50 youths from Orlando to the soiree at an Airbnb in Davenport, FL.

Judd said the Airbnb was rented to an adult on behalf of a 16-year-old girl, who was in charge of the party.

After everyone showed up at the bash, Judd said Oral Walker --  an 18-year-old gang member -- whipped out a gun and opened fire. Grady said in a news conference Walker has 76 previous charges.

Another attendee allegedly pulled out his gun and returned fire, killing Walker, and then fled.

Judd said the shooter may have acted in self-defense and encouraged him to come in and talk to investigators.

During the shooting, six other people between the ages of 15 and 21 were wounded by gunfire, Judd said.

The sheriff noted that the 15-year-old girl was in critical condition, while the other surviving victims suffered non-life-threatening injuries.

#3334. Forget Photorealism: How ‘Wildwood’ Made Its Handmade Digital Artistry Visible

WETA FX has been called upon to do visual effects for everything, from orc armies to superheroes, alien planetscapes to the innards of a whale. On each project, they have to match the movie’s consistency. The goal is to make sure that the VFX blends perfectly into the overall visual style, not so unlike a certain Springfield dad creeping into a hedge.

Meeting that challenge often means the teams at WETA match and then build on live-action footage to get as close to a photorealistic look as possible. But adding digital effects to the wonderful world of stop-motion animation, as with “Wildwood,” WETA FX got to have more fun with creating a world that looks as textured and handmade as the puppets designed and animated by Laika Studios. Related Stories ‘Odyssey’ Cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema Was More Interested in the Intimate Than the Epic ‘Cliff Booth’ Brings Back a Fan-Favorite ‘Once Upon a Time in Hollywood’ Face

“Everybody was super stoked about this film because it’s so different from what we usually do. People got to be artists,” VFX supervisor Sabine Laimer told IndieWire. “We’re really good at making effects invisible, but here we could actually showcase the artistry. All of our people here loved it.”

This applies to the way that WETA helped intensify battle sequences, the way they expanded sets so that they feel as fast as the impassible woods where most of “Wildwood” takes place, and the way they were able to match cinematographer Caleb Deschanel’s lighting to bring a unity to the digital and puppetry work within individual scenes. When designing the ivy that Alexandra (Carey Mulligan) seeks to control and that Prue (Peyton Elizabeth Lee) seeks to pacify, WETA’s digital leaves weren’t meant to mimic real leaves in nature. They were built to look like the paper leaves a stop motion animator would use.

“[The leaves in ‘Wildwood’] have a different light transmission. They have a different level of detail, depending on how close the camera is to them,” Laimer said. “[We developed] this sort of stage realism, if you want to call it that, rather than realism, and that makes a huge difference.”

One element where WETA needed to heighten the realism most was the ivy, which is eventually summoned into a sentient spire that threatens to overwhelm the entire world. “It’s alive, but it’s not a person. It has character, but it can’t feel like it’s a boss. It has to have intent, but it can’t be so direct that it feels like there’s a brain that’s going after the characters,” VFX supervisor Dan Macarin laid out the challenge of Laika’s brief to IndieWire.

“It had to creep, it had to attack, it had to consume, it had to overgrow,” Laimer added. “There was a lot of material there for us to work with, which was amazing, but we had to translate all of this intricate detail that they’ve built on their practical sets into a digital plinth environment and build it in a way that was malleable for us, and we had different stages of everything.”

Laimer and her team tested ways to mimic the Laika animators’ practical work and drew inspiration from the natural world, like time-lapses of pea shoots with an uncanny, jerky motion as they grow. They built different vignettes that could be placed inside specific shots so the ivy would read as dangerous, but not distract from the drama between the characters. For the moments where the ivy threatens to overwhelm the entire plinth, the WETA team actually used fluid simulation to get the feel of the ivy being like a tsunami, this swelling of constant, growing motion that is headed in a definite direction, not just moving at random.

“We looked at practical references like schools of fish, where they move in unison and create shapes and change directions on purpose. It was a similar thing, or like flocks of starlings in the air. You have to sculpt the [ivy] cyclone per shot so that it’s not distracting in the background, it’s not too busy, but at the same time still feels like it’s alive,” Laimer said.

Hitting that visual effects sweet spot was important in all the visual effects collaborations between WETA and Laika. The path to do that always ran through story, and what visuals would make the storytelling the most immediately legible to the audience. “WETA is really, really fantastic at doing third act battles,” Macarin said. “We’ve done a tremendous number of them over the years and decades, and so it’s not the scope that we have to worry about. We can handle all of that. It’s always, ‘How do we tell this story?’”

In the case of “Wildwood,” telling the story with visual effects meant simplifying a lot, so that even when we placed it behind the explosion of cannon fire (where it would never be safe for a practical camera to go), we still cared about the characters. “We were able to create aesthetic choices that still allow the audience to engage in the battle, but not necessarily put you suddenly into this photorealistic explosion or feel. This is a very colorful, emotionally driven sequence that just happens to have a battle around it,” Macarin said.

The most fantastical-seeming choices in “Wildwood” are all about character. “They shot everything with two suns,” Laimer said. “They had a smaller, sharper key light and then a softer, wider one, which created this really beautiful falloff on the faces that we had to create digitally. That was really cool.”

Getting to build expressive, beautiful worlds in animation — whether digital, stop-motion, or a combination of the two — usually is pretty cool, to be fair. And clearly, in the case of “Wildwood,” it brings out some of WETA’s best work.

#3332. Grand Theft Auto 5: 17 Secret Areas That You Had No Idea About

The enduring popularity of Grand Theft Auto 5 means that millions of people have taken the game for a spin, but many of these players have never discovered all the secret locations in GTA 5. This is unsurprising considering the scope of the game, which provides you with a large, open-world map to explore and enjoy all the virtual free will you please.

Being an expansive game with hundreds of different areas and locations, it's easy to get lost in the exciting adventures one can go on in San Andreas. The most well-hidden and little-known locations scattered about the map can be hard to find without being especially observant. These range from tiny, yet useful areas that can provide shelter from potential enemies to simply creepy, mysterious locations that have a number of unanswered questions.

Whether searching out secrets with friends in GTA Online or taking on the hunt alone in the single-player campaign, if you want to discover the best GTA 5 secret locations, you have plenty to look forward to. You can enjoy finding these and, now that GTA 6 is out, discover even more secret locations in Vice City and Leonida.

The Humane Labs is a research facility that is found in a more secluded area of GTA 5's map, and with a few sneaky game tricks, you can find yourself exploring the secret spaces inside this private building.

The interior of this laboratory can be accessed as follows: approach the building, accept a job invite from your character's phone, and back out of the job menu that displays. This will spawn you inside the Humane Labs itself.

In GTA 5, entering the property will immediately deploy a four-star wanted level, but no such repercussions happen in GTA Online. With a submarine, you can also find a tank at the bottom of the water just east of Humane Labs.

From there, you can roam about and discover the miscellaneous Easter eggs that it has to offer. Unlike the other hidden labs or bunkers found in Grand Theft Auto 5, the interior of this facility is completely empty, leaving less chance of making enemies while exploring the space. It is quite a large secret area, with numerous rooms and wide spaces that you may potentially even find yourself getting lost in.

Grand Theft Auto 5 is known for having quite a few useful bunkers on the map, though this one's a little harder to find. In online mode, one of these can be stumbled upon at the Los Santos airport; you can access the location either by sneaking down a hatch on the roof or through the back doors of the area's building.

Inside, the place houses quite a few objects to interact with, including a number of vending machines and a water cooler. While it's a large enough bunker, the doors inside sadly read "Authorized Personnel Only," leaving not a lot to do or explore. However, it's a suitable location to hide from the cops as a wanted felon on the run.

It's also not known for sure whether Rockstar had initial plans for this room to play a more integral role in GTA 5's main campaign, given its level of interactivity. As it stands, it has the unusual feeling of a not-quite-finished space that's still interesting to uncover.

Hidden on the side of a disused country road sits a gold-glowing tree that many players speculate is at the center of a GTA 5 mystery. The golden tree is located nearest Braddock Pass on Mount Gordo. It can be seen clearly from the road, so interested players need only drive around the area until they find it.

Its gold color can only be seen at night; during the day, it looks like any other tree. This could very well be a glitch; other bushes in the game are occasionally seen to randomly glow gold.

However, some have speculated that the golden tree is somehow tied to GTA 5's Mount Chiliad mystery, a complicated conspiracy theory involving aliens, jetpacks, and a mysterious underwater hatch. While none of this has ever been solved, let alone officially concerned, the golden tree still keeps watch over Los Santos from its perch on the hill.

As one of the more expansive hidden locations in GTA 5, this secret mine tunnel is as interestingly designed as it is mysterious. Found in the more mountainous region of the map, you can access this secret area by detonating the wooden doors that block the place from outside entry.

This isn't accessible in the original console version of the game, introduced as a surprise in the PlayStation 4 and Xbox One versions of Grand Theft Auto 5.

Upon being blown up (either by grenades or any other explosive weapon), a dark entrance is revealed that leads to an eerie mine tunnel—one that extends to cover a wide range of ground, even branching off into different directions at some points in the area.

You'll also discover a perplexing dead body upon venturing inside—a man dressed in typical '40s fashion. This solves the side mission "Murder Mystery" and unlocks some camera filters for the game.

In a much more elusive part of the map, this hidden area can be located among one of the tiny islands of the Pacific Ocean. You'll have to access this via some form of water transport, and carefully seek out a portion of land with two trees standing side-by-side.

When you reach the base of one of these trees, GTA 5 players will suddenly find themselves transported into a secret underground bunker, complete with mercenaries and FBI agents standing guard.

With the main part of the base designed to look like a garage, it's also easy to find a variety of vehicles on display, including a red monowheel bike. When further explored, you may also stumble upon a few police operatives having a confidential meeting in what looks like a combined office and lounge, with fancy-looking sofas, a sleek TV system, and untouched, filled shot glasses.

GTA 5 contains countless references to icons of pop culture, including a faithful recreation of the final scene from the 1991 film Thelma and Louise. Starring Susan Sarandon and Geena Davis, it follows the titular characters as they embark on a crime spree across the United States.

In the film's final scene, Thelma and Louise are cornered by a group of police cars at the edge of the Grand Canyon. Rather than give themselves up, they instead decide to drive forward, ending the film in a final freeze-frame as their car flies off the cliff.

You can watch this scene play out in real time in GTA 5 by perching a helicopter near Raton Canyon around 7 PM. They'll see a group of police cars chase a Tornado to the edge of a cliff, at which point the Tornado will drive off, creating a near-perfect imitation of Thelma & Louise's final moments.

Yet another secret hideout, this one is elusively situated among the Tongva Hills. It is a small cave that overlooks the mountains of the San Andreas map, carefully hidden away for Grand Theft Auto 5 players to find, hidden from the rest of the territory. You can arrive at this location through the simple means of a helicopter (or any other form of aircraft).

However, it may take a while to spot, as at first glance, it may seem like a mere shadow or boulder. There is a narrow entrance into a small, dark cave with a beautiful view of the region's mountainous horizon. Inside, a pile of rocks and a spaceship part can be found, although the area is otherwise empty.

All the same, it makes for a perfect place to hide away from enemies. As a bonus, it's a properly defensible area, as bombs or booby traps can be placed around the entrance to ward off potential bounty hunters.

In the original version of GTA 5, some players reported finding a mysterious, smiling face in black paint on the side of a Mt. Chiliad rock wall. It's located on the north-facing slope and can easily be accessed from the cable car station.

Although many players believed this was merely a game developer who inserted their own Easter egg, there was some speculation that this was related to the wider Mount Chiliad mystery, which similarly involves paintings on the mountainside.

However, the former explanation appears to be correct, as in the Enhanced Edition of GTA 5, the face was removed and replaced with a rather risqué rooster. This one is done in the style of the other Mount Chiliad mystery graffiti and seems to be an indication of how higher-ups at Rockstar felt about noticing a developer had inserted their own face into the game unbidden.

If You're looking for a large, unique assault vehicle (and are a fan of tacos), this secret GTA vehicle location should be quite useful. Located to the north of Sandy Shores, a huge taco van can be found along a dirt road, right next to a few people who were probably down with the afternoon cravings.

You must arrive at this secret Grand Theft Auto 5 location between 1:00 PM and 2:00 PM, as the vehicle is only spawned onto the map during this time. The van is unoccupied, saving you the worry of having to kick someone out of their precious food truck.

One can easily hop inside and drive off with the vehicle, and—having the mechanics of a van—a second person can safely stand on its roof and be completely immune to falling onto the road. Although the location where the taco van spawns isn't one of the most interesting spots in GTA 5, it does provide one of the most useful secrets

Everyone knows about GTA 5's alien mysteries, which generally allow you to occasionally sight UFOs once you've completed 100% of the game's content. Fewer, however, know about the alien frozen under the ice during GTA 5's prologue, before Michael and the gang have even left North Yankton.

In order to find it, you'll need to forge your own paths shortly after you gain control. When the tutorial mission instructs them to make the railroad crossing, they'll instead want to make a right and drive onto the ice under the bridge. There, clear as day, will be an alien frozen beneath the river, reaching futilely for the surface. There's no further interaction with this extraterrestrial, but it is a fun detail.
