Apple AirPods Pro 3 are not only my favorite earbuds I've ever owned, they might also be my favorite headphones of all time. The Pros sound great, come with excellent noise cancellation and transparency modes, and are packed with modern features that go beyond listening to music. I'd recommend these to any Apple user looking for the best overall audio experience at full price, but when they're $100 off, I actively encourage you to buy these now.

On the surface, Apple's third-generation AirPods Pro are among the best ways to listen to audio on your Apple devices. I frequently turn to mine when I want to pay close attention to a new album, or watch a show or movie with intricate sound design. Plus, like other AirPods, the Pros are great for jumping between your various Apple devices. The noise cancellation on these AirPods is also stellar. I used to take my AirPods Max with me on planes, but lately, I've been fine with just my Pros, since the noise cancellation seemingly blocks just about as much background sound as my over-the-ear headphones. Equally great are both the transparency modes, which pump in outside sounds while you're wearing your AirPods, and Adaptive Transparency, which automatically adjusts the level of transparency based on how loud or soft your surroundings are. #3330. Lee Child Reveals Why He Doesn’t Mind ‘Reacher’ Fans Writing Their Own Fanfiction

Given that Lee Child spent more than 20 years writing a new Jack Reacher novel every year, I was quite curious to find out whether he actually enjoys reading the books now that somebody else is writing them. One of the things Child has spoken about over the years is that when he sits down to write a Reacher novel, he doesn't necessarily know how it's going to end, which means he's finding out what's happening to Reacher at much the same pace as the person who'll eventually read the book. I wondered whether that was still the case now that his younger brother, Andrew Child, has taken over, and whether the two would have conversations about what Andrew was planning to do with the character.

During a conversation to discuss the latest Reacher novel, Chain Reaction, Child revealed to Collider that he doesn't actually get to read the new Jack Reacher novels until they're submitted to the publisher. Andrew has inherited his older brother's approach to writing the books, which makes it rather difficult for him to tell anybody what he's planning to do with Reacher, given that he doesn't necessarily know himself.

“When I was doing it, I hated showing anybody anything, and I generally wouldn't, because the style that I had and that Andrew's continued is completely improvised. There's no plan, there's no arc view. You can't say this is what it's going to be. We don't know," explained Child. "It'll be what it is, and so until it's finished, I don't know really what it is or what it's about, and so, I don't like to show anybody, and he's the same. I just get it when the publisher gets it, and I read it out of interest.”

The show that claimed the most of your answers is the world you were built for. If two tied, both are shown — you're complicated enough to straddle two Sheridan universes.

You are a Dutton — or you might as well be. You understand that some things are worth protecting at any cost, and that the modern world's indifference to history, to land, to legacy, is not something you're willing to accept quietly. You lead from the front, you carry your family's weight without complaint, and when someone threatens what's yours, you don't escalate — you finish it. You're not cruel. But you are absolute. In Yellowstone's world, that combination of ferocity and loyalty doesn't make you a villain. It makes you the only thing standing between everything that matters and everyone who wants to take it.

You thrive in the chaos of high-stakes negotiation, where the money is enormous, the margins are thin, and the wrong word in the wrong room can cost everyone everything. You're a fixer — the person called when a situation is already on fire and needs someone with the nerve to walk into it. West Texas oil country rewards exactly what you are: sharp, adaptable, unsentimental, and absolutely clear-eyed about what people want and what they'll do to get it. You're not naive enough to think this world is fair. You're smart enough to be the one deciding who it's fair to.

You are a Dwight Manfredi — someone who has served their time, paid their dues, and arrived somewhere unexpected with nothing but their reputation and their wits. You adapt without losing yourself. You build loyalty through respect rather than fear, though you're not above reminding people that the two aren't mutually exclusive. Tulsa King is for people who are still standing when everyone assumed they'd be finished — who find, in an unfamiliar place, that they're more capable than the world gave them credit for. You don't need a throne. You build one, wherever you happen to land.

You carry the weight of a system that is broken by design, and you do it anyway — because someone has to, and because you're the only one positioned to do it without the whole thing collapsing. Mike McLusky's world is for people who are comfortable operating where there are no good options, only less catastrophic ones. You speak every language: law enforcement, criminal, political, human. That fluency makes you invaluable and it makes you a target. You've made your peace with both. Mayor of Kingstown belongs to people who understand that keeping the peace is not the same as being at peace — and who do the job regardless.

It's perhaps not all that surprising that Child is comfortable with the arrangement, given that he's already had the experience of watching two other people bring their own interpretations of Reacher to life in Tom Cruise and Alan Ritchson. As far as Child is concerned, though, he'd already given Reacher away long before anybody had bought the rights to make a movie about him.

“People think that's weird, you know, that I've given away this character, but the entire point of writing is to give away the character. You want the reader, first of all, to own it, and for the character to live as a reality in the reader's mind. That's the whole point. You want to give it away, and then you give it away to movies or television or whatever. It's no different giving it away to a different author.”

Child even extended that sentiment to those who've taken to writing their own Jack Reacher fanfiction, saying: “Let them have it, let them enjoy it.” The first four seasons of Reacher are streaming on Prime Video. Stay tuned to Collider for more from our exclusive conversation with Lee Child.

With nothing but his wits, he must figure out what is happening in Margrave, Georgia. The first season of Reacher is based on the international bestseller The Killing Floor by Lee Child.

#3328. ‘Odyssey’ Cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema Was More Interested in the Intimate Than the Epic

Christopher Nolan‘s adaptation of Homer’s “The Odyssey” was one of the most awe-inspiring cinematic achievements of 2026, an epic worthy of comparison with the grandiose visions of David Lean and Stanley Kubrick. Yet what interested cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema was less the story’s vast scale than the details of the human faces inhabiting the film‘s sweeping vistas.

“We never really treated it in an epic way,” van Hoytema told IndieWire. “Even though we all know ‘The Odyssey‘ and understand the scale of the story, making some sort of a tourist film was never on our agenda. It was the characters and the visceral sense of their experience that we were interested in, so even standing in the most crazy places in the world — on mountaintops or wherever — we were never motivated by the landscapes. The settings take care of creating the scale and scope of the film — our perspective on the story was a very intimate one.” Related Stories Forget Photorealism: How ‘Wildwood’ Made Its Handmade Digital Artistry Visible ‘Cliff Booth’ Brings Back a Fan-Favorite ‘Once Upon a Time in Hollywood’ Face

Given that, van Hoytema tried not to be seduced by the beauty of his surroundings if it didn’t serve the emotional experience. “It was less about showing how beautiful a beach was than about showing how shitty those men felt when they were on the beach,” he said, noting that a key tool in getting across the characters’ internal feelings was shooting the film entirely in IMAX.

“Shooting an entire film in IMAX has been a pursuit of ours for quite a long time now, and we’ve been tweaking the lenses and tweaking the cameras in order to get there,” van Hoytema said. “We’ve managed to wrangle the equipment and technology around it to enable us to be right there next to you, looking straight into your eyes.”

This again plays into that idea of intimacy versus scale, which was something van Hoytema and Nolan had experimented with in “Oppenheimer.” In that film, IMAX was used not only for major set pieces like the atomic bomb test, but quiet dialogue scenes shot largely in close-up. Van Hoytema says that he and Nolan have long been aware that IMAX has historically been used mostly to depict the wonders of the world, but they wanted to expand its grammar.

“The lenses that we use today are an evolution of different iterations of lenses that we have been building through the years, lenses that focus extremely close and that can open wide so that you can work with natural light or in half-darkness,” van Hoytema said. “We’ve found that IMAX is an intimate format because it’s such a good replicator of the human experience and perspective.”

The biggest obstacle toward shooting an entire movie in IMAX before “The Odyssey” was always the sound — IMAX film cameras are famously noisy, making it difficult to get decent production recordings. “We built a blimp on ‘Tenet,’ but it didn’t work,” van Hoytema said. “This was the first film where we felt that the technology had gotten far enough to actually shoot the entire thing on IMAX. There’s been an evolution in development not only in my department but in the sound department — they have come up with better microphones, better filtration, and in this film it came together beautifully.”

Van Hoytema and Nolan always had a backup plan in case the IMAX cameras became too unwieldy or got in the way of performance, particularly in lengthy dialogue scenes that would outlast the cameras’ short magazines. Once Matt Damon and Anne Hathaway proved that they could pull off a complicated sequence in close collaboration with van Hoytema and the other departments, however, Nolan and his crew were confident they could rely on IMAX as their format of choice. “That day was the hardest, and we shot everything on IMAX, so for the rest of the film we just committed — no plan B,” van Hoytema said.

While van Hoytema and Nolan were enthusiastic about committing to IMAX, it did create massive logistical challenges — not just when it came to getting the heavy camera and blimp in and out of remote locations, but in terms of performance. The actors’ eyelines, for example, were often blocked by the enormous camera. “Here we are bragging about the intimacy we can achieve, and suddenly you’re on set with a gigantic black box in front of the actors, and they can’t look each other in the eyes,” van Hoytema said. “It was a huge problem.”

To solve the problem, van Hoytema and his crew built a system that would allow the actors to see each other. “It was based on a teleprompter that has an angled mirror in front of the lens, and people can look straight into the lens reading a teleprompter because it has projected text on it. But instead of text, we had another mirror, and we had an actor sitting here. So basically what actors see is a little surface with a mirror with the other actor in there, and they can look straight into the other actor’s eye.”

Van Hoytema could fine-tune the eyelines by adjusting the angles of the mirrors in what he called “a very analog but very effective solution. And the actors loved it, because instead of looking at a wall they’re literally looking at their co-stars.” Van Hoytema reiterated the idea that everything in the movie was geared toward character and performance — including, at times, making the actors as uncomfortable as possible.

“It’s not for nothing that Chris loves to go out at sea with a ship and do things that are almost physically impossible,” van Hoytema said. “The more miserable or real or wet the situation is, the more the actors have to react to and play with. And that also goes for my way of working. I love different weather situations. I love different light situations. I love kinetic and physical challenges. It adds something unexpected and something visceral. The camera’s always fighting something and the actors are fighting at that very same moment, so it becomes a weirdly symbiotic relationship to the elements.”

In spite — or perhaps because — of the arduous shoot, van Hoytema didn’t want to see it end. “This was an extremely difficult film, but it was also the film where everything we’d been working toward came together,” van Hoytema. “We were much more light-footed. Weirdly enough, when what you’re doing becomes subjected to elements that you cannot control, you become a bit less precious. And that lack of preciousness is very liberating. We just went in headfirst.”

The LG OLED evo C6 and Samsung S90H are worth considering for movie enthusiasts and gamers who want excellent contrast and smooth motion, while the Hisense U7 and TCL QM64L offer mini-LED alternatives for brighter living rooms. For a large screen at a relatively affordable price, the 75-inch Hisense U6 Pro at $699.99 stands out, while the 65-inch Roku Plus Series at $449.99 makes sense for everyday streaming on a tighter budget. If screen size is your priority, the 98-inch TCL F8D is also worth a look, provided you have the room for it.

Choosing between OLED and QLED is an important decision you need to ask yourself before you go shopping for TVs. If you can afford an OLED and want the best image possible, go for the OLED. Just make sure you're okay with the dimmer lights they emit. If you need brightness and don't want to blow out your budget on a TV, go with a QLED.

If you're seeing the deals on this post, they're real. But don't think every deal out there is real. Retailers are known to manipulate prices to make you think you're getting a better deal than you actually are. We vet our deals to make sure that doesn't happen, though.

#3325. CBS Is Finally Bringing Back TV's Best Show In 2027

After an extended hiatus, TV's best show will officially return in 2027. Since its 2024 premiere, CBS's Matlock has consistently proved that network television is still worth watching. While the Kathy Bates-led legal drama initially drew audiences in with its clever reinvention of the classic Andy Griffith series, it has since established an identity entirely its own. Much of that comes down to creator Jennie Snyder Urman's ability to develop compelling characters whose lives are every bit as fascinating as the cases they take on.

As engaging as it's been to watch Matty pursue justice for her daughter, Matlock is at its best when it explores the characters' complicated relationships. The unlikely friendship between Matty and Olympia has become the series' emotional backbone, while Olympia's history with Julian adds another layer of complexity to their professional and personal lives.

Even beyond those central relationships, Julian's complicated dynamic with his father and Sarah's ongoing attempts to find her place among her colleagues give audiences reasons to tune in every week. Few network dramas make nearly every character's personal journey feel essential to the overall narrative. It's what makes Matlock the best show currently on network television and why its prolonged absence has been so disappointing.

Unfortunately, unlike many of CBS's returning dramas, Matlock was noticeably absent from the network's fall 2026 programming lineup. However, after months of uncertainty about when audiences would finally reunite with the lawyers of Jacobson Moore, CBS has officially confirmed when Matlock season 3 will premiere in 2027.

After spending most of 2026 without knowing exactly when Matlock would return, audiences finally have a date to look forward to. On November 16, CBS announced its 2027 midseason programming schedule, confirming that Matlock season 3 will premiere on Thursday, January 21, 2027. With the legal drama's sophomore season having concluded on April 23, 2026, this puts approximately nine months between seasons.

However, the premiere date isn't the only noteworthy revelation from CBS's midseason schedule. While Matlock is retaining its Thursday night placement, the legal drama is moving back an hour to 10 pm ET. For the first two seasons, Matlock occupied the 9 pm ET time slot, serving as the lead-in for another critically acclaimed CBS procedural, Elsbeth.

With Elsbeth having moved into Matlock's former time slot in the fall of 2026, the two dramas will effectively switch places come January. The shift for CBS's newest legal drama, Cupertino, from Thursdays to Sundays also allows the network to reunite two of its most compelling female-led procedurals without disrupting Elsbeth's established season 4 schedule.

Fortunately, Matlock's January premiere means audiences won't have to wait until the latter half of the traditional midseason premiere window to see Kathy Bates return. Some of CBS's midseason offerings aren't scheduled to debut until February; the network could have easily extended the legal drama's hiatus even further.

While nine months is an unusually long break for a network television drama, it's comforting to know Matlock's absence isn't indicative of CBS losing confidence in the series. In fact, the decision to hold Matlock season 3 until 2027 was made with the show's best interests in mind.

Considering Matlock's incredible success so far, CBS's decision to remove the legal drama from its fall programming lineup initially seemed questionable. However, unlike some of the network's other scheduling decisions for the 2026–2027 television season, Matlock's move to midseason was motivated by creative necessity rather than programming strategy.

In an April 2026 interview, Jennie Snyder Urman revealed that she personally approached CBS about delaying Matlock season 3. After spending the first two seasons unraveling the mystery of Jacobson Moore's involvement in concealing the Wellbrexa study, Urman wanted additional time to develop the next overarching mystery.

One of the biggest reasons Matlock has been so successful is how meticulously its writers have incorporated elements of the larger mystery into its episodic storytelling. Even when an episode's central case had seemingly little to do with Matty's investigation, certain developments would become significant several episodes later. Replicating that level of storytelling requires considerable preparation.

Kathy Bates' Matlock series is successful for many reasons, including her Madeline Kingston character's covert disguise as Madeline "Matty" Matlock.

Furthermore, resolving the Wellbrexa investigation means fundamentally changing Matty's motivations for practicing law. Everything she's done since the series premiere has been informed by her desire to hold those responsible for her daughter's death accountable. Now that she's accomplished what she originally set out to do, the writers have to establish an equally compelling purpose for the character.

What's particularly encouraging about CBS agreeing to Urman's request is that it demonstrates the network's willingness to prioritize Matlock's quality over the immediate benefits of having one of its most acclaimed dramas on the fall schedule. In an industry where successful network procedurals are generally expected to maintain a consistent production schedule, giving a creative team additional time to develop its story is a welcome change.

As frustrating as the extended hiatus has been, rushing Matlock into its next chapter could have undermined everything that made its first two seasons so exceptional. The conclusion of the Wellbrexa investigation presents an opportunity for the series to prove its longevity isn't dependent on its original premise. Giving Urman and her writers time to explore that opportunity is ultimately in everyone's best interests.

When Matlock returns in January 2027, the legal drama will look considerably different from when audiences last saw it. Urman recently revealed that season 3 will begin with a time jump of approximately six to nine months. Additionally, the midseason premiere means Matlock season 3 will consist of fewer episodes than its predecessors.

Perhaps the most exciting development, however, is that Matty and Olympia will officially be business partners. Matlock season 3's first promotional image confirms that the two women have opened their own law firm, Lawrence Matlock. After two seasons of watching their friendship develop under circumstances that frequently put them at odds, audiences will finally get to see what their partnership looks like without the limitations imposed by Jacobson Moore.

Of course, just because the Wellbrexa mystery has been solved doesn't mean its ramifications won't continue to influence the characters' relationships. Julian's decision to implicate himself in the cover-up to protect Matty was arguably his most significant moment of character development. Having finally shown he can be a better man than his father, Julian must now navigate the consequences of that decision, both as a lawyer and as a father.

How that experience further shapes his relationship with Olympia is equally intriguing. Throughout Matlock season 2, the former couple gradually rediscovered their ability to trust one another. With Julian's future still uncertain following his arrest, there's considerable potential to explore how their relationship evolves now that neither is beholden to Senior's expectations.

There's also the matter of Sarah finally learning the truth about Matty's identity. Urman has confirmed that audiences will see the aftermath of that revelation in the season 3 premiere. Considering how much Sarah values earning the respect of those around her, discovering that two of her mentors kept something so significant from her could fundamentally alter her relationship with both women.

While the specifics of Matlock season 3's new mystery remain largely unknown, the emotional foundations for another exceptional season are already in place. Ultimately, Matlock's greatest accomplishment in its first two seasons was making audiences care enough about these characters that the resolution of its central mystery didn't diminish their desire to see more. Regardless of what investigation awaits Matty and Olympia, simply spending more time with these characters makes January 2027 worth looking forward to.

Matlock season 3 premieres on CBS Thursday, January 21, 2027, at 10 PM ET.

#3324. Forget 'The Last of Us,' Netflix's 6-Part Near-Perfect Survival Thriller Is Your Next Binge

Giovana Gelhoren is a High-Trending Topics Writer at Collider, covering the most-talked-about stars, movies, and TV shows. Before joining Collider, she was a Digital News Writer at People Magazine and served as Associate Editor at SheKnows, where she honed her expertise in celebrity coverage and entertainment journalism.

A proud Latina from Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, Giovana graduated from Northwestern University with a degree in Journalism and International Studies. She has interviewed countless celebrities, including Anne Hathaway, Halle Berry, Pamela Anderson, Jamie Lee Curtis, and Brenda Song, and is known for her encyclopedic knowledge of film, TV, and pop culture.

Over the years, a number of TV shows have explored what life during and after an apocalypse could look like. From Paradise to The Walking Dead and The Last of Us, each of these shows has their own either alarming, horrifying or even hopeful versions of a post-apocalyptic future. But while these three shows have received worldwide attention, another Netflix title has its own original and chilling story of survival, and it's equally a must-watch.

First premiered on April 30, 2025, the Argentinian series The Eternaut was a hit on the streaming giant, debuting at #1 on Netflix’s Global Top 10 for non-English language series, and earning over 10.8 million views worldwide in the first week, per Netflix. Led by Ricardo Darín, the critically acclaimed series follows a father facing unforeseen circumstances, and a country coming to terms with its own destruction.

Adapted from the iconic 1957 graphic novel El Eternauta by writer Héctor Germán Oesterheld and artist Francisco Solano López, The Eternaut follows a group of longtime friends in Buenos Aires, Argentina, as their casual night at home having drinks and playing cards takes a turn. After the power goes out across the city and a mysterious snow begins to fall, they begin to raise their suspicions. When one of them leaves to return home, the ones who stayed make a shocking realization: the white, fluffy flakes are toxic, and kill anyone who makes direct contact.

Stranded inside, with no power or means of contacting anyone (other technology, like cell phones and cars, have also gone dead), the longtime friends become desperate to check in with their loved ones. That's when the series' protagonist Juan Salvo (Darín) makes an impromptu protective suit and soon braves the snowstorm in search for his daughter, Clara (Mora Fisz), who was spending the night at a friend's house. The series, which has a dad's mission to save his daughter at the center, follows a group of friends as they embark on a desperate struggle for survival and how they must band together to fight an enemy from another planet.

While fans of Darín have certainly already tuned in, The Eternaut's Rotten Tomatoes score might be enough to convince anyone unfamiliar with the show or the actor to watch. On Rotten Tomatoes, the series accomplished a near-perfect 96% from critics, as well as 88% on the popcornmeter. From the reviews, while the series' slow-burning storyline and uneven pace is a sore spot, the rest of the series, including its performances and production value, are home runs. "With phenomenal production values, cast and care by its creators, The Eternaut does enough to hook the audience and entertain them, while overcoming some bumps on the snowy road," reads one review.

In Collider's very own review by Carly Lane, the series received a 7/10. Among the highlights was the series' very beginning, in which it establishes mundane, daily life, with an impending doom slowly simmering in the background. "In depicting these early moments of mundanity before the cataclysmic turning point, The Eternaut becomes a sci-fi story that anyone can identify with, even as it still adheres to the Argentine setting from the original graphic novel," Overall, the series delivers a gripping watch for the audience. "With a captivating performance from Darín, who brings both gravitas and vulnerability to Juan Salvo, as well as stunning visuals and clever narrative swerves, Netflix's adaptation deserves to be lauded right alongside the groundbreaking sci-fi story it adapts," Lane wrote.

Ultimately, while post-apocalyptic shows aren't exactly a rare find on TV, Netflix's The Eternaut brings something new to the genre. Starring one of Argentina's most celebrated actors, as well as a beloved story that goes back to the 1950s, The Eternaut is a must-watch for fans of the genre, one that will grip viewers from beginning to end.

I've read more than 30 books in the past year, all of them on an e-reader with a screen roughly the size of a credit card. If you think that sounds untenable, I say: Don't knock it 'til you've tried it. Once you're immersed in a book, you'll find the size doesn't matter, and the convenience of being able to slip it into any pocket and forget it's there means you need never be without it.

Right now, the Xteink X4 Pro, the best tiny e-reader I've tried so far—and Lifehacker's pick for the 2026 E-Reader Gift of the Year—is on its best sale yet for Black Friday: When ordered directly from Xteink, you'll save 15% off the usual $99 price, bringing it down to $84. The X4 Pro is the newest and best e-reader from Xteink, the Chinese tech startup that turned the e-reading world upside down last year with the launch of the original X4 pocket e-reader. While the X4 Pro is the same size as the basic X4 Classic, it adds two big upgrades—a temperature-adjustable front light and a touchscreen—plus a faster processor and more memory. But if you can jump those hurdles, you might just discover it's the weirdest, most lovable piece of tech you've used in years.

#3320. This Apple Watch Is a Lifehacker 'Gift of the Year' Award Winner, and It's $50 Off During Black Friday

Apple has three main Apple Watch "lines." There's the flagship, currently the Series 12, which represents Apple's mainstream wearable. For athletes and users who think they'll put their watches through some extreme scenarios, there's the Ultra line, currently the Apple Watch Ultra 4. And while both the Series 12 and Ultra 4 are excellent devices in their own right, they can be pretty pricey (particularly the Ultra). That's why the third category, the SE, is actually best for most people, and Lifehacker's choice for best smartwatch gift of the year. Better yet, the third-generation SE is currently $50 off ahead of Black Friday, perfect for most people asking for an Apple Watch this year.

The SE 3 does just about everything you'd expect an Apple Watch to do. It, of course, has a heart rate sensor to keep tabs on your pulse, including high and low heart rate alerts; the ability to track dozens of different workouts and exercise types (including swimming, thanks to the device's water resistance); a sleep tracker with daily analyses available in the Health app; notification forwarding to check in on your alerts without opening your iPhone; and the ability to send and receive text messages.

It comes in two sizes (40mm and 44mm) depending on how large or small you prefer your watch. No matter which model you get, the watch comes with the S10 chip, Apple's last-generation watch processor. While it isn't as fast as the current S11 chip, the S10 is more than capable of running watchOS 27. Apple says the SE 3 can run for up to 18 hours on a single charge, and up to 32 hours in Low Power Mode, with fast charging from 0% to 80% in 45 minutes.

The majority of the features missing from the SE 3 aren't essential. Apple's other watches have things like bigger, brighter displays, additional health tracking tools like hypertension alerts and an ECG sensor, longer battery life, and Audio Intelligence—the latter of which might be a benefit to miss, depending on who you are.

If your giftee wants or needs any of those additional features, Series 12 or Ultra 4 might be a better choice. But for anyone who wants the essential Apple Watch experience, the SE 3 is simply the best-value watch Apple sells right now—especially at this discount. Right now, the watch starts at $199 for the 40mm watch, or $229 for the 44mm. You can also save on the cellular versions of these watches: $249 for the cellular 40mm watch, and $279 for the cellular 44mm model.

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, Nov. 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday, Nov. 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by Dec. 2, 2026.

#3317. 'Bond Meets Slow Horses' Series With 12 Episodes Is Hands Down Netflix's Best Show

Netflix churns out so much original content that it can be very hit-and-miss. Whereas HBO has a quality-over-quantity policy, Netflix will just throw as much stuff as it can afford at the wall and see what sticks. And honestly, it’s a winning strategy. We remember the hits (Adolescence, Baby Reindeer, The Queen’s Gambit) and forget the stinkers (Jupiter’s Legacy, Iron Fist, Disjointed).

Over the past couple of months, Netflix’s output has been way more hit than miss. His & Hers emerged as one of the streamer’s biggest ever hits earlier this year. The Body was a fascinating mix of the horrors of Satanic rituals and the horrors of high school. East of Eden was a riveting, comprehensive adaptation of the Steinbeck classic. While Ozark and Stranger Things and BoJack Horseman and House of Cards have all ended (the latter with a whimper, not a bang), Netflix still has some great shows on the go.

Arguably the best show on Netflix right now — better than Beef, better than Wednesday, better than Haunted Hotel (although I adore Haunted Hotel) — is Black Doves. Keira Knightley stars as a honeypot agent from the titular spy agency, who’s drawn into a sinister conspiracy when her lover is killed.

Black Doves recently returned for its second season, and it solidified this show as the best thing Netflix has to offer right now. What the series lacks in realism (seriously, the British Prime Minister’s wife would not be free to roam around London with a gun in her hand), it makes up for with gripping action, compelling characters, and high-wire dramatic tension.

Black Doves almost feels like the Winter Olympics version of Slow Horses. It recaptures Slow Horses’ intoxicating blend of high-octane action spectacle and witty British banter, but in a Christmas setting. It has all the shootouts and showdowns we’ve come to expect from Slow Horses, but set against a chilly yuletide backdrop. It’s as if Shane Black wrote a UK spy show; it’s The Long Kiss Goodnight set in London.

Knightley’s Helen Webb makes for an intriguing antihero, raising kids in a sham marriage to gather intelligence for the British government, but Ben Whishaw steals the show as her friend and partner-in-espionage, Sam. Sam is a cold-blooded secret agent with a license to kill, so Whishaw has essentially graduated from playing Q to playing 007 himself. The character of Sam is probably the closest we’ll get to seeing a gay James Bond, and it’s an interesting new spin on that archetype.

Spy thrillers are a dime a dozen in the streaming age (Lioness, The Old Man, Day of the Jackal, the aforementioned Slow Horses), but Black Doves stands out from the crowd, because it’s more the story of a mother than the story of a spy. It’s not so much about the espionage plots as it is about Helen’s double life, and the inherent emotional strain of her web of lies and deceit.

The plot of Black Doves was inspired by a real 2010 scandal involving British intelligence officers who had gone undercover with a radical environmentalist group and gotten so entrenched in their community that they started relationships and built families. What creator Joe Barton thought was interesting about that story was the dramatic tension of the kids getting caught in the middle. They didn’t ask for any of this, and yet their lives are most affected by it.

Black Doves is as much about mistrust in a marriage as it is about the inner workings of a fictional spy organization. Helen’s husband doesn’t trust her, and he has no reason to, and it’s interesting to see how that affects their relationship day to day.

#3316. The 10 Most Action-Packed War Movies of All Time, Ranked

Most war movies will showcase some kind of combat, even if those scenes aren’t necessarily action ones. It makes sense, because wars are fought, and fighting involves violence. It is responsible, on the part of many war movies, to showcase such combat as horrifying rather than exciting, but depending on the movie and overall tone, war films can also work as action movies.

Now, these ones aren’t necessarily the best war movies that also function as action films, but they are right up there among the most action-packed war movies ever made. The quantity of action is important here, but thankfully, a few of the movies here are actually pretty darn good anyway (and those that aren’t quite as good might at least make for some mindless fun/entertainment, even if they're all technically war films).

So, it’s not the best of samurai movies, nor one of the more authentic ones, but The Last Samurai still works as a good entry point to samurai-adjacent cinema, maybe because it’s very Hollywood. That makes some sense, given it follows an American man hired to educate the Japanese army about more modern weaponry (well, modern by the standards of the late 1800s).

As you might expect from a movie about a Western man going to an unfamiliar place, he comes to appreciate their samurai culture and eventually endeavors to join their ranks. This leads to plenty of conflicts and, eventually, warfare, with the action present throughout The Last Samurai being fairly frequent and also quite exciting to watch. There’s undeniable spectacle here, and it’s one of many good showcases for Tom Cruise’s talent as an all-time great action movie star.

Even by the standards of something that came out in 1968 (New Hollywood, as a movement, was underway here, if only just), Where Eagles Dare feels a little old-fashioned, but it is an impressively made and sometimes quite exciting World War II movie. It's about a daring rescue mission to retrieve an American general who's being held captive inside a heavily guarded castle in Germany.

That’s the basics. It takes this premise and stretches it to about two and a half hours all up, and thankfully makes it work. It starred Clint Eastwood, and he was at the center of another pretty great action/war movie that’ll be mentioned very shortly. Eastwood was well-matched with Richard Burton, too, who’s typically good and makes it all feel a bit more prestigious than you might expect a rollicking sort of war movie to be.

Bam, Eastwood’s back, as promised. Kelly’s Heroes has a remarkable cast, as it gave Clint Eastwood another early starring role that wasn’t in a Western, and then as far as supporting cast members here go, you’ve got the likes of Donald Sutherland, Telly Savalas, and Don Rickles. It’s also one of the funnier World War II movies out there, with it being about a chaotic mission where American soldiers go AWOL and then behind enemy lines so they can rob a bank.

There’s a novelty in seeing a heist movie take place during World War II, and making things comedic also helps give Kelly’s Heroes a distinctive identity. It’s good escapist fun, even if it can ultimately be a little strange to see a story set during the deadliest war of the 20th century be so jam-packed with comedy and general silliness, and that sense of humor carries over to much of the action, too. It’s all very breezy and broad, yet also pretty hard to resist, truth be told.

A classic 1960s war movie, The Train takes place during World War II, and revolves around a German Colonel’s plans to steal valuable artwork from France and transport it back to Germany. The conflict comes about because a group of French resistance fighters aren’t too thrilled by that idea, setting in motion a fairly small battle of sorts within the broader Second World War, sure, but it’s still a microcosm of some of that bigger conflict.

The Train has aged remarkably well for a movie that’s now more than 60 years old, standing as something that’s likely to prove engaging for contemporary viewers in much the same way it would’ve been for audiences all those decades ago. It’s a movie that understands how surprisingly cinematic trains are, and how they're very conducive to the action genre in particular, so it ends up being an overall – and undeniably – gripping World War II film.

It’s honestly a bit surprising to see The Last of the Mohicans within the filmography of Michael Mann, because when he does go back into the past to tell a story, he doesn’t usually go back centuries. And then plenty of his best-known movies were set around the times during which they were made/produced, and such films often lean into crime/thriller territory, sometimes with a bit of action, too.

As for The Last of the Mohicans, this one showed Mann also had what it took to make an impressive, stirring, and action-packed historical epic. Though shorter than most epics, what the film ended up being is still pretty much perfect, feeling epic regardless of how long it actually is. The final act in particular is great, and The Last of the Mohicans looks and sounds immense, all the while being unsurprisingly helped by the fact that Daniel Day-Lewis stars in it, and he can do (almost) no wrong, as an actor.

Not to be mixed up with Quentin Tarantino’s Inglourious Basterds, which was made just over 30 years later, 1978’s The Inglorious Bastards (those words were spelled correctly for this one) is an underrated World War II movie and an explosively fun viewing experience. It has the same kind of chaotic energy and pacing as 1967’s The Dirty Dozen, and follows a squad of soldiers undertaking a dangerous mission to steal a valuable weapon from German forces.

It probably has even more action than The Dirty Dozen, though, so that’s why it’s here. “Most action-packed” is different from “best action-packed,” though The Inglorious Bastards is still pretty great for what it is. No one’s going to call it an example of high art, by any means, but no one should, because it’s clearly not trying to be anything so lofty. It’s good, old-fashioned, and high-energy entertainment, and those looking for a bombastic war movie with plenty of action and explosions will likely come away from this one satisfied.

The best Wolfgang Petersen epic is not Troy, since he was also behind Das Boot, but that one isn't really an action movie, so it can’t really be here. Watch Das Boot, though, for the record. It’s about as good and effective as anti-war movies get. Troy, though, is heavy on action, prioritizing that more than its source material, The Iliad, which is a defining story generally, and also definitely significant if you're talking books/stories about warfare.

Don’t go in expecting something faithful. That’s a reasonable ask, because condensing something as complex and immense as The Iliad into just one movie would be almost impossible. Troy does enough with the basics, and when all else fails, it does have a good deal of spectacle, not to mention some huge battle sequences (and also a fairly high number of battle sequences, too.

Famously, the first movie in what became the Rambo series wasn't too excessive when it came to action, but then its sequels kept on upping the explosiveness and action considerably. They were a little less gritty and intense than First Blood, though. So, when it came to do a fourth one (just called Rambo now), there was an attempt to do a bit of both.

This movie’s brutal in a way that delivers a different sort of intensity and nihilism to what was found – and felt – in First Blood.

Like, there is a ton of action here, but it’s not always fun and definitely doesn’t feel escapist, because this movie’s brutal in a way that delivers a different sort of intensity and nihilism to what was found – and felt – in First Blood. There’s Rambo on a mission, and then he comes into contact with some bad people, and ultimately, he once more has to be a one-man army against some sadistic soldiers, leading to a huge body count. And speaking of bodies, few remain intact, owing to just how much blood and gore there is throughout this film.

While Sisu takes place during the Second World War, it’s not really about actual people or events, instead functioning mostly as a survival/action movie that just so happens to take place during that war. It’s about a Finnish ex-commando turned gold prospector clashing with a group of German soldiers in 1944, since they try to steal his gold and kill him, but find that’s much easier said than done.

Like, the main character here doesn’t talk all that much, and he’s almost supernaturally powerful and about as determined as fictional characters get, too. Sisu is never grounded, by any means, even near the start, but does prove willing to get more and more ridiculous as an action movie as it goes along, to the point that it almost feels like a live-action cartoon by the end. If you don’t mind some grisly violence, it proves to be broad, pulpy, and fairly ridiculous fun.

Honestly, 300 plays around with “historical accuracy” to such a great extent that if some soldiers had pulled out guns at any point and started blasting, then maybe it’d be possible to just go with it. Though the battle depicted here did technically happen long ago, 300 retells it as a legend, or maybe even something of a myth, rather than trying to keep things realistic or grounded.

It’s pretty close to outright fantasy, just not to quite the same extent as something like The Lord of the Rings. It is direct and not very deep at all, possibly being even more straightforward than previously mentioned blunt action/war movies like Rambo and Sisu. 300 is fun and compelling in a mindless sort of way, though, and even if all the action is a bit overwhelming, it’s hard to complain too much when it all looks so stylish and visually bold.

#3313. Two billion credentials publicly exposed, including everything needed for identity theft

A security researcher has discovered a publicly exposed database containing approximately two billion credentials. The database was neither password-protected nor encrypted.

The scariest part of it is around 400,000 documents came from separate folders for individual victims, creating a detailed profile with all the personal data needed to “own that person” …

Cybersecurity researcher Jeremiah Fowler says that the database contains a huge array of information, including login details for Tor .onion addresses used to access the dark web.

I also observed thousands of Tor .onion addresses associated with account names and passwords. The Tor .onion services are generally categorized as part of the dark web, and these credentials could potentially provide access to private forums, marketplaces, communication platforms, or other hidden services. While .onion accounts alone do not imply criminal or malicious activity, it is estimated that as much as 60% of dark web sites host illegal material and illicit activities. This is the first time I have seen a large number of dark web accounts in breached credentials. It should be noted that legitimate organizations, journalists, whistleblower platforms, and news organizations also operate .onion services to provide anonymity and bypass censorship.

But the most frightening aspect of it is separate folders for individual victims containing all of the information needed for identity theft.

Fowler told Wired that this data appears to have been obtained through advanced malware.

The “scariest” thing in the database, Fowler says, was around 400,000 documents that appeared to come from “more advanced malware” compiling information about individual victims […] that create a detailed profile of an individual and their digital life. “If you had that, you own that person,” Fowler says.

There’s no information about the specific sources of the data, but it seems likely to be aggregated from a range of data breaches. Fowler contacted the hosting company to have the database removed, but it’s not known how many people may have had access to it.

The best protection is to use a password manager like Apple’s Passwords app to ensure you have strong, unique passwords for each individual website and service you use, with two-factor authentication enabled wherever possible. When given the choice of 2FA code delivery, you should always opt for an authenticator app rather than a text message to protect yourself against SIM-swap attacks.

#3310. TIME’s Top 100 Photos of 2026 list includes a shot taken on iPhone 18 Pro

In September, Apple held a photography exhibition in New York City to show off the iPhone 18 Pro camera. Now, an image of the Bugaboo Mountains from that exhibit, shot by photographer Jimmy Chin, is included in TIME’s Top 100 Photos.

TIME publishes its Top 100 Photos list each year. The list showcases the pictures that the TIME Photo Department determines best capture that particular year.

The essence of TIME’s Photos of the Year, selected by our photo editors and presented below, is the authentic, sometimes staggering, reality captured by photojournalism. Someone was there. A news photographer lifted a viewfinder, pressed a button, and captured an instant happening in front of them.

Chin’s image was shot in Bugaboo Provincial Park, Canada, on iPhone 18 Pro. He explained that a traditional production creates a layer of separation between the photographer and the subject, with equipment, crew, and all the moving parts of a shoot. Shooting on iPhone 18 Pro meant that he could create a more intimate environment, allowing for a sense of comfort and spontaneity that comes through in the images.

Image Courtesy of Apple (as featured in the What Holds Us exhibition)

Chin’s goal was to capture the intersection of human ambition and the pursuit of wonder against the backdrop of a timeless natural landscape.

“The resolution and the sharpness on iPhone 18 Pro surprised me. I could shoot a few inches of rock and ice, or a massive panorama, and trust it would hold at size. That is what this work needed. It also meant I carried almost nothing. In the mountains, everything you carry is a decision. I was not thinking about gear. I was thinking about what was in front of me.”

Apple’s “What Holds Us” exhibit ran in New York City in September, featuring work from photographers Alex Prager, Jack Davison, and Jimmy Chin, with each artist using the iPhone 18 Pro to explore the “people, places, and ideas that connect and ground humanity.” Kathy Ryan, the former longtime director of photography for The New York Times Magazine, curated the exhibition.

The exhibit is now headed to London, where it will open to the public on December 4, from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. It will also be open from Saturday, December 12 through Sunday, December 13, from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

#3309. Marvel’s New Iron Man Is Officially A Hulk-Level Threat

Marvel's new Iron Man is a character with the same level of strength as the Hulk. Tony Stark has created an extraordinary arsenal of powerful Iron Man armors designed to push human technology past every conceivable limit. Among the mightiest are the Godkiller Armor Mark II, a Celestial-sized mech built to brawl with Dark Celestials; as well as the Godbuster Armor, a virtual-reality construct brought into physical existence that effortlessly outclassed Tony's entire armory at once. Others include the Galactus armor imagined by Tony to defeat Reed Richards, the Thorbuster powered by an Asgardian crystal, and the Mysterium Armor, forged from mutant-mined cosmic metal capable of resisting magic and crushing Adamantium.

But even with those godlike inventions at his disposal, the Hulk will always defeat Iron Man’s best suits pound for pound in a pure test of strength and endurance. The Hulk possesses virtually limitless physical power that increases indefinitely in direct relation to his rage. Whenever Tony Stark does manage to neutralize the Green Goliath, he owes his victory either to his own ingenuity or to the timely backup of teammates like the Avengers and the Fantastic Four. As powerful as Iron Man's strongest Hulkbusters might be, the Hulk eventually catches up.

Time and again, Marvel has made it quite clear that mystical power beats technology, particularly through the transdimensional nature of Hulk's unparalleled might.

In Marvel's The Infernal Hulk, the titular Eldest-possessed Hulk transforms Earth’s Mightiest Heroes into his demonic Infernal Avengers, starting with Iron Man. Failing to stop the raging monster, Tony Stark undergoes a terrifying transformation that finally puts a dark Iron Man on the exact same physical tier as the Green Goliath. As the Infernal Hulk’s first major victim, Stark is twisted into the hulking "Iron Thing", a nightmarish mass of bulging gamma-mutated flesh. While the rest of the Infernal Hulk are just as monstrous, the Iron Thing’s sheer size and oversized muscles make him one of the team’s most overwhelming brutes, towering above the Infernal Hulk himself.

Iron Man's traditional Hulkbuster suits rely entirely on state-of-the-art technology that inevitably breaks down under prolonged use in battles against Hulk-level enemies. The Iron Thing removes the classic mechanical bottleneck that has always kept Iron Man a step behind Bruce Banner in a pure slugfest. Although he lacks the same level of control over his body as the Infernal Hulk, the Iron Thing has become an unstoppable living juggernaut capable of trading earth-shaking blows directly with most gamma monsters.

The Infernal Hulk clearly knows what hurts Iron Man the most, so he strips away the cutting-edge technology and refined sophistication that make the billionaire futurist so famous in the Marvel Universe. As the Iron Thing, Iron Man transforms into a bloated, misshapen brute of bulging muscle, with barely any defined anatomy. Gone are Tony Stark's legendary intellect and playboy charm, and instead he's cursed with a demonic mutation that reduces one of Marvel’s greatest minds to a mindless physical mass, in short a cruel mockery of everything Stark has spent his life building.

Iron Man's armors have always been flashy and awesome, but sometimes, Tony Stark builds a truly devious suit of armor in order to combat evil.

The Infernal Hulk corrupts the entire Infernal Avengers team in a similar manner. Spider-Man’s monstrous Arthropod transformation parades Peter Parker’s limp body across New York like a puppet, Captain America’s rotting War Dead form mocks his status as a symbol of wartime honor, and Vision’s Diaboli Ex Machina form reduces an android who has always fought to have his own soul and emotion into a giant exposed brain inside a machine devoid of visible humanity. In every case, and most visibly in Tony Stark’s transformation into the Iron Thing, the Infernal Hulk weaponizes body horror to humiliate Earth’s mightiest heroes from the inside out.

#3307. Netflix's 12-Part Horror Rom-Com Is Too Good To Miss for 'Ghosts' Fans

Over the last five years, CBS' Ghosts has bloomed into quite an impressive story success. The sitcom's ongoing popularity continues to be a welcome surprise, even though a single episode can sufficiently articulate the reason it has accumulated a loyal audience. Ghosts' sly, gently unassuming charm emerges from the awkwardly heartfelt cohabitation shenanigans that result when two living leads and a circus' worth of zany, deceased characters congregate in the same location.

Spooky in Love, a 12-episode K-Drama boasting a semi-comparable premise, premiered on Netflix as part of the platform's summer programming slate. The 12-episode series immediately followed Ghosts' lead, becoming one of the year's highest-streamed Korean sensations. Led by actor Park Eun-bin of Extraordinary Attorney Woo fame, Spooky in Love is a mischievous genre-blending exercise in horror-adjacent thrills-and-chills, comedic warmth, scheming familial power struggles, and case-of-the-week procedurals.

When Cheon Yeo-ri (Park), the heir apparent to her family's prestigious conglomerate, strides across the floors of her luxurious Reina Hotel, every click of her expensive heels conceals a hidden life. Yeo-ri's secret isn't the traditional kind one associates with opulent CEOs, either. Almost drowning in the same accident that claimed her friend's life years earlier granted her the rare ability to communicate with ghostly apparitions. Despite the unsettling nature of these visitations, Yeo-ri has accepted death as a routine companion by helping these restless, wronged souls find peace.

What's more, Yeo-ri unintentionally transfers her otherworldly side effect to anyone with whom she shares skin-to-skin contact. She responds to this specific imposition by wearing gloves and resigning herself to total seclusion. Her ensuing reputation as a reclusive and heartless ice queen couldn't be further from the truth; Yeo-ri's fundamentally good and lonely heart aches to help others. Protecting family, friends, and strangers from being literally haunted is why she denies herself that figurative lifeline of human connection.

This show is based on a popular web novel.

As far as her foil is concerned, Ma Kang-wook (Yang Se-jong) is an evidence-driven prosecutor who, at the faintest hint of ghoulish activity, petrifies himself into a shrieking frenzy. Kang-wook's courage lies in his unshakable idealism. He seeks justice on behalf of the murder victims whom the system failed, even when resisting institutional corruption costs him a promotion. Coincidence, as it does, pushes Kang-wook and Yeo-ri into an unlikely alliance. The duo use their separate skills to solve a confluence of mysteries, ranging from cold-case investigations to threats against Yeo-ri's status, and perhaps the biggest obstacle of all — whether Yeo-ri can ever find true, lasting happiness.

Some promising K-Dramas tend to introduce themselves with a strong hook and streamlined focus, only for their threads to unravel into frustrating (not endearing) contrivances. It's also not uncommon for the cast's chemistry to balance out these structural mishaps. Both phenomena hold true in this case. Overall, Spooky in Love's light-hearted tone works in its favor. It aspires to channel the rom-com formula's beats, like forced proximity, slow-motion montages, improbable kisses, "there's only one bed," and miraculous recoveries from outrageous injuries that, if beholden to real-world physics, would be fatal.

Yet playing in a tried-and-true sandbox needn't preclude a series from finding an efficient balance. If Spooky in Love had excavated the deeper potential buried within its conceit, it could've articulated some genuinely distinct and introspective arcs. Instead, the show overcrowds its unbalanced back half with duplicitous corporate machinations and rushed resolutions.

Never fear, however, for the driving-force relationship and the leads' accompanying performances both justify and compensate for their semi-insubstantial surroundings. Likewise, they prove to be fertile ground for Spooky in Love's strongest subversions, starting with a bickering grumpy-sunshine dynamic where the woman assumes the reserved role and the man embodies open-hearted extroversion. Many K-Drama heroines' controlling demeanor and curdled hearts spring from their traumatic pasts. Yeo-ri's attitude is an affectation. She's a self-sacrificing and compassionate protector who shoulders an exhausting weight on her own, even though maintaining her distance exacerbates her private misery. The heiress' greatest desire is the sole thing she believes she cannot have — a partner.

Four love stories, four completely different ideas of what it means to be somebody's person. This is the one that matches how you actually fall, and what it would ask of you.

You do not fall for strangers. You fall for the person you have already been talking to for years, which is the slowest and by some distance the most durable way anybody has found to do this.

You want a partner, not an audience. Somebody who wants their own life as badly as you want yours, and who would never ask you to be smaller to make the relationship easier.

The intensity was never the problem. The secrecy is. You are drawn to a love that lives entirely in private, and to the particular ache of wanting somebody you are not supposed to want.

You do not do this cautiously. When it happens for you it is immediate and total and it rearranges everything, and you would not accept a smaller version of it.

Although her unconventionality springs from the text, immense credit must go to the ever-hypnotic Park. Her effortlessly layered spin on a known archetype exchanges clichés for calculated composure and buried hurt, not to mention hesitant vulnerability as, against Yeo-ri's better judgment, her long-maintained defenses crumble into hesitant trust. Kang-wook, meanwhile, is honest, sensitive, altruistic, and empathetic to a relentless fault. His self-awareness reframes his ghost-based fears into gratitude time and again; choosing to love and celebrate Yeo-ri is worth every discomfort.

United in their mutual compassion and beneficial push-and-pull, the duo make for an idyllic, equitable, and healthy match. Rather than rely on steamy attraction, it's their smitten shyness and understanding acceptance of each other that melts the heart. Even their inability to hold hands adds an intimate texture to the torturous slow-burn tension; the couple's affection encounters a believable barrier that's born from the heroine's exterior circumstances and her emotional walls. The ghosts' unresolved situations carry tragically poignant punches as well, even though their individual stories don't operate on the same devastating level as Hotel del Luna. Broader structural weaknesses aside, Spooky in Love is another record-book example of pristine romantic yearning — a sprightly romp with comforting, quiet stakes and earnest rewards.

#3303. iPhone Handoff: Here’s the latest on carrier availability and pricing

iPhone Handoff is a new feature in iOS 27 that lets you use the same phone number across two different iPhones. However, the feature requires carrier support, so it isn’t available to everyone. Here are the carriers that currently support iPhone Handoff and those that have promised support.

9to5Mac is sponsored by Sony: Score Sony’s INZONE noise-canceling earbuds for 38% off. These deliver immersive 360 Spatial Sound, active noise canceling, low-latency wireless connectivity, and much more.

With iPhone Handoff, you can use the same phone number on two different iPhones. Your number automatically moves between the two phones, depending on which one you pick up. This includes calls, voicemail, messages, and Find My location.

Simply unlock whichever device you want to use and you’re ready to go. Other data synced with iCloud will automatically update across your devices. Third-party apps work across both devices, following each app’s own syncing behavior.

iPhone Handoff is available on iOS 27 and later. The phones must be connected to Wi-Fi, share the same Apple Account, use Messages in iCloud, and be signed into FaceTime and iMessage with the same Apple Account.

The biggest limiting factor of iPhone Handoff is that it requires carrier support. Currently, just three carriers support the feature:

What about carriers that are working on the feature? In the United States, Verizon has promised it “will support iPhone Handoff,” but it’s unclear when the feature will launch. Verizon says it will charge $10 per month for the service.

AT&T, meanwhile, has no plans to support iPhone Handoff. In a statement in September, the carrier said that its focus “remains on delivering innovations that make life simpler and keep customers connected with confidence.” The carrier noted that there “could be potential in capabilities like iPhone Handoff,” but that customers should use “existing eSIM activation and transfer options” instead.

No other carriers have promised support for iPhone Handoff, so it’s unclear how quickly the feature will expand around the world.

In my testing, iPhone Handoff works really well. I have it set up between my iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. I use the iPhone Duo 90% of the time, but when I do pick up my iPhone 18 Pro, my number instantly switches to it. There’s a cute animation that expands from the Dynamic Island, confirming that the number has moved.

Have you tried iPhone Handoff? Are you willing to pay extra for it? Let us know down in the comments.

#3300. Mark Wahlberg’s ‘Reacher’-Style Detective Franchise Officially Gets a New Release

Given how frequently Mark Wahlberg and director Peter Berg had worked together by 2020, there was something quite appealing about the prospect of the pair making a crime thriller set in Wahlberg's hometown of Boston. Their previous collaborations, including Lone Survivor and Patriots Day, had been based on real events, but this time around, they were taking on a character that readers of crime fiction had been familiar with since the 1970s. That movie didn't exactly endear itself to critics, although plenty of people watched it on Netflix, and while we're still waiting to see whether Wahlberg will get another outing, the character himself has been considerably busier.

Robert B. Parker's Framed, the 54th novel in the Spenser series, was officially released on November 24. The 352-page novel comes from Mike Lupica, who's been writing the series since 2023, having also continued Parker's Jesse Stone and Sunny Randall novels. This time around, Spenser is looking into a conspiracy involving his longtime friend Martin Quirk, whose reputation within the Boston Police Department has been destroyed by an unknown adversary. With the department unwilling to let Quirk defend himself, it's up to Spenser to establish who's behind it all.

There's certainly no shortage of source material for Wahlberg and Berg, given that their first movie was loosely based on Wonderland, the 42nd book in the series, written by Ace Atkins. Long before Wahlberg took on the role, of course, there was Robert Urich, who played the Boston private investigator for three seasons of ABC's Spenser: for Hire in the 1980s.

Berg previously discussed plans for a second movie with Wahlberg, although six years on from the release of Spenser Confidential, we've yet to see it materialize, which is a surprise given that Netflix is more in the business of views and minutes watched than caring much for the opinion of critics.

The movie features Wahlberg (The Departed) as Spenser, Winston Duke (Black Panther) as Hawk, Alan Arkin (Little Miss Sunshine) as Henry Cimoli, Iliza Shlesinger (Good on Paper) as Cissy Davis, Bokeem Woodbine (Fargo) as Driscoll, and Marc Maron (GLOW) as Wayne Cosgrove.

Robert B. Parker's Framed is available now, while Spenser Confidential is streaming on Netflix. Stay tuned to Collider for all the latest news and updates.

#3299. Muse safety debate continues as the AI agent rolls out in the UK

The debate over the wisdom and safety of using Meta’s Muse AI agent continues as the app rolls out in the UK. It follows a warning by a number of regulatory bodies about the potential risks of AI agents …

Meta yesterday announced the UK availability of Muse.

Muse, Meta’s personal Al agent, is now available to adults in the UK. Think of it as a helping hand for the jobs that pile up, like chasing a refund, renewing car insurance or keeping on top of the school calendar. To get those jobs done you can connect Muse to the apps you already use, from your email and calendar to the retailer apps you shop on.

A forum representing four different UK regulatory bodies last month issued a warning about the potential dangers involved in using AI agents. The Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum said:

AI agents may amplify and accelerate risks and introduce new ones. These risks may increase as the capabilities of personal agents grow and adoption rises. Questions of consumer protection, competition and data protection – for example the risk of fraud and scams, personal information sharing not in line with user expectations and misleading recommendations, decisions or information provided – must be addressed to ensure innovation develops in ways that earn and maintain public trust.

Meta has pushed back against suggestions that Muse has accessed personal data without permission, insisting that users are in control and must approve important actions. The company has admitted to some “isolated incidents,” but says other reported breaches were either hallucinations or took place on internal versions of the app while undergoing testing. In a new blog post, Meta says:

Muse only works with the apps and services you choose to connect it to, and you control the access it gets […] Once you’ve decided what Muse is connected to and what you want it to do, with your oversight, it can handle tasks like searching, comparing and planning for you. But before it does anything like sending an email or buying something, it shows you exactly what it’s about to do and waits for your go-ahead. A separate security agent checks Muse’s actions and the information it sends out against the permissions you’ve granted. You can also choose how often it checks in with you in Settings.

At the time of writing, Muse remains the second most popular free app in Apple’s US App Store, with more than 10 million downloads. We reported yesterday that some banks are already blocking AI agents, while others are warning that they will not be responsible for the consequences of any actions taken by them.

#3296. iOS 27 breaks 15 years of muscle memory on iPhone and iPad

Since iOS 5 in 2011, the iPhone and iPad have included Notification Center, a central place to find alerts from various apps in chronological order.

Starting with iOS 27, Apple is making a major change to how users open Notification Center on iPhone and iPad.

iOS 27 is here after a summer of beta releases. The behavior changed slightly between the first two releases. However, this change shipped, and I’m still adjusting to it.

Opening Notification Center is unchanged on iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 by default. However, enabling Siri AI changes a key swipe gesture on both iPhone and iPad.

One of the many ways of invoking Siri AI, once enabled, is by swiping down from the center of the top edge of your iPhone or iPad display. This previously opened Notification Center.

You can still access Notification Center by swiping down from the top-left corner once Siri AI is enabled. Alerts now animate in from the top left corner. This is a way to point users toward Notification Center’s smaller surface area.

Apple is greatly prioritizing Siri AI access in iOS 27. The majority of the top edge is devoted to invoking the new Siri experience.

The last time Apple made a change to accessing Notification Center came when Control Center moved from a swipe up gesture from the bottom to a top-right corner swipe down gesture on iPhone X. Apple later unified this experience across devices.

Now it’s Notification Center’s turn to be put in the corner. On iPadOS 27 beta 1 in particular, the area above Home screen app icons was pretty much devoted to invoking Siri AI. The area for opening Notification Center actually shrank if you disable displaying AM/PM or the date.

I've been always swiping from the left corner to see my notifications. I didn't even know you could swipe from the center to get to it as well 😂 I guess I'm good then?

Apple improved this with iPadOS 27 beta 2, creating a more uniform region on either side. It’s roughly the size of two app columns with Notification Center on the left and Control Center on the right. The rest is for invoking Siri.

After 15 years of muscle memory, it’ll take some time to determine if this change is worth it or something that should be reconsidered. In the meantime, early feedback sounds overwhelmingly positive around Apple’s new Siri AI system. Hearing that Siri is good now will also take some getting used to, I’m sure.

After months of using the new behavior, I’m certain I’d toggle it off if there were a setting to do so. Since there’s no option to disable invoking Siri from the top middle swipe down, the only thing to do is build new muscle memory around avoiding the center.

What do you think? Would you change this back if you could? Is accessing Siri from the swipe-down gesture worth the change? Share your thoughts in the comments.

#3294. iOS 27 adds new Messages app setting I instantly started using

iOS 27 brought several new features to the Messages app, including a setting that’s long been a popular request: the ability to customize or turn off the audio button. Here’s how to use it.

With iOS 27, Apple fixed a lot of bugs and also granted many feature requests from over the years.

Siri AI is the biggest example of that, offering a big upgrade over the old Siri. But smaller changes in apps like Calendar, Mail, and Messages reflect this focus on wish fulfillment.

In Messages, there’s a new setting that I instantly starting using. It lets you turn off the audio button that normally lives on the right side of the text input field.

Even if you turn the audio button off, you can still send audio messages by hitting the + button to open your iMessage apps then selecting ‘Audio.’

If you prefer to keep the button active, you can alternately now select ‘Record Audio’ or ‘Start Dictation’ as its function. That way the button will always stay set to your preference instead of dynamically changing like it did before.

#3293. You Can Get One of These Pocket E-Readers for As Little As $55 During Black Friday

Black Friday is usually a great time to grab a new e-reader, but the ongoing RAM crisis has made that a question mark this year: Amazon recently raised the prices of all its Kindles by around $50 and refreshed the entire lineup, which means your odds of grabbing one at a big discount are low. But you aren't totally out of luck: If you haven't noticed, micro-e-readers—I'm talking credit card-sized, with screens that measure around four inches—are all the rage in 2026, and right now, you can pick up one of them for around $55.

If you too can see the appeal of carrying all of your books with you on a device so small you'll forget it's even in your pocket, it's a great time to jump in: The recently released Xteink X4 Classic is currently 38% off for Black Friday, bringing it down to $54.87, a record-low price. Meanwhile, the smaller X3 is $55.72, or 19% off. Both are available in either "mist grey" or "space black." The discounts should last through the end of Cyber Monday on Nov. 30.

Xteink is a Chinese startup that shook up the e-reading world last year with the launch of the X4, a super bare-bones device that made up for its lack of features and usability with a cheap sub-$70 price point. Since then, a huge online community of fans has formed, sharing tips on Reddit and even coming together to crowdsource an alternate operating system that fixed a lot of early problems. Xteink quickly followed up the X4 with a slate of other devices, including the 3.7-inch X3 and the X4 Pro, which adds a front light and touchscreen (at the cost of screen clarity and two physical buttons).

The X4 Classic and the X3 improve on the original X4 with quality-of-life upgrades like a larger battery, relocated page-turn buttons, a real-time clock, and a tilt-to-turn-page feature. They're also lighter and thinner than the X4, though there is a trade-off involved: They drop the USB-C charging port in favor of magnetic pogo pins that require a separate adapter (included).

These upgrades also increased the cost: The X4 Classic typically retails for $89, $20 more than the discontinued X4 and only $10 less than the X4 Pro, while the X3 launched at $79. But right now, the X4 Classic is just under $55, or around 38% off, and the X3 is about a dollar more. Either is a great option for those who prioritize crisp, readable text above the conveniences of a built-in light or touchscreen, as those add extra layers between the inner screen and outer glass. It's also important to understand what you're getting into: These devices support only e-books without Digital Rights Management (DRM), which means you can't use it to read your existing library of Kindle books. On the plus side, there's no longer a need to worry about flashing new firmware if you don't want to, as the native version has been totally overhauled and is now one of your best options (though the new firmware, called "Licorice," isn't available on the X3 quite yet).

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.
